docs.title: The Civilization Restart Manual
docs.text:
How to walk from a single stone back to electricity, after industrial civilization breaks.

This book does not bet on whether collapse will come. It assumes one situation: a generation is left with land, stone, timber and fire, and nobody remembers how to turn those into tools. Fifty-six chapters in eleven parts, starting from building a measurement system and making fire, running through glass, iron and steel, electricity, paper and ink, medicine, and the institutions that hold a workforce together.

docs.title: How to read it
docs.text:
• Every procedure that can only be learned by doing is written as a process card. Each card has the same eight fields: input materials, tools required, operation sequence and control points, experiential parameters and calibration method, in-process observation items, accept / rework / scrap criteria, common failures and troubleshooting order, and L1 / L2 / L3 evidence.
  • A card is meant to be copied onto one page and carried to the bench — chalked on a board, nailed to a wall, folded into a tool bag. There are 286 of them, one set in Chinese and one in English.
  • Wherever a figure is experiential, the card says so and says it must be calibrated against local material. No invented precision.
  • Field 8 of each card states what evidence that particular procedure has to produce before it counts as passed.

docs.title: Status of this edition
docs.text:
Fifth edition (v5.0): 56 chapters, 11 parts, 286 eight-field process cards, Chinese and English chapter by chapter. Every technical parameter carries a source or an explicit calibration requirement; nothing was filled in to make a table look complete.

This is a snapshot, not a continuously updated site. Issues are welcome; revisions ship as new editions.

docs.title: One caution
docs.text: Some procedures here involve fire, furnaces, molten metal, electricity, explosives precursors, and medicines. They are written for a world without hospitals, regulators or suppliers — which is exactly why they carry red lines. Read the red lines in Appendix C before you do any of it.

docs.title: 01 · Restart Conditions and Iron Laws (: Seven Laws)
docs.text: This document is one of the constitutions of the whole book. When any chapter conflicts with this document, that chapter shall be revised in accordance with this document. adds Iron Law Six and Iron Law Seven, and aligns the wording of the original five Iron Laws with the process card system (Document 02).

docs.title: 1. Restart Conditions: Where the Reader Starts
docs.text:
All ambiguity in technical routes stems from an unclear starting point. The book defines three starting points:

Starting point Initial conditions Main challenge Role in this book A: Purely natural start No tools, containers, clothing, or any artifacts Survival and manufacturing from natural resources Baseline verification line: Part Two is written to this standard B: Limited leftover artifacts Clothing, a few metal tools, and containers, but no way to replenish them Use the existing tools to build a sustainable production system Accelerated route: chapters are tagged with "leftover-artifact shortcuts" C: Knowledge preserved People remember modern scientific knowledge but have no modern industrial products Convert knowledge into actual production capability Main line

Why C is the main line: the value of this book is not to let readers rediscover scientific laws, but to teach readers to rebuild the technology system in a realistically feasible order. But one distinction must be kept in mind at all times—

Knowing the principle of a technology does not mean possessing the ability to manufacture that technology.

A person can describe precisely how integrated circuits work and still be unable to produce silicon wafers, fabricate fine patterns, deposit thin films, or test chips. The book distinguishes three levels for every technology:

  1. Knowledge comprehensible: the reader can explain the principle.
  2. Technology reproducible: the reader can manufacture it using available resources.
  3. Production sustainable: the reader can repeatedly manufacture, test, and repair it, and replenish the tools and materials consumed.

The three must not be conflated. Chapter acceptance criteria must state which level is achieved.

docs.title: Iron Law One: No Tool Time Travel
docs.text:
No chapter may invoke a tool that has not yet been manufactured.

  • The pottery chapter may not presuppose metal molds.
  • The iron-smelting chapter may not presuppose modern blowers.
  • The hand-forging chapter may not presuppose electric grinding wheels.
  • The precision machinery chapter may not presuppose CNC machine tools.
  • The early power-generation chapter may not presuppose modern insulating materials.
  • The semiconductor chapter may not presuppose modern chemical reagents and precision instruments.
  • The vacuum-device chapter may not presuppose matched-expansion sealing wire — sealing materials must either provide their own route or be explicitly listed as an external dependency.

If a tool is indispensable, you must first go back to the chapter that manufactures it. Chapter numbering is the dependency order: Chapter N may only cite results numbered less than N.

docs.title: Iron Law Two: All Precision Must Have a Source
docs.text:
You may not merely say "machine the parts to sufficient precision." You must explain:

  • How is a dimension defined? (reference datum)
  • How is a dimension replicated? (gauges, templates)
  • How are two dimensions compared? (comparative measurement)
  • How is error discovered? (inspection methods)
  • How do you make a tool more precise than the tools you already have? (bootstrap routes, e.g. three-plate mutual lapping)
  • How do you judge whether the precision meets requirements? (acceptance criteria)

Precision manufacturing cannot start from the lathe; it must start from straightedges, square references, marking tools, measuring gauges, standard parts, and error comparison — only then come scraping, lapping, reference surfaces, precision sliding pairs, thread cutting, and mechanical mother machines (machine tools). The book has only two legitimate sources of precision: Chapter 3 (natural references and comparative measurement) and Chapter 20 (bootstrapping geometric references).

docs.title: Iron Law Three: Every Material Must Have a Complete Chain
docs.text:
Writing "use steel" or "use glass" does not settle the matter. Every key material must be traceable:

Natural resource → collection → sorting → primary processing → purification or smelting → forming → inspection → use

Iron ore is not iron; iron is not steel; and steel is not necessarily steel fit for pressure vessels. Sand is not optical glass; ordinary glass is not a qualified lens; silicon-bearing minerals are not semiconductor-grade silicon. Every "equals" between two material names is a process chain that must be accepted on its own.

docs.title: Iron Law Four: Every Technology Has Verifiable Success Criteria
docs.text:
"It looks like it came out right" is not acceptance. Acceptance criteria must state three things clearly: what to measure, under what conditions to measure it, and what observation counts as pass/scrap. Examples:

  • Pottery: filled with water for 24 h, the level drops < 2 mm; 3 boiling-water → cold-water cycles without cracking.
  • Ironware: a fractured test bar shows no large slag-inclusion layers; the spark test for carbon and the fracture grain structure corroborate each other.
  • Lenses: can form a sharp image that can be observed repeatedly (resolution-target criteria, see Chapter 24).
  • Steam engines: a hydraulic test at 1.5 times working pressure, held for 30 min without leakage — only then is operation discussed.
  • Generators: "it spins but gives no electricity" must first pass the troubleshooting checklist (residual magnetism → windings → brush neutral plane, see Chapter 31); condemning it as scrap outright is not allowed.
  • Integrated circuits: the specified logic functions are realized in independent testing, repeated across three batches.

Acceptance criteria must correspond to real use, not appearance.

docs.title: Iron Law Five: Every Key Technology Must Have a Fallback
docs.text:
The absence of one material must not interrupt the entire civilization route. An alternative route must state explicitly its performance loss, resource cost, applicable boundaries, and final bottleneck; the theoretical existence of a substitute does not license the claim that it can fully replace the original technology.

  • No high-grade iron ore → which partial technologies can copper, wood, bone, and stone advance?
  • Lacking lens raw materials → start with pinhole imaging, reflective observation, and simple measurement.
  • No coal → charcoal, water power, wind power.
  • No conditions for silicon chips → first build relay, vacuum electronic device, or germanium transistor routes.
  • No matched sealing wire → carbon electrodes, transitional sealing with coarse lead wires, or demoting vacuum tubes to an external dependency (Chapter 33).

docs.title: Iron Law Six: Every Parameter Has a Calibration Method, Every Process Has Failure Criteria, Every Acceptance Preserves Evidence
docs.text:
This Iron Law is new in and targets "silent failure" — for smelting, annealing, winding, and vacuum processes, a mistake often does not fail at once but fails invisibly: what comes out is cast iron instead of wrought iron, looking almost identical; unannealed glass does not crack that day, then shatters on a hot plate three days later; a generator with miswired windings and one with insufficient residual magnetism show the same symptom, "it spins but gives no electricity." A reader without criteria will not know they are wrong; they will only think their luck is bad, and then repeat the same batch of scrap. Therefore:

  1. Parameters: any "empirical value" must be written together with its field calibration method; a parameter without a calibration method is a placeholder and may not be used for acceptance.
  2. Failure criteria: every process must answer "what does a botched job look like, and how do you verify where it went wrong"; the manual may omit a shortcut, but it may not omit a single failure mode.
  3. Evidence: every acceptance leaves behind physical items (test bars, test coupons, failed parts) and written records (parameters, criteria, dates), filed into the ledger (Chapter 43). A pass without evidence is not a pass; it is an impression.

docs.title: Iron Law Seven: Labor Is the Primary Asset
docs.text:
Depreciation of equipment, furnaces and kilns, and power grids can all be rebuilt; the death or maiming of a craftsman cannot. Therefore:

  1. In every chapter, the safety boundary ranks equal to the process itself: for any step that can kill, maim, or cause chronic poisoning, safety measures are not "precautions" but part of the process steps; skipping them counts as not completing the step.
  2. Production planning must account for people: the minimum shift crew of continuous processes (blast furnaces, kilns, steam-engine tending) is written into the labor-hours block (Chapter 37); a process book written from a single-person perspective collapses at the second step.
  3. Medicine, hygiene, and occupational health (Chapters 44–49) carry the same weight as metallurgy and machinery: they are the "human maintenance system," the only safeguard in the book that lets the reader live through a twenty-year horizon. Epidemics and silicosis kill a workforce faster than equipment wears out, and irreversibly.

docs.title: 3. Technologies Explicitly Excluded (Writing Them into the Book Would Turn It into Pseudoscience)
docs.text:
The following technologies are not given manufacturing routes; the relevant chapters only explain the reasons for exclusion and the conditions for future restoration. Readers who try to force them by the book will die:

Technology Reason for exclusion Conditions for restoration Vaccines, antibiotics, biological preparations Require controlled culture, aseptic filling, batch testing, and a cold chain Microscope + aseptic technique + strain library + assay system (Chapters 44–46 define the boundaries) Electrolytic aluminum Requires high-purity alumina, corrosion-resistant high-temperature electrolytic cells, and stable high current Far beyond the "millimeter-scale handcrafted process" ceiling; aluminum is listed as an external dependency of this route Tungsten filaments for incandescent lamps The powder metallurgy, sintering, swaging, and wire drawing of tungsten are high-purity heavy industry The carbon-filament route is usable (Chapter 33); tungsten filament is listed as a Class-C item Marine chronometers and longitude determination An independent precision-machinery tech tree that departs from the main line Astronomical rough positioning is usable (Chapters 3 and 25)

docs.title: 4. The Tool Lineage Concept: Every Tool Must Answer Four Questions
docs.text:
Both writing and reading check themselves against this:

  1. What is needed to manufacture it?
  2. How were those things manufactured in turn?
  3. During manufacturing, which tools will be damaged, worn out, or need replacement?
  4. If one of those resources is missing, can another route be taken?

Example — you may not merely write "use an iron chisel to work stone"; it must be traceable:

Iron chisel ← usable iron stock ← reduction of iron ore and forging ← furnaces/kilns and charcoal ← refractory materials and temperature-control capability ← pottery kilns, fuel processing, and basic measurement

The iron chisel also needs: abrasives that allow repeated regrinding, a hand hammer to deliver impact, a fixture that holds the workpiece safely, a method for judging the edge condition, and the ability to re-heat-treat when necessary. When a tool is damaged, the manual must state whether it can be repaired and what repair requires — not "replace it with a new one."

docs.title: 5. From One-Off Fabrication to a Production System
docs.text:
Manufacturing one part ≠ building a system that can keep producing that part. In the acceptance criteria at the end of each chapter, the book separates "single-part success" (L1) from "system established" (L3). The minimum elements that sustain continuous production:

  • Raw-material stockpiles and resupply routes (Chapter 38, materials ledger)
  • Sustainable consumption rates for fuel/energy (Chapter 38, energy ledger)
  • Tool wear rates and repair/replacement arrangements (Chapter 39, maintenance and spare parts)
  • Process records (parameters, failure cases) (Chapter 43, archival system)
  • Quality inspection methods (Chapters 22 and 27 + Chapter 39, quality traceability)
  • Skilled labor and transmission (Chapter 37, labor organization; Chapter 43, master–apprentice system)

The ceiling of a technical route is often set not by tools but by the scale of the division of labor. This is also why the environment versions of Part Eleven evaluate the "labor and time" dimension.

docs.title: 02 · Chapter Framework and Process Card System ()
docs.text: This document is one of the constitutions of the whole book. The goal of the first-edition template was "complete structure"; the goal of is forced executability — it revises the defects exposed by the first edition: the template allowed every item to stay at the noun level (an A-list entry reading only "glass lampworking (Chapter 14)", acceptance criteria reading only "magnify at least 5x"), so the form was complete while the content remained a table of contents. makes "every process must deliver a process card filled with all eight fields" a hard rule: if the eight fields cannot be filled, the process has not been thought through.

docs.title: 1. The Three Tiers: Every Section First Declares Which Tier It Is
docs.text:
Tier Meaning How to tell Tier 1 After reading, you know it exists Can recite the step names, cannot recite the parameters and criteria Tier 2 Can follow it once and succeed by luck If it works, cannot say why; if it fails, does not know where it went wrong Tier 3 Can manufacture repeatedly, judge acceptance, diagnose failures A different person or a different batch of raw materials can still reproduce it from the records

The book's commitment for main-text processes is Tier 3. A subsection that cannot reach Tier 3 must open by declaring "this section is Tier X" and state what is missing to move up a tier.

Mapping between the three tiers and the three acceptance levels (L1/L2/L3): L1 = Tiers 1–2 (the phenomenon has been seen); L2 = the manufacturing face of Tier 3 (qualified output can be produced repeatedly); L3 = Tier 3 plus the system face (raw materials, spare parts, records, transmission). The implementation system for L3 is in Chapters 37–39.

docs.title: 2. The Chapter Skeleton: Nine Blocks (fixed order; a missing block is disqualifying)
docs.text:
# Block Content requirement One-vote-veto counterexample 1 Capability boundary What can be done, what explicitly cannot be done, what is an external dependency (named and entered into the C list) Writing only what can be done 2 Pre-work verification A check-box list. Each line says "confirm you have XX in hand; the criterion is XX," not "see Chapter X" Pushing the pre-checks onto the reader to figure out 3 Materials list Five items per material: identification standard (how to recognize it) / minimum specification (how poor it can be before unusable) / acceptable substitutes (and the performance loss) / signs of defective stock / quantity per piece Only material names 4 Tools list Three items per tool: source chapter / precision requirement / pre-use calibration method Only the source chapter 5 Process steps Three questions per step: what to do / to what degree (observable criteria) / how to roll back or salvage if done wrong "then operate carefully" 6 Parameter table All key parameters collected into one table; every empirical parameter carries a field calibration method (see §4) Isolated numbers with no source 7 Failure modes and diagnostics Table: symptom → candidate causes → verification method → disposition → prevention. Sorted by "most common / hardest to detect" None 8 Acceptance methods For L1/L2/L3 respectively: criteria + test conditions + evidence to be preserved (test bars, records, samples) Target values without conditions 9 Labor hours, manpower, and consumption Head count, skill tier, days, fuel and material unit consumption — supports production planning and the "is it worth doing" judgment None

The first edition's closing blocks (the three A/B/C lists, safety boundary, acceptance criteria, next-step dependencies) are all retained, in the same positions and written the same way; entries in the A/B lists must reach the density of blocks 3 and 4 of §2. The fifteen-module self-check table continues to serve as the writing-side checklist.

docs.title: 3. Process Cards: One Card per Process Topic
docs.text:
One card = one independently executable operation (e.g., "anneal a batch of glass", "quench a file blank", "scrape a pair of surface plates"). The main text explains why; the card explains how. A card can be copied out on its own and taken to the workstation; when it wears out, copy it again; when it changes, reissue it.

The eight fields (uniform across the book; missing any one voids the card):

Field What to fill in 1 Input materials For each: minimum specification, acceptable substitutes (with performance loss), quantity per run 2 Required tools Source chapter, precision requirement, pre-use calibration 3 Operating sequence and control points Numbered steps; the "to what degree" criterion for each step; key control points in bold 4 Empirical parameters and calibration methods Parameter value + how to set that value in the field (test bars, controls, gradient tests) 5 In-process observation items The colors / sounds / hand-feel / readings to be recorded, and in which column 6 Accept / rework / scrap criteria The three-way split: what counts as accept, what can be reworked (and how), what is scrap 7 Common failures and troubleshooting order For "multiple causes of the same symptom," give a verification order, not just a list of causes 8 L1/L2/L3 evidence What physical items and written records to preserve after acceptance at each level
  • Card number rule: chapter number - sequence number (e.g., 20-01). Card numbers are unique across the book; Appendix A carries the master index.
  • Card length: 1–2 pages (about 1500–3000 characters). Failure to fill all eight fields = a downgrade declaration for that process; adjectives may not be used to fill the gaps.
  • Hospital operating procedures, factory process cards, and flight checklists all have this structure — it is not a new invention; it is the industry baseline this book must meet.

docs.title: 4. Writing Rules for Criteria and Parameters
docs.text:
1. Three elements of a parameter: value + applicable conditions + calibration or verification method. Example: you may not write "annealing temperature about 500 ℃"; write "soda-lime glass annealing point 500–540 ℃ (empirical range); field calibration: take three pieces of glass from the same batch, treat them at 480/520/560 ℃ respectively, then drop them into 60 ℃ warm water — any that crack are below the lower limit."
  2. Criteria must be observable: who, using what, seeing what counts as accept/scrap. Example: "lapping complete" fails; "spot-color inspection shows ≥ 20 contact points within a 25×25 mm area, evenly distributed, and any two of the three plates give consistent results in pairwise mutual lapping" passes.
  3. Silent failure first: for processes where a mistake is not immediately visible (metallurgy, annealing, winding, vacuum, concrete curing), write "how to discover the mistake" before writing "how to do it right." For such processes, placing the failure-mode table before the steps is also not an error.
  4. The ◎ hand-feel marker: steps that cannot be fully put into words (the feel of scraping, forging heat, blowpipe rhythm, thread-twisting tension) are marked ◎ and given two things: a practice method (how many repetitions, on what material) and misjudgment compensation (what measurable physical evidence replaces hand-feel: test bars, test coupons, weighing, templates).
  5. Three-way criteria: accept / reworkable / scrap. A two-way split by default means there is no rework path and will tempt readers to force defective parts into service.

docs.title: 5. Numerical Discipline
docs.text:
1. The book is metric throughout: length in mm, mass in g, temperature in ℃, time in min/h; pressure uses both atm and mmHg (the conversion is given at first occurrence).
  2. Every "about, roughly, approximately" must carry an order of magnitude: write "about 3 kg (±0.5)", not "a few jin".
  3. Order-of-magnitude self-check: every calculated result is followed by a "reasonable-range check" (example: the computed airflow is 200 L/min; check: an adult's lung capacity is about 4–5 L, one bellows bag about 8–15 L; demanding 200 L per minute means 15–25 full compressions per minute — a single person can sustain that briefly but not through a full shift on watch; conclusion: this furnace needs a two-person rotation or a different bellows).
  4. Transmission rule: all parameters marked "empirical value, must be field-calibrated" must be transcribed into the ledger (Chapter 43) once calibration is complete. The next generation may not work from memory; they may only consult the ledger. Losing the ledger counts as that process being demoted back to Tier 1.

docs.title: 6. Physical Layout of a Chapter (unified layout)
docs.text:
# Chapter X Chapter title
## Objectives of this chapter
## Capability boundary (Block 1)
## Pre-work verification (Block 2)
## X.1–X.n  Main subsections (Blocks 3/4/5 embedded; key operations insert [Process Card X-nn])
## Master parameter table (Block 6)

docs.title: 7. Revision Order (execution plan for the rework)
docs.text: The framework comes first; the main text is then rewritten in the silent-failure-first order: measurement (3) → machine tools (20) → steel (19) → iron (18) → high-temperature furnaces (12) → glass (14) → steam (28) → generators (31) → agriculture (10) → electronic devices (33), with the remaining parts to follow. The newly added Parts Eight, Nine, and Ten (production organization and system governance; knowledge carriers and transmission; medicine, hygiene, and occupational safety — Chapters 37–49) fill in the "human maintenance" and "knowledge carrier" blocks that were missing wholesale from the first edition.

docs.title: 8. Terminology Unification (book-wide usage)
docs.text: Process card = workstation card = a numbered job sheet of the form "Card 20-01"; the three are the same thing: the main text calls it a "process card," posted at the workstation it is a "workstation card," and the numbering format is always "chapter number - sequence number." Fixed blocks = the five fixed closing subsections of every chapter (failure modes and diagnostics / process card index / acceptance criteria / safety boundary / next-step dependencies). Preview = a forward declaration that "this capability will be established in Chapter N"; preview items may NOT be used as existing (the determination method is in Chapter 4). Downgrade declaration = the explicit declaration at the start of a process that has not reached Tier 3.

docs.title: 03 · Six Technology Lineages
docs.text: The six capability chains that run through the whole book. Each time you write or read a chapter, you should know where it sits on these six chains: what it consumes from upstream, and what it provides to downstream.

docs.title: Lineage 1: Materials
docs.text:
The upgrade chain from natural raw materials to industrial materials.

Natural minerals → ore dressing → smelting → primary metals → forging → heat treatment → machine parts

By the same logic: clay → pottery → refractory materials; sand → glass → optical glass; fibers → yarn → fabric → industrial fabric. Every link corresponds to the complete chain of Iron Law 3: raw materials → collection → sorting → primary processing → purification/smelting → forming → inspection → use.

docs.title: Lineage 2: Tools
docs.text:
From simple tools to "tools for making tools".

Stone flakes → stone hammers → woodworking tools → metal tools → measuring tools → precision machinery → machine tools

Criterion: a tool counts as "established" if and only if, once damaged, it can be repaired or remade (lineage self-sufficiency).

docs.title: Lineage 3: Energy
docs.text:
Fire → charcoal → furnaces and kilns → water-powered machinery → steam engines → generators → electric motors

Each energy level determines the processing ceiling for the previous level's materials: without charcoal and blast there is no iron; without stable mechanical power there are no precision machine tools; without a continuous electricity supply there is no electrochemistry and no semiconductors.

docs.title: Lineage 4: Measurement
docs.text:
Visual estimation → simple comparison → standard dimensions → gauges → precision mechanical measurement → optical measurement → electrical measurement → materials and device testing

This is the lineage most easily overlooked, and yet the most pervasive: from the bow drill (Chapter 7) to semiconductors (Chapter 34), the capability that truly runs from start to finish is reliable measurement and repetition. Every upgrade in measurement comes from the "more precise tools" manufactured by the previous level of measurement (bootstrapping).

docs.title: Lineage 5: Chemistry
docs.text:
Combustion → lime → glass → basic acids, alkalis, and salts → metal purification → industrial reagents → material purification and surface treatment

Not every region can develop in this order, but every technology should state the chemical capability it requires. End-state awareness: the semiconductor route is, in essence, the comprehensive examination of "chemical purity capability".

docs.title: Lineage 6: Information
docs.text:
Oral experience → graphical records → unified metrology → process records → technical drawings → standardization → production records → automatic control → electronic computation

Civilizational recovery depends not only on physical tools but also on knowledge that can be preserved, transmitted, and reproduced. This lineage reminds every settlement: ledgers and archives are infrastructure, on the same level as kilns.

docs.title: Feedback Loops: Civilization Is Not a Tree That Grows in One Direction
docs.text:
Reinforcing loops exist among the six lineages; the true engine of rebuilding is these loops, not the chains themselves:

  • Precision instruments → improved materials research → better materials → more precise tools
  • Better generators → support electrically driven machining → better machine tools → better generator parts
  • Better measurement → higher-quality mechanical and electrical products → feeding back into the manufacture of measuring instruments
  • Electronic control → higher automation of production equipment → acceleration of all manufacturing

In the early phase (Parts 1 through 3), advance mainly along the chains; in the middle phase (Parts 4 and 5), build the feedback loops deliberately; in the late phase (Part 6), each loop should begin reinforcing itself. Each chapter's "next-step dependencies" block should state which loop it feeds.

docs.title: II. Five Critical Chains (Priority Verification Targets for Writing and Auditing)
docs.text:
1. Stone tools → woodworking tools → simple machinery (Chapters 5, 7, 9)
  2. Fire → furnaces and kilns → refractory materials → metal smelting (Chapters 6, 12, 16–18)
  3. Metal tools → measurement → precision machining → machine tools (Chapters 19–22)
  4. Mechanical power → electromagnetism → generators → electric power systems (Chapters 21, 28–32)
  5. Glass and chemistry → material purification → semiconductor processing → integrated circuits (Chapters 14, 23–26, 33–35)

Chains 3 and 5 are the most prone to unexplained tool anachronisms; check them node by node during review.

docs.title: III. Priority Decision Framework
docs.text:
Technically feasible ≠ technologically worth prioritizing. A comparison framework (for discussion, not a computable scientific law):

Priority = survival contribution × resource availability × repeatable-manufacturing capability × support value for downstream technologies

Each technology must further answer five questions:

  1. If it is not built, which downstream technologies will be blocked?
  2. Is there a cheaper alternative?
  3. How much non-renewable resource does it consume?
  4. Does it raise the efficiency of other production steps?
  5. When is it worth committing more labor?

The reader must know not only how to build a tool, but also when not to build it.

docs.title: IV. Environment Assessment Table (Unified Model for the Four Versions of Part Eleven)
docs.text:
Resource or capability Question to answer Technology routes affected Water Stable, storable, treatable? Agriculture, chemistry, metallurgy, cooling Fuel Sustainably obtainable? Pottery, lime, glass, metallurgy, heat engines Clay and refractory materials Can reliable furnaces and kilns be built? High-temperature processes and metal smelting Metal ores Are there usable ore sources? Metal tools, machinery, electrical equipment Quartz and silicon-bearing raw materials Raw material supply and subsequent purification conditions? Glass, optics, and semiconductor routes Timber and fiber Sufficient and sustainable? Tools, construction, transport, some machinery Available power Water flow, wind, sunshine, fuel? Mechanical power and power generation Transport conditions Can ore, fuel, and equipment be moved? Industrial layout and specialization Maintenance capability Can tools and equipment be repaired continuously? Long-term sustainability of the technology Manpower and time How many people can take part over the long term? Route selection, capacity, division of labor

Core principle: environmental differences change not only where materials come from, but the entire developmental order of the civilization. The four environment versions share technological knowledge, but they do not share the same technological sequence.

docs.title: V. Technology Boundaries: Three Goals That Must Not Be Conflated
docs.text:
Taking the integrated circuit as the example (Chapter 35 enforces this table strictly):

Goal Meaning This book's stance Understanding Able to explain the working principles and the main manufacturing steps Delivered continuously throughout the book Manufacturing simple devices Building and verifying devices of limited complexity on top of established materials, equipment, and measurement The ultimate challenge of Part Six Rebuilding modern industry Sustained production of high-performance, complex, reliable, competitive products Honestly labeled as beyond the capability of a single volume, with a list of the required conditions

Writing the boundary honestly is worth more than inventing a route that looks complete but cannot actually be executed. Chapter 36, "Which modern technologies cannot yet be rebuilt", is part of the book's credibility, not a defect.

docs.title: Chapter 1 What Civilization Restart Really Means
Chapter Objectives
docs.text:
• Establish three judgment capabilities:

  • Determine the restart starting point you are at (A/B/C);

  • Determine which level of L0–L3 any given technology is at;

  • For any target technology, list its dependency chain and find the critical path and the bottleneck.

  • This chapter builds no physical artifacts. Its deliverables are four "paper tools" (the starting-point determination checklist, the level determination table, the dependency-tracing four-question card, and the blank dependency graph template), which every later chapter will invoke.

  • This chapter also defines the book's lowest-layer boundary rules: what counts as "direct use of natural objects" and what counts as a "tool".

docs.title: Minimum Prerequisites
docs.text: Item Requirement Source Knowledge The seven Iron Laws (no crossing, precision has a source, materials have chains, acceptance is provable, technology has a fallback, every process must have failure criteria and evidence, labor is the first asset) General Constitution G01 Knowledge The three-level acceptance system and the chapter template General Constitution G02 Knowledge The six technology lineages and the feedback loop concept General Constitution G03 Knowledge The master dependency graph and the priority decision framework General Constitution G04 Supplies None. This chapter is purely a methods layer and needs no artifacts — Manpower At least 1 reader; L3 acceptance requires ≥2 people —

docs.title: 1.1 The Three Restart Starting Points
docs.text:
The three starting points are the fork for every technology route in the book. They must be determined on day one and written up as a "starting-point checklist".

Starting point Initial conditions Main challenge Role of this manual A: Pure natural starting point No tools, containers, clothing, or any artifacts Surviving and manufacturing from natural resources Baseline verification line (Part 2 is written to this standard) B: Few leftover items starting point Clothing, a few metal tools, and containers, but no way to replenish them Using the existing tools to build a sustainable production system Accelerated route (chapters flag "leftover-item shortcuts") C: Knowledge-retained starting point Modern scientific knowledge remembered, but no modern industrial goods Converting knowledge into actual production capability Main line

Determination steps (complete on day one):

  1. Inventory the artifacts available within 24 hours: clothing, metal tools, containers, cordage.
  2. Rule: ≥1 metal tool present and not replenishable → B; no artifacts at all → A; modern knowledge in the group's memory and no industrial goods → C.
  3. Record the determination result together with the inventory details in the starting-point checklist. Mixed states (e.g., clothing but no tools) are handled at the lowest tier.

Starting-point resource inventory — every starting point holds three classes of assets:

  1. The body: hands, fingernails, teeth, body temperature, physical strength, stride, heartbeat. These are the first "measuring instruments" (formally put to use in Chapter 3).
  2. Natural objects: stones, sticks, vines, shells, and animal bones that can be picked up and used as-is. **Boundary rule (valid book-wide): an unprocessed natural object picked up and used directly in the hand does not constitute tool crossing; once it has been chipped, ground, or carved into shape, it counts as a tool and belongs to the deliverables of Chapter 5 and later.** Wherever later chapters write "striking with a stone held in the hand", they mean the usage this rule permits.
  3. Knowledge and record-keeping capability: the core asset of starting point C. But knowledge must first pass the "memory reliability" check — a wrong memory is more dangerous than no memory (see Section C of this chapter).

Failure modes:

  • Misjudging the starting point. The most common error at starting point B: treating a leftover steel knife as a sustainable capability, using it until it wears out and fails, and never building the capability to remake it (usable iron stock does not arrive until Chapter 18). Rule: leftover items may only be used to accelerate the making of "lower-level tools that can be self-sustained" (example: use the steel knife to carve the first standard rod, then immediately switch to a route that can be sustained without the steel knife).

  • Treating the knowledge of starting point C as the whole of your assets. Knowledge is a route map, not production capacity. See 1.2.

Three rules for leftover-item management at starting point B (to prevent "eating the mountain bare"):

  1. Register and catalog: give every leftover item an archive entry (item name, material, current condition, date placed in service), incorporated into the Chapter 3 archive system.
  2. Tier the usage: use them only to accelerate the making of "lower-level tools that can be self-sustained" or for one-time reference-standard making; everyday consumptive use is forbidden. Example: a leftover steel knife may not serve as a kitchen knife; it may only carve the first batch of standard rods.
  3. Failure contingency: annotate next to every leftover item "after damage, replaced by the deliverables of Chapter N"; items for which no replacement plan can be written are treated as "end-of-life resources" — the replacement route must be built before they are used.

docs.title: 1.2 What Counts as Truly Rebuilding a Technology
docs.text:
The book splits "possessing a technology" into four levels; levels must never be mixed in reporting:

Level Name Criterion L0 Knowledge comprehensible Without the manual, can write out the principle and the main process steps L1 Proof of principle Done once successfully, with records of date and observed behavior, but unstable L2 Repeatable manufacture Following the recorded process, produce conforming pieces 3 times in a row (the conformity criteria must be written down first) L3 Sustainable production Damaged tools can be repaired or remade; raw-material supply interruptions can be bridged; another person following the records can produce

Level-up conditions (interrogate level by level):

  • L0→L1: what is missing is one hands-on run. Schedule the time and the materials.

  • L1→L2: what is missing are parameters and records. Write out the conditions of every run in full (material batches, parameters, weather) and identify what distinguished successes from failures.

  • L2→L3: what is missing is the system. Answer: what is the tool attrition rate? What are the raw-material resupply routes? Who knows the second way of doing it? Where are the spares?

Three telltale signals of "treating L1 as L3" (self-check):

  1. No failure records — only successes and no failures means you have not tried often enough.
  2. No second product — something made only once is not a technology; it is an event.
  3. No consumables replenishment plan — if you cannot answer "what happens when the raw materials run out", you have not reached L3.

False-claim phrasing cross-reference (for self-check):

Common claim Actual level Corrective action "I studied it and watched someone do it" At most L0 Schedule one hands-on run "I made one once" L1 Make 3 conforming pieces in a row, with records throughout "Following the process, it basically works" Below L2 Add the parameter window and the failure records "I can make it whenever I want anyway" Unverified Aid-interruption test + reproduction by a different person (see 1.4)

Running example (a preview only; the artifact is established in Chapter 5): an edged stone tool. Being able to state "flaking stone requires homogeneous rock with a conchoidal fracture" = L0; having flaked one stone flake that can cut a grass stem = L1; flaking 3 flakes in a row, each able to cut 20 dry grass stems without edge chipping = L2; the stone source recorded on the resource map, the flaking hammer replaceable by re-picking and re-dressing after wear, and another person able to flake by following the records = L3.

docs.title: 1.3 Why Modern Technology Cannot Be Copied Directly
docs.text:
Behind every modern product stand four layers of hidden dependencies, and none of them exists in the early restart phase:

Hidden dependency Default condition of the modern world Early-restart reality Energy density Power grid and liquid fuel, available on demand Only muscle, fuel wood, and fire (from Chapter 6) Material purity Reagent-grade chemicals, specification steel Only minerals, clay, and biomass (from Chapter 2) Standardization Tolerances, interchangeable parts, thread standards Not even a unified unit of length (from Chapter 3) Supply chain Thousands of factories behind a single device Everything within a one-day walking radius (Chapter 2 resource map)

The "chase three layers" exercise (to be done once in this chapter): pick any modern object and interrogate three rounds in a row: "What is it made of? → Where do those things come from? → What, in turn, are the processing tools for those things?"

  • If you hit bottom within three layers (landing on natural objects such as stone, wood, clay, and fire) → the object can be attempted relatively early.

  • If you still have not reached bottom after three layers (example: stainless steel knife → steel mill → iron ore + coke + refractory bricks → chase each of those one more layer) → the upstream must be built first; a direct attempt is not allowed.

Conclusion: the true asset of starting point C is "knowing where to go and knowing which roads are dead ends", not "already owning". The manual's task is to exchange "knowing" for L1, L2, and L3, chapter by chapter.

Four common illusions of knowledge retainers (check one by one):

  1. "Understanding the principle means knowing how to make it" — the principle is only L0; between it and L2 lie the parameter window and the failure library (3.7).
  2. "Skip the old technology and go straight to the better solution" — the preconditions of the better solution (materials, measuring tools, energy) are established precisely by the old technology.
  3. "Modern numbers can be taken over as they are" — without standard gauges, numbers such as "a few millimeters" or "so many degrees" have no measurement source (Iron Law 2) and can only be expressed through the self-built references of Chapter 3.
  4. "One person can be all-capable" — the depth of division of labor in modern technology dictates that rebuilding must be divided too (1.4); the realistic ceiling of a solo route ends at Part 2.

docs.title: 1.4 From Making One Piece to a Production System
docs.text:
Making one part ≠ establishing a system that can keep producing that part. The six minimal elements of a system (checked item by item at every chapter's L3 acceptance):

Element Interrogation Record medium Raw-material stock Current stock? Resupply cycle? Resource map (Chapter 2) Energy consumption rate How much firewood burned / how many labor-hours per unit of product? Process card (3.7) Tool attrition rate Which tools will fail? How often? What happens when they do? Tool archive (Chapter 3 archive system) Process records Are the parameters and the failure cases written down? Clay-tablet archive (3.6) Quality inspection What are the conformity criteria? Who inspects? Acceptance criteria (each chapter) Manpower and succession How many people can do it? Does it still work when the person changes? Mentoring records (3.7)

Two quantitative criteria:

  1. Output rate = number of conforming pieces ÷ total labor-hours invested. Start tracking only after L2.
  2. Sustainability criterion: resource consumption rate ≤ resource regeneration/resupply rate. Example (previewing Chapter 11): the wood consumed by one kiln load of pottery must fall within the annual regeneration of that forest stand; otherwise pottery production will cut off its own supply within a few years.

The blunt test of whether a system exists: the aid-interruption test — imagine (or actually) stop all external inputs for 30 days: can this technology's output still be sustained? Only what can be sustained counts as "possessed" by the settlement.

**Example (the numbers are fictitious; the format is for imitation):** A settlement produces 30 pottery jars per month, 24 of them conforming, investing 60 working days → output rate 0.4 jars/labor-day; fuel consumption is 3 dan of firewood per kiln load, 4 kiln loads per month; measured against the forest stand's annual regeneration of 200 dan → about 70 percent taken up. Record both figures once each month; the trend matters more than any single value: when the output rate falls for three consecutive months, check tool attrition and raw-material batches first instead of pushing for more labor-hours.

Failure mode: treating "a certain artisan can make it" as "the settlement can produce it". The artisan falls ill and production stops = the system lacks element 6. The countermeasure is in 3.7 (from personal experience to replicable processes).

docs.title: 1.5 The Technology Tree, Bottlenecks, and Dependencies
docs.text:
Backward dependency tracing (the four-question card): for any target technology, answer in order:

  1. What does making it require? (tools, materials, energy, knowledge — the four dependencies, expanded in Chapter 4)
  2. How are those things themselves made? (repeat the question for each item until you land on the natural resources of Chapter 2 or on deliverables already established in earlier chapters)
  3. Which tools in the manufacturing process will be damaged, used up, or need replacement?
  4. If one of them is missing, can another route be taken? (alternative routes must state the performance loss, the resource cost, the applicability boundaries, and the final bottleneck — Iron Law 5)

Example (quoted from the outline, for imitation): iron chisel ← usable iron stock ← reduction of iron ore and forging ← furnaces/kilns and charcoal ← refractory materials and temperature-control capability ← pottery kilns, fuel processing, and basic measurement. Side branches: abrasives, hand hammers, clamping devices, edge-quality judgment methods, re-heat-treatment capability. The artifacts of the links are established in Chapters 18, 12, 11, 6, 3, and 2 respectively.

Second example (the reader should practice once in this format): pottery jar ← clay purification and batching ← pottery kiln and fuel ← refractory materials ← controlled combustion ← tinder and dry firewood ← resource map. Side branches: shrinkage-rate records (Chapter 3 gauges), firing cycle (Chapter 3 time anchor), acceptance criteria (watertightness and resistance to thermal cycling — Iron Law 4). The artifacts fall in Chapters 11, 12, 6, 3, and 2 respectively. The common node of the two chains is "controlled combustion and the resource map" — it blocks both chains at once, and that is the bottleneck: manpower goes to bottlenecks first, because once one is cleared, several chains advance at the same time.

Definitions of critical path and bottleneck:

  • Critical path = the longest prerequisite chain from the starting point to the target. It determines the earliest completion time; the other chains can run in parallel.

  • Bottleneck = a node on which multiple downstream items depend at the same time (examples: a controlled fire source is the common prerequisite of pottery, charcoal, lime, and metallurgy; the measurement system is the common prerequisite of almost all L2 acceptances). Bottlenecks should receive manpower first.

Priority decision (quoted from General Constitution G04): priority = survival contribution × resource availability × repeatable-manufacture capability × supporting value for subsequent technologies. This is a discussion framework, not a computable formula. The accompanying five questions: if we do not build it, what gets stuck? Is there a cheaper substitute? How much nonrenewable resource does it consume? Can it raise the efficiency of other links? When is it actually worth adding people?

Deliverable: the blank dependency graph template. Node fields: name / source chapter number / current level (L0–L3) / side-branch dependencies / alternative routes. Maintain it on inscribed clay tablets or a ground-inscription area (medium in 3.6). Rule: until any node reaches its labeled chapter, its status on the drawing is always "not yet built", no matter how sure you are that you could make it.

docs.text:
• No physical tools (this chapter sits at the book's lowest layer).

  • Method tools (source: General Constitution G01–04): the seven Iron Laws, the three-level acceptance definitions, the six lineages, the priority formula, the five-question checklist.
