Tool Manufacturing source Use Starting-point determination checklist (with the natural-object boundary rule) This chapter 1.1 Day-one self-assessment; the boundary rule is cited book-wide Technology level determination table (L0–L3) This chapter 1.2 (per General Constitution G01) Every chapter's acceptance; guards against "treating L1 as L3" Dependency-tracing four-question card This chapter 1.5 (rewritten from General Constitution G01, Item 3) Guards against tool crossing Blank dependency graph template This chapter 1.5 Target planning, finding the critical path

Note: the "tools" of this chapter are all paper/oral methods. The record media do not exist yet — until the inscribed clay tablets, the catalog boards, and the rest are established in Section 3.6, this chapter's outputs may be held provisionally by oral transmission + ground inscription, and should be transcribed into the archive as soon as possible.

docs.title: C. Unresolved Dependencies
docs.text:
• There is no way to verify whether the reader's memory of modern knowledge is accurate. Wrong memories contaminate the entire dependency chain. Mitigation: key numbers and criteria are cross-checked against the independent recall of ≥2 people; where they conflict, physical experiments prevail; the quantitative verification method is established in Chapter 25.

  • No physical production capability of any kind yet — this depends on every manufacturing chapter from Chapter 5 onward.

  • The problems of manpower scale and division of labor can only be raised here, not solved (handled by the per-environment versions of Part 10).

docs.title: Failure Modes and Diagnosis [methods chapter]
docs.text: This chapter has no processes; its failure modes are method misuse: (1) treating leftover items as sustainable capability (bootstrap-line preview in Chapter 18); (2) treating previews as existing (criteria in Chapter 4); (3) memory contamination (key numbers cross-checked by ≥2 people; quantitative verification awaits Chapter 25).

docs.title: Process Card Index [methods chapter]
docs.text: This chapter sets no process cards — its deliverables are method pieces (checklists/tables/cycles), see inventory B; the cards of every process chapter are used with the 4.7 cycle of this chapter.

docs.title: Safety Boundaries
docs.text:
• No physical operations in this chapter.

  • The single clause: no one may cite "knowing the principle" as a reason to skip verification and go straight to hazardous processes (high pressure, high temperature, toxic substances). The relevant hard prohibitions are in each chapter's "safety boundaries" block; in Part 6 (steam, electricity, chemicals) especially, proceeding on knowledge alone is absolutely not allowed.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• L1 proof of principle: for a given technology (example: pottery jar), can state the L0–L3 differences and one's own current level, and can say whether one is caught by any of the three "treating L1 as L3" signals.

  • L2 repeatable manufacture: complete the starting-point checklist for this environment + at least 1 complete backward dependency graph (with side branches and alternative routes), independently reviewed by a second person with the four-question card, and no tool crossing found.

  • L3 sustainable production: ≥2 people in the settlement can independently use this chapter's tools to run dependency analysis on new targets; the deviations between the analysis conclusions and the actual subsequent progress are recorded and used to revise the analysis method itself.

docs.title: Next-Step Dependencies
docs.text:
• 1.1 Starting-point determination and boundary rules → the scope, priorities, and permitted sampling means of the Chapter 2 resource survey.

  • 1.2 Level determination → the Chapter 3 error-recording system and the acceptance criteria of every chapter book-wide.

  • 1.5 Dependency graph and four-question card → the prerequisite checks of all chapters book-wide and the reading method of Chapter 4.

  • This chapter feeds the entry point of Lineage 6 (the information lineage): oral experience → determination rules → (Chapter 3) graphical records.

docs.title: Parameter Notes
docs.text: This chapter is a position and methods chapter; its capability boundary is the boundary of the book itself (natural objects may be used directly, every tool must be traceable); it contains no process parameters and no master parameter table; the only quantitative content of this chapter is one capability-level determination (the three-level L0–L3 table, see 1.2). The parameters and criteria of every process chapter fall in the chapters after this one — this chapter pre-issues no numbers, which is in itself a demonstration of the ban on tool crossing.

docs.title: Chapter 2 Know the Natural World First
Chapter Objectives
docs.text:
• Build the "resource survey" capability: conduct a systematic census of rocks, soils and clays, plant materials, water and common raw materials, fuels and natural energy within the activity radius.

  • Produce three physical deliverables: a resource survey record sheet (≥20 entries), a resource map (1 sheet), a symbol key table (2 backup copies).

  • This chapter does only identification, simple tests, recording, and rating; it processes no material. All conclusions must be tagged with a confidence level (confirmed / suspected / unknown); "suspected" items are backfilled after verification by calcination and trial burning in later chapters.

docs.title: Minimum Prerequisites
docs.text: Item Requirement Source Knowledge Iron Law III (materials must have a complete chain) — the survey is the first link of the chain General Outline G01 Method Starting-point determination checklist, natural-object boundary rules (unprocessed natural objects may be used directly), grade determination table Chapter 1, Sections 1.1, 1.2 Supplies No artifact requirement; picked-up stones, sticks, rattan, shells used directly Chapter 1, Section 1.1 Manpower 1–2 people suffice; marsh and cliff zones require 2 people together This chapter's safety boundaries

docs.title: 2.1 The Difference Between Rocks, Minerals, and Ores
docs.text:
Three engineering definitions:

Concept Definition Question to ask during the survey Rock A natural aggregate of multiple minerals (granite, sandstone, limestone) Can it serve, as a whole, as building material / millstone / dimension stone? Mineral A single natural compound or element (quartz, calcite, hematite) What are its streak, hardness, and luster? Ore Rock in which the grade of some useful component is high enough to be worth recovering Is the amount picked up on site worth hauling back?

Key insight: **ordinary rocks are everywhere, ores are rare.** A reddish-brown stone is not the same as iron ore. Criteria always take priority over color impressions.

First-tier clues (naked-eye, ordered by reliability):

  1. Streak: the color of the powder a sample leaves when scratched on a coarse quartz-sandstone slab. Streak color is far more stable than the color of the bulk exterior.
  2. Fracture form: conchoidal fracture (an arced surface like the inside of a shell) is characteristic of homogeneous glassy stones such as flint and obsidian — these are the first choice for knapped stone tools in Chapter 5. Flat fractures and bedding planes indicate sedimentary rock.
  3. Hardness grades (see 2.6): the fingernail (about 2.5) and quartz (about 7) bracket out three grades.
  4. Luster: metallic / vitreous / greasy / earthy.
  5. Crystal form: for crystals with visible faces (hexagonal-prism quartz, cubic pyrite), record the shape.

Common streak table (memorize 5 rows on site to get started):

Mineral Bulk appearance Streak Notes Hematite Red-brown to black Red-brown The most common source of iron (Chapter 18) Magnetite Black, metallic luster Black Markedly dense; iron source Limonite Yellow-brown, earthy Yellow-brown Hydrous iron oxide; iron source Pyrite Golden yellow, cubic crystals Greenish-black "Fool's gold": harder than gold (about 6); gold is soft (about 2.5–3) with a golden streak Graphite Black, greasy, stains the fingers Black, shiny Extremely soft (1–2); used later for lubrication and marking

Failure modes:

  1. Memorizing a list of mineral names with no evidence of occurrence. Countermeasure: the manual gives only criteria; "whether there is ore under your feet" must be answered by the field survey of 2.7.
  2. Being fooled by bulk color (pyrite taken for gold, red sandstone taken for hematite). Countermeasure: make the streak before drawing conclusions.
  3. Taking a single pretty crystal for an "ore vein". Countermeasure: records must state the distribution extent (see the 2.7 table); for a single crystal, honestly write "scarce" in the "workable amount" column.

docs.title: 2.2 Soils, Clays, Sands and Gravels, and Sediments
docs.text:
Clay is the common raw material of pottery (Chapter 11), clay tablets (3.6), and construction (Chapter 13); it has the highest priority.

Four field tests for clay (all bare-handed + water):

  1. Wet-roll test: knead a knuckle-sized soil sample thoroughly with water and roll it into a strip on the palm. It can wrap a full loop around the little finger without breaking = good plasticity, high clay-particle content; it snaps as soon as bent = sandy or low clay content.
  2. Finger-rub test: smear a wet sample flat on the fingertip pad. Slick like paste = fine; an obvious gritty feel = sandy. Record the feel in three grades: paste / powder / sand.
  3. Settling test: fill a natural container (a split large bamboo segment, a large shell, a folded bark bucket) with water, drop in a knuckle-sized soil sample, disperse it, and let stand (duration counted in heartbeats, see 3.1). Coarse sand sinks within a few beats; silt needs several quarter-hours to clear; the water is still turbid after most of a day = fine clay particles present. The settling-time boundaries are empirical values and must be field-calibrated: settle a sample of known river sand alongside as a control.
  4. Dry-shrink test: press the wet sample into a palm-sized clay cake and shade-dry it for two days. Compare the scribed marks: large shrinkage, cracked into several pieces = extremely high clay content; used directly for pottery it will crack, so sand must be mixed in (the recipe is handled in Chapter 11); almost no cracking or shrinking = sandy, insufficient plasticity.

Sands, gravels and sediments:

  • River sand: rounded grains, usually fairly clean; sea sand contains salt (salty taste, trace-level confirmation) and must be rinsed with fresh water before later use in mortar and glass (the rinsing step belongs to Chapters 13 and 14; here only the "contains salt" property is recorded).

  • Quartz sand (mainly white, vitreous-luster grains): enter it on the map and tag it "high priority" — it is the raw material of the glass route (Chapter 14).

  • Reading depositional environments: river bends, lake deposits, old channels, wind-deposited loess layers — zones with thick and fine soil are candidates for clay and farmland (Chapter 10) alike; tick both columns when recording.

Failure mode: declaring "there is clay" after testing only one spot. Countermeasure: take at least 3 samples along the same valley and run the four tests on each, recording the entries separately — clay quality can change drastically within a few dozen paces.

docs.title: 2.3 Wood, Bark, Fibers, Resins, and Natural Binders
docs.text:
One record per candidate tree; survey dimensions:

Dimension Field judgment Species grouping Deciduous / evergreen; conifer / broadleaf. Conifers often have resin Trunk form Straight length of the trunk (measured in paces), curvature, fork height — decides whether straight stock can be taken Material feel Weigh same-hand-length broken branches in three grades: light (paulownia types) / medium / heavy (oak types); heavy ones later become hammers and axles (Chapter 7) Grain Along-grain split test: drive a picked-up stone along the grain into a crack; splits easily along the grain = good for taking boards / strips Moisture state Standing deadwood (dead but not fallen) is drier than fallen wood and burns more readily than green wood — first-choice fuel (Chapter 6) Bast Peel off a strip of inner bark; does not break when pulled by hand = bast fiber usable (rope candidate, verified in Chapter 7) Exudates Resin and gum oozing from trunk wounds: pinch for softness, smell, record color (binder and waterproofing candidates, verified in Chapter 8)

Other fiber sources: grass stems (the long, tough ones), rattan, tree rootlets, animal hair and sinew (if there is game). At this stage only the hand-test result "does not break when pulled" is recorded; twisting into rope is the craft of Chapter 7.

Sustainable harvest rules (starting values): in each woodland's first harvest year, take no more than one tenth of the trees (empirical value, must be field-calibrated: mark 20 sample trees, record the regrowth year by year, then revise the cap). Standing deadwood and fallen wood are harvested first. Each woodland gets its own separate entry on the resource map, including an "annual harvest cap" column.

Failure mode: the resource map records only "there is forest" without species composition and stock volume, and three months later it turns out the good timber species numbers just seven trees. Countermeasure: the distribution and estimate columns must state pace-count dimensions and the dominant species.

docs.title: 2.4 Water, Salt, Limestone, Sulfur, and Other Common Raw Materials
docs.text:
Water (a separate entry for each source):

  • Type: spring / stream / river / lake / rain / snow. Springs and live streams take priority.

  • Record: location, seasonality (if unknown, mark "observe for one year"), turbidity (clear / slightly turbid / turbid), odor, water-temperature feel, downstream pollution signs (carcasses, algal blooms, bad smells).

  • Drinking-water criterion for this stage (very limited, stated honestly): live water + clear + odorless + no signs of human or animal carcasses upstream. This is not disinfection — pathogenic microorganisms are invisible. Until the boiling-disinfection capability is established in Chapter 6, standing water and shallow-pool water is in principle not drunk.

Salt: rock-salt outcrops (white / colorless, salty taste, soft enough to crumble between the fingers), salt springs (white salt efflorescence by the spring mouth), salt lakes, seashores. Taste judgment is limited to trace-level confirmation of samples already identified as salty; tasting unknown samples is forbidden. Use preview: food preservation (Chapter 10), the starting point of the chemical industry (Chapter 23). Salt-poor areas are honestly marked "none" on the map.

Limestone (criterion set for a no-acid era): gray-white to bluish-gray; can be scratched into powder marks by a quartz block (hardness grade 3–4, below quartz's 7); fracture fairly flat; often contains shell or coral fossils; often occurs together with karst caves and spring-mouth travertine (loose, porous white lime sinter) — fossils and travertine are the most valuable indirect evidence. Final verification relies on calcination: lighter after burning, gives off heat and slakes into powder with water (requires the fire of Chapter 6 and the kiln of Chapter 12; backfilled then).

Sulfur: yellow, brittle, easily crumbled to powder, distinctive smell; found in volcanic and hot-spring regions. Non-volcanic regions often have no sulfur — record honestly; the lack of sulfur is a hard boundary for certain later chemical and disinfection routes, and is not solved in this chapter.

Other separately listed raw materials: flint nodules and bands (in limestone; first choice for Chapter 5); obsidian (glassy volcanic rock, conchoidal fracture, sharp but brittle); kaolin (white earth; the white earth of termite mounds as a clue); ochre pigments; natural grinding stones (large flat slabs of fine sandstone); graphite (see the 2.1 table).

Failure mode: treating "should theoretically exist" as "already found". Countermeasure: every map entry must have a location and a physical sample; conjectures without samples go into the "to-investigate list", never into resource entries.

docs.title: 2.5 Fuels, Heat Sources, and Usable Natural Energy
docs.text:
Fuel resources (survey only, no trial burning — trial burning needs fire, which belongs to Chapter 6):

Fuel Identification Notes Standing deadwood / fallen wood Dead trees, dry branches The first main fuel Green wood High moisture, smoky Record but do not harvest Animal dung Steppe / pastoral areas Combustible once dried (verified in Chapter 6) Peat Black fibrous soil of wetlands, visible plant remains Extraction carries collapse risk (safety boundary) Coal outcrop Black, lighter than a same-sized rock, brittle and stains the hands, layered Record as "suspected coal"; trial-burning verification postponed until a fire source is obtained

Natural energy (record existence and location; utilization is long-term):

  • Hydropower: for candidate sites record the head (paces and eyeball estimate; precise measurement waits for 3.3) and flow speed (the number of beats for a leaf to drift past a two-pace interval; rough measure). Water wheels and drive trains are in Chapter 21.

  • Wind: prevailing wind direction (indicated by flag-shaped crowns), a feel-based wind scale: still / leaves moving / branches moving / trunks swaying. Windmills belong to Chapter 29.

  • Sunshine: slope aspect (record sunny slopes), cloud-cover grades. Solar energy use belongs to Chapter 52.

  • Animal / human power: current livestock species and numbers, and the labor hours that can be invested.

**Failure mode: treating energy existence as energy availability.** A river does not mean hydropower — without head and a water wheel (Chapter 21), river water is just water. The "possible uses" column of an entry may only say "candidate + target chapter number", never "usable".

docs.title: 2.6 How to Identify Materials by Appearance, Hardness, Density, and Other Simple Tests
docs.text:
Pocket test kit (all picked-up natural objects, unprocessed):

Tool Use Streak plate: a palm-sized flat coarse quartz-sandstone slab Streak color Fingernail (hardness about 2.5) Lower reference Quartz reference block (a white crystal block confirmed to be quartz, hardness about 7) Upper reference Bark bucket / large shell + water Settling, float-sink, absorption tests Leaf or grass-stem ruler Record length grades (no numeric values marked)

If start point B has bronze artifacts left over, a "copper (about 3)" grade may be added; start points A/C have none — do not add one.

Pocket hardness ladder table (completed in v2 — match directly on site when prospecting and selecting material, no numbers to memorize):

Test object (scratcher) Hardness grade Reading Scratchable by fingernail <2.5 Very soft: galena, gypsum, micas — metal-ore candidates Not scratchable by fingernail, scratchable by a copper sheet (start point B) 2.5–3 Soft: most sulfide ores Scratchable by knife / iron nail (this grade added after Part 4) 3–5.5 Medium: malachite, cuprite, fluorite, apatite Not scratchable by knife, not scratchable by a coin 5.5–7 Hard: magnetite, hematite, feldspar, pyrite Not scratchable even by quartz (reference block) ≈7 Very hard: quartz, cassiterite, corundum

Usage: test grade by grade from top down; stop at the first "cannot scratch" grade — that is the object's hardness grade — compared against the 2.1 mineral tables this eliminates half the candidates. Experience note: a scratch counts only if it "leaves a line that cannot be rubbed off"; a powder mark that rubs off does not count (that is the scratching tool's own powder).

Ten-step identification procedure:

  1. Record the collection location and setting (riverbank / slope / outcrop).
  2. Naked eye: color, luster, bedding, crystal form.
  3. Fracture: conchoidal / flat / jagged / earthy.
  4. Streak: scratch on the streak plate, record the color.
  5. Hardness three grades: scratchable by fingernail (<2.5) / not scratchable by fingernail but scratchable by quartz (2.5–7) / not scratchable by quartz (≈7).
  6. Density three grades: weigh same-hand-sized pieces — light (clearly lighter than average stone) / medium / heavy (hefty in the hand, mostly metal minerals).
  7. Water test: float or sink (wood / lightweight); drip water to see absorption (clay absorbs water and turns sticky, shale does not).
  8. Magnetism: a weak criterion in an era without iron tools — record "suspected magnetism" only if fragments attract each other; the main criteria remain streak + density.
  9. Compare against the tables of 2.1–2.5 and give a judgment + confidence level (confirmed / suspected / unknown).
  10. Bag and number (tied with grass stems), backfill into the 2.7 record sheet.

Misjudgment recording method: every time an error is discovered after the fact, add a "misjudgment entry": original judgment / what it actually was / which criterion failed. Misjudgment entries are archived on a par with resource entries — they are the basis for revising the criteria tables.

Failure mode: skipping steps to reach a conclusion (writing "hematite" from color alone). Countermeasure: the "judgment" column may be filled only after all ten steps of the procedure card are done; if unfinished, fill in "unknown".

docs.title: 2.7 How to Build Your Own Resource Map
docs.text:
Three elements of the map:

  1. Datum point: stand a head-sized stone at the exact center of the camp; every position on the map takes it as the origin.
  2. Direction: the equal-shadow standing-pole method determines north-south — in the morning mark the pole-shadow endpoint A; in the afternoon mark endpoint B when the shadow length equals the morning's; the line AB is east-west, and its perpendicular is north-south. This method depends on no tools and can be re-measured for verification on any clear day.
  3. Distance: pace counts. Note "non-standard unit, to be upgraded in Chapter 3". First do a personal calibration of pacing itself: walk 100 paces, measure the length, and record your personal pace length (see the example process card in 3.7).

Recording media (by durability): shade-dried scribed clay tablets (fear water; stored on elevated racks off the ground), carved wood, knotted cords (reminder index only, no parameters stored), the camp-ground scribing field (large-scale diagrams). The symbol system is agreed at ≤20 carved symbols (water / clay / stone / flint / iron / fuel / danger / premium ...); the symbol key itself is an archive item, with two backups stored apart.

Resource survey record sheet template (this chapter's core deliverable; every column mandatory):

Column Content to fill Example Number / date / surveyor Sequential number + day name 007 / Day 9 / Jia Location Direction relative to the datum + paces + landform East by south, about 1200 paces, north bank of a river bend Category Rock / soil / plant / water / fuel / energy Soil Judgment + confidence level Name + confirmed / suspected / unknown Clay, suspected (not verified by calcination) Test record Streak / hardness grade / fracture / density grade / four-test results Rolled strip wraps the finger without breaking; still turbid after most of a day of settling Distribution and estimate Outcrop or area size (paces) + workable amount scale (scarce / medium / abundant) About 200 paces along the bank, about 3 fingers thick, scale: abundant Collection difficulty Bare hands / tools needed / multiple people needed / carry paces Diggable by hand Possible uses Candidate uses + target chapter numbers Pottery (Chapter 11), clay tablets (3.6) Verification status Unverified / verified (note the chapter number) / misjudged (note the entry number) Unverified Priority High / medium / low (per the Chapter 1 priority framework) High

Survey plan (layered expansion): week 1 covers the half-day-walk circle; month 1 extends it to a full-day walk. Clay, stone, fuel, and water sources are the four priority targets; each day one category is the main line.

Backfill rule: the map is a living archive. When later chapters verify or falsify an entry, backfill the "verification status" column within the same month. A map to which entries are only added but never backfilled is, a year later, a pile of expired information.

Failure modes:

  1. Recording "presence" but not "quantity" — when Part 3 plans production capacity there is nothing to start from. Countermeasure: the estimate and amount-scale columns are mandatory.
  2. No datum point or vague landmark descriptions, so a second person cannot revisit. Countermeasure: all three elements of the location column (direction / paces / landform anchor) are indispensable; acceptance is by the revisit test.
  3. Symbols lost when the recorder changes. Countermeasure: double backups of the symbol table; the newcomer's first lesson is the symbol table.

docs.title: A. Existing Tool Inventory
docs.text:
• Chapter 1 method tools: starting-point determination checklist, grade determination table, dependency-tracing four-question card, dependency graph template (source: Chapter 1).

  • Physical items: none (this chapter still lies before the manufacturing chapters).

docs.title: B. New Tools Introduced in This Chapter
docs.text: Tool Made in Use Resource survey record sheet (template + filled entries) This chapter 2.7, medium: clay tablet The book-wide resource ledger Resource map (scribing field + reduced clay-tablet copy) 2.7 Site selection and planning Symbol key table (≤20 symbols, double backup) 2.7 Recording standardization (the lineage's six starting points) Streak plate (a ready-made coarse quartz-sandstone slab, picked up) 2.6 Mineral streaks Hardness reference set (fingernail + quartz reference block) 2.6 Hardness grading Ten-step identification procedure card 2.6 Identification protocol Natural container set (bark bucket / large shell / bamboo segment, picked up unprocessed) 2.2 Settling and water tests

docs.title: C. Unresolved Dependencies
docs.text:
• All "suspected" judgments (ore grade, limestone, coal, heating value) must wait for calcination / trial-burning verification by the fire of Chapter 6 and the kiln of Chapter 12; this chapter's conclusions stop at the "suspected + confidence level" grade.

  • Chemical criteria are entirely absent: no acid, no reagents, composition unmeasurable. Purification of salt and sulfur is in Chapter 23.

  • Distance in paces, quantity in "scarce / medium / abundant" — key entries must be re-estimated after Chapter 3 upgrades them to standard units.

  • The microbiological safety of water cannot be judged; only indirect signs can be used for avoidance (disinfection capability belongs to Chapter 6).

docs.title: Failure Modes and Diagnostics [methods chapter]
docs.text: This chapter's failure modes: ① step-skipping judgment (writing conclusions before the ten steps are done — the procedure card enforces them); ② treating 'suspected' as 'confirmed' (the confidence level must be tagged); ③ treating energy existence as energy availability (a river ≠ hydropower, Chapter 21); ④ fixing an ore site from a single sample (close the boundary only after three consecutive points show no mineralization).

docs.title: Process Card Index [methods chapter]
docs.text: This chapter sets up no process cards — the deliverables are method items (checklists / tables / loops), see list B; the cards of the various process chapters use the loop of this chapter's 4.7.

docs.title: Safety Boundaries
docs.text:
• Tasting unknown minerals and soils is forbidden; taste is limited to trace-level confirmation of samples already identified as table-salt class, and nothing may be swallowed.

  • Cliffs and cave mouths: observe from afar and mark out the rockfall zone before approaching; do not strike the rock mass overhead. At this stage there is no lighting and no support; mine shafts and deep caves are forbidden.

  • Peat-bog sampling requires 2 people together, probing the way with a long pole; no one steps onto soft mud.

  • Without a boiling means (before Chapter 6) do not drink standing water; outdoor cooking is not yet established (same as above).

  • Felling on steep slopes and climbing for rattan are prohibited outright — woodworking and safety ropes are in Chapter 7.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• L1 proof-of-principle: complete the first census round of the half-day-walk circle: ≥20 entries + 1 resource map, each entry containing the three location elements and a confidence level.

  • L2 repeatable manufacture: draw any 3 entries at random; a second person independently revisits them by "direction + paces + landform" and locates all of them successfully; the clay, fuel, and stone/ore categories each have ≥1 entry at "suspected" or above; the ten-step procedure card executed with trace records on 5 samples.

  • L3 sustainable production: the record-backfill system is running (≥10 entries verified / falsified and backfilled); the symbol table and map double backups checked consistent every quarter; the survey circle extended to a full-day walk; ≥1 misjudgment entry and a revision of the criteria table based on it.

docs.title: Next Dependencies
docs.text:
• Clay entries → Chapter 3 (clay-tablet archive medium), Chapter 8 (natural chemical materials), Chapter 11 (pottery).

  • Stone entries (flint / quartzite / obsidian) → Chapter 5, the first stone tool.

  • Fuel and water-source entries → Chapter 6, the first controllable energy source.

  • Wood and fiber entries → Chapter 7, wood, fiber, and rope.

  • Limestone, quartz sand, salt, sulfur entries → Chapters 13, 14, 23.

  • Hydropower / wind / sunshine entries → Chapters 21, 29 and the environment variants of Part 10.

  • The resource map as a whole → the master entry point of Part 10's four environment variants.

docs.title: Parameter Notes and Capability Boundaries
docs.text: Capability boundary: what this chapter produces is the "identify and register" capability — all criteria are comparative (streak color / hardness grade / density feel / water tests); no chemical quantification is done, nothing is burned, no material is modified. Explicitly cannot do: quantitative mineral composition (after Chapters 16, 23); quantitative strength (after the balance of Chapter 3). Parameter table: this chapter's only tabulated quantitative criteria are the pocket hardness ladder (2.6) and the density feel grades (2.6), both given in the main text; this chapter has no process parameters, so no master parameter table is set up.

docs.title: Chapter 3 Building a Measurement System Without Standard Tools
Chapter Objectives
docs.text:
• Establish physical carriers and reproduction methods for four classes of temporary standards: length (the standard rod), mass (the equal-arm balance + weight-stone set), time (solar shadow, beats, and the water clock), temperature (the phase-change anchor card).
  • Establish three geometric standards (straight line, right angle, circle) and one physical standard (level), all directly constructible from natural objects.
  • Establish body-unit error statistics (using data to prove why cross-person handover is forbidden) and the true-north determination by construction method.
  • Establish the error-recording method (repeat measurement, range, two-person cross-measurement) and the unit management system (primary standard + secondary standards + monthly check).
  • This chapter is cited repeatedly throughout the book: from Chapter 6's combustion timing to the process control before Chapter 35, the capability that runs through everything is reliable measurement and repetition (lineage IV). The only legitimate sources of precision in this book are this chapter and Chapter 20.

docs.title: Capability Boundaries
docs.text:
Can do: length halved down to the "finger" level, balance equilibration at 1–2% of load, time anchored to the day + water-clock segments, temperature with four anchors + feel grades; true-north orientation to half-finger-width-level deviation (multi-day re-measurement).

Explicitly cannot do: interpolation between temperature anchors (awaits the glass thermometer, Chapter 25); short-duration high-precision timing (the water clock is nonlinear; the constant-head method is only a mitigation); uniform ten-way division of scribed lines (awaits a hard scribe point, Chapter 19); tracing units back to old-world standards (no impact; external settlements convert by mutual comparison).

This chapter starts from zero: every procedure is bare-handed + picked-up natural objects, with no prerequisite tools.

docs.title: Pre-Work Verification
docs.text: # Verification item Criterion Source 1 Boundary rules Picked-up objects may be used directly; this does not constitute time travel Chapter 1 2 Materials 3 straight-grained dry wooden rods, rattan / long grass stems (untwisted), clay, a set of stones, a palm-sized flat stone Chapter 2 survey 3 Recording medium Clay-tablet temporary-storage system in place Chapter 2 4 Manpower Cross-measurement needs ≥2 people (error statistics recommend ≥6) —

docs.title: 3.1 Length, Weight, Time, and Temperature
docs.text:
Why these four classes: length constrains every dimension; mass constrains every ratio; time constrains every process cycle; temperature constrains every thermal process. The pre-industrial overall strategy: compress "absolute measurement" to a minimum and solve most problems with "comparative measurement" — comparison needs no true value, only stability.

Master table of natural anchors for the four classes of standards:

Class Absolute anchor (naturally existing) Comparative means (established in this chapter) Length No stable natural absolute anchor (solar shadow length varies with the season) Standard rod + secondary rods; body units (single-person self-use only) Mass None Equal-arm balance: comparison and equilibration only; it never reads "how much" Time Day, sunrise, noon (astronomical anchors, highly reliable) Beats; water clock (segmented calibration) Temperature Ice water 0; body temperature about 36–37; beeswax about 63±2 (if available); boiling water about 100 (at sea level) Feel grades + phase-change anchor card

Using the temperature anchor card, and its honest boundaries: - Four feel grades: icy (≈0–5), cool, neither cold nor hot (about 32–35 — the neutral point where skin "feels no difference" lies below body temperature; empirical value), warm (tolerable for long contact), hot (withdrawn at one touch); - The boiling point varies with altitude and solutes: roughly 1 ℃ lower per about 300 m of elevation; salt water boils higher (approximately +0.5–1). Take "the locally measured boiling point" as your anchor; - Fire-color temperature estimation is auxiliary only: error on the order of ±100 ℃, must not be treated as quantitative detection; its formal placement is in Chapter 12.

Key insight for the mass standard: the equal-arm balance gives only "equal / not equal"; only with a weight-stone set does it become counting. Proportioning by ratio is nothing but repeated equilibration, which suffices to support all proportioning from Chapter 8 onward.

docs.title: 3.1.1 Error Statistics of Body Units (Setting the Rule with Data)
docs.text:
The problem with body units (elbow, hand-span, finger, pace) is that they differ from person to person. Do not trust "roughly about the same" — measure on the spot:

Measurement protocol (once, half a day, ≥6 people): 1. Each person measures in turn: index-finger width (widest point of the proximal phalanx face), hand-span (thumb tip to little-finger tip at full stretch), elbow (elbow tip to middle-finger tip), pace (mean of 10 natural paces), arm span (tip to tip of the two middle fingers with the arms raised horizontal); 2. Each item is measured 3 times per person and the median taken; all readings go into the error record sheet; 3. Compute for each item the in-team range (max minus min) and the range/median percentage.

Empirical intervals (prefilled values, to be overwritten by the team's own measurements):

Item Typical median In-team range (empirical) Relative difference Finger width 17–20 mm 5–7 mm ≈30% Hand-span 180–220 mm 40–60 mm ≈25% Elbow 420–490 mm 60–80 mm ≈15% Pace length (natural) 650–780 mm 100–150 mm ≈18% Arm span ≈ one's own height Varies with height ≈15%

Conclusion written into the unit charter: a relative difference of 15–30% means — Jia's "five hand-spans" may be Yi's "four hand-spans". Body units are permitted for single-person self-use only (you make it, you check it yourself); cross-person handover and entry into archives are forbidden. For cross-person handover, the smallest permitted unit starts from the "standard rod". The personal pace calibration card (3.7) solves the reliability problem of "using your own pace for your own work".

[Card 03-05 Body-Unit Error Statistics] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: ≥6 subjects from the same team; a standard rod (as the conversion reference); a clay scribing field or tablets.
  2. Tools required: standard rod, marking tool, error record sheet (the 3.4 template). Calibration source: body units record only the differences among people and are never converted outward; every outward conversion is made against the standard rod.
  3. Sequence and control points: each person measures in turn finger width (widest point of the proximal phalanx face), hand-span (thumb tip to little-finger tip at full stretch), elbow (elbow tip to middle-finger tip), pace (mean of 10 natural paces), arm span (tip to tip of the two middle fingers) → 3 measurements per item, median taken → all readings onto the sheet → compute the in-team range and the range ÷ median percentage → write the conclusion into the unit charter. Control points: one protocol per item (landmarks fixed in the sheet header); re-zero between the 3 runs.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: ≥6 people, half a day; prefilled empirical intervals — finger width median 17–20 mm, in-team range 5–7 mm (≈30%); hand-span 180–220 mm, 40–60 mm (≈25%); elbow 420–490 mm, 60–80 mm (≈15%); pace 650–780 mm, 100–150 mm (≈18%); arm span ≈ one's own height (≈15%). All empirical values, to be overwritten by the team's own measurements.
  5. Observations to record: person / item / the 3 readings / median / in-team range / range ÷ median percentage / measurement conditions (wet-dry, cold-hot).
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = all five items present, 3 readings each, ranges and percentages complete; rework = an item short of 3 readings or measured at inconsistent landmarks — retest; scrap = fewer than 6 subjects (too thin to set a rule; the conclusion is reference only and may not enter the charter).
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) one item's range is abnormally large → first check the landmarks (finger width at the widest point of the proximal phalanx face is the easiest to place differently), then whether anyone spread or curled deliberately; (2) the hand-span / arm-span ratio is clearly off → check whether the hand-span was taken at full stretch; (3) pace dispersion is large → first check for a deliberate pace, then the ground state; (4) the conclusion will not go into the charter → too few subjects or missing items; retest (the commonest cause of rework).
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one five-item statistics table for ≥6 people; L2 = the conclusion written into the unit charter and used to forbid cross-person handover; L3 = a second team repeats the method and lands in the same relative-difference order (15–30%).

docs.title: 3.2 How to Make the First Straight Lines, Right Angles, and Circles
docs.text:
Straight lines (three kinds, each with a reliable source): 1. Plumb line: a stone hammer tied to rattan and hung freely; a gravity-defined line, the most reliable (doubles as the vertical standard); 2. Stretched cord: taut untwisted rattan / grass stem approximates a straight line — the error is sag from the cord's own weight; beyond a span of about 20 paces the mid-span sag becomes perceptible and intermediate support is required; 3. Three-rod mutual-check straightedges: fit three dry wooden rods against each other pairwise, grind away the high spots and repeat, until all three rods fit pairwise without gaps. Two rods can only detect bending; three are needed to average the curvature out (the straight-line prototype of Chapter 20's "three-plate mutual lapping"). Hand-shaved rod straightness reaches only "no gap visible against the light"; quantified testing awaits Chapter 20.

Right angle (the 3-4-5 cord method): 1. Take rattan about 14 elbows long; using any stick as a temporary unit, measure off 12 equal segments, one hard knot per segment (12 knots, 13 points); 2. With small stakes form a triangle of sides 3, 4, 5 knot-spacings, all three sides taut; 3. The angle between the 3 side and the 4 side is the right angle; 4. Error control: knot spacings all measured with the same stick (the systematic error cancels automatically); readings uniformly referenced to knot centers; work on a leveled clay platform; 5. Self-check: flip it over and fit it back in place; a uniform gap means it is true.

Circle: staked-circle method — the stake is the axis, the rattan the radius, a hardwood-tipped scribe; one full turn scribes the circle. Roundness check: measure the radius of the same circle in 8 directions; a range ≤1 finger width passes as a rough circle. To copy a circle, compare against a radius-scribed rod.

docs.title: 3.2.1 True-North Determination by Construction (Equal-Shadow Method, Multi-Day Re-Measurement Orientation)
docs.text:
Orientation is the common prerequisite of layout (Chapter 13 kiln foundations, house orientation) and of the calendar (farming times, Chapter 10). Do not rely on a magnetic needle (magnetic declination is unknown and varies widely by region; the compass must wait for calibration until after Chapter 30's magnetism) — use the sun:

Construction steps (completed in one day, verified by re-measurement the next day): 1. Level a clay surface of about 2×2 m (leveled with the A-frame); stand a rod at the center (about 1.5 m tall), trued plumb (plumb line against the rod in two directions); 2. In the morning (about 2–3 h after sunrise) drive small stake A at the rod-shadow tip, and immediately, as a graduated compass, scribe an arc with the "rod-base-to-A distance" as radius and the rod base as center; 3. All day long, at intervals of about one section (command beats), drive a recording stake at each shadow tip — the shadow-tip track is an arc swinging outward through the morning, shortest at noon, swinging back in the afternoon; 4. In the afternoon, when the shadow length again equals the arc radius (the shadow tip has returned onto the arc), drive stake B; 5. The line joining A and B is the east-west line; construct the perpendicular bisector of AB (the rattan fold-in-half midpoint method, the bisection technique of 3.5) through the rod base — this line is the north-south line; in the northern hemisphere, the side where the shadow tip lies is north (the noon shadow points north); 6. Fixing the line: scribe a groove along the north-south line and bury stakes at both ends.

Verification and precision: re-measure every 1–2 days; the angle difference between the two lines should be ≤ half a finger width (eyeball estimate, ◎; compensation: measure the distance difference between the end stakes of the two lines). Multi-day averaging can lower the error further. Principle of equal-shadow symmetry: the sun is symmetric about noon between morning and afternoon, so two shadows of equal length are necessarily symmetric about the north-south line — this is given by geometry and does not depend on any tool precision.

[Card 03-02 True-North Determination by Construction] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: one straight-grained dry wooden rod (about 1.5 m tall); small stakes; rattan for scribing the arc; a scribe; a level clay surface about 2×2 m.
  2. Tools required: plumb line (to true the rod), A-frame level (to level the clay surface), scribing tool. Calibration source: the plumb line relies on gravity and needs no calibration; the arc radius is the "rod-base-to-A distance", taken with the same length of rattan that scribes the arc.
  3. Sequence and control points: level the clay surface → stand the rod and true it plumb (plumb line against the rod in two directions) → in the morning drive stake A at the shadow tip and scribe an arc about the rod base → all day, every one section or so, record the shadow-tip stake → in the afternoon, when the shadow length again equals the arc radius, drive stake B → the A–B line is the east-west line → fold the rattan in half to take the midpoint, construct the perpendicular bisector of AB through the rod base: that is the north-south line → scribe a groove along it and bury stakes at both ends. Control points: the rod must be plumb; B may be driven only when the equal shadow finally arrives.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: clay surface 2×2 m; rod about 1.5 m; drive A about 2–3 h after sunrise; recording interval about one section (command beats); re-measure every 1–2 days — a two-day inter-line angle difference ≤ half a finger width passes (eyeball, ◎; compensation: measure the distance difference between the end stakes); multi-day averaging lowers the error further.
  5. Observations to record: day name / section count at staking / morning and afternoon shadow-tip stake positions / inter-line angle difference (eyeballed in half-finger units) / weather (overcast days are not used).
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = re-measurement inter-line angle difference ≤ half a finger width; rework = over limit — re-measure and average over several days; scrap = the site is obstructed or the clay surface collapses — move to a new site and start over (the old scribed line may not be reused).
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) large angle between two runs → first check whether the rod is plumb, then whether the arc radius was misread (it must be the original radius of the arc-scribing rattan), last whether the afternoon really waited for the equal shadow (staking B early is the commonest error); (2) scattered shadow-tip stakes → the recording interval is too coarse; tighten it to "about one section"; (3) no usable shadow on an overcast day → stop and redo another day; (4) the scribed line will not line up with the shortest noon shadow → north and south are swapped (in the northern hemisphere the shadow-tip side is north).
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one scribed true-north line plus a next-day re-measurement record; L2 = two consecutive months of shadow-position re-measurement; L3 = a second person constructs the line from this card alone, within half a finger width.

docs.title: 3.2.2 Bootstrapping the Angle Standard (the Sole Source of Every "Angle Plate" in This Book)
docs.text:
Later chapters cite the "angle plate" in many places (chisel edge angles 40°–50°, mesh-texture angle 45°, turning-tool angles, etc.) — it does not appear out of thin air in Chapter 5; it is generated by this section's three bootstrap lines:

  1. 45°: fold the right angle made by the 3-4-5 cord (the diagonal is 45°) — construction: with the right-angle vertex as center, scribe an arc of arbitrary radius crossing both legs at A and B; then with A and B as centers and the same radius, scribe arcs intersecting at C; the line vertex–C is the 45° bisector;
  2. 30°/60°: trisect the 45° (approximate construction: probe the two division points against the arc intersections; close within ≤2° and accept — honestly labeled "approximate 30/60"); the interior angles of an equilateral triangle (three cords of equal length closed up) are exactly 60°, which is the harder source;
  3. Making the angle plate: carve the above standard angles on the edge of a hardwood board / bone plate, fitted with "snap-plate" fit testing (fit the angle under test against the plate angle and hold up to the light; an uneven gap is an error).

Honest boundary: this section can guarantee only the three hard standards 90/45/60 plus the ±2–3° approximate grade; arbitrary angles (e.g., 73°) cannot be done at this stage — any process requiring an arbitrary angle is rewritten as a combination of the three grades or as "functional-test acceptance".

docs.title: 3.3 How to Use a Water Surface to Establish a Level Standard
docs.text:
Principle: a still water surface is a level surface. Four methods (progressing by range): 1. Basin-water scribe-line method (local): let water in a container stand still, scribe a line on the vessel wall at the water surface; 2. A-frame level (portable): tie two equal-length wooden rods into an A shape, connect the midpoints of the two legs with a crossbar, hang a stone-hammer line from the apex, scribe a mark at the crossbar midpoint — when the hammer line passes the midpoint, the frame face is level. Key self-calibration — the reversal method: read the offset in the normal orientation, turn the whole frame around 180° and read again; the midpoint of the two offsets is the true midpoint (it eliminates the systematic error of unequal legs and may not be omitted); 3. Plumb line: the vertical standard; mutually 90° with the horizontal; 4. Segmented level transfer (long distance): basin-water scribe lines set the heights + the A-frame and range poles transfer level segment by segment; error accumulates per segment (about half a finger per segment; calibration: transfer back and forth between the same two points and compare the closing error). Precise leveling awaits Chapter 25.

Application preview: workbench leveling (Chapter 9), kiln-foundation layout (Chapter 12), channel gradient (Chapter 13 — when a deliberate slight slope is intended, express it with proportional rules of the "raise one finger per pace" type).

Failure modes: wind acting on the hammer line (windbreak); rattan stretching when damp (calibrate the dry and wet states separately); tie cords loosening (run the reversal self-check before every use).

[Card 03-03 A-Frame Reversal Self-Calibration] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: two equal-length wooden legs; one crossbar; one stone hammer; rattan (for lashing and for the hammer line).
  2. Tools required: plumb line (stone hammer on rattan, hanging free), marking tool. Calibration source: no external standard — self-calibration rests only on the 180° reversal, not on the legs being equal.
  3. Sequence and control points: lash the two legs into an A → connect the midpoints of the two legs with the crossbar → hang the stone-hammer line from the apex → scribe a mark at the crossbar midpoint → read the offset in the normal orientation → turn the whole frame 180° and read again → take the midpoint of the two offsets as the true midpoint. Control points: the reversal must turn the whole frame (legs not swapped); the reversal step may not be omitted.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: reversal angle 180°; criterion = the hammer line passing the true midpoint, meaning the frame face is level; residual error is of the "about half a finger per segment" order (accumulating per segment in segmented level transfer; empirical value — must be calibrated to local conditions); calibrate the dry and wet states separately (rattan stretches when damp).
  5. Observations to record: frame number / normal-orientation offset (in finger widths) / offset after reversal / true-midpoint correction / pre-use self-check date / weather (wind).
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = the true midpoint is fixed after reversal and the hammer line passes it; rework = both offsets equal and in the same direction (the ground or the support is at fault — re-shim and recalibrate); scrap = a leg is cracked or the lashing will not tighten — replace the stock.
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) the hammer line swings without settling → add a windbreak first (wind is the first cause), then check whether the stone hammer is too light; (2) the offset is identical before and after reversal → not unequal legs but an uneven support or ground; shim level and recalibrate; (3) accuracy drifts away after some use → the tie cords have loosened; run the reversal self-check before every use; (4) overall deviation grows in the rainy season → rattan stretched when damp; calibrate the dry and wet states separately.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one reversal self-calibration record; L2 = two consecutive months of re-checks; L3 = a second person calibrates the same frame from this card alone, and the two true midpoints agree by scribed-line overlap.

docs.title: 3.4 How to Repeat Measurements and Record Errors
docs.text:
Iron Law II made concrete: every measurement must answer "how large is the error", and the lowest-cost answer is repetition.

Repeat-measurement protocol: 1. Measure every quantity at least 3 times, re-zeroing and re-reading each time, without memorizing the previous result; 2. Record all readings and compute the range R = max − min; 3. Report the median as the value, R as the dispersion flag, with the uncertainty roughly estimated as ≈R/2; 4. Two-person cross-measurement: for the same nominal value, 2 people each measure independently 3 times; if the difference between the two reported values is greater than either person's R, judge a systematic error — switch person, tool, and method in turn to localize the source.

Error record sheet template:

Column Content Example Date / recorder Day name + person name Day 31 / Yi Object Number + name Standard rod 1 vs secondary rod 2 Nominal value Expected value Should be equal length Readings Each measured value 3 comparisons: equal / shorter by one finger / equal Range R Max − min One finger Tools used Tool numbers Rod 1, rod 2 Conditions Weather / wet-dry / temperature anchor Dry season, overcast, cool grade Disposition Conclusion + follow-up R over limit, re-measure next month

Naive discrimination between systematic and random error: if the value stabilizes after repeated averaging, random error dominates (measuring more helps); if averaging leaves an overall offset (someone's pacing always runs long), it is a systematic error — change the standard or add a correction; more measuring is useless.

Drift detection of the standard rod (monthly check): at each full moon compare the primary rod with the two secondary rods pairwise; if any pair differs by more than 1 smallest graduation, replace and remake. Wood's wet swelling and dry shrinking is the main drift source — the dryness criterion = rod weight unchanged across two consecutive monthly checks (weighing on the balance to judge moisture stability; a closed loop).

docs.title: 3.5 How to Establish Unified Units of Measure
docs.text:
Principles: 1. The absolute magnitude of a unit is unrelated to the old world, and that is fine — what matters is stability, shareability, rebuildability; 2. Body units are permitted for single-person self-use only (per the 3.1.1 measured data); cross-person handover is forbidden.

Length unit charter: - Primary unit = the full length of the standard rod (the "rod"), made of shade-dried hardwood, cross-marks at both ends, the rod body numbered; - Sub-units by halving: half-rod, quarter-rod ... down to the "finger". No decimal graduations — hand-scribed marks cannot achieve uniform tenths; halving can be achieved exactly by the fold-in-half method; - 2 secondary standards, the three rods stored in three places (against simultaneous loss); monthly check per 3.4; if the three rods mutually exceed tolerance, remake the third rod by majority rule.

Mass unit charter: - Unit weight = the calibrated stone: equilibrate the two pans repeatedly to select one of handy size and number it; - Multiple copies via a binary equilibration chain: obtain a 1/2, 1, 2, 4, 8 weight set; any integer mass can be composed; - Weight stones are notch-marked and registered into the archive.

Time unit charter and water-clock calibration method:

Public anchors: sunrise, noon (the shortest-shadow moment on the north-south line), sunset. Two short-duration levels: 1. Beats: agree a fixed command or chant as "one section"; each person long-term records "heartbeats per section" and takes the average; the beat is governed by the command, heartbeats serve only as a cross-check; 2. Water clock: a bamboo segment or gourd holds water; a small hole is pierced in the bottom with a natural sharp point. Defect declared honestly: the drip rate slows as the water level falls, so timing is not linear. Two responses:

[Card 03-01 Drip-Rate Segmented Calibration] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: one bamboo-segment or gourd water vessel (inner wall blackened with soot so the water level is visible); a natural sharp point to pierce the bottom hole; a scribe needle; clay tablet and charcoal for records.
  2. Tools required: scribe needle (to score the inner-wall graduations), command beats as the time ruler, marking tool. Calibration source: graduation spacing comes from the fold-in-half bisection, not from a rule; the only time ruler is the command beat — no outside clock is borrowed.
  3. Sequence and control points: pierce the bottom hole → score equal divisions on the inner wall (4–8 divisions by fold-in-half bisection) → calibrate division by division (while the level falls from line i to line i+1, count command sections, repeat 3 times and record the range) → make the "division-to-time table" and hang it beside the pot. Control points: each division is calibrated on its own; never infer the rest from one division; a new pot means recalibrating the whole table.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: 4–8 divisions; 3 repeats per division; range criterion ≤1/10 of that division's total section count; winter drip rate slows by 5–10% (empirical value — must be calibrated to local conditions), recalibrate on season change; two-pot cross-comparison difference <10% (L2 criterion).
  5. Observations to record: per division — pot number / division number / the 3 section counts / range / water-temperature grade (Chapter 3 anchors) / recalibration date.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = the 3 runs of every division fall within ≤1/10 of that division's total section count; rework = one division's range is over limit — recalibrate that division only; scrap = the pot body cracks and leaks — replace the pot and recalibrate the whole table (a new pot means a new table; the old table may not be carried over).
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) readings always run slow → first check whether another division's table is in use, then whether the season changed without recalibration (winter slowing 5–10%); (2) the drip runs as a continuous thread → hole too large, fit a finer hole and recalibrate the whole table; (3) no drops form → first check whether the hole is blocked (clear it with a bamboo sliver), then whether the level is too low; (4) two runs of the same division far apart → the command beat is unsteady; have one person call the beat.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one division-to-time table; L2 = a two-pot cross-comparison difference <10%; L3 = the season-change recalibration system running, with recalibration records on file.

Constant-head water clock (upgrade technique; switch as soon as materials allow): the root of the uneven drip rate is: water level changes → pressure changes. Cure: twin-pot constant head — the upper pot is continuously topped up and overflows from a side port, holding the dripping pot's liquid surface constant at the overflow-port height → constant pressure at the drip hole → constant drip rate. The upper pot can be a pierced pottery jar (after Chapter 11). The constant-head pot needs only one calibration of "drips per beat", and all divisions take the same time.

Unit charter clay tablet: all unit definitions are written only on the "unit charter" tablet; changing a unit = issue a new charter tablet, deprecate the old one and archive it. On contact with external settlements, exchange standard-rod copies and record mutual comparisons.

docs.title: 3.5.1 Process Card for Making the Equal-Arm Balance (3-06, the Root of the Proportioning Line)
docs.text:
The balance on which all later proportioning (from Chapter 8 on) depends is given its manufacturing method here, no longer just "pick a stone":

[Card 03-06 Equal-Arm Balance] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: one straight hardwood beam (70–90 cm, knot-free, straight-grained); cord in three grades; two shell / hardwood hanging pans; a set of calibration stones (chosen by repeated balancing of the two pans, each numbered); a scribing needle and charcoal; a clay tablet (for the record and the notch numbers).
  2. Required tools: scribing needle (zero line and end lines); chisel (shallow V notch); hard-bone / hardwood seat block (carrying the V); crossbar (to hang the beam); pillar (three lines scribed); fine needle (pointer); the smallest-unit calibration stone. Calibration sources: equal arms are measured with one and the same cord wrapped round the beam and cross-checked by the reversal method (same method as Card 03-03); weights are copied level by level as a binary balancing chain (1/2, 1, 2, 4, 8) — no external weights are borrowed.
  3. Operating sequence and control points: ① scribe the zero line at the exact middle; at both ends wrap the same cord to measure equal distances and scribe the end lines → ② reversal cross-check: place the same stone at each end and swap them — if it does not balance, the ends differ in weight or in arm length; repair until the tilt direction is unchanged after swapping → ③ chisel a shallow V notch in the top midline, seat it on a hard-bone / hardwood block, hang the beam from the crossbar → ④ hang a fine needle from the bottom midline; scribe three lines on the pillar (left / middle / right, one finger width apart) → ⑤ sensitivity test: after balancing empty, add the smallest-unit stone — a pointer deflection ≥ half a line width passes → ⑥ weight multiplication 1→2 (duplicate by placing two stones side by side) →4→8, copying level by level with the balance, each piece notch-numbered and archived. Control points: the V notch is where the whole balance's precision resides — ground smooth, never chipped; if sensitivity falls short, only lighten the beam or shorten the hang distance — never add stones to fake a reading; the pans and hanger cords must never lift loads or people (structural strength unverified).
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration methods: beam 70–90 cm, straight-grained, knot-free; end lines measured with one and the same cord (no rule); V notch shallow and ground smooth, seated on hard bone / hardwood; the three pillar lines one finger width apart (Chapter 3 body unit, single-person use only); sensitivity criterion = the smallest-unit stone deflects the pointer ≥ half a line width; weight chain binary 1/2, 1, 2, 4, 8, calibrated by level-by-level balancing duplication with each piece notch-numbered and archived.
  5. In-process observation records: beam number / beam length and weight / zero-line and end-line scribes / tilt direction in the two reversal cross-checks / V-notch condition (grooved, chipped) / sensitivity measurement (stone added, pointer deflection) / notch numbers and balancing result at each level of the weight chain / handler.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = tilt direction unchanged after reversal + empty balance + smallest-unit stone deflects the pointer ≥ half a line width + weight chain 1→8 balanced level by level on file; rework = sensitivity short (lighten the beam or shorten the hang distance, then re-measure), unequal end lines (re-scribe and cross-check again); scrap = cracked beam, chipped V notch, or a beam warped by moisture (replace the beam; the old weight chain must be re-balanced).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: ① the same object weighs differently twice → first check whether the V notch has worn a groove (new seat, re-grind) → then check hanger-cord lengths and the two pans' weights (equal-length cords, swap the pans) → finally check whether the beam has taken up moisture (weigh it to judge dryness, remake); ② pointer does not move, or moves sluggishly → first check whether the fulcrum is binding → then whether the beam is too heavy or the hang distance too long → finally whether the "smallest-unit" stone is itself a reject; ③ pans at unequal height → first adjust the beam midpoint, then fit equal-length hanger cords.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one usable balance + weight chain 1→8 notch-numbered on file; L2 = two consecutive monthly balancing re-tests (same object weighed twice, difference within the range, recorded and explained) + the weight chain reviewed by a second person; L3 = a second person builds one blind from this card and it is verified usable (Chapter 3 acceptance L3) + a damaged standard rebuilt within two days per the charter, old-to-new deviation ≤ one finger width.

docs.title: 3.6 How to Preserve Technical Drawings and Process Records
docs.text:
Recording media list:

Medium Advantages Drawbacks and countermeasures Shade-dried clay tablet Scribeable, high volume, locally sourced Destroyed by water: store elevated off the ground, cover boards, transcribe a second copy at another site before the rainy season; fired hardening awaits Chapter 11 Carved wood Water-resistant Small capacity, short entries only Knotted cords Portable Reminder index only, cannot store parameters Ground scribing field Large drawings possible Weathers; important drawings must be transcribed to clay tablets

Drawing standards: 1. Scales in integer multiples only: 1:1, 2:1, 1:2. Arbitrary scales are forbidden — there is currently no fine-division capability, and arbitrary scales cannot be re-verified; 2. Dimensions marked with scribe symbols: one rod = primary-unit symbol, one finger = sub-unit symbol; quantities counted with scribed dots (five dots and one bar); 3. Three kinds of drawing: outline, assembly relationships, full-size layout field (1:1 ground layout).

Archive system: one tablet, one matter; numbering = date + serial; build the catalog tablet before establishing files; key drawings and recipes kept in two copies at different sites; symbols follow the Chapter 2 key table, and new symbols are updated in both copies simultaneously. Failure mode: damp tablets, lost symbols, the gamble of "keeping it in the head" — results at L2 level and above must be put in writing.

docs.title: 3.7 From Personal Experience to Reproducible Craft
docs.text:
Turning "I can do it" into "it works from the record": four means: 1. Retelling test: the artisan dictates the complete procedure → another person executes blind, following only the dictation → differences backfilled item by item. Until the dictation is proven by blind execution, it is deemed "an incomplete procedure"; 2. Parameter-window method: for each parameter record three values — minimum usable / usual / maximum usable. A failure outside the window is not a surprise; it is a known boundary; 3. Process card format (one card per tablet): procedure steps + parameter window + failure modes + acceptance criteria + version number; 4. Journeyman criterion: an apprentice may work independently only after N consecutive acceptable pieces (generally N=3; critical materials and safety parts N=5, empirical value).

Version management: every improvement issues a new version of the process card; the old card is archived marked "superseded by version X", searchable in both directions. Verbal changes to processes are forbidden — any practice change that has not entered a new card version is logged as an operational error.

[Card 03-04 Pace Calibration] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: one standard rod (the primary "rod" unit, shade-dried hardwood); small stakes (to mark the ends of the measured distance); clay tablet or marking board.
  2. Tools required: standard rod, marking tool, error record sheet (the 3.4 template). Calibration source: every pace count is converted into "rods", never into millimetres — this chapter has no millimetre-level absolute standard.
  3. Sequence and control points: pick level, dry, firm ground → measure off a known distance with the rod (say 10 rods, stakes at both ends) → the person walks it at a natural pace and counts paces → walk it out and back once each → repeat 3 times and take the median → compute "paces per rod" and score it onto the personal pace calibration card. Control points: a natural pace only (no deliberate overstriding); restart the walk each time without carrying the previous count.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: the natural pace is read as the mean of 10 paces; each item is measured 3 times per person and the median taken; typical median pace length 650–780 mm with an in-team range of 100–150 mm (empirical value — must be calibrated to local conditions); pass criterion = pacing dispersion 1–2%; a round-trip difference >2 paces per 10 rods means change the venue (slope, grass height, soft mud all alter pace).
  5. Observations to record: person / venue / measured distance in rods / outbound paces / return paces / median of 3 / paces per rod / weather and ground state.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = round-trip difference ≤2 paces per 10 rods and the 3 runs inside the 1–2% dispersion; rework = over limit — recalibrate on level, dry, firm ground; scrap = the same person's results from two venues are systematically inconsistent (that pace may be used only at that venue, never generally).
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) the round-trip difference grows with every calibration → check the venue first (slope, grass height, soft mud) and change it; (2) two counts of the same walk disagree → a deliberate pace was used; switch to a natural pace and restart; (3) the pace is markedly shorter than at the last calibration → fatigue or load; record the current state separately without overwriting the historical value; (4) the converted distance will not match the rod measurement → first check whether someone else's pace table is in use (body units may not be handed across persons).
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one personal pace calibration card (paces per rod); L2 = one calibration record per venue at two venues, each stating where it applies; L3 = pacing a distance with the card and landing within the 1–2% dispersion of the standard-rod measurement.

docs.title: 3.8 Calendar and Farming Times (C3 supplement)
docs.text: Solar-term determination: measure the rod shadow length at noon every day and enter it in a table — the longest-shadow day = winter solstice, the shortest-shadow day = summer solstice (judgment error ±2 days; take the mean over three consecutive years); between the two equinoxes and two solstices, use linear interpolation of shadow length to divide out the eight sections. Season marking by star rise/set: choose the last bright star in the eastern sky before dawn (heliacal rising) and the first bright star in the western sky after dusk (heliacal setting), and record the star names day by day — the same star rising and setting at the same time year after year is a natural yearly calendar. Leap-year correction: fix the year by the winter solstice — if the "year length" (the interval between two winter solstices) consecutively exceeds 365 days by more than one beat, insert an intercalary month to realign (folk rule: 12 lunar months fall short of the year by about 11 days; three years one leap as a starting point). Farming-time alignment: sowing window = solar term + local correction (phenological anchors: record when a certain tree flowers / a certain insect first chirps, and revise year by year against yields — corrections transcribed into the ledger; doing it from memory is forbidden).

docs.text: Parameter Value Class Body-unit in-team relative difference Finger width ≈30%, hand-span ≈25%, elbow/pace ≈15–18% Measured-protocol prefilled Balance equilibration discrimination limit 1–2% of load (calibrated by the small-stone increment method) Empirical Minimum reliable hand-scribed line spacing 2–3 mm (mean of 10 successive divisions) Empirical Pacing dispersion 1–2% (change the venue if the round-trip difference is >2 paces per 10 rods) Empirical Rough roundness check 8-direction radius range ≤1 finger width Criterion True-north re-measurement Two-day inter-line angle difference ≤ half a finger width Criterion Water-clock division range ≤1/10 of that division's total section count Criterion Winter drip-rate change Slows by 5–10%, recalibrate on season change Empirical Cord sag Span >20 paces requires mid support Empirical

docs.text: Symptom Candidate causes (by probability) Verification Disposition Dimensions mismatch on two-person handover A body unit was used across persons Check the "tools" column of the record sheet Switch to the standard rod across the board; re-measure Standard-rod monthly check mutual difference over limit Rod not fully dry / absorbed moisture Weigh and compare against the monthly-check records Replace and remake the rod; add moisture protection to the storage Right-angle layout skewed Uneven knot spacing / uneven ground / wet rattan stretched Flip self-check Measure with the same stick; level the platform; re-test in the dry state Large angle between the two true-north lines Rod not plumb / arc radius misread / afternoon did not wait for the equal shadow Re-check plumb; re-measure Re-measure and average over multiple days Water-clock readings always slow Wrong division table used / winter viscosity / hole worn larger Cross-check against the table; recalibrate on season change Follow the table; recalibrate Balance pans unequal height Beam midpoint offset / hanger cords of unequal length Hang the empty beam and fine-tune Adjust the midpoint; equal-length hanger cords Cross-measurement difference greater than either party's range Systematic error (someone's technique / a rod's defect) Switch person and tool, bisect to localize Add a correction or change the standard

docs.title: Process Card Index
docs.text:
[Card 03-01] Drip-rate segmented calibration (card in 3.5, before the constant-head drip section) | [Card 03-02] True-north determination by construction (card at the end of 3.2.1) | [Card 03-03] A-frame reversal self-calibration (card at the end of 3.3) | [Card 03-04] Pace calibration (card at the end of 3.7) | [Card 03-05] Body-unit error statistics (card at the end of 3.1.1) | [Card 03-06] Equal-arm balance (card in 3.5.1)

All six cards copy out onto a single page with the eight fields complete: input materials / required tools (including calibration sources) / operating sequence and control points / empirical parameters and calibration methods / in-process observation records / pass–rework–scrap criteria / common failures and troubleshooting order / L1–L3 evidence.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• L1: one physical anchor built for each of the four classes of standards, each with 1 recorded measurement; the true-north line scribed with a next-day re-measurement record; the body-unit error statistics table completed.
  • L2: two consecutive monthly checks (three-rod mutual comparison, equilibration re-test, shadow-position re-measurement); ≥10 entries in the error record sheet with no column missing; the two-person cross-measurement difference recorded and explained; the water-clock division-to-time table verified by a two-pot cross-comparison; the charter and catalog tablet in the archive.
  • L3: any damaged standard rebuilt within two days per the charter, with an old-to-new deviation ≤1 finger width; at least 1 process card verified usable by a second person's blind execution; the double-backup archive running, with one transcription drill completed before the rainy season. Evidence: monthly-check sheets, transcription records, blind-execution records.

docs.title: Labor Hours, Manpower, and Consumption
docs.text: Item Manpower Hours (empirical) Body-unit error statistics ≥6 people Half a day Standard rod, three rods + mutual check 1–2 people 1 day (material selection and shade drying counted separately) True-north determination + re-measurement 2 people 2 half-days Water clock making and full-table calibration 1 person Half a day per pot Balance and weight chain 1 person 1 day Monthly check 1 person Half a day per month

docs.title: Safety Boundaries
docs.text:
• The balance hanging pans and hanger cords must never hoist heavy loads or people — structural strength unverified;
  • Guard against scalds from boiling water and molten wax (beeswax at 63 ℃ can already cause injury): never touch hot objects bare-handed, insulate hot containers with multiple layers of dry leaves; the full heat-safety procedure is in Chapter 6;
  • Solar shadow observation reads the shadow tip; looking directly at the sun is forbidden;
  • The hanging stone hammer must never be suspended overhead; while working with a scribing point, the other hand must never be placed along the extension of the scribe line.

docs.title: Chapter 4: How to Use This Manual — Navigation, Process Cards, and On-Site Work Organization
Chapter Objectives
docs.text:
• Master the manual's navigation system: prerequisite chapter numbering rules, the four-dependency check, core/alternative route selection, chapter start gates, failure logging and version management, and recognition of technical jumps.
  • Master the on-site use cycle of the process card (new in v2): how one complete job runs, from "pre-start verification" to "archive and transcribe".
  • Produce four method tools: the four-dependency checklist, the chapter start triple-check table, the reader's chapter completeness self-check list, and the technical log format and version naming rules.
  • This chapter and General Outline G02 (the author template) mirror each other: General Outline G02 constrains how authors write; this chapter constrains how readers read and how they judge "have I completed this chapter". From v2 on, General Outline G02 grows to seven Iron Laws and the eight-field process card system — this chapter is synchronized with it.

docs.title: 4.1 Dependency Levels and Prerequisite Chapter Numbering
docs.text:
The number is the dependency: Chapter N may cite only results numbered below N. This is the book-wide mechanical criterion against tool anachronism, and the reader's first check.

How the reader uses it (three actions):

  1. Scan prerequisites before reading: open any chapter and read its "Minimum Prerequisites" table first, checking the chapter number in the "Source" column line by line. Any unsatisfied line: go back and fill it, then return.
  2. Watch citations while reading: every tool is tagged with its source (chapter number or General Outline document number) on first appearance in the body text. Any untagged tool you see goes into the "jump register" (see Section 4.6).
  3. Check the lists after reading: cross-check the chapter's List A (existing tools) and List B (new tools) against your physical stock. Items on List A you should already own; anything missing is prerequisite debt.

"Preview" versus "available" (the most misread rule in the book): the manual permits writing "this capability will be established in Chapter N" — that is a preview (a forward declaration), and preview items may NOT be used as existing. The test is very simple: which chapter's List B does it appear in, and have you accepted that chapter to the corresponding level? Example: Chapter 2 may preview "calcination verification will be backfilled in Chapter 12", but Chapter 2 itself may not burn anything.
