Reader-created content follows the same rule: any process record you add for your own settlement must also carry a source chapter number and is audited by the same rules. What these rules protect is not the manual's authority but the traceability of your own dependency chain.

docs.title: 4.2 The Four Dependencies: Tools, Materials, Energy, and Knowledge
docs.text:
Every "stuck" state falls into one of the four dependency classes. The check action and gap handling for each:

Dependency class Check action (what to ask) What to check Gap handling Tool dependency Are the required tools physically present and in good condition? Each chapter's A/B lists + your tool archive Look up the tool's manufacturing chapter and build it first; if no substitute exists, that chapter has not met its start conditions Material dependency Are the required raw materials enough for this run plus two trial runs? Resource map + reserve ledger (Chapter 2, Section 3.6) Check that chapter's alternative-route section; if reserves are short, gather more first Energy dependency For the required heat/mechanical energy, are fuel and power sufficient? Fuel entries + energy entries (Section 2.5) Check upstream in the energy lineage (fire, Chapter 6; hydropower, Chapter 21) Knowledge dependency Without the manual, can you write out the principle and the key parameter windows? The chapter body + your recitation test (Section 3.7) Re-read + oral examination; a knowledge gap must not be replaced by "just trying it"

Combined example — the four-dependency rehearsal for Chapter 6 (fire-making):

  • Tools: no hard prerequisite (the bow drill belongs to Section 7.6; Chapter 6 friction fire-lighting uses a fire bow board makeable by hand — the Chapter 6 text governs);
  • Materials: fire-starting material (fine dry grass, inner birch bark), tinder, fuel (the standing deadwood entry in Section 2.5);
  • Energy: human power;
  • Knowledge: the three elements of combustion, fire-starting material grading, ventilation principles.

With all four columns filled, Chapter 6 meets its start conditions. Any chapter can have a start card filled out this way.

docs.title: 4.3 Core Routes and Alternative Routes
docs.text:
The core route = the manual's default mainline order; its skeleton is the five critical chains (from General Outline G04):

  1. Stone tools → woodworking tools → simple machines (Chapters 5, 7, 9)
  2. Fire → furnaces and kilns → refractory materials → metal smelting (Chapters 6, 12, 16–18)
  3. Metal tools → measurement → precision machining → machine tools (Chapters 19–22)
  4. Mechanical power → electromagnetism → generators → electrical power systems (Chapters 21, 28–32)
  5. Glass and chemistry → material purification → semiconductor processing → integrated circuits (Chapters 14, 23–26, 33–35)

The fixed annotation format for alternative routes (Iron Law 5; no element may be omitted): performance loss / resource cost / applicability boundary / final bottleneck. Example (preview): a flint-free region takes the quartzite/obsidian stone-tool route (Chapter 5) — performance loss: poorer edge retention or excessive brittleness; resource cost: collection from greater distances; applicability boundary: covers only chopping/scraping-class tools; final bottleneck: cannot provide fine-machining edges, so the metal route (Chapters 16–18) must be entered as early as possible.

Three-step route selection:

  1. Fill in your current state row by row using the environmental assessment table (General Outline G04 part four, ten rows);
  2. Verify each row against the resource map (Chapter 2);
  3. Cross the two tables to fix this settlement's mainline and the chapters to advance or delay. Principle: environmental differences change not only material sources but also the order of development (example: hydropower-rich regions may advance some machine chapters; fuel-poor regions must push the glass and metallurgy chapters back and solve energy first).

Alternative-route usage rule: once a substitute goes into service, that chapter's acceptance criteria must be re-validated; the core route's acceptance values must not be carried over. Substitute materials almost always behave differently (shrinkage, thermal stability, strength); carrying over old criteria misses real defects.

docs.title: 4.4 How to Judge Whether a Chapter May Start
docs.text:
The three start checks (one column each; fill the start card):

  1. Prerequisite completeness check: verify item by item against the Section 4.2 four dependencies; all source chapters must have met their own acceptance standards (at least L1; safety-related chapters follow their own stricter requirements).
  2. Resource margin check: from the chapter's "resource cost", estimate the materials and fuel for this run plus two failures. Do not start when the margin is below twice planned consumption (rule of thumb: at the L1 stage trial-and-error rates are generally above fifty percent; revise in the field from failure records).
  3. Manpower and time check: the chapter's work-hour estimate ÷ available people = schedule; chapters exceeding one continuous work season must be split into segments.

"Can be done but should not be done": passing the three checks ≠ it should be done immediately. Re-run the priority framework (General Outline G04 part three): what gets blocked if this is not built? Is there a cheaper substitute? What is the opportunity cost of the manpower at this moment? Answer the five questions of Chapter 1 Section 1.5 one by one before starting work.

Pause criterion: the same failure mode appearing 3 times in a row (rule of thumb) → mandatory pause; re-examine prerequisites (did the material batch change? are tools worn? a knowledge gap?). Consecutive same-mode failures are almost always a prerequisite problem, not a craft problem.

Reader's chapter completeness self-check list (core deliverable; tick item by item; one missing item means incomplete):

(A) Before starting - [ ] This chapter's start card has been filled out (four-dependency check + resource margin + manpower and time) - [ ] All prerequisite chapters have met their acceptance standards, with levels recorded - [ ] This chapter's safety boundary has been read, and the prohibition conditions for dangerous operations excerpted somewhere visible on site

(B) During the work - [ ] Every operation is logged in the technical log format (date/parameters/result/failure mode) - [ ] Failures are filed under the five classifications (see Section 4.5); an unfiled failure counts as never having happened and must never be repeated - [ ] Parameters are recorded by the window method (minimum usable / typical / maximum usable)

(C) After completion - [ ] Every acceptance criterion of this chapter has been physically measured; "it looks done" was not accepted as a substitute - [ ] The level reached (L1/L2/L3) has been judged honestly and recorded; L2 requires evidence of 3 consecutive conforming pieces - [ ] New tools on this chapter's List B have been numbered into the tool archive, with repair/rebuild paths on damage written down - [ ] List C (unresolved dependencies) has been copied into your own dependency map, with target chapters marked - [ ] Relevant resource-map entries have been backfilled with verification status (Chapter 2 backfill rules) - [ ] The next chapter's start card can now be begun from this

docs.title: 4.5 Failure Records, Process Improvement, and Version Management
docs.text:
Technical log format (one volume per chapter, on clay tablet or carved wood, carved column by column):

Column Content Date/operator day name + person name Goal what this entry's operation is meant to achieve Prerequisite check are all four columns of the start card green (if a gap is only discovered now, record it honestly) Operation record working parameters (length/mass/time/temperature anchor readings) — recorded per the four benchmark classes of Chapter 3 Result finished-piece dimensions, phenomena observed, pass status of each acceptance criterion Failure classification one of the five classifications (below) Improvement hypothesis which variable the next entry will change (one only)

The five failure classifications (troubleshoot in this order, eliminating class by class):

  1. Missing prerequisite: tool out of condition, different material batch, insufficient energy — back to the start card;
  2. Parameter out of bounds: operating parameters ran outside the process card's window — back to the Section 3.7 parameter windows; where no window exists yet, run window trials first;
  3. Material difference: same-named material from a different source behaves differently — back to Chapter 2 for retesting; split the entries;
  4. Operating error: step order or technique deviated from the process card — supplement the step descriptions via the recitation test;
  5. Wrong criterion: the acceptance criterion itself does not match the real use — revise the criterion field of the process card and bump the version.

Improvement loop (single-variable method): hypothesis → change one variable only → record → if it works, issue a new version of the process card; if not, revert the variable and void the hypothesis on the record.

Version naming rule: process name + version number + date index (example: pace-survey calibration v2 / Day 45). New and old cards are linked both ways by "supersedes"; old cards are archived, not destroyed. Oral process changes are forbidden (settled in Section 3.7; this is the enforcement point).

Three anti-patterns (self-check):

  • Changing several variables at once — attribution becomes impossible; you turn the experiment into a gamble;
  • Retrying without records — 3 failures repeated with the same method triggers the Section 4.4 pause criterion;
  • Mistaking a fluke for a process — anything not reproduced 3 times gets no card and does not enter List B.

docs.title: 4.6 How to Recognize Unreasonable Technical Jumps
docs.text:
A jump = some step invoking something that does not exist. Readers audit any technical material with the six signals below — including this manual, external oral knowledge, and other settlements' processes — and register findings on discovery:

Signal Test question 1 Tool with no source Does this tool appear nowhere in Lists A/B and the chapter numbers? 2 Precision with no source It says "accurate to such-and-such" — in which chapter are the datum, the measuring instruments, and the inspection method established? 3 Broken material chain It simply says "use steel/glass/reagents" — where is the manufacturing chapter? (Iron Law 3) 4 One piece claimed as a system "Mastered" is declared with a finished piece but no maintenance, no spares, no resupply plan 5 Acceptance by appearance The success criterion is "it looks right", with no functional or repeatability test (Iron Law 4) 6 Substitution at no cost The substitute is presented as equal to the original, with no performance loss or boundary statement (Iron Law 5)

Audit exercises (two items; readers answer for themselves):

  • Example 1: "Burn lime in an iron pot." — Which chapter does the iron pot come from? (Signals 1 + 3: ironware comes only after Chapter 18, and pot-class castings carry their own prerequisites; the correct vessel route for lime burning is in Chapters 12–13.)
  • Example 2: "Cut six timbers to equal length precisely per the drawing." — In which chapter are the datum and measuring instruments behind "precisely" established? (Signal 2: the length datum is Chapter 3; copying a dimension relies on the standard rod and notch comparison, not on the word "precise".)

Handling flow: a jump is found → write it into the "jump register" clay tablet (date/source/signal type/missing dependency) → decide chain repair (return to the missing chapter) or reroute (take an alternative route) → if the entry points at this manual, handle it under the conflict rules at the head of General Outline G01: revise with the Iron Laws and prerequisite numbering as the authority.

What the register is for: the jump register is the settlement's technical immune system. Left unmaintained, within three months oral experience quietly mixes in "sounds plausible" anachronisms — and by then nobody remembers where they came from.

docs.title: 4.7 The On-Site Use Cycle of the Process Card (new in v2: the complete course of one job)
docs.text:
From v2 on, the book's key operations are delivered as process cards (numbered like Card 20-01); a card can be copied onto a single sheet and carried to the workstation. One complete on-site job runs in five steps:

  1. Pre-start verification: without reciting the body text, run this chapter's "pre-start verification" table and tick each line — no start unless the criteria pass. Whichever item is missing, go back to that chapter and fill it; never start impaired;
  2. Operate by the card: follow the card's field order (input materials → tools → operations and control points → parameters). Steps marked ◎ are hand-feel steps — execute them by the practice method and compensation criteria given on the card; do not improvise by feel;
  3. In-process recording: for every item on the card's "in-process observation entries", make one entry per band (color/sound/reading), on the spot and in the original words — any observation added after knock-off must be marked "added later";
  4. Three-way disposition by criteria: results are sorted into "pass / rework / scrap"; "close enough" is not allowed. Rework follows the card's rework path; scrapped pieces are handled as the card directs (mostly kept as samples in the failure sample library);
  5. Archive and transcribe: wherever this batch's measured parameters differ from the card's default values, transcribe them into the ledger after field calibration (Chapter 43) — the next batch consults the ledger, not memory. Retire the worn card to the archive.

This cycle is the field form of Iron Law 6 (every acceptance leaves evidence). A job that skips step 5 has only "got the work done", not "established a capability" — the next batch must grope forward from your starting point all over again.

docs.title: A. Existing Tools List
docs.text:
• Chapter 1: starting-point determination checklist (including the natural-object boundary rules), level determination table, four-question dependency-tracing card, dependency map template.
  • Chapter 2: resource survey record sheet, resource map, symbol key, streak plate, hardness reference set, ten-step identification procedure card, natural container set.
  • Chapter 3: standard rod and secondary rod, 12-division rope, 3-4-5 rope method, plumb line, Type A level frame, equal-arm balance and weight-stone set, solar shadow pole, temperature anchor card, error record sheet, units charter and archive system.

docs.title: B. New Tools in This Chapter
docs.text:
Tool Manufacturing source Use Four-dependency checklist 4.2 The attribution starting point for every "stuck" state Chapter start triple-check table 4.4 The start gate Reader's chapter completeness self-check list (three sections, A/B/C) 4.4 The mandatory actions at every chapter's opening and close Technical log format 4.5 The record carrier for failures and parameters Five-classification failure troubleshooting method 4.5 Failure attribution order Process version naming rule 4.5 (together with the Section 3.7 process card) Supersession-chain management Six-signal jump checklist + jump register 4.6 Auditing all technical material

All are method tools; their carriers follow the Chapter 3 archive system (clay tablet / carved wood + dual backup).

docs.title: C. Unresolved Dependencies
docs.text:
• The self-check list's force depends entirely on the Chapter 3 archive system actually running (dual clay-tablet backup, monthly inspection, catalog board). With a hollow archive, the list is a formality idling in place.
  • The reliability of external knowledge (oral transmission, other settlements' processes) can only be first-screened with the six signals; it cannot be verified quantitatively — until the systematic experimental verification methods of Chapter 25 exist, treat every imported process as L0 first.
  • The priority framework is a discussion tool, not a formula; a quantitative conversion method for manpower and time must wait for the Part 10 environmental edition to provide a draft algorithm.

docs.title: 4.8 Minimal Drafting Method (a field, board-carried version of three views, datums, and tolerances)
docs.text:
This section is the temporary-carrier version of Chapter 42 (engineering drawing and version control): paper only arrives in Chapter 41, but from Chapter 5 on you already need to draw — on wooden boards, bark, and clay tablets. The rules are identical to formal drafting; only the carrier differs.

Three views (front/plan/side): draw the same object's outline from three directions, under the three mnemonics "aligned, flush, equal width" — the front view and the plan view align vertically; the front and side views are flush left to right; the plan and side views have equal width. Scribe on clay tablets with a scriber (the Chapter 5 pointed tool); on wooden boards, lay out with a charcoal stick and set the lines with a carving knife.

Datum first: the first stroke on any drawing is always the datum (a face or an edge); every other dimension is measured from it. Chain relaying is forbidden — chains accumulate error; measured from the datum, errors do not stack (the forerunner of the Chapter 22 tolerance idea).

Nominal size plus upper/lower deviation: every dimension is written as "target value + tolerance", e.g., "shaft diameter 20, acceptable 19.8–20.2". When a clay tablet has no room, use tally marks (groups of five with a bar, the Chapter 3 method). A drawing that gives only target values without tolerances is judged a non-conforming drawing under Section 4.6 Signal 5.

Scale and drawing number: use only integer scales (1:1, 2:1, 1:2; Chapter 3 discipline); carve the drawing number (date + serial, the Chapter 3 archive method) and the drafter's mark in the lower-right corner of every drawing. Wooden-board drawings are branded at a corner (scorched mark from a fire awl) to prevent erasure.

◎ Drawing hand-feel: lay out straight lines by pressing a taut hemp cord into the surface (long lines); use the edge of a straightedge for short lines (the rule after the Chapter 20 three-ruler mutual check). Practice method: draw the same object three times and overlay the three sheets — outlines that coincide pass.

docs.title: 4.9 Minimal Record Carriers (writing surfaces before paper)
docs.text:
The paper of Chapter 41 is an upgrade route, not the starting point. Starting carriers, in order:

Carrier How made Advantage Loss risk and countermeasure Clay tablet (Chapter 3, Section 3.6) Flatten local clay and inscribe; shade-dry Zero cost, inscribable Water destroys it — store on high racks under cover; transcribe before the rainy season Wooden board Chapter 7 planed thin stock; charcoal stick/carving knife Water-resistant (when inscribed) Wood checks, writing wears faint — carve, not just write, anything important Bark (birch inner layer) Stripped with the Chapter 6 tinder source Bendable, light Brittle, cracks — store in rolls Leather (offcuts) Chapter 15 tanned offcuts Durable, rollable Costly — record only "permanent-class" entries (units-charter class)

Transcription upgrade chain: temporary carrier → fired hardening (Chapter 11 ceramicized clay tablets) → paper (Chapter 41). "Permanent-class" content recorded on temporary carriers (units charter, thread standard, batch ledger) must be transcribed when the carrier upgrades, with the old pieces archived — no "rewriting in passing during a carrier change"; go through the loan register of Section 4.10.

docs.title: 4.10 Minimal Archive System (three things: numbering, duplicates, loans)
docs.text:
The complete archive system is Chapter 43; from Chapter 5 on only three things are required, and they are the seed of the Chapter 43 system:

  1. Numbering: every record piece is carved with "date + serial" (the Chapter 3 method) + attribution (which chapter, which card). An unnumbered record piece counts as scrap paper;
  2. Two copies, two places: permanent-class records are always kept in duplicate, stored apart (two buildings, or a house and a cellar) — a single-copy record equals no record;
  3. Loan register: record pieces do not leave the premises. If one is needed on site, copy a working duplicate and take that; the master stays in the cabinet, carved with an "on loan" mark — a record whose master is lost counts as that process demoted back to the first tier (a pass without evidence is called an impression; Iron Law 6).

Interface to later chapters: Chapter 41's paper and ink deliver the "durable and duplicable" carrier; Chapter 42 upgrades this section's "tolerance notation" into full tolerance annotation and version control; Chapter 43 expands this section's "three things" into tiered archives, a negative-results library, and master–apprentice transmission. This section is their root — written into Chapter 4 because from Chapter 5 on, every acceptance uses them.

docs.title: Failure Modes and Diagnosis [methods chapter]
docs.text: This chapter's failure modes: ① checking prerequisites but not criteria (work starts only after every line of the verification table is ticked); ② treating previews as existing (checked against List B); ③ oral process changes without a new version (version discipline); ④ reading the ledger without transcribing into it (step 5 of the Section 4.7 cycle).

docs.title: Process Card Index [methods chapter]
docs.text: This chapter sets no process cards — its deliverables are method items (checklists/tables/cycles), see List B; the cards of the process chapters are used through the Section 4.7 cycle of this chapter.

docs.title: Safety Boundary
docs.text:
• This is a methods chapter with no physical operations. The one hard clause: in any chapter whose self-check list section (A) has not passed, operations involving fire, high temperature, heavy loads, deep water, or falls are barred from starting — reading yes, hands-on no.
  • No one (including readers with modern knowledge) may claim exemption from the three start checks on the strength of "I understand the principle"; the knowledge dependency is checked precisely by the recitation test (Section 4.2).

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• L1 proof-of-principle: for any chapter read, state orally its four dependencies, its current level, and what the next level lacks; for any external suggestion, say which of the six signals it hits.
  • L2 repeatable manufacture: actually walk one subsequent chapter (recommend Chapter 5 or 6) with the three start checks + the completeness self-check list, with complete technical log and process card traces, re-verified item by item by a second person against the list.
  • L3 sustainable production: the settlement runs it as an institution — every process carries a version number and a supersession chain; the jump register has a maintainer and a quarterly review; one new member reproduces a level-one process (e.g., pace-survey calibration or the clay settling test) from the archives alone (process card + log + symbol table) and passes acceptance.

docs.title: Next-Step Dependencies
docs.text:
• Part 1 (Chapters 1–4) closes here: rules (1), resources (2), measurement (3), methods (4) — the four-piece set is in place. This is the only part of the book needing no physical manufacture, and the only part whose deliverable is "institutions".
  • From Chapter 5 on, physical manufacture begins: its start card will cite the Chapter 2 resource map (stone material entry), the Chapter 1 boundary rules (picking up natural stone), and the Chapter 3 standard rod (dimension recording).
  • The information lineage (Lineage 6) takes shape in this chapter: oral experience → decision rules → graphical records → unified measurement → process records are established; technical drawings and standardization upgrade in Part 4 (Chapters 20–22); production records and automatic control come after Part 6.
  • The four-dependency check and the jump register will feed the "Safety Boundary" block of every chapter and the appendix audit tools (this list is included when Appendix A recompiles the master map).

docs.title: Capability Boundary and Parameter Notes
docs.text: Capability boundary: this chapter delivers method tools (four-dependency checklist, start triple-check table, self-check list, log format, process card use cycle), all institutional pieces — no physical product is manufactured and there are no process parameters. A methods chapter's "acceptance" is evidence of use: the tables were actually used and left records (see Acceptance Criteria), not that the paperwork is complete. Parameter table: this chapter has no process parameters and keeps no master parameter table; every parameter in the book is delivered with its own process chapter. This chapter sets only the check rule that "parameters must carry a calibration method" (Section 4.6 Signal 2).

docs.title: Chapter 5: The First Tool — Stone
docs.text: Part 2 · Survival, Fire, and Primitive Materials. This chapter is written to the pure-natural Starting Point A standard: it depends on no artificial artifact whatsoever. Any operation needing fire, cord, or adhesive is given here only as a placeholder; the formal solutions are in Chapters 6, 7, and 8 respectively.

docs.title: Chapter Objectives
docs.text:
• From the bare-hand state, establish the first generation of reproducible manufacturing capability: identify knappable stone → detach flakes and cores → pressure-flake and trim → produce the four tool classes of cutting, scraping, drilling, and chopping → accept against executable criteria.

  • Deliverables: a set of stone tools that pass functional testing (flake knife, scraper, pointed tool, hand axe, hard hammer, soft hammer, pressure flaker), plus the first tool-wear archive.

  • This chapter is the start of the tool lineage (Lineage 2): stone flakes → stone hammers → all subsequent tools.

docs.title: Minimum Prerequisites
docs.text: Item Requirement Source Knowledge The three rock classes, common mineral appearances, hardness scratch test Chapter 2 Records Resource survey record format and resource map Chapter 2 Measurement Length datum, wooden straightedge, rope scale, right-angle and angle boards Chapter 3 Archive Process record sheet template, three-level capability definitions Chapters 1, 3, 4 Materials Dense siliceous rock from river-gravel bars or bedrock outcrops Chapter 2 resource survey Tools None. This chapter is the tool starting point —

docs.title: 5.1 How to Identify Stone Suitable for Knapping
docs.text:
Five criteria for knappable stone; all must be satisfied before test-knapping:

  1. Homogeneous: color and grain size uniform across the fresh fracture; no banding, mottling, or interlayers.
  2. Fine-grained: no crystal grains detectable by eye or fingertip. The fracture surface should look like "solidified syrup", not "granulated sugar".
  3. Conchoidal fracture: a freshly knocked-off fracture shows a curved surface, often with concentric ripples; the edge is naturally sharp.
  4. Isotropic: striking from any direction produces the same conchoidal fracture; no fixed splitting plane (unlike the bedding of slate and shale, or the cleavage planes of feldspar-class crystals).
  5. Fresh: "rotten stone" with whitened weathered surfaces and powder that scrapes off under a fingernail is usually riddled with microcracks; forbidden.

Four-step field procedure:

  • Step one, find: prefer river-bank gravel (the water has already done the sorting; weak stones were eliminated by transport and abrasion); second, nodules in limestone hills (lumpy masses along the limestone bedding planes); third, conglomerate cementation zones and volcanic slope deposits.

  • Step two, knock: knock a corner off with a stone in hand and inspect the fresh fracture; listen at the same time: a crisp "ring" means dense and crack-free; a dull thud suggests internal cracks or porosity.

  • Step three, scratch: grade by mutual-scratch testing (against Mohs hardness: fingernail ≈ 2.5, bone splinter ≈ 3, quartz ≈ 7). Qualified edge material should be scratched by quartz and yet able to scratch bone — that is a siliceous rock of roughly Mohs 6–7.

  • Step four, record: location, lithology, fracture description, and test-knapping results, registered into the resource map (Chapter 2 format).

Exclusion list:

Excluded Characteristics Reason Shale, slate, schist Splits into sheets when struck; bedding planes flat Bedding controls the cracking; a controlled cutting edge cannot be made Coarse-grained granites Grains visible to the eye Spalls at grain boundaries; edge discontinuous Strongly weathered stone Whitened surface; powder scrapes off with a fingernail Internal microcracks well developed; collapses entirely when struck Porous volcanic rock (except pumice, which has other uses) Many gas vesicles Cannot form a continuous edge

docs.title: 5.2 Flint, Cherty Rocks, and Other Knappable Stones
docs.text:
Stone Common occurrence Fracture quality Edge quality Main limitation Priority Flint/chalcedony/jasper Limestone nodules, gravel Conchoidal, flat Best; edge about 0.01–0.05 mm thick Only in sedimentary-rock regions First choice Obsidian Volcanic glass slope deposits Flattest and glossiest About an order of magnitude thinner than flint; sharpest of all Extremely brittle; collapses under chopping; cutting only Use if available Quartzite Metamorphosed sandstone, river gravel Disturbed by grains, rough Oversized edge serrations, short service life Thickened edges only Second choice Siliceous limestone nodules Limestone regions Near-flint Good Often interlaced with white calcite veins; cracks along the veins Test nodule by nodule Hornfels, dense basalt Contact-metamorphic zones, igneous regions Tough, not brittle Unsuitable for knapped thin edges Take the grinding route (Section 5.5) First choice for ground tools Rhyolite/felsite Pyroclastic regions Moderate Moderate Limited occurrence Backup Quartz crystals Vein quartz Cracks run along healed fissures and grain boundaries (no cleavage; fracture discontinuous; often milky/smoky inclusions) Uncontrollable Use only as a battering hammer Excluded as edge material

Search strategy: river gravel first, limestone nodules second, obsidian slope deposits in volcanic regions third. Marker of ancient quarry sites — large piles of sharp stone debris on slopes that natural transport cannot explain.

Alternative-route boundary (Iron Law 5): in flint-free environments the realistic order is quartzite/siliceous limestone (knapped) + hornfels/basalt (ground). Performance losses must be stated: edge angles need thickening by 10°–20°; cutting life on the same task is roughly halved (rule of thumb, must be field-calibrated); the knapping reject rate rises and long thin flakes become hard to obtain. Conclusion: the alternative route does not affect the validity of later chapters' technical chains; it only lowers efficiency and yield.

docs.title: 5.3 Flakes, Cores, and Sharp Edges
docs.text:
Principle — the Hertzian cone: a hard object striking a stone surface propagates stress downward in a cone (cone angle about 136°, an empirical constant). When the strike point lands at the edge of the core's striking platform and the platform angle (the angle between the platform and the side face to be flaked) is less than 90°, the cone intersects the core edge and the crack runs along the predetermined path "platform edge — core side face", detaching a flake with a sharp edge. At a platform angle ≥ 90°, the impact energy turns into local crushing, and what you get is debris, not a flake.

Three geometric parameters (measured with the Chapter 3 angle board):

Parameter Definition Control range Platform angle Angle between platform and flaking face Flaking requires < 90°; ideal 70°–85° Edge angle Angle between the two faces of the flake's edge Set by use (see Section 5.5) Length-to-thickness ratio Flake length/thickness About 2:1 with hard-hammer flaking; 3:1 and above with a soft hammer

Flaking procedure:

  1. Select the core: fist to two fists in size, no visible cracks, at least one flat face usable as a platform.
  2. Dress the platform (hard hammer): with a 300–600 g dense-gravel hammer, knock a continuous flat band along the core edge, 10–20 mm wide.
  3. Detach flakes (hard hammer): hold the core in the left hand (always padded with hide or thick bark) and strike 5–10 mm in from the platform edge with the right-hand hammer in short snapping blows (swing amplitude 30–40 cm). Accurate placement outranks force.
  4. Fine flaking (soft hammer): switch to an antler section or hardwood bar (200–400 g) and "brush-strike" close against the platform edge to detach longer, thinner flakes.
  5. Blades (upgrade item): dress the core into a prismatic shape and detach parallel long blades in sequence along the ridges — the most economical use of material and the straightest edges.

Failure troubleshooting (expanded to five patterns in v2): ① all debris → strike point too far from the platform edge or platform angle too large; re-dress the platform; ② flake splits lengthwise → internal cracks in the stone; discard the material; ③ hammer slips → platform edge too rounded; knock a sharp ridge out again; ④ step (hinge) — the flake breaks midway and leaves a stepped shelf on the core → insufficient strike energy or placement too deep; restart the next flake from the outer edge of the shelf; do not force blows directly from the base of the shelf; ⑤ over-half edge collapse — more than half the ring of the edge has spalled away → hammer blows are standing in for pressure flaking; switch to light soft-hammer flaking.

The three lashings of the stone axe and load testing (completed in v2; connects to the quadruple attachment of Section 9.1):

Knot How tied Used for Characteristics Slip loop (slip knot) Wrap the cord one turn and pull tight to lock First positioning of edge to handle Fast; must be re-tightened under load Cross-wrapping knot Figure-eight wraps, 6–10 turns, at the "edge–handle" crossing; finish with a square knot Main load-bearing lashing Shear-resistant Stick-twist tensioning knot After lashing, insert a short stick and twist the cord 2–3 turns; press the free end in Prevents handle-end slip Tightest; can be loosened and readjusted

Load test (mandatory after every hafting; current lashing material = temporary binding of vine/wet rawhide strips; cord and knots are a Chapter 7 preview — backfill the formal lashing once Chapter 7 is unlocked): swing the axe into bare wood 20 times — lashing displacement < 2 mm and no creaking is a pass; then re-check with 1.5x impact (5 full-force blows into hardwood). If displacement exceeds the limit, twist it tighter and retest first; if still loose, re-lash with a longer binding section. Lashings are consumables: bindings soaked by rain or immersion must be retested (wet expansion and dry shrinkage change the binding force).

[Card 05-01 Platform Preparation and Hard-Hammer Flaking] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: a core from fist- to double-fist size (no visible cracks, at least one flat face usable as a platform); a dense cobble hammer, 300–600 g; one piece of hide or thick bark as a hand pad. Reject any blank with a visible crack without test-striking it — a cracked blank shatters ten times out of ten and wastes hours.
  2. Tools required: hard hammer (inspect its striking face once every half-day; on any penny-shaped spall, turn it or replace it), angle gauge (Chapter 3, for platform angle), anvil block (keeps the core from rolling). Calibration source: hammer weight balanced on the Chapter 3 balance into the 300–600 g band; angle gauge self-checked by the 3-4-5 cord method.
  3. Sequence and control points: select core → dress the platform (strike a continuous flat band 10–20 mm wide along the core edge) → flake (strike 5–10 mm in from the platform edge, 30–40 cm stroke, short snapping blow) → inspect the flake. Two control points: the platform angle must be <90° (measured with the gauge; ideal 70–85°); the strike must land 5–10 mm from the edge — placement beats force.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: platform angle 70–85° (eyeballing is unreliable; always use the gauge — with no gauge, cut a 75° template by the 3-4-5 cord method and compare); hammer 300–600 g (balanced); stroke 30–40 cm (about one-third of arm length); length-to-thickness target 2:1 (before calipers exist, judge by pinching the flake between two fingers; measure directly once Chapter 20 gauges appear).
  5. Observations to record: per core — measured platform angle / hammer weight / whether the strike drifted / number of good flakes / share of debris / failure-mode number (field 7).
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = five or more consecutive flakes from the same core, length-to-thickness ≥1.8:1, edge flat with no step; rework = a step has formed, restart the flake from the outer edge of the step (never hammer straight into the step floor); scrap = the blank splits lengthwise (internal crack) or three consecutive strikes yield only debris (wrong stone).
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) all debris → first check whether the strike is too far from the edge, then whether the platform angle is ≥90°; (2) lengthwise split → internal crack, discard the blank, do not blame technique; (3) hammer skids → platform edge too rounded, dress a sharp ridge; (4) hinge → insufficient force or strike too deep; (5) edge crumbling past halfway → switch from hard to soft hammer (go to Card 05-02).
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one acceptable flake plus one record sheet; L2 = ≥60% success over ten consecutive cores plus per-core records; L3 = a second person reaches L2 from this card alone, and the two batches' platform-angle distributions can be compared.

[Card 05-03 Stone Axe Hafting and Load Test] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: a knapped axe head (bifacial, tough stone 15 cm or longer); a straight dry handle (diameter matched to the hafting groove — too thin it twists, too thick it will not bind); vine or wet rawhide strip (temporary binding only in this chapter; the proper cord and knots arrive in Chapter 7 and are back-filled); one short stick for tightening; a wooden tablet for records.
  2. Tools required: stone knife (trimming vine ends), wooden wedge (opening the groove), scored tablet (displacement datum). Calibration source: no dedicated gauge; displacement read against scored lines to about 1 mm.
  3. Sequence and control points: slip knot to locate (blade to first pass on the handle) → cross wrapping (figure-eight 6–10 passes at the blade-handle crossing, finished with a flat knot) → toggle-stick tightening (2–3 turns, end tucked in) → load test (mandatory after every hafting, never skipped). Control points: wrap count and tightening turns are written into the record, not left to "looks about right".
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: 6–10 cross wraps (fewer and shear strength fails); 2–3 tightening turns (more snaps the vine); test standard = 20 swings into empty air, binding displacement <2 mm, no creaking; recheck = five full-force blows into hard wood (1.5× impact). Displacement judged against scored lines; failure means rework.
  5. Observations to record: per axe — wrap count / tightening turns / measured displacement after 20 swings / any creaking / whether it got wet.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = displacement <2 mm after 20 swings and no creaking; rework = displacement over limit, tighten and retest first, and if still loose, lengthen the binding and re-haft; scrap = the hafting wood splits or the axe groove chips (change the head).
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) large displacement → check wrap count first, then tightening; (2) creaking → knot not seated, or the vine is too dry (switch to wet rawhide); (3) after rain or soaking the binding must be retested — swelling and shrinkage change the binding force, and this is the main cause of a flying axe head; (4) loosens after a few swings → binding section too short, load concentrated.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one hafted axe plus test record; L2 = five passing axes, at least one with a post-rain retest record; L3 = a second person hafts independently from this card and passes the test, with both batches' displacement data comparable.

docs.title: 5.4 Stone Hammers, Bone Tools, and Wooden Aids
docs.text:
Two classes of stone hammer:

  • Hard hammer (direct percussion): dense rock (quartzite, flint nodules), 300–600 g, egg-shaped, one end slightly narrowed for aiming. Inspect the striking face every half day of use; when biscuit-shaped impact scars appear, switch faces or replace.

  • Soft hammer (fine flaking): antler section or hardwood bar, 200–400 g. Why the soft hammer works: local deformation of the contact surface absorbs the impact spike, and the crack starts inside the core rather than at the hammer mark, so the flakes come off thinner and longer; the cost is fast wear.

Bone tools (raw material from collected bones of naturally dead animals and scavenger leftovers):

Bone tool Making Use Pressure flaker Antler tip ground round and blunt Pressure-flaking and edge retouch (Section 5.5) Bone awl Long bone split lengthwise into strips; tip wet-ground on a sandstone slab Holes in leather goods, aid to cordage work Bone needle Fine bone strip ground to shape with water on a fine sandstone slab, 1–3 h per needle (rule of thumb, must be field-calibrated) Sewing and net making (awaits Chapter 7 fibers and Chapter 15 textiles) Bone scraper blade Shoulder-blade edge ground to an edge Scraping residual flesh from hides (more durable than stone blades)

Bone preparation: air-dry fresh bone to half-dry before working; too wet and it gums up the grinding stone, too dry and it chips and snaps. Fatty bone smells after long storage but does not affect use.

Wooden aids: wooden anvil (a short stout block to pad the core and stop it rolling), bark or hide hand-guard pad (mandatory under the hand holding the core), spare wedge stock (for the Section 5.7 placeholder).

Every tool in this section can be rebuilt from "collection + stone hammer + grinding stone"; the lineage is self-sustaining, meeting the requirement.

docs.title: 5.5 How to Make Cutting, Scraping, and Drilling Tools
docs.text:
Specification table for the four tool classes:

Tool Material/shape Edge angle Use boundary Flake knife 8–15 cm straight-edged flake; ridges and corners in the grip zone knocked blunt to prevent cuts 20°–40° Cutting meat, hides, grass stems; no chopping Scraper Thick flake with end or side edge blunted 45°–70° Scraping hides and wood surfaces; only a large edge angle withstands vertical scraping force — a blunt edge is a design requirement Pointed tool (drill-point blank) Short stout point pressure-flaked symmetrically on both sides Point angle 60°–80° Drilling and incising; drill points for Chapters 7 and 9 Hand axe/chopper Bifacially knapped; tough stone (quartzite, hornfels) 15 cm or larger 60°–90° Chopping wood, cracking bone; never for prying

Pressure-flaking retouch (turning "can cut" into "works well"): press the antler pressure flaker against a spot 2–3 mm above the edge at about 45° to the stone surface (rule of thumb), pushing down with combined arm and chest force to pop off small flakes 2–5 mm wide; work segment by segment around the edge to produce uniform serrations shallower than 1 mm. Uniform serrations = uniform loading = no local edge collapse. After retouch the edge shows a regular ripple rather than uneven notches — this is the conforming visual criterion.

Serrated flake (the embryo of the saw): select a long straight flake and pressure-flake continuous serrations with a 2–3 mm tooth pitch along one edge. This chapter makes only the blank for a hand reciprocating saw; the formal bow saw, mounted in a frame, is in Section 9.2.

Grinding placeholder: hornfels and basalt blanks can be given an edge by wet grinding on a sandstone slab — time-consuming (on the order of hours) but the edge body is tough; this is the proper route for felling tools. The complete grinding process unfolds after tooling-up in Section 9.2.

All outputs of this section are numbered in one scheme and registered into the tool archive (wooden tablet, Chapter 3 record format).

[Card 05-02 Pressure Flaking and Edge Retouch] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: a struck flake blank (edge cuts but is ragged); an antler billet or hardwood billet, 200–400 g, as soft hammer; an antler tip ground blunt as pressure flaker; coarse and fine sandstone slabs; hand pad.
  2. Tools required: soft hammer, pressure flaker, sandstone slabs, angle gauge. Calibration source: billet weight balanced on the Chapter 3 balance; pressure-point position by eye plus marker (measured once Chapter 20 arrives).
  3. Sequence and control points: soft-hammer "stroke" along the platform edge (hug the edge, do not strike air — yields longer, thinner flakes) → seat the pressure flaker 2–3 mm above the edge at about 45°, press with arm-and-chest weight, removing 2–5 mm chips → work once around the edge. Control points: 2–3 mm from the edge and about 45°; deviation in either causes edge collapse.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: soft hammer 200–400 g; pressure point 2–3 mm from the edge (empirical, calibrate to local stone); pressure angle about 45° (empirical); chip width 2–5 mm; finished serration depth <1 mm. How to establish "45°": cut a 45° template by the Chapter 3 3-4-5 cord method and hold it against the edge face; do not rely on feel.
  5. Observations to record: per pass — chip width / serration depth / collapse locations and count / whether the step spacing stayed even.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = edge shows an even wave (not a jagged notch), serration depth <1 mm, still cuts after 20 strokes; rework = local collapse, retouch from both sides of the notch inward, do not patch only the notch; scrap = edge worn below 3 mm (reclassify as scraper or discard).
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) edge collapse → check whether the pressure angle is too steep, then whether force is excessive; (2) flakes will not come off → flaker too blunt, or seated too far in (>3 mm); (3) uneven serration → uneven step spacing, switch to counting steps; (4) edge getting thinner and thinner → chips too wide, back off to 2 mm.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one retouched knife edge plus an edge photo (or rubbing); L2 = five consecutive passes plus serration-depth records; L3 = a second person reaches L2 from this card alone with a scrap rate <20%.

[Card 05-04 Edge Grinding and Bevel-Angle Verification] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: dulled flake or ground blank (tough stone such as hornfels or basalt); coarse and fine sandstone slabs; water; hand pad.
  2. Tools required: sandstone slabs (coarse for shaping, fine for establishing the edge — never interchange), pressure flaker, angle gauge, wooden tablet. Calibration source: bevel angle measured with the Chapter 3 gauge; slab flatness verified by rubbing two slabs face to face and checking for light gaps (rough precursor to the Chapter 20 three-plate method).
  3. Sequence and control points: coarse sandstone to shape (remove notches, true the edge line) → fine sandstone with water to establish the bevel → pressure-flake the serration (go to Card 05-02) → verify bevel angle. Control point: the bevel angle must fall inside the use band — flake knife 20–40°, scraper 45–70°, awl blank 60–80°, axe 60–90°; anything outside is rework.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: the four use bands above (from the 5.5 specification table); grinding takes hours (empirical, varies with local stone hardness, must be calibrated); grind with a single-direction push, never pull back (pulling rounds the edge).
  5. Observations to record: per session — measured bevel angle / edge-line straightness (check for light gaps) / grinding time / any one-sided bias.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = bevel in the use band, no light gap along the edge line, still cuts after 20 strokes; rework = bevel out of band or biased, re-true and regrind; scrap = body thinner than 3 mm or a through-crack in the edge line.
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) will not cut → bevel too large (blunt), return to coarse grinding to reduce it; (2) chips on first use → bevel too small (brittle), increase it or switch to pressure flaking; (3) growing asymmetry → one side ground too long, alternate sides by count; (4) edge shiny but will not bite → over-ground into a round bevel, return to pressure flaking for serration.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one acceptable edge plus measured bevel record; L2 = one of each of the four tool types with per-item bevel records; L3 = a second person reaches L2 from this card alone, with the two people's same-use bevel measurements within 5°.

docs.title: 5.6 How to Check Whether a Stone Tool Suits Its Intended Use
docs.text:
Visual inspection (100% inspection):

  1. Edge serrations uniform, serration depth < 1 mm.
  2. Rotate slowly against the light; the edge's reflected highlight must be continuous — an interruption is a microcrack or nick.
  3. Flick the back of the stone with a finger: a crisp sound means no internal cracks; a dull sound means cracks — downgrade or scrap.
  4. No through cracks, and no radiating hidden cracks near the bulb of percussion.

Functional testing (sampled, on standardized workpieces):

Test Standard Pass line (rule of thumb, must be field-calibrated) Cutting 50 consecutive strokes through hide or fresh meat; one stroke = one 10 cm pass ≤ 1 nick and ≤ 2 mm Scraping 30 reciprocating scrapes on a wet hide, 5 cm per stroke No nick > 2 mm; edge angle increase < 5° Drilling Pointed tool ground and rotated on hardwood for 20 minutes Point does not break off; no ring-shaped cracks Chopping Hand axe chops hardwood 20 times Crushed zone < 10% of edge length

Blunting and edge collapse must be distinguished: blunting is uniform rounding of the edge, normal wear; it can be reworked by pressure flaking and counts within service life. Edge collapse is local spalling, pointing to material microcracks, a wrong platform angle, or use beyond the tool's purpose (e.g., taking a cutting knife to chopping); find the cause first, then rework.

Scrap criteria: edge body too thin after 3–5 cumulative reworks; edge length loss over 1/3; a through crack appears. Scrapped pieces are converted into battering-hammer cores or pressure-flaking stock.

Every test and rework goes into the tool archive: number, stone material, date, test data, rework count, scrap reason. This archive format is the record template for the book-wide tool lineage (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 5.7 How to Go from Stone Tools to Composite Tools
docs.text:
Why haft at all: it multiplies the lever arm (with the same swing force, edge velocity ≈ arm speed × (arm length + handle length) / arm length); the hand leaves the impact zone; strike kinetic energy concentrates along the edge line.

This chapter's boundary: cord (Section 7.4), adhesive (Section 8.5), and bow drill (Section 7.6) have not appeared; this chapter does two "placeholder validations" only:

  • Option one (semi-composite): split the end of a short wooden handle along the grain, seat the flake blade in the split, and wrap temporarily with fresh bark strips or rawhide strips. Drawback: it loosens as it dries and must be re-wrapped before each use. This option only validates blade-to-handle shape matching; it is not a formal tool.

  • Option two (fire-burned groove, to be implemented after the Chapter 6 stable fire): first scorch the planned groove line of the handle into a char line, then scrape deeper with a flake. Hot working replaces precision working, dropping the groove's precision requirement by one grade.

Placeholder acceptance: swing the hafted hand axe empty 20 times → lightly chop a wooden block 20 times; lashing displacement < 2 mm and no blade-body shift passes the placeholder.

Pre-registration of dependencies for the formal composite tool (to prevent later-chapter tool anachronisms):

Step Dependency Solved in Cutting the handle groove Charring + scraping; rows of drilled holes with the bow drill 6.5; 7.6 Lashing Cordage, rawhide strips, sinew 7.3, 7.4 Bonding Birch-bark tar/pine resin glue 8.5 Locking Wooden wedges 7.5

The complete hafting procedure is given in one place in Section 9.1.

docs.title: Capability Boundary
docs.text: Can do: both percussion and pressure flaking; functional-level acceptance of six stone-tool classes (chopper/scraper/point/blade/stone drill/hand-axe blank); field reading of platform angle and strike point; load testing of lashed composite handles (see the Section 5.4 supplement block). Explicitly cannot do: mass production of long pressure-flaked blades (needs soft pressure tools and practiced skill; listed as an upgrade item); standardization of micro-serrations on stone edges (no microscope; rely on cutting trials). External dependencies: none. This chapter is the book's first "zero-tool start" chapter.

docs.title: Master Parameter Table
docs.text: Parameter Value Class Platform angle < 90° (85° ± 5° best); ≥ 90° yields only debris Criterion Strike point from platform edge 5–10 mm Empirical Hard hammer weight 300–600 g; soft hammer 200–400 g Empirical Hand axe edge angle 60°–80°; stone knife 20°–40° Specification Lashing load acceptance Displacement < 2 mm after 20 empty swings; 1.5x impact × 5 Criterion

docs.title: Failure Modes and Diagnosis
docs.text: Symptom Candidate causes (by probability) Action All debris, no flakes Platform angle too large; strike point too far out Re-dress the platform; practice "5 mm from the edge" Flake breaks midway (step/hinge) Insufficient energy or placement too deep Restart the flake from the shelf's outer edge Over half the edge collapsed Hammer blows standing in for pressure flaking Switch to soft hammer; reduce swing amplitude Blade edges not parallel Core prism not straight Re-dress the core before flaking; never force it Handle loose as soon as hafted Groove too shallow / bond not filled Re-cut the groove; heat the adhesive and re-seat

docs.title: A. Existing Tools List
docs.text:
• Wooden straightedge, rope scale, angle board, plumb bob, record tablets (Chapter 3).

  • Resource map and survey records (Chapter 2).

  • No power tools and no heat source of any kind.

docs.title: B. New Tools in This Chapter
docs.text: Tool Specification Manufacturing source Hard hammer Dense gravel, 300–600 g Selected directly from river gravel bars Soft hammer Antler/hardwood bar, 200–400 g Collected + cut to length Pressure flaker Antler tip Collected + ground Flake knife 8–15 cm, edge angle 20°–40° Flaking + pressure-flaking retouch Scraper Edge angle 45°–70° Thick flake with blunted edge Pointed tool (drill-point blank) Point angle 60°–80° Symmetric pressure flaking Hand axe ≥ 15 cm, edge angle 60°–90° Bifacial knapping Serrated flake Tooth pitch 2–3 mm Serrations by pressure flaking Bone awl, bone needle, bone scraper blade See Section 5.4 Bone stock + sandstone-slab grinding Wooden anvil, hand-guard pad — Hand axe + collected stock

docs.title: C. Unresolved Dependencies
docs.text:
• No cord: hafting can only be temporary wrapping (solved in Section 7.4).

  • No adhesive: composite tools are not secure (solved in Section 8.5).

  • No stable heat source: groove burning, drying, and heat straightening are all infeasible (solved in Chapter 6).

  • The bone needle has no thread to work with (meaningful only after Chapter 7 produces fibers).

  • Knapping depends on individual skill; the reject rate is unquantified — to be backfilled after the Section 9.5 capacity ledger is established.

docs.title: Safety Boundary
docs.text:
• During knapping, the 3 m fan-shaped zone in front of the strike point is off-limits; observers may only stand to the knapper's side and rear.

  • The hand holding the core must be padded with hide or thick bark; gripping a small core bare-handed for hard blows is forbidden — always use the wooden anvil.

  • Check edges with a light sweep of the back of the hand; stroking along the edge with a fingertip is forbidden.

  • Obsidian debris is extremely sharp and hard to see; it must be swept up and collected at knock-off.

  • Cracked stone is forbidden as hammer stock — it will burst apart and fly in mid-strike.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• L1 proof-of-principle: knock off at least one sharp flake with a conchoidal fracture that can cut through a grass stem and strip bark.

  • L2 repeatable manufacture: following the archive-recorded selection–flaking–retouch process, complete 1 set (knife + scraper + point + hammer) on each of 3 different collection days, all passing the Section 5.6 functional tests; per-piece time and reject rate recorded.

  • L3 sustainable production: stone sources registered in the resource map ≥ 2; hard/soft hammer wear rates known with replacement sources; tool archive holding ≥ 20 items; rework procedure executed ≥ 5 times; novice reproduction success rate from the archives ≥ 50% (empirical criterion, assessed within the team).

docs.title: Next-Step Dependencies
docs.text:
• Chapter 6 (fire): flake knives shape drill shafts and fire boards and shave tinder; flint serves as the percussion fire-striking stone (Section 6.4).

  • Chapter 7 (timber and cord): the stone axe and stone adze are the first felling-and-splitting tools; the pointed tool mounted on a bow drill becomes a drill point (Section 7.6).

  • Chapter 8: resin-tapping cuts (Section 8.5) are made with the flake knife.

  • Chapter 9: this chapter's tools enter compositing (Section 9.1) and tooling-up (Sections 9.2–9.4).

docs.title: Chapter 6 The First Controllable Energy Source — Fire
docs.text: Part 2 · Survival, Fire, and Primitive Materials. Starting Point A standard: fire lighting may depend only on natural materials such as stone, wood, fungi, and minerals. The bow drill requires cord, whose full specification is given in Section 7.6; this chapter's official routes are the hand drill, fire plow, fire saw, and percussion fire lighting.

docs.title: Chapter Goals
docs.text:
• What is established is not "being able to light a fire once," but a repeatable energy technology: fire lighting (friction and percussion routes) → ignition → stable heat source (coal-bed management) → fuel management (firewood grading, wood → charcoal conversion) → temperature and airflow control → safety boundaries.
  • Deliverables: each of at least two fire-lighting methods succeeding multiple times; one fire bed that can be banked overnight; one batch of qualified charcoal from a kiln; one combustion log.
  • This chapter is the starting point of the energy lineage (Lineage 3): fire → charcoal → furnaces and kilns. Its results directly support Chapter 8 (pyrolytic glue), Chapters 10–13 (cooking, pottery, furnaces and kilns, lime).

docs.title: Minimum Prerequisites
docs.text:
Item Requirement Source Tools Stone-flake knife, scraper, hand axe, hard hammer, pointed flake Chapter 5 Knowledge Fuel and heat-source resource survey, combustible identification Chapter 2 Measurement Length and volume measurement, record sheets Chapter 3 Materials Dry firewood, tinder materials (fungi, grass, birch bark), (optional) pyrite nodules Chapter 2 resource map Constraint No cord — the bow drill is not yet available Completed in Section 7.6

Bow drill material-matching preview (configure this way when the bow drill unlocks in Section 7.6; v2 completion): the drill board uses straight-grained wood softer than the drill shaft (willow, poplar types — produces powder fast and gathers heat); the drill shaft uses hard straight wood (or a later-era steel rod); the bearing block uses hardwood with a soapstone/bone-plate socket (wear-resistant and low friction) — the three-part hardness mismatch (soft board, hard shaft, slippery bearing) is the hidden prerequisite of bow drill efficiency; an all-hard configuration only polishes and produces no powder.

docs.title: 6.1 Natural Fire Sources and Combustible Materials
docs.text:
Natural fire sources: lightning fires (patrol along the smoke line within 24 hours after a thunderstorm; approach from crosswind when closing in), margins of volcanic eruptions, and rare self-ignition of peat or coal seams. Iron Law: once you have an ember, the first task is keeping the fire, not using it — keep the ember alive and you need not strike fire again for a week.

Two methods of keeping an ember:

  • Banked fire bed: heap the coals into a pile, cover with 5–10 cm of dry ash, press a thin layer of soil over the ash, and leave one finger-thick air hole. Next morning, pull it open and blow — it ignites.
  • Ember tube: roll thick birch bark into a tube holding a dark-smoldering piece of rotten wood (or a tinder-fungus chunk) together with semi-dry moss; leave air gaps; inspect every 2–4 hours and replace the chunk when the ashen, burnt-down part grows short.

Four-tier table of combustible materials:

Tier Representative materials Size criterion Function Tinder Cattail down, dry-grass down, thin inner-bark sheets of birch, pounded tinder-fungus fluff, dry bird and beast down A pinch can be kneaded into a ball Receives the smoldering ember and is blown into open flame Kindling I Fine dead twigs, pine-needle bundles Toothpick to chopstick thick Bridges from open flame to firewood Kindling II Small branches Finger thick Establishes a stable small fire Main fuel Branch and trunk wood Wrist thick and up Maintains the heat source, produces charcoal

Dryness criteria: dry grass snaps with a brittle crack; inner bark held to the cheek feels not cool and not sticky; standing dead wood beats fallen wood (fallen wood regains moisture from the ground); after rain, all firewood is split open to check core color (dark = damp).

docs.title: 6.2 How to Select Tinder Materials and Fuel
docs.text:
Three qualification criteria for tinder (usable for formal fire lighting only when all three pass):

  1. Fully dry: no cool feeling against the lips (cool = moisture absorbed).
  2. Elasticity: kneaded into a ball and released, it springs back without collapsing.
  3. Pre-burn: shaped into a nest and gently blown for 5 seconds, it gives off a scorched smell or shows faint smoke.

Tinder preparation:

  • Tinder fungus (the hoof-shaped polypore on standing birch and oak): cut away the outer crust, pound the inner flesh into fluff on a stone slab, air-dry and store in a bag. This is the first-priority tinder.
  • Dry grass: roll and rub it into fluff on a flat stone; remove the stems.
  • Birch bark: discard the hard outer skin; tear the inner layer into thin rolls matchstick-wide; it contains oils and remains flammable even in light rain.

Charring preparation (v2 completion: "bake" the tinder before storing it): pack young-twig bast and cloth-grade plant fluff into a pottery jar (after Chapter 11) or bury in an ash pit; smother-roast over a low fire until evenly scorched brown throughout, igniting at a touch yet not self-igniting — when the color turns from yellow-white to brown-tan it has reached doneness (◎ judge by color; compensation: light a pinch as a test — sparks spreading into a patch without raising open flame passes). Charred fluff ignites at a far lower temperature than raw fluff and is the key intermediate layer for turning smolder into open flame.

Smolder-to-flame transition (breath-volume control, v2 completion): after the tinder smolders and smokes, blowing is "pulsed," not "one long blow" — two or three short puffs (each on the order of a tenth of a lungful), with pauses that let the smoke recede and deepen; when the red spot inside the tinder has widened to cup-mouth size, wrap it in fine kindling and one long breath raises open flame. One long blow all the way through = blowing the heat away, and the red spot dies instead — "blowing the fire out" is not a metaphor; it is a real operational failure. Practice method: rehearse 20 times with scrap tinder and count the minimum number of puffs needed "from smolder to open flame."

Fire-lay structure (fire nest): the tinder forms the innermost nest; toothpick-sized sticks form a cone, each outward layer growing coarser up to finger thickness; sticks within each layer cross loosely, never fitted tight, preserving air gaps; the cone's opening faces the upwind side and the lighting port stays on the lee side. Wrong sequence is the number-one cause of ignition failure: sticks too thick, gaps too dense, or an opening facing the wind that gulps air too hard — any one of the three will blow the flame out.

Fuel grading management:

Wood class Representative species Burning characteristics Use Softwood Willow, poplar, linden, pine Ignites fast, tall flame, does not burn long Kindling, quick fire Hardwood Oak, locust, elm Steady fire, good charcoal, long-burning Coal bed, charcoal making Resinous wood Pine knots, burls, old pine roots Fierce fire, moisture-resistant Embers, wet-weather kindling

Reserve quantities (empirical values; must be field-calibrated): heating one person through one night takes roughly 15–25 kg of wrist-thick firewood; cooking one meal about 2–4 kg; double the reserve for the rainy season. Stack the woodpile raised off the ground and roof it with bark against rain.

[Card 06-02 Preparing Charred Tinder] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: inner bark of young shoots or plant down at rag grade (dry grass down, bast fiber both work); a clay pot (after Chapter 11) or a freshly dug ash pit; storage pouches. Raw and charred tinder must be labeled and stored apart — mixed together, you cannot tell a material problem from a firing problem when it fails to light.
  2. Tools required: clay pot or ash pit (deep enough to bury the charge), stone slab (for spreading to dry), an established ember bed (Section 6.5). Calibration source: readiness is judged by color plus a burn test, not by a thermometer.
  3. Sequence and control points: load pot or bury in ash pit → slow bake over low heat (never over open flame — a flame turns the batch to ash in seconds) → watch the color turn from yellow-white to brown → pull a pinch and test-light it. Control points: low heat throughout; both the color change and the burn test must pass — color alone runs under-charred.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: readiness = uniformly char-brown, ignites when touched to a spark but does not self-sustain; fallback when color is ambiguous = pull a pinch out, it should spread sparks in a sheet without breaking into flame (flame = under-charred; ash = over-charred). Bake time varies with material and fire position — no fixed minutes are given; judge by color plus test, and record this batch's time for the next person.
  5. Observations to record: per batch — source material / bake time / final color / burn-test result (sheet of sparks / flame / ash) / date bagged.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = char-brown, burn test gives a sheet of sparks with no flame; rework = color short or test gives flame, return to heat in 10-minute steps, testing between; scrap = self-burned to ash (heat too high — redo the batch and note the fire position to avoid next time).
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) will not light → check for moisture first (is the pouch sealed), then under-charring; (2) turns to ash at a touch → over-charred, fire too close or too long; (3) half raw, half charred in one batch → uneven heating, pot packed too full (fill to seven-tenths).
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one passing batch plus burn-test record; L2 = three batches from three different source materials, all passing, with times and final colors comparable; L3 = a second person produces a passing batch from this card alone, with matching burn-test results.

[Card 06-03 Pulse-Blowing an Ember into Flame] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: an established ember (black powder cake or a glowing spot in charred tinder); fire-nest material (toothpick twigs → fine twigs → finger-thick sticks, added in layers); tinder. Build the nest before you blow — blowing first and gathering wood after is a common way to lose the ember while it waits.
  2. Tools required: none beyond breath; a small reserve of tinder for re-seeding.
  3. Sequence and control points: two or three short puffs (each about one-tenth of a lungful) → pause to let the glow deepen → glow spreads to the size of a cup mouth → tuck fine twigs around it → one long breath brings flame. Two control points: blowing is pulsed, not continuous; do not add twigs before the glow reaches cup-mouth size (twigs added early smother it).
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: about one-tenth lungful per puff; two or three puffs per set, resting two or three breaths between sets; cup-mouth (about a palm wide) is the moment to add twigs. Individual variation is large — practice method: run 20 trials on waste tinder and count the minimum number of puffs from glow to flame; record that number as a personal yardstick for judging ember quality.
  5. Observations to record: per attempt — puff count / pause length / peak glow diameter / whether the glow shrank at any point / time to flame after twigs went on.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = flame established and nest intact; rework = glow shrinking (heat blown away), stop blowing at once, let it recover, restart the count; scrap = ember out, go back to Card 06-01 and record the puff count to find the cause.
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) glow shrinking → blowing too long or too hard, carrying heat away ("blowing the fire out" is not a metaphor, it is a real operating failure); (2) heavy smoke but no flame after adding twigs → twigs too thick or packed too tightly, rebuild the nest with air gaps; (3) flame pushed to one side → nest opening faces upwind, turn the opening upwind and keep the lighting gap downwind; (4) repeated failures → check tinder for moisture (back to Card 06-02 for a burn test).
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one successful light plus puff count; L2 = after 20 practice runs the minimum count is stable (last five within 2 puffs); L3 = a second person succeeds from this card and the two counts are comparable (a wide gap means one of you has different tinder quality).

docs.title: 6.3 Principle and Tools of Friction Fire Lighting
docs.text:
Principle: friction power = normal force × sliding speed. The drill shaft rotates in the hole of the hearth board; the abraded wood powder accumulates in the hole; once the interface temperature rises to about 300–400°C (empirical value; must be field-calibrated), the powder pyrolyzes into black charcoal dust and begins to smolder, forming a glowing ember — no open flame. Move the ember into the tinder nest and blow to add oxygen; only when the temperature rises above about 500°C (empirical value) does open flame appear. The process therefore has four stages: friction → black-powder smolder → transfer ember into tinder → blow to flame — not "drilling out a flame."

Hand drill method (this chapter's official route):

Component parameters:

Component Specification Material Drill shaft Length 40–70 cm, diameter 0.6–1.2 cm, straight and round Dry straight-grained medium-hard wood (willow, elder, etc.) Hearth board Thickness 1.5–2.5 cm, width about 5 cm, length 30 cm or more Dry softwood Powder notch V-notch on the board's side, deep enough to reach the hole's center Carved with the stone-flake knife

Operation: stand the shaft in a shallow depression; with the palms pressed together around the shaft, roll it back and forth while pressing down; speed about 120–200 rpm, combined palm pressure 3–6 kg (empirical values; must be field-calibrated); as the hands reach the shaft's lower end, quickly return them upward, keeping the shaft seated in its hole; drill continuously for 1–5 minutes. Criterion chain: white smoke appears → smoke thickens and holds → stop and inspect the powder pile — black powder pressed into a cake and, with the light blocked, a dark-red glow visible = the ember is established.

Failure troubleshooting table:

Symptom Cause Remedy Powder brown, board hole polished Insufficient pressure or board too hard Add pressure; switch to a softer board Shaft slips Hole worn oversize Move aside and open a new hole Powder black but no glow Powder damp or drilling stopped too early Switch to dry material; extend the drilling run Shaft scorched and breaks Pressure too high Reduce pressure, raise speed

Fire plow method (backup for hand injury or cold weather): cut a longitudinal groove in a softwood board; push a hardwood plow head rapidly back and forth along the groove; the powder is pushed together at the groove's end into an ember. Laborious; moderate success rate.

Fire saw method (in bamboo regions): saw a thin bamboo strip rapidly back and forth inside a kerf of a dry bamboo board; the powder falls into a carved notch below and forms an ember.

Upgrade preview: the bow drill (Section 7.6) drives the shaft with a cord bowstring — less effort and stable speed, with a success rate several times that of the hand drill (empirical value). Until cord technology is established, the hand drill is the mainline; hand-drill training must not be omitted from the records.

[Card 06-01 Hand-Drill Fire Making, Full Sequence] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: drill shaft (40–70 cm long, 0.6–1.2 cm diameter, straight and round, dry straight-grained medium-hard wood such as willow or elder); fireboard (1.5–2.5 cm thick, about 5 cm wide, 30 cm or longer, dry soft wood); tinder passing the three tests in field 4; birch bark or a broad leaf to catch powder. Shaft and board must be equally dry — one dry and one damp grinds the hole smooth without producing black powder.
  2. Tools required: flake knife (Chapter 5, to cut the V-notch), a spare fireboard (for when the hole wears oversize), record tablet. Calibration source: speed and pressure cannot be instrumented — infer from the result: black powder means the parameters are right, brown powder means pressure is short.
  3. Sequence and control points: seat the shaft in a shallow dimple → clasp between the palms and rub while pressing down → just before the hands reach the bottom, snap them back up (the shaft must not leave the hole) → drill continuously 1–5 minutes → stop and check the powder pile. Control points: the V-notch must reach the center of the hole (too shallow and powder will not exit, too deep and the shaft wobbles); never release pressure during the hand reset.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: about 120–200 rpm; combined palm pressure 3–6 kg; interface reaches about 300–400 °C where black powder forms (empirical, calibrate on site); decision chain — white smoke appears → smoke thickens and holds → stop and inspect, black powder caked together with a dull red spot visible in shade = ember established. Speed and pressure constrain each other: too slow usually means too little pressure, too much pressure and it will not turn; use powder color as the arbiter.
  5. Observations to record: per attempt — drilling time / powder color (black / brown / white) / smoke color and density / whether a dull red spot appeared / failure-mode number (field 7) / humidity that day.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = caked black powder with a dull red spot in shade; rework = brown powder or a glazed hole, add pressure or switch to a softer board and redrill; scrap = shaft scorches and snaps (reduce pressure, raise speed, replace shaft).
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) brown powder and glazed hole → pressure too light or board too hard, add pressure first, then change board; (2) shaft skids → hole worn oversize, move over and start a new hole (do not fight the old hole); (3) black powder but no glow → powder damp or drilling stopped too early, dry the material and drill longer; (4) shaft scorches and snaps → pressure too high, reduce and speed up.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one ember obtained plus record; L2 = five consecutive successes including at least one in damp weather, with the success rate entered in the combustion log; L3 = a second person succeeds from this card alone, and both success rates and times can be compared.

docs.title: 6.4 Principle and Applicability of Percussion Fire Lighting
docs.text:
Principle: when pyrite or marcasite (both FeS₂, Mohs 6–6.5, pale brass-yellow with metallic luster, nodular or with cubic crystal faces, greenish-black streak) is scraped briskly against a sharp flint edge, the tiny iron-sulfide flakes peeled off oxidize violently in air and release heat, spraying out as incandescent particles — essentially "hot particles carrying their own oxidation reaction"; landing on fluffy tinder, they become smolder points.

Applicability conditions: (1) pyrite nodules are available (look in volcanic rock areas, coal-seam outcrops, and black shale; register them in the resource map, Chapter 2); (2) a sharp flint edge exists (Chapter 5); (3) the tinder is extremely dry and fluffy (tinder-fungus fluff is best).

Operation: the left hand holds the tinder patty with birch bark underneath to catch ash; the right hand holds the pyrite and strikes its surface obliquely and quickly with the sharp flint edge; sparks spray into the fluff; when fine blue smoke appears, close the fluff around them and blow gently into open flame. Each scrape yields several sparks; success typically comes in 5–15 strikes (empirical value; must be field-calibrated).

Boundaries and limitations (must be stated):

  • Mineral sources are extremely unevenly distributed. In regions without pyrite this route is zero and must not be the mainline.
  • In overcast or rainy weather the spark survival rate drops sharply.
  • Common misconception: flint struck against flint, or flint against ordinary rock, produces only cold spalls — no sparks, no fire.
  • The pyrite striking face dulls after repeated use; rotate to a corner or knock out a fresh edge.

Combined strategy: mainline = friction fire lighting (feasible anywhere wood exists); percussion = an accelerated route in mineral-bearing regions. Run both in parallel and register success rates in the combustion log.

docs.title: 6.5 From Campfire to Stable Heat Source
docs.text:
Four standard fire configurations:

Type Structure Use Cone Sticks leaned into a cone, fire nest at the cone's heart Fast ignition, lighting Log-cabin Layers of sticks crisscrossed in a square lattice Stable coal bed, supporting a grill Star Long sticks with ends toward the center, pushed in as each burns Overnight fire tending, wood saving Dakota fire pit Combustion well 25–30 cm in diameter, 40–50 cm deep; a 45° air tunnel dug slantwise from the windward side connects to the well bottom Wind-resistant, efficient, low smoke, concealed fire

Dig the Dakota pit with a pointed stick and the hand axe (Chapter 5); the air-tunnel mouth must sit on the day's windward side — when the wind reverses, efficiency collapses, so re-dig or set wind-guiding stones at the tunnel mouth.

Coal-bed management: after 30–60 minutes of open burning the wood turns to charcoal. Spreading or gathering the coals creates an adjustable heat surface. Three heat levels:

  • High fire: add sticks elevated off the ash (ample airflow).
  • Medium fire: gather the coals into a pile, lay sticks flat.
  • Low fire: spread the coals out, cover with a thin layer of ash.

Cooking and baking rely on the coal bed, not on open flame.
