Banking the fire overnight: gather the coals into a pile → cover with 5–10 cm of dry ash → press thin soil around the edges → leave one finger-thick air hole. Success criterion: next morning the coal core is dark red and rekindles when blown. Failure causes: ash layer too thin or too damp; too little coal before banking (keep at least a bowl-mouth-sized coal pile).

Turning the heat source into a hearth: build a stove from stone slabs. Slab selection: dense sedimentary or igneous rock; layered stone, vug-bearing stone, or water-absorbing stone explodes when heated. Trial-burn method: roast a candidate slab over a small fire for 10 minutes; if it does not burst, crackle, or crack, it is usable. This stone stove is the prototype of the Chapter 11 pottery kiln and the Chapter 12 furnace.

[Card 06-04 Banking the Fire Overnight and the Ember Tube] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: a charcoal bed after 30–60 minutes of open burning (at least a bowl-mouth-sized heap); dry ash, 5–10 cm (must be dry — damp ash smothers the fire); a thin layer of soil; an ember tube (bamboo section or small clay pot, lidded, with a pinhole in the lid).
  2. Tools required: a wooden or stone paddle (for raking coals and spreading ash), ember tube, a small bag of spare dry ash. Calibration source: no instrument — next morning's ember condition is the verdict on last night's banking.
  3. Sequence and control points: rake coals into a heap → cover with 5–10 cm dry ash → press a thin soil rim around it → leave a finger-width air hole. For the tube: put a small red coal plus charred tinder inside, lid on, pinhole open. Control points: ash depth and hole size — sealing the hole smothers it, opening it burns it out; one finger-width is the empirical middle.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: wood turns to charcoal after 30–60 minutes of open burning; ash cover 5–10 cm; air hole about one finger wide; heap no smaller than a bowl mouth (below that there is not enough thermal mass to last the night). A banked bed holds 8–12 hours (empirical, varies with ash depth and overnight temperature, calibrate locally).
  5. Observations to record: per night — heap size when banked / ash depth / hole condition / ember color next morning / whether it relit on the first try / overnight low temperature.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = ember dull red next morning and relights on a breath; rework = warm but no glow, feed dry kindling to revive; scrap = cold ash — establish which of the three causes applied (ash too thin, ash damp, heap too small) and record it.
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) cold in the morning → check ash depth first, then whether the ash was damp, then whether the heap was big enough (in that order of frequency); (2) glow present but will not relight → air hole blocked or ash packed too deep; (3) coal dies inside the tube → tube not pre-warmed, or pinhole too large (convection carries the heat away).
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one successful night plus record; L2 = seven consecutive nights including at least one cold or rainy night, with complete nightly records; L3 = a second person achieves it from this card alone, and the two seven-night records can be compared.

docs.title: 6.6 Wood, Charcoal, and Combustion Conditions
docs.text:
Three stages of combustion: below 150°C moisture evaporates (white smoke); 200–400°C pyrolysis releases combustible gas (a flame is essentially wood gas burning); above 400°C fixed carbon glows red without flame. Two engineering conclusions: (1) smoke = unburned combustible gas = heat loss + carbon monoxide risk; (2) the key to raising temperature is not piling on more wood but getting air to the root of the flame.

Wood → charcoal conversion (earth-mound kiln):

  1. Build the mound: a cone-shaped wood pile 1–1.5 m in diameter; straight billets stand packed tight; leave a central vertical shaft as the ignition core.
  2. Cover: first with grass or leaves, then with 5–10 cm of earth; leave 1–2 fist-sized air inlets at the bottom and a bowl-mouth-sized smoke port at the top.
  3. Light: drop the ember into the central shaft and let the fire burn outward through the pile.
  4. Control the burn, using smoke color as the criterion sequence: white smoke (water vapor) → yellow-brown smoke (tar) → pale blue smoke (combustible gas nearly spent) → thin smoke. Each time the smoke color advances one stage, shrink one air opening with earth; after blue smoke, keep only the top port.
  5. Seal the kiln: close all openings and add more earth cover; smother-cool for at least 4 hours before opening. Opening early = it reignites into ash.

Total time about 4–10 hours (empirical value; must be field-calibrated; larger mounds take longer).

Charcoal acceptance criteria: a strike rings crisp like "ding"; fracture faces are jet black and glossy and the piece is light; no brown wood core (underburned); it does not crumble under finger pressure nor shed black powder (overburned charcoal turns whitish, is brittle, and sheds ash).

Yield (empirical value; must be field-calibrated): mass yield about 20%–25%, i.e. 4–5 kg of dry wood yields 1 kg of charcoal; volume is roughly halved.

Use registry: this chapter's charcoal serves roasting heat and drying; charred tinder fungus is the best fire-lighting medium; the large-scale consumers come in Chapter 12 (furnace and kiln fuel) and Chapter 18 (smelting reducer).

docs.title: 6.7 How to Control Temperature, Airflow, and Burn Time
docs.text:
Three airflow principles: low inlet, high outlet (air inlet low and facing the wind, smoke outlet high); the fire channel's cross-section must not be blocked by collapsed wood; rake out the ash when it accumulates to a finger's thickness (an ash layer insulates and blocks air, but a thin ash layer left in place protects the coals).

Adjustment measures table:

Goal Operation Raise temperature Add dry wood; elevate wood off the ash; gather coals together; open the air ports Lower temperature Stop adding wood; cover with ash; spread the coals; half-close the air ports Hold temperature Burn large hardwood billets slowly; add small amounts of wood at fixed intervals Concentrate heat Bank the coals into a nest; stand windbreak stones on all sides

Judging temperature by fire color (auxiliary empirical method, not quantitative): dull red about 500–600°C; bright red 700–800°C; orange-yellow 900–1100°C; bright yellow-white above 1100°C (empirical values; must be field-calibrated). Limitations: strongly affected by ambient light, flame brightness, and viewing angle; use only for coarse grading and never as a quantitative basis (style rule 3).

Standard-sample method (a reproducible substitute): place small clay pieces, dough, and rosin lumps of the same batch at the same position as the workpiece. The changes the samples show (drying out, scorching brown, softening) calibrate the temperature step of that fire position, and anyone following the record can reproduce the same criteria. Sample recipes and preparation are unified in Section 8.6. This method lays the groundwork for formal high-temperature measurement in Chapter 12.

Burning schedule (empirical values; must be field-calibrated): finger-thick softwood sticks 2–4 minutes each; palm-wide split wood 15–25 minutes; wrist-thick hardwood billets 40–90 minutes whole; a banked coal bed 8–12 hours. Scheduling rules: overnight use fire banking, long cooking use a hardwood coal bed, quick heat use softwood open flame.

docs.title: 6.9 Stone Boiling and Drinking-Water Disinfection (Delivering Chapter 2's Promise)
docs.text: Chapter 2 declares twice that "until boiling-disinfection capability is established in Chapter 6, do not drink still water" — this section delivers on it: stone boiling in the pre-pottery era. Method: hold the water in a wooden/leather container (never set it directly on the fire); drop in dense, non-spalling stones burned through in the stove (river pebbles; trial-burn method: only pebbles that survive one dry firing without cracking may be used — quartz-bearing pebbles tend to burst when heated, and flying stone fragments are this section's number-one hazard); add 3–5 stones per liter of water, stir, and once rolling bubbles appear, add another round; a full rolling boil sustained for one period (about 3–5 min) is the disinfection criterion; lift the stones out with a clean branch. Drink only after it has cooled completely. Batch disinfection and water storage upgrade to routine boiling once pottery (Chapter 11) and metal pots (Chapter 18) unlock.

docs.title: 6.8 Fire Prevention, Smoke, and Carbon Monoxide Risk
docs.text:
Carbon monoxide (CO) risk — this chapter's number-one safety item: CO is colorless and odorless, produced by oxygen-starved incomplete combustion (sealed shelters, smothered fires, green wood piled onto a fire). Poisoning progression: pressure pain in the forehead and temples → nausea → dizziness and weak legs → loss of consciousness. Mild poisoning response: move immediately to fresh air and rest lying down; after recovery, avoid smoke exposure for 24 hours.

Four Iron Rules:

  1. Any indoor overnight fire must have both a low air inlet and a high smoke outlet (outlet diameter ≥20 cm, vertical separation ≥1 m; empirical value; must be field-calibrated). Ports at equal height = no draft.
  2. Banking is not sealing: always keep the flue open.
  3. A flame turning yellow, soft, and lazy, or indoor smoke accumulating and refusing to clear = poor combustion: open the door to ventilate and evacuate people immediately.
  4. Fires under eaves or inside shelters must be attended at all times; the attendant must not turn their back to the fire and must not fall asleep.

Fire separation: keep the fire's outer edge ≥1.5 m from dry grass, woodpiles, and shelter walls; vertically, sparks can reach over 3 m (resinous wood throws them farther) — no drooping branches within 3 m above; clear the ground to mineral soil and ring it with stones; never light a fire directly over root mats, peat, or a thick humus layer — smolder can creep along roots for days and reappear far away.

Extinguishment acceptance: pour water → stir apart → pour again → hold the back of a hand against the ash for 60 seconds with no sensation of warmth before leaving the site. When water is short, bury with wet soil and tamp it firm; the hand-back test applies equally.

Burn treatment: flush immediately with cold water, continuing to cool for at least 15 minutes; never apply mud, ash, or grease; do not puncture blisters.

docs.title: Capability Boundaries
docs.text: Can do: at least two of the four fire-lighting methods (hand drill / fire plow / fire saw / percussion) reproducible in all weather; three-tier tinder preparation and charring preparation; ember storage overnight; controlled coal bed and fire banking. Explicitly cannot do: bow drill (unlocked by Chapter 7 cord — see the three-material mismatch preview in this chapter's prerequisites); gunpowder-grade ignition; maintenance-free embers in humid rainforest conditions (weighted further in the rainforest edition, Chapter 50). External dependencies: dry tinder — fire-lighting success rates in the humid season are subject to this team's own measurements; no promises.

docs.text: Parameter Value Category Three tinder criteria Fully dry / rebound / pre-burn faint smoke Hard procedure Charred-tinder doneness Yellow-white → brown-tan; test-lighting gives patching sparks without flame ◎ color judgment Smolder to flame 2–3 pulsed short puffs; never one long blow Technique Banked fire bed Coals covered with 5–10 cm dry ash; leave one finger-thick air hole Specification Ember tube inspection Every 2–4 h Regime

docs.title: Failure Modes and Diagnostics
docs.text: Symptom Candidate causes (by probability) Remedy Board smokes but no ember Powder not gathered into a nest / damp / board too hard Gather the powder into a nest and blow; switch to a soft straight-grained board Tinder dies when blown Fluff too coarse or damp; blowing too hard Remake fine fluff; switch to pulsed short puffs Ember tube dead by morning Air hole too large (burned out) / too small (smothered) Adjust the air hole; log a comparison of both hole sizes No ember from the banked bed in the morning Air hole blocked Rake the ash and rebuild the pile; keep two holes for redundancy Percussion sparks fail to ignite Tinder insufficiently charred Remake with an added charring step

docs.title: C. Unresolved Dependencies
docs.text:
• Bow drill (needs a cord bowstring): completed in 7.6; fire-lighting efficiency will rise several times over.
  • Quantitative temperature measurement (a reproducible scale): awaits Chapter 12.
  • Charred-cloth tinder: no textiles yet, awaits Chapter 15; charred tinder fungus substitutes for now.
  • Indoor flues and cookhouse construction: awaits Chapter 13.
  • Scaling charcoal up to kiln production: awaits Chapter 12; this chapter's earth-mound kiln is small-batch only.

docs.title: Safety Boundaries
docs.text:
• The four CO Iron Rules (6.8) are absolute; no "warmth first" excuse holds.
  • Opening the charcoal kiln during the smother-cooling period is strictly forbidden: reignition not only ruins the charge, kiln CO can kill.
  • Never bring the ember tube into a closed overnight shelter.
  • In thunderstorms, do not light or tend fire under lone trees, on ridges, or on open high ground.
  • Fire-lighting training takes place on cleared mineral ground, far from woodpiles.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• L1 proof-of-principle: complete one successful friction fire lighting and raise a campfire; complete one pyrite percussion fire lighting (in mineral-bearing areas).
  • L2 repeatable manufacture: complete friction fire lighting to flame in 3 weather conditions (sunny, overcast, after rain); the Dakota pit burns for 30+ minutes without dying; the banked fire rekindles next morning with ≥2 successes; one kiln batch of charcoal with a pass rate (jet black, hard, no wood core) ≥60% (empirical value; must be field-calibrated).
  • L3 sustainable production: standing tinder stock from ≥3 sources; fuel reserves >7 days' use, raised off the ground against damp; 3 consecutive kiln batches pass; the combustion log and attendance regime are on the books and in force; two or more members independently pass the L2 assessment.

docs.title: Next-Step Dependencies
docs.text:

  • Chapter 8: controlled pyrolysis for birch-bark tar (8.5); chemical use of ash (8.3); drying and roasting pre-study of clay samples (8.6).
  • Chapter 10: cooking, smoking, and drying food.
  • Chapters 11–13: pottery firing, furnaces and kilns, lime burning — all built on this chapter's airflow control and coal management.
  • Chapter 18: charcoal as smelting reducer.

docs.title: Chapter 7 Wood, Fibers, and Rope
docs.text: Part 2 · Survival, Fire, and Primitive Materials. The Starting Point A standard remains in force: use only the capabilities established in Chapters 1–6 (stone tools, fire, measurement). This chapter delivers the first generation of woodworking tools, cordage, and mechanical joints, providing the foundation for all timber structures, load moving, and later mechanical power transmission.

docs.title: Chapter Goals
docs.text:
• Establish the complete process chain of wood evaluation — drying — splitting and shaping; establish the harvesting and processing of plant and animal fibers; establish the reverse-twist rope-making process and complete static-load and impact calibration.
  • Deliverables: qualified timber stock, cordage in three diameter classes, the full bow drill (the first reusable rotary tool), composite-handled stone adze/stone axe, specifications for wedge and mortise-tenon joints, and lever/roller/tripod load-moving devices.
  • This chapter is the first "tool bootstrap" on the measurement lineage (Lineage 4): the bow drill's rotary capability will be tooled up into a drill-press prototype in Chapter 9.

docs.title: Minimum Prerequisites
docs.text: Item Requirement Source Tools Stone-flake knife, scraper, pointed flake, hand axe, hard hammer, soft hammer, pressure flaker Chapter 5 Heat source Stable fire, coal bed, fire banking (charring grooves, fire straightening, drying) Chapter 6 Measurement Length, angle board, plumb line, records Chapter 3 Materials Standing and fallen trees, bark, grasses, hides and sinew Chapter 2 resource map

docs.title: 7.1 How to Identify Wood Suitable for Working
docs.text:
Field three-level hardness criteria (without relying on any metal tools):

  1. Fingernail pressed into the sapwood: a deep mark with slow rebound = softwood; almost no mark = hardwood.
  2. Cross-cut scoring with the stone-flake knife: a smooth cut face and flaky chips = fine, dense, good stock; a rough, torn cut face = coarse or slanted grain.
  3. Heft and tap pieces of the same size: heavy with a crisp ring = dense; light with a muffled thud = loose or porous.

Four structural checks: straight grain (the grain lines do not twist when followed along the length); few and live knots (dead knots have a black ring around them and drop out); no cracks (especially radial splits on the end face); no wormholes (reject pieces where holes and powder appear together).

Moisture state: freshly felled wood is wet-heavy; fine surface checks and a clearly lighter weight = it has entered the air-dried state.

Species selection by use table:

Use First choice Reason Tool handles, levers Oak, locust, elm hardwoods Hard and tough, bending-resistant Bow drill board/shaft Willow, poplar, linden Soft, fine friction powder, easy hole formation Wedges Straight-grained Mongolian oak, hawthorn Strong in compression along the grain, does not splinter Containers (chiseled out) Whole softwood sections Easy to burn-hollow Kindling/charcoal See 6.2 —

Register bark appearance in the resource map (Chapter 2): for each woodland, record species, diameter class, quantity, and distance. Felling rules: take fallen trees and standing dead wood first; cut living trees during the cambium-active season (when bark peels easily), and only fell — never girdle.

docs.title: 7.2 Drying, Splitting, and Shaping Wood
docs.text:
Drying: green wood moisture content is about 30%–60% (empirical value; must be field-calibrated); the usage target is air-dried to 12%–18% (empirical value; must be field-calibrated).

Procedure:

  1. Debark (protects the sapwood from borers).
  2. Seal the ends: wrap the end grain with wet mud or bark — wood ends evaporate fastest; unsealed ends crack.
  3. Stack raised off the ground with gaps between pieces; air-dry in a shady, ventilated place; avoid direct sun (differential surface-to-core shrinkage causes cracking).
  4. Estimate air-drying time for thick boards at "about 1 year per 2.5 cm of thickness" (empirical value, dry climate; must be field-calibrated); small-section tool handles are usable in about 1–2 months (empirical value).

Splitting: splitting along the grain is the most efficient woodworking method — the crack tracks the wood grain automatically and needs no cutting force.

Procedure: read the grain direction on the end face → with the hand axe or hard hammer, drive a stone wedge in on the end-face grain line → once the crack starts, follow with the second and third wedges in sequence, advancing down the crack line → boards result. Twisted grain will not split into straight boards; such stock can only be used whole.

Radial-split boards (through the pith) are dimensionally more stable than tangential-split boards: tangential shrinkage is about 1.5–2 times radial shrinkage (empirical value; must be field-calibrated), so tabletops and ways use radial-split boards.

Shaping: rough-hew with the hand axe (cut from the far end toward the body; cutting against the grain always tears) → fine-shave with the stone adze (see 7.8) → smooth with the scraper → fire straightening (wet the bent section, bake it near the fire until hot to the touch, then press and hold the shape while it cools).

Crack-prevention management: rough-shape large pieces before drying (a cracked rough blank is a small loss); cut holes and grooves only after drying; keep thickness ratios ≤2:1 at thick-thin transitions.

docs.title: 7.3 Bark, Vines, Grass Fiber, and Animal Fiber
docs.text:
Plant fiber table:

Source Harvesting Processing Characteristics Linden and paper-mulberry inner bark Strip during the spring–summer cambium-active season (take only 30 cm segments of cut per tree, never a full girdle) Rett 7–14 days (empirical value; shorter in warm water) → pound soft with a wooden mallet → comb and wash the fiber bundles out in water Long and strong; the cordage mainstay Nettle stems Cut in autumn Dry until they snap brittle → crush the outer skin → draw out the inner-core fiber High strength, but prickly to harvest Thatch grass, sedge, cattail leaves Cut in the dry season Pound soft → comb straight into bundles Quick coarse rope, weaving Fresh bark strips Take as needed Use immediately Turns brittle when dry; temporary tying only Vines Harvest live Soak soft, remove knobby growths Whole-length tying, good elasticity

Animal fibers:

  • Sinew (hind-leg tendon, back strap): dry to half-dry and shred into bundles. It wraps wet and shrinks dry — after binding a stone edge it dries and self-locks; the first-choice hafting binding material (9.1).
  • Rawhide strips: spiral-cut a hide into strips; wet-bound, dry-shrinking, as above.
  • Horsehair and down: aids for braiding and sewing.

Selection criteria: fiber length ≥10 cm is preferred; pull test by hand — a single bundle pulled repeatedly 20 times without breaking; no mold spots or black specks. Storage: hang dry; wet-moisten before use to restore suppleness.

docs.title: 7.4 Rope Twisting, Weaving, and Basic Joints
docs.text:
Mechanics of reverse twisting: once a single strand is twisted, the fibers inside it grip through friction and helical geometry; but a single strand has an untwisting tendency — let go of one end and it falls apart. The solution is reverse plying: twist the two strands each in the Z direction, then ply the two strands around each other in the S direction. The strands' untwisting tendency is exactly canceled by the ply's winding — the whole is in torsional equilibrium, and the rope neither kinks nor loosens. This is the fundamental difference between a usable rope and "a handful of grass twisted once," which is not.

Retting time vs. water temperature (v2 completion; linden/paper-mulberry inner bark): retting is microorganisms digesting pectin; each roughly one-step rise in water temperature ("warm" against "cool") about halves the time (empirical value; must be field-calibrated):

Water-temperature class (Chapter 3 anchors) Retting period (empirical starting point) Mid-course check Cool (<15 ℃) 14–20 days Day-7 spot check: can the outer skin be separated from the woody core? Neither cold nor hot (15–25 ℃) 7–14 days Spot check every other day Warm (25–30 ℃) 4–8 days Daily spot check — over-retted fiber turns brittle (snaps like paper when pulled)

Fiber wet-strength comparison (v2 completion; quick species reference; comparative terms):

Fiber Dry strength Wet strength Notes Linden/mulberry inner bark High Higher Cordage mainstay: gets stronger when wet Nettle High High Fine cord and sewing thread Dry grass stems Medium Plummets Dry-state tying and fuel only Sinew High Medium Softens when wet; for seams only (7.3)

[Card 07-01 Retting and Degumming] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: linden or paper-mulberry inner bark (ring-cut in spring-summer when the cambium is active; only a 30 cm strip per tree, never a full girdle); retting water.
  2. Tools required: wooden mallet (pounding soft), clean water (combing out), temperature anchor card (to judge the water grade), record board. Calibration source: water temperature by the Chapter 3 feel grades (cool / neither cold nor hot / warm), no thermometer; time anchored to the day.
  3. Sequence and control points: strip the bark (30 cm per tree) → ret in water → set the retting period by the water-temperature class → mid-course spot checks (does the outer skin separate from the woody core?) → pound soft with the mallet → comb the fiber bundles out in water → store hung dry. Control points: take it out early rather than over-ret — over-retted fiber snaps like paper when pulled.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: cool (<15 ℃) 14–20 days, spot check on day 7; neither cold nor hot (15–25 ℃) 7–14 days, check every other day; warm (25–30 ℃) 4–8 days, check daily; each roughly one-step rise in water temperature about halves the time (empirical value — must be calibrated to local conditions). Criteria: outer skin separable from the woody core; fiber surviving 20 repeated pulls.
  5. Observations to record: species / stripping date / water-temperature class / retting start and end / spot-check dates and results (separable or not, feel, smell) / wet strength (whether it actually improves when wet).
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = the fiber combs out into bundles and survives 20 pulls; rework = not fully separated — extend the ret and check daily; scrap = over-retted (snaps like paper), discard the whole batch.
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) fiber retts into mush → over-retting: first check whether the schedule was set by the highest temperature class (the warm class needs a daily check), discard the batch and shorten the next; (2) the outer skin will not peel → not the cambium-active season; collect in another season; (3) fiber is brittle and snaps → first check over-retting, then whether it dried too fast (dry storage must be hung in the shade); (4) strength collapses when wet → the wrong fiber was used (dry grass stems plummet when wet); switch to linden/mulberry inner bark.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one batch retted and combed into bundles; L2 = one batch at each of two water-temperature classes, with retting periods and spot checks that line up; L3 = a second person rets a batch from this card alone with the same fiber yield and strength feel.

Rope-making procedure:

  1. Take two bundles of equal thickness (the bundle diameter is half the finished rope's diameter).
  2. The right hand twists each strand tighter in the same direction (Z twist) while the left hand, keeping pace with the twisting, winds the two strands around each other in the opposite direction (S ply).
  3. Rolling on the knee or thigh is least tiring; two-person teamwork: one feeds and splices material, one twists and plies.
  4. Splicing: stagger the two strands' splice tails ≥10 cm apart, roll the overlap into the strands, and keep the joint no thicker than the rope body.
  5. Finishing: tuck-braid the end three turns or whip it dead with fine cord.

[Card 07-02 Reverse-Twist Rope Making] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: two bundles of equal-thickness bast fiber (the bundle diameter decides half the finished rope diameter); fine cord (for whipping the ends).
  2. Tools required: bare hands (rolling on the knee or thigh); a stone-flake knife for cutting rope; known-weight stones and water bags (for the 07-03 calibration). Calibration source: rope diameter estimated at the standard rod's sub-unit grade; load steps only from known-weight objects.
  3. Sequence and control points: take two equal bundles → twist each strand tight in the same direction (Z twist) → with both hands in step, wind the two strands together in the opposite direction (S ply) → on splicing, stagger the two splice tails ≥10 cm and roll the overlap into the strands → tuck-braid the ends three turns or whip them dead with fine cord. Control points: single strands Z, plying S, uniform across the whole team (a reversed direction will kink the rope).
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: bundle diameter = half the finished rope diameter; splice overlap ≥10 cm, staggered, joint no thicker than the rope body; ends tucked three turns; diameter classes 3/6/10/16 mm with static breaking loads 30–60 / 80–150 / 200–350 / 500–800 kgf (empirical values — must be calibrated to local conditions).
  5. Observations to record: fiber species / batch number / bundle diameter / twist direction (Z/S) / rope diameter / splice positions / maker.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = the rope neither kinks nor back-twists, the ends do not unravel, joints no thicker than the body; rework = the rope kinks into loops (plying direction reversed) — unply and re-ply with S/Z swapped; scrap = fiber over-retted and brittle (snaps when pulled) — replace the whole batch.
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) the rope will not hold and falls apart as soon as it is released → first check whether the twist is insufficient, then whether the two strands are uneven (match thicknesses); (2) the rope kinks into loops → the plying direction is reversed; unply, swap S/Z, re-ply; (3) breaks always at the splice → first check whether the overlap is shorter than 10 cm, then whether the two splice tails sit at the same place (they must be staggered); (4) strength plummets when wet → dry-grass-type fiber was used; switch to bast fiber.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one length of rope that neither kinks nor unravels; L2 = 10 m made in each of the three diameter classes and filed; L3 = two or more people can make rope to the file independently, with the same diameter and twist direction.

Rope diameter vs. breaking load table (empirical values; must be field-calibrated; based on three-strand linden-bark/nettle rope):

Rope diameter Static breaking load (order of magnitude) Use 3 mm 30–60 kgf Tying, sewing, bow drill string (4–6 mm steadier) 6 mm 80–150 kgf Tool hafting, general hanging 10 mm 200–350 kgf Load lashing, tripods 16 mm 500–800 kgf Load hoisting (with pulley sets)

Calibration methods (mandatory for every batch):

  • Static-load test: suspend the rope and load it in steps (stones/water bags of known weight), holding each step for 1 minute, and record the breaking step. The breaking value divided by 5 is that batch's working-load ceiling; divide by 10 when lifting people.
  • Impact test: drop a weight equal to half the static breaking load in free fall from 1 m onto a tensioned rope; surviving 10 drops qualifies it as a lifting sling.

[Card 07-03 Static-Load Stepping and Calibration] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: the rope batch to be calibrated (sampled from the batch); known-weight stones or water bags (stepped load); a fixed suspension point (crossbeam or tree limb) and slings.
  2. Tools required: hanging cord, water bags and stone set (stepped ballast), wooden caliper or standard rod (to measure diameter), record board. Calibration source: load comes from known-weight stones or water bags (Chapter 3 weighing), not from eyeballing.
  3. Sequence and control points: suspend the rope → load in steps → hold each step 1 minute → record the breaking step → divide by the safety factor for that batch's working load → impact test (half the breaking load, 1 m free fall, 10 drops). Control points: every step must be held 1 minute (loading fast misjudges); for lifting people divide by 10 instead.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: safety factor — working load = breaking value ÷ 5, ÷ 10 for lifting people; the impact test drops half the static breaking load from 1 m, surviving 10 drops qualifies as a lifting sling; step increments keyed to the diameter class's empirical breaking magnitudes 30–60 / 80–150 / 200–350 / 500–800 kgf, to be overwritten by on-site measurement.
  5. Observations to record: batch number / rope diameter / load and hold result at each step / breaking step / break location (rope body, splice, knot eye) / impact drops and result / calibrator and date.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = the breaking step is not below that class's empirical magnitude and the rope survives 10 impact drops; rework = the break is at a splice — lengthen the overlap, stagger it, re-splice and recalibrate; scrap = specimens from one batch scatter widely in breaking step (batch inhomogeneity — the batch is not used for load-bearing).
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) breaking steps scatter within a batch → first check whether specimens came from the same splice section, then whether fiber batches were mixed; (2) breaks always at a knot eye → first check whether that knot passed the three load-bearing checks, then whether the rope surface is fuzzed (a fuzzed knot drops to 50% load); (3) the rope stretches visibly and will not recover → wet rope or over-twisted; dry it and retest; (4) it parts on the first impact drop → first check whether the drop weight exceeded half the breaking load, then whether the rope was wetted and dried again (strength already lost).
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = a stepped-loading record for one batch; L2 = one calibration table per diameter class stating the working load; L3 = the table in use for real hoisting, with a recorded working-load ceiling per batch and refusal above it.

Basic knots (function-oriented):

Knot Function Key points Square knot Joining two ropes of equal thickness Both ends loaded together, no slip Sheet bend Joining ropes of different thickness The thin rope wraps the thick and locks Bowline Fixed loop, no slip, no jam Still untieable after loading Clove hitch Fast pole lashing Tighter the harder it pulls; can be tied one-handed Cross lashing Binding two crossed poles (scaffolds, tool handles) 3 turns each in the order horizontal–vertical–horizontal–vertical, then add frapping coils to cinch dead

Weaving (plain and twined) produces mats and baskets — the interim grain-storage container solution until Chapter 10.

docs.title: 7.5 Wooden Wedges, Mortise-and-Tenon Joints, and Mechanical Connections
docs.text:
Wooden wedges:

  • Stock: straight-grained hardwood (Mongolian oak, hawthorn), grain parallel to the load direction.
  • Wedge face angle 8°–12°: too steep and vibration pops it out; too shallow and it splits the workpiece (empirical value; must be field-calibrated).
  • Leave a 2–3 mm blunt edge at the head to prevent mushrooming when driving.
  • Drive dry wedges into wet holes: as the hole dries and shrinks it locks the wedge dead — tighter with use.

Mortise-and-tenon (pre-chisel-era techniques):

  • Two ways to cut mortises: burn-chiseling — char it through locally with coals → scrape away the char layer with a stone flake → repeat to depth; drill-and-enlarge — the bow drill (7.6) drills a continuous row of holes along the mortise line → break through → scrape and true the walls (efficiency multiplies once tooled up in Chapter 9).
  • Specifications: tenon width = 1/3–1/2 of the handle width; tenon length 2–3 times its width; fit a dry tenon into a wet mortise with 0.5–1 mm of interference (empirical value; must be field-calibrated); once the tenon protrudes through, drive in a cross-grain wedge to swell it dead (through-wedge lock).
  • Three anti-crack rules: hole centers at least 2 hole-diameters from the end of the wood; no holes along split-sensitive directions; for large holes, burn a small hole first and enlarge stepwise.

Joint lineage (strength and reversibility):

Level Joint Characteristics 1 Lashing (rope) Fast, removable, needs periodic re-lashing 2 Wedge + lashing Semi-permanent 3 Mortise-and-tenon + through wedge Permanent, load-bearing in bending 4 Tar glue + wedge + lashing Strongest; depends on 8.5

Acceptance: apply a static load of 1.5 times the working load to the joint and hold for 1 minute; displacement <2 mm with no cracking or noise passes (record working loads by use).

docs.title: 7.6 Simple Bow Drill and Rotary Tools
docs.text:
Full bow drill parameter table:

Component Specification Material/source Bow arm Length 60–80 cm, straight-grained elastic wood; strung, the arc stands about 5 cm high 7.1 species selection + 7.8 shaping Bowstring Rope diameter 4–6 mm, wraps the drill shaft 1.5–2 turns 7.4 rope making Drill shaft (for boring) Length 20–25 cm, diameter 2–2.5 cm, round straight hardwood; stone drill point fitted at the end Stone point = Chapter 5 pointed flake Drill shaft (for fire lighting) Diameter 2–2.5 cm softwood, rounded end See 6.3 Hearth board See 6.3 — Bearing cap Hardwood block or a stone with a socket; grease the socket with animal fat to reduce drag Chapter 5 toolworking

Operating parameters: stroke length 25–35 cm; 50–70 strokes per minute; speed about 200–400 rpm; downward force 5–10 kg (empirical values; must be field-calibrated). Solo operation: left hand presses the cap, right hand works the bow; two-handed cooperation (one presses, one saws the bow) for deep holes and hard stock.

Boring procedure:

  • Wood: scribe a cross to mark the hole position (Chapter 3 datums) → the drill point starts a locating dimple → steady pressure, slow rotation → lift the drill to clear the chips every 20–30 seconds. A hole through 2 cm thick hardwood takes about 5–15 minutes (empirical value; must be field-calibrated).
  • Deep-hole anti-runout: drill from both faces toward the middle; correct the meet-up deviation with the angle board.
  • Bone and stone: switch to a hollow bone-tube/bamboo-tube bit + wet quartz-sand abrasive — grinding rather than cutting; see 9.2 for details.

Fire-lighting reuse: swap in a softwood shaft and a hearth board and it becomes the bow drill upgrade of 6.3, with a success rate and efficiency several times the hand drill's (empirical value).

Maintenance: restring as soon as the string loosens (wrap count unchanged); dulled drill point → retouch by pressure flaking (Chapter 5); bearing-cap socket worn deep and slipping → re-cut the cap face.

[Card 07-04 Bow Drill Component Making] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: bow-arm stock (straight-grained elastic wood, 60–80 cm); bowstring (4–6 mm rope); shaft stock (round straight hardwood for boring, softwood for fire lighting); stone drill point (Chapter 5 pointed flake); bearing cap (hardwood block or stone with a socket); animal fat.
  2. Tools required: stone-flake knife, scraper, adze (shaping, 7.8); grinding stone (truing the shaft round); angle board (checking shaft and hole position); marking tool. Calibration source: component lengths measured against the standard rod's graduations; shaft roundness judged by rolling it.
  3. Sequence and control points: shape the bow arm (arc about 5 cm high when strung) → string it (1.5–2 turns around the shaft) → shave the shaft round and fit the stone point → cut the socket in the bearing cap and grease it → trial spin (does the point trace a circle?) → boring. Control points: the wrap count and stroke length may not be changed casually (change them and the speed changes); a socket worn deep and slipping means re-cut the cap face.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: bow arm 60–80 cm, arc about 5 cm high; string 4–6 mm, 1.5–2 turns; shaft 20–25 cm long, 2–2.5 cm diameter; stroke 25–35 cm; 50–70 strokes per minute; about 200–400 rpm; downward force 5–10 kg (empirical values — must be calibrated to local conditions); a hole through 2 cm hardwood takes 5–15 minutes.
  5. Observations to record: component number / bow length and arc height / string diameter and wrap count / shaft diameter / strokes per minute / time per hole / lifts to clear chips / socket depth.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = the point traces a circle in free spin, holes do not skew, and a 2 cm hardwood hole is done in 5–15 minutes; rework = restring a slack string (wrap count unchanged), retouch a dull point by pressure flaking, re-cut a worn socket; scrap = the bow arm cracks or loses its spring — replace the stock.
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) the point slips without biting → first check whether the point is dull (retouch by pressure flaking), then whether downward force is short (the 5–10 kg grade), last whether the stock is too hard (change stock or switch to abrasive drilling); (2) holes skew → first check for a starting dimple, then whether the cap hand is adding lateral force, last whether the stock face is tilted; (3) the string keeps going slack → first check whether the wrap count changed, then whether the string is under 4–6 mm; (4) speed will not come up and it only smokes without cutting → first check whether the stroke is too short (25–35 cm), then whether the bearing cap lacks grease.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one assembled bow drill that bores one hole; L2 = 5 aligned holes in hardwood, drilled from two faces with deviation <2 mm; L3 = bow, string, shaft, and wrap count on file, and a second person reproduces a bow drill of the same speed from the file.

docs.title: 7.7 Levers, Pulleys, and Simple Load-Moving Devices
docs.text:
Lever: three elements — fulcrum, effort point, load point. Effort saved = distance from fulcrum to load ÷ distance from fulcrum to effort. Practice: when prying a heavy stone, the packing stone acts as the fulcrum and sits as close to the load as possible; the longer the effort arm, the more effort is saved, but the larger the stroke.

Rollers: place equal-diameter logs under the load and feed them in one by one from the front. The rolling friction coefficient is about 0.05–0.1 versus about 0.4–0.6 for sliding (empirical values) — effort saved 3–5 times. Key points: keep the path level; roller spacing 50–80 cm; fan the rollers out when turning.

Inclined plane: an earth ramp with a 1:4 grade saves effort down to 1/4 in theory (ignoring friction). Chock behind the load on the way up to prevent backsliding.

Rope-and-pulley arrangements (limited by having no metal axles):

  • Turning a line over a tree limb or smooth log: efficiency <50%, heavy rope wear; for direction changes only.
  • Simple wooden pulley block: hardwood with a grooved wheel + wooden pin axle, efficiency about 60%–70% (empirical value; must be field-calibrated); a single movable pulley saves nearly half; a one-fixed-one-movable combination saves more than half, but descent speed and stroke double.
  • Tripod hoisting: bind three equal-length hardwood legs at the top (cross lashing + through wedge) and hang the pulley set; used for loading carts, lowering into pits, and erecting members.

Rafts and sledges:

  • Raft: buoyancy = displaced volume × water density. Assessment: dry wood density about 0.5–0.7 (empirical value); a log's displacement minus its own weight is the gross load capacity; halve that again for the safe load.
  • Sledge: for hauling over snow and mud; hardwood runners underneath; lash the load with cross lashing.

All load-moving devices undergo 1.5-times static-load verification before use (method of 7.4).

docs.title: 7.8 How to Make Reusable Woodworking Tools
docs.text:
First batch of composite-handled woodworking tools (hafting uses joint lineage level 2 of 7.5: wedge + lashing; level 4 awaits the 8.5 glue):

Tool Edge Haft angle Use Stone adze Ground stone edge (hornfels/basalt) or a thick flake Edge to handle about 60°–75° Transverse shaving, gouging channels Stone axe Bifacially knapped or ground Edge line perpendicular to the handle axis Felling, splitting rough stock Wood chisel/graver Small flake bound to a short handle, edge angle 30°–50° In line with the handle Gouging channels, truing holes; cutting and prying only — hammer strikes forbidden Scraper/flat blade Thick flake end edge 45°–60° In line or slightly angled Surfacing, bark removal Wooden mallet Large-diameter short hardwood section, ends flat One piece Driving wedges, truing shape; spares the edge

Auxiliaries: marking gauge (hardwood point + charcoal stick for scribing); whetstone set (one coarse and one fine sandstone slab); plumb line and angle board (Chapter 3) carried with the toolbox.

Grinding process (the proper route for adze and axe edges): grind the blank on a coarse sandstone slab with water to remove excess → medium-grind to shape → polish with fine sand + leather. Keep the original edge angle constant throughout: consistent grinding-striation direction, parallel to the edge, is the evidence the angle has not changed. Grinding one stone axe takes 3–8 hours (empirical value; must be field-calibrated).

Maintenance regime:

  1. Wipe clean after use and coat thinly with animal fat against moisture.
  2. Re-sharpen as soon as the edge dulls, angle unchanged (checked against the grinding striations).
  3. Re-lash immediately when lashings loosen — follow the standard lashing pattern (7.4 cross lashing); no temporary wrappings.
  4. After 3–5 regrinds a stone-edged tool's blade is too thin and is scrapped; the edge blank is recycled for re-knapping (back to 5.5).

Wear ledger: for every tool, record manufacture date, labor hours, regrind count, and scrap date. Summarize the wear rate monthly to feed capacity planning in Section 9.5.

docs.title: Capability Boundaries
docs.text: Can do: retting-combing-grading of three bast fibers; two- and three-strand reverse-twist rope; a field-measured rope diameter–load table on file; bow drill assemblies and basic wooden workpieces (mortise-tenon and lashing). Explicitly cannot do: machine rope twisting (the rope walk is an upgrade item); single-fiber strength quantification (bundle-strength comparatives substitute). External dependencies: retting water sources and seasonal water temperature (see the 7.4 addendum block for the table).

docs.title: 7.9 Knot Atlas: Ten Knots and the Three Load Checks
docs.text:
The five knots of 7.4 cover "joining and lashing"; this section completes the ten-knot atlas and gives a unified slippage risk grading: low = self-locks even under pulsating loads and vibration, may be left unattended overnight; medium = self-locks under constant load but backs off under pulsating loads, must be checked the same day; high = for temporary positioning or attended use only, untie immediately after use.

Knot One-line tying method Use Slippage risk Clove hitch Wrap the rope twice around the pole, the second wrap trapping the first wrap's end Lashing starting point on poles; opening stage of the tripod top joint Medium (stable under constant load, backs off under pulsating load; finish with a half hitch) Figure-eight knot Wrap the rope end around the standing part into a figure "8" and pass back through Rope-end stopper against pull-through (safety end before threading holes) Low (tightens the harder it pulls; the cost is being hard to untie after loading) Rolling hitch The short rope takes three snug turns around the standing rope facing the load side A temporary power-grip handle on a tensioned rope (rope-tightening work) Medium (rigged backwards it slips: the wrapped face must face the load direction) Bowline The rope end goes up through to form a loop, around the back of the standing part, and down back into the loop Fixed loop: lifting people, around stakes, starting netting Low (no slip, no jam, untieable; tuck the tail back through into a double bowline to finish) Sheet bend The thin rope end passes through the thick rope's bight, folds back around the bight's bottom and traps itself Joining a thick and a thin rope Medium (thin-end tail ≥10 cm; tie it doubled at critical points) Double fisherman's knot The two rope ends each wrap the other's standing part twice, then pull against each other to tighten Permanent joining of equal thin ropes; closing loops Low (extremely self-locking; cannot be untied after loading — permanent joins only) Sheer lashing With two poles side by side, the rope takes several connected turns around both, then fraps tight horizontally between the poles to close A-frames, shears legs (set the angle before closing) Medium (the close-off backs off under vibration; re-tighten daily) Carrying-pole lift hitch Once the load sling loop is set, the carrying pole's end passes through the loop, traps the sling root, and takes one more back turn Two-person carrying: joining the carrying pole to the load sling Low (vertical load presses it ever tighter; must be re-closed after setting the load down) Ladder hitch The short rope wraps the standing rope one turn and passes through to form a self-gripping loop; rungs are lashed horizontally between two loops Rope-ladder rung fixing Medium (slips unloaded: re-tighten rung by rung before climbing) Anchor hitch The rope end takes two turns around the ring or post, finished with a half hitch Fixed ends between rope and rings, posts, anchors Low (self-locks under constant load; switch to three turns for stiff, thick rope)

Three checks for load-bearing knots (any knot that will take a load must be checked after tying; miss one, do not use):

  1. Check the load direction: does the knot's locking face square with the actual pull direction? A rolling hitch or sheet bend rigged backwards is as good as untied; the bowline's loaded side must be the standing part, not the end.
  2. Check the finish: tail ≥10 cm; required re-threading done and required half hitches added; a figure-eight knot pre-tied on a rope end must not be stripped for convenience.
  3. Check the wear point: pinch the knot's eye (the tightest bend) and twist-inspect — fuzzing = outer fibers cut; a cut-through feel = the core is about to fail. A fuzzed knot drops to 50% load; a cut-feel knot is retied at a new spot immediately.

◎ Hand-feel marker: whether the finish is tight enough is judged not by eye but by "two fingers clamping the tail cannot pull it out, and a knuckle tap on the knot gives a muffled sound." Practice method: everyone ties each of the ten knots 20 times with 3 mm rope (about 2 hours total, empirical value), then ties each 5 times blindfolded; thereafter, each week 3 knots are drawn at random and re-tied against the clock, with scores entered in the rope ledger.

Field Content Input materials Calibrated rope (7.4, any of the 3–10 mm classes); wooden poles or ring posts; practice usage about 50 cm of rope per knot per run Tools required Bare hands for the most part; stone-flake knife for cutting rope (Chapter 5); known-weight stones for verification (Chapter 3 weight records) Operation sequence and control points Tie per the atlas → run the three checks for load-bearing knots → register item by item. Control points: failing either the load direction or the finish forbids hanging any load Empirical parameters and calibration Tail ≥10 cm; calibration: run 3 pull-to-failure tests per knot type and record "slippage load ÷ breaking load"; a knot type with a ratio <0.7 is banned for that use (empirical criterion; must be field-calibrated) In-process observation items Knot type, rope diameter, load step, slip amount (mm), fiber state at the knot eye; enter in the rope ledger Pass / rework / scrap Displacement <5 mm under working load with no slip = pass; slips then re-locks = reworkable (add a half hitch or retie doubled); slips out = that knot type is scrapped for that use Common failures and check order Slip: (1) check whether the load direction is rigged backwards (2) check whether the finish lacks a half hitch (3) check whether the rope surface is too slick (newly twisted rope lacks fuzz; pre-fuzz it before use) L1/L2/L3 evidence L1: one demonstration of each of the ten knots; L2: 3 pull-test records per knot on file; L3: knot-type vs. use ledger + quarterly retraining records

[Card 07-05 Knot Atlas] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: calibrated rope (7.4, any of the 3–10 mm classes, about 50 cm per knot per practice run); wooden poles, rings, stakes to tie onto.
  2. Tools required: bare hands for the most part; stone-flake knife for cutting rope (Chapter 5); known-weight stones (for the slippage-load ratio calibration). Calibration source: diameter and breaking load from the 07-03 calibration table; load applied in known-weight stone steps.
  3. Sequence and control points: tie per the atlas → run the three checks for load-bearing knots (load direction, finish, wear point) → register item by item in the ledger. Control points: failing either the load direction or the finish check forbids hanging any load.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: tail ≥10 cm; run 3 pull-to-failure tests per knot type and record "slippage load ÷ breaking load"; a knot type with a ratio <0.7 is banned for that use (empirical criterion — must be calibrated to local conditions); practice load: each of the ten knots 20 times with 3 mm rope (about 2 hours), then 5 times blindfolded, thereafter 3 knots drawn at random each week against the clock.
  5. Observations to record: knot type / rope diameter / load step / slip amount (mm) / fiber state at the knot eye (fuzzed or cut-feel) / tier and date.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = displacement <5 mm under working load with no slip-out; rework = it slips then re-locks (add a half hitch or retie it doubled); scrap = it slips out — that knot type is scrapped for that use; change knot type.
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) it slips → first check whether the load direction is rigged backwards (a rolling hitch or sheet bend rigged backwards is as good as untied), then whether the finish lacks a half hitch or the tail is under 10 cm, last whether the rope surface is too slick (newly twisted rope lacks fuzz; pre-fuzz it); (2) it cannot be untied after loading → that knot belongs to permanent joins only (double fisherman's type); switch to an untieable knot; (3) the knot eye fuzzes → first check whether the tightest bend is taking the load (move the knot), fuzzed knots drop to 50% load; (4) slip amounts differ widely between two runs → first check whether the rope is the same diameter class, then whether the tying followed the atlas step by step.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one demonstration of each of the ten knots; L2 = 3 pull-test records per knot on file; L3 = a knot-type vs. use ledger plus quarterly retraining records.

docs.title: 7.10 Net and Mat Weaving
docs.text:
Starting a net: first tie a row of base loops on the spreader bar (bowlines, loop spacing = one mesh size); the loop count is the net's mesh count across the width. Weave row by row: take the cord and tie two consecutive half hitches around the two mesh posts of each mesh in the row above and tighten (interlocking knot); rows interlock into a sheet.

Decreasing and increasing meshes row by row:

  • Decrease (narrowing the net): at the row end, combine two adjacent meshes of the row above into one and tie a single knot.
  • Increase (widening the net): tie two knots on the same mesh post.
  • Rule: the number of decreases and increases per row must be left-right symmetric, or the net draws up skewed (the whole sheet twists into a trapezoid).

Mesh gauge (sizing board): one hardwood board, width = mesh side length × 2, thickness 3–5 mm, edges rounded off. Cast the starting loops around the board so every mesh comes out the same width; mesh tolerance is judged by "the gauge slides through the full row with uniform snugness." Fishing-net mesh 30–50 mm (start from half the target fish's body height; one live fishing run calibrates it); cargo-net mesh 80–120 mm (sized so cargo cannot slip out).

◎ Weaving-tension hand feel: tighten each interlocking knot to the degree that "mesh posts do not twist and the gauge slides in and out without binding." Practice method: weave three 10 cm × 10 cm test pieces first; when the third matches the first row by row in mesh count, you have graduated (empirical value; must be field-calibrated). Misjudgment compensation: run the gauge through the full row — rows it will not pass are too tight and rows it falls through freely are too loose; correct the hand-feel record against the gauge results.

Item Specification Labor hours (empirical value; must be field-calibrated) Use Fishing net 1 m², mesh 30–50 mm, 3 mm bast rope 6–10 h Blocking streams, drag fishing Cargo net 1.5 m × 1.5 m, mesh 80–120 mm, 6 mm rope 8–12 h Hoisting and load binding, hanging storage Grass mat (plain weave) 1.8 m × 0.9 m 3–5 h Sleeping mat, underlay Grass mat (twill) Same as above 4–6 h Rain cover (twill is denser and seeps more slowly)

Two mat weaves: plain weave alternates one-over, one-under — fast, flat surface; twill advances two-over, two-under in offset rows — diagonal texture, denser weave. Pound the grass soft and comb it straight first (7.3 processing); press each column tight as you weave — "finish a column, press a column."

Selecting cord: nets use bast rope that does not lose wet strength (linden/paper-mulberry inner bark; 7.4 wet-strength table); mats can use dry grass, but it must be stored hung dry to prevent mildew.

Field Content Input materials 3–6 mm bast rope (wet-strength-retaining type, 7.4); one spreader bar; stock estimate = net area × mesh density plus a 15% allowance Tools required Mesh gauge (self-made in this section); stone-flake knife for cutting rope (Chapter 5); verification: the gauge passes through the full row Operation sequence and control points Cast loops → interlocking knots row by row → decrease/increase meshes per the plan → finish edges with three tucked turns. Control point: count the meshes as each row completes; a miscount unravels that row Empirical parameters and calibration Mesh size = gauge width ÷ 2; calibration: first weave a 10 cm × 10 cm test piece, count the meshes per row and re-measure the mesh wet (wet swelling passes as long as the gauge is not jammed) In-process observation items Mesh count per row, tension hand feel (◎ criterion), rope batch number; stop the row for inspection on any mismatch Pass / rework / scrap Mesh deviation <10% with no skipped knots = pass; two consecutive rows deviating the same way = rework (unravel two rows, reweave, and re-check the gauge); rope stock over-retted and brittle (snaps when pulled, 7.4 criterion) = scrap and replace the stock Common failures and check order Net draws skewed: (1) check whether decreases/increases are piled on one side (2) check the interlocking knots for uneven tightness (3) check whether the gauge has worn narrow L1/L2/L3 evidence L1: a 10 cm × 10 cm test piece kept as a reference; L2: one fishing net survives one launch without losing meshes; L3: net output, losses, and wet-strength spot checks entered in the ledger

[Card 07-06 Net Weaving] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: 3–6 mm bast rope (wet-strength-retaining type: linden/mulberry inner bark); one spreader bar; stock = net area × mesh density plus a 15% allowance.
  2. Tools required: mesh gauge (hardwood board, width = mesh side × 2, thickness 3–5 mm, edges rounded, self-made); stone-flake knife for cutting rope (Chapter 5). Calibration source: mesh size = gauge width ÷ 2; wet swelling passes as long as the gauge is not jammed.
  3. Sequence and control points: cast a row of base loops on the spreader bar (bowlines, spacing = one mesh) → interlocking knots row by row (two consecutive half hitches around the two mesh posts of each mesh, tightened) → decrease/increase meshes per plan (left-right symmetry is mandatory) → finish edges with three tucked turns. Control point: count the meshes as each row completes; a miscount unravels that row.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: mesh size = gauge width ÷ 2; fishing net 30–50 mm (start from half the target fish's body height, calibrated by one live fishing run); cargo net 80–120 mm; mesh deviation <10% passes; weave three 10 cm × 10 cm test pieces first, and graduating means the third matches the first row by row in mesh count (empirical value — must be calibrated to local conditions); labor 1 m² fishing net 6–10 h, 1.5 m × 1.5 m cargo net 8–12 h.
  5. Observations to record: mesh count per row / mesh size (gauge full-row test) / tension hand feel (◎ mesh posts untwisted, gauge neither binding nor slack) / rope batch number / mesh re-measured wet.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = mesh deviation <10% with no skipped knots; rework = two consecutive rows deviating the same way — unravel two rows, reweave, re-check the gauge; scrap = rope stock over-retted and brittle (snaps when pulled) — replace the stock.
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) the net draws skewed into a trapezoid → first check whether decreases/increases are piled on one side (they must be left-right symmetric), then whether the interlocking knots vary in tightness, last whether the gauge has worn narrow; (2) mesh size wanders → first check whether every starting loop was cast on the same gauge board, then whether wet rope was re-measured (wet swelling); (3) a skipped knot inside a row → add it when counting that row; never carry it into the next row; (4) the cord snaps mid-weave → first check for over-retted stock (switch to linden/mulberry inner bark), then whether the diameter is under 3 mm.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = a 10 cm × 10 cm test piece kept as a reference; L2 = one fishing net survives one launch without losing meshes; L3 = net output, losses, and wet-strength spot checks on the ledger.

docs.title: 7.11 Splitting Strips and Rattan-Bamboo Work
docs.text:
Fixed-blade strip-splitting method: stand the bamboo tube upright on the ground with a shallow cross kerf pre-cut in the end face; set the blade (stone axe edge or thick-backed flake) into one of the kerf lines; from then on the blade position does not move — press down on the blade spine with both hands or strike the spine with the wooden mallet, letting the tube's own weight and the strikes drive it downward in one split to the end. The fixed blade is the key to equal-width strips: move the blade midway and the strips are sure to come out uneven.

Splitting order: first split crosswise into four blocks (through the pith) → split each block into strips → scrape the inner diaphragms clean (diaphragms are hard and brittle; left in, strips snap mid-weave).

Strip grading:

Grade Position Characteristics Use Green strip The outer layer with the green skin High strength, over 2 times the yellow strip's (empirical comparative; calibration: hang weights on equal-width strip pairs and compare breaking steps) Load-bearing warp strips, basket bottoms, bending members Yellow strip Inner layer Low strength, soft Weft winding, filling woven walls

Strip width specifications: warp strips 6–8 mm with faces free of split wounds (a wounded strip is a future break point); weft strips 3–5 mm. Moisten dry strips in water for about 10 minutes before weaving; the brittle-snap rate drops markedly (empirical value; must be field-calibrated).

Rattan working:

  • Straightening: bake bent sections near the fire until hot to the touch (same fire-straightening method as Chapter 6), press straight, and cool naturally; twice per spot is the limit — a third baking scorches the rattan skin and it is discarded.
  • T-joint: the horizontal bar's split end clamps the upright; close with cross lashing; used for frame tops and tool racks.
  • Splicing (lengthening): split each rattan end into three strands; interweave the strands into one another; whip the outside with fine cord to close. Joint strength is about 60%–70% of the parent stock (empirical value; must be field-calibrated: hang loads on spliced and whole sections and compare breaking); critical load points must avoid joint positions.

◎ Strip-splitting blade hand feel: the along-the-grain criterion is "the blade spine sinks evenly and the sound runs continuous without popping"; a popping sound = hitting a node or going against the grain — stop and withdraw immediately and re-open the kerf. Practice method: split 20 strokes on a scrap bamboo tube; ≥80% equal-width strips means graduation (empirical value). Misjudgment compensation: compare strips two by two, side by side; pull out any with a width deviation >2 mm for re-splitting or demote them to weft strips.

docs.title: 7.12 Rope Bridges and Hoisting
docs.text:
Twin-cable suspension bridge (design span limit 10 m, empirical value; must be field-calibrated):

  • Structure: 1 main cable (10–16 mm, passing static-load calibration) + 2 handrail cables (6–10 mm) + the tread set.
  • Main cable sag: 8%–12% of the span (empirical value; must be field-calibrated) — too tight and the anchor-point loads run to several times the bridge load; too loose and every step is a trap. After tensioning, verify by "hanging 75 kg at mid-span and the extra sag stays <50 cm."
  • Anchoring: wrap the main cable three turns around a living trunk + anchor hitch (7.9), or bury ground stakes (hardwood ≥15 cm in diameter, buried ≥1 m deep, with a cross-bar on top of the stake). Handrail cables anchor at chest height at both ends.
  • Tread lashing: short timbers (40–50 cm long, 6–8 cm diameter) hang from the main cable with clove hitches, spaced 30–35 cm, each tread end given a half hitch against sliding; every 3–4 treads, run a hanger rope from a handrail cable diagonally to the main cable, forming triangles against sway.
  • Verification: before carrying people, hang 1.5 times the rated load (water-bag ballast) and let it stand 10 minutes; anchor displacement <5 cm passes; thereafter inspect the anchor hitches and tread half hitches weekly.

Three-point hoisting:

  • Center-of-gravity judgment: the test lift is the measurement — once the sling lifts the object, it rotates until the center of gravity hangs directly below; if it tilts, set it back down, shift the sling loops, and try again until it lifts level.
  • Sling layout: two-point slings + one top point make three points. With the two legs at an angle <90°, each leg carries <0.75 times the weight; at 120°, each leg carries the full weight; lifting is forbidden at angles >120° (empirical criterion; measure on site with the Chapter 3 angle board).
  • Test-lift procedure: lift 10 cm off the ground and hold 1 minute → observe the tilt and the slip at every knot → set down and adjust → second test lift, level → formal hoist. No one stands below at any point during the lift; lifting and lowering follow the called-command system of this chapter's safety boundaries.

Stringing a rope across a river (leader-line method):

  1. Tie a stone or a piece of floating wood to the fine leader line's end (3 mm rope), throw it across, or carry it while swimming over.
  2. Pull the leader line taut across the river and anchor it temporarily on the far bank.
  3. The leader line drags the middle rope (6 mm), and the middle rope drags the main cable (10–16 mm) — scale up step by step, each step a rope-diameter ratio of about 1:3; if any step will not budge, stop and check for snagging; throwing the main cable across directly is forbidden.
  4. Anchor and tension the main cable to the twin-cable bridge specification; run the 1.5-times static-load verification first, then use it as a crossing bridge or a traverse line.

docs.title: Parameter Summary Table
docs.text: Parameter Value Category Retting period table Warm class 4–8 days; cool class 14–20 days Empirical, settled by spot checks Over-retting criterion Fiber snaps like paper when pulled = gone too far Red line Z twist / S ply Single strands Z, plying S, uniform across the team Procedure Splice overlap ≥10 cm, staggered and rolled in Procedure Working load Breaking value ÷ 5; lifting people ÷ 10 Safety factor

docs.title: Failure Modes and Diagnostics
docs.text: Symptom Candidate causes (by probability) Remedy Rope will not hold together, loose Insufficient twist / uneven strand thickness Add twist and re-ply; match the thicknesses Rope kinks into loops Plying direction reversed Unply and re-ply (swap S/Z) Break at the splice Overlap too short or aligned Lengthen the overlap, stagger it, re-splice Fiber retts into mush Over-retting Shorten the retting period; discard over-retted batches Strength plummets when wet Dry-grass-type fiber was used Switch to bast fiber (wet-strength table) Uneven meshes, net draws skewed Decreases/increases concentrated on one side; interlocking knots uneven in tightness Unravel the deviating rows and reweave; recount every row; re-check the gauge Bridge main cable gradually loosens and sags Anchor regression (stake creep, living-tree growth) or wet-stretch of the rope Retie the anchor hitch and re-tension; shorten the inspection cycle and record it Strips snap mid-run and splinter Yellow strips used in load-bearing; blade met a node against the grain Switch to green strips at load points; re-open the kerf with the grain; demote broken strips to weft

docs.text:
• Chapter 5 full stone kit (knife, scrapers, points, axe, hammers, pressure flaker, bone tools).
  • Chapter 6 full heat-source kit (campfire, coal bed, charcoal kiln, ember tube).
  • Chapter 3 measurement and records.

docs.title: B. New Tools Added in This Chapter
docs.text: Tool Specification Manufacturing source Timber stock (air-drying) See 7.2 Hand axe + wedges Fiber stock (linden bark/nettle/grass) Stored dry Retting + pounding and combing Cordage, three classes (3/6/10 mm) Calibrated 7.4 reverse twisting Full bow drill See 7.6 Chapters 5 + 7 combined Stone adze, stone axe (composite handle), wood chisel, scraper, wooden mallet See 7.8 Chapters 5 + 7 combined Wedge set, mortise-tenon joints See 7.5 Split from hardwood Rollers, tripod, sledge, raft See 7.7 Lashing + mortise-tenon Mats and baskets Plain/twined weaving 7.4 weaving

docs.title: C. Unresolved Dependencies
docs.text:
• No adhesives: the haft-strength ceiling is limited by lashing (tar glue in 8.5 completes it).
  • Flatness and angle accuracy rely on grinding + eyeballing; there is no surface datum or gauges (solved in Chapter 20; for now use the Chapter 3 datums + templates).
  • Wood drying cycles are long (months), so capacity is constrained by stock; kiln drying awaits the Chapter 12–13 buildings and kilns.
  • Pulley bearings are wooden pins — fast wear, no lubricant system (animal fat barely covers the bearing cap).

docs.title: Safety Boundaries
docs.text:
• When splitting, no one within 3 m of the wedge ejection direction; follow-up wedges must be driven in one by one in sequence — hammering a single wedge hard is forbidden.
  • Retting water carries putrefactive bacteria: wash hands after processing fiber and keep wounds away from retting water.
  • The bow drill string wrapping around fingers is a major injury source: string length and bow grip follow the 7.6 specifications.
  • Tripods, pulley sets, and rafts must pass 1.5-times static-load verification before use; rafts carrying people run at half load.
  • Swing the stone axe through empty air and confirm no one is behind before working (called-command system, see 9.5).

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• L1 proof-of-principle: complete a length of reverse-twist rope (no kinking, no unraveling ends); one successful fire lighting with the bow drill; produce one radial-split board.
  • L2 repeatable manufacture: make 10 m in each of the three rope diameter classes and complete static-load calibration, with the calibration values filed; the bow drill bores 5 aligned holes in hardwood (drilled through from two faces, deviation <2 mm); a composite-handled stone adze completes a surfacing task and passes the 1.5-times static-load haft test; a mortise-tenon sample passes the hold-load test.
  • L3 sustainable production: fiber feedstock from two or more sources, registered; monthly rope output and wear rate on the books; air-dried timber stock >3 months' use; every woodworking tool has regrind and re-lashing records; two or more people can independently make rope and bow drills per the files.

docs.title: Next-Step Dependencies
docs.text:
• Chapter 8: tar glue completes the hafting upgrade (joint level 4); resin collection; rope used in hanging tests and bound samples.
  • Chapter 9: the bow drill tooled up into a drill-press prototype; stone saws and frame saws; toolbox and workbench.
  • Chapter 10: farm tools (hoe, lei digging-stick plow) and storage containers (woven baskets, hemp rope).
  • Chapters 11–13: kiln timber framing, building timber structures, formwork, and scaffolding.
  • Chapters 20–21: the woodworking and lashing foundations for shafts, bearings, and belt transmission are established in this chapter.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Clay, Ash, and Natural Chemical Materials
docs.text: Part 2 · Survival, Fire, and Primitive Materials. This chapter establishes the first batch of "chemical capabilities": clay evaluation, ash alkali, pigments, binders, and — more important — the methodology of small-scale materials testing and recipe record-keeping. No pottery, no glassware: all liquid operations use gourds, shells, wooden troughs, and hide bags.

docs.title: Chapter Objectives
docs.text:
• Establish the complete workflow of clay prospecting — identification — performance evaluation (pre-study and stock preparation for pottery in Chapter 11).
  • Establish the collection and preparation processes for plant-ash lye leaching, limestone registration, natural pigments, resin and tar glues, and hide glue.
  • Establish the materials-testing system of "standard specimens + single-variable trials + record sheets" — this is the common starting point of the chemistry lineage (Lineage 5) and the information lineage (Lineage 6).
  • Deliverables: a clay test archive, the first tar glue and bond-strength data, and a recipe record system.

docs.title: Minimum Prerequisites
docs.text: Item Requirement Source Tools full stone tool set, woodworking tools, cordage, bow drill Chapters 5, 7 Heat source fire pit, charcoal bed, charcoal kiln (pyrolysis, roasting) Chapter 6 Measurement length and volume standards, record-keeping Chapter 3 Materials clay outcrops, wood ash, birch/pine, hides, ochre Chapter 2 resource map Containers gourds, large shells, fire-carved wooden troughs, hide bags Chapter 7 carving tools

docs.title: 8.1 How to Find and Identify Clay
docs.text:
Prospecting locations (in priority order): inner point bars of river bends (slowing water deposits fine grains); floodplains; lake and marsh margins; slope wash below springs; fresh-cut faces of landslides; subsoil turned up by termite mounds and animal burrows (fine-grained, sticky when wet).

Outcrop appearance criteria: sticks to shoes and hands when wet and takes a fingerprint when squeezed; on drying the surface shrinks into polygonal cracked blocks; the fracture is fine and grit-free; gray, yellow-brown, red-brown, or blue-gray color are all acceptable (color is used only for labeling, never for selection).

Three field tests (run in order; record every one):

Test Method Pass criterion Rejection criterion Lick test a soybean-sized bit of soil — touch to the tongue tip, then immediately spit it out and rinse (no chewing, no swallowing — guards against pathogens and grit wearing the teeth) fine and slick, no grit clearly gritty — sand content too high; pan it or change sites Coil test knead with water into a 6 mm diameter coil, roll it out to 15–20 cm does not break, no transverse cracks; if it can further be rolled to 3 mm and bent into a ring without breaking, plasticity is high snaps as soon as it is rolled — plasticity insufficient Shrinkage test knead a 4 cm clay ball, shade-dry 24 hours visible shrinkage but only hairlines on the surface deep cracks — shrinkage rate too high; temper must be added

Settling method for sand content (glassware-free version): fill a gourd, large shell, or fire-carved wooden trough with water, drop in an equal volume of soil sample, stir, and let stand 1–2 hours. Read the layers: bottom coarse sand, middle silt, top suspended fine clay. A clay layer more than 50% of the total thickness is excellent (rule of thumb, must be field-calibrated). Carefully pour off the top slurry — what you pour off is the initially panned fine clay.

Registration: for every source site, record location, description, three-test results, estimated workable quantity, and test-block numbers in the Chapter 2 resource-map format. Bring back a representative sample of 1–2 kg for the Section 8.2 and 8.6 tests.

docs.title: 8.2 Clay Plasticity, Shrinkage, and Cracking
docs.text:
Moisture-by-feel ladder: dry powder → damp (will not ball) → plastic zone (balls without sticking to the hands or cracking; feels like an earlobe) → soft mud → slurry. The plastic zone holds about 18%–28% water (rule of thumb, must be field-calibrated). All forming operations happen only in the plastic zone.

Wedging: before use, knead and press repeatedly (spiral kneading) for 10–15 minutes; purpose: homogenization + expelling air bubbles. Air bubbles will blister and crack during later drying and firing.

Shrinkage-rate measurement: make a standard clay bar (12×2×2 cm), scribe a 10 cm standard line on its surface (Chapter 3 scribed rule), and measure the line after shade-drying. Dry shrinkage = (10 − measured length)/10. Common range 5%–10% (rule of thumb, must be field-calibrated). The shrinkage rate of a given clay batch is the basis for later pottery layout scaling.

Temper (inclusions against shrinkage cracking):

Temper Grain size First-use ratio (by volume) Notes Washed quartz sand 0.5–1 mm 10%–20% general purpose Crushed shell powder coarse-sand grade 10%–20% good thermal-shock resistance Crushed old pottery — — unavailable in the pre-pottery period; activated after Chapter 11

Temper gradient test: make one set of test bars at each of 0%, 10%, 20%, 30% (per the Section 8.6 system), and select by "no cracks after drying + highest strength."

Four-cause crack triage: drying too fast (sun exposure, drafty spots) → slow the drying; inhomogeneity (bubbles, dry or wet lumps) → re-wedge from scratch; temper excessive or too coarse → lower the ratio; abrupt thickness change → thickness ratio ≤2:1 with a transition.

Drying procedure: shade-dry in a cool place under grass or large leaves; full-dry criterion: the bar lightens in color, feels cool-free against the lip, and its weight no longer drops. Record all data in the test sheet.

[Card 08-02 Clay: Three Field Tests and Settling Grading] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: 1–2 kg of soil from candidate deposits (a representative sample, surface soil scraped away); water; one control lump of known-good clay (for hand-feel reference only). Take samples from at least three spots per deposit — river-bend sediment is layered even within one site.
  2. Tools required: a stone flake (to cut a fresh test face), a wooden trough or gourd or large shell for settling (must show layers visibly), scored rule (Chapter 3), record sheet. Calibration source: rule scored against the Chapter 3 standard rod; settling fractions read by eye, no instrument.
  3. Sequence and control points: lick test → ribbon test → shrinkage test → settling test for sand content, in that order, recording each. Control points: after the lick test spit it out and rinse — do not chew, do not swallow (pathogens and grit); the shrinkage test must run a full 24 hours — reading early mistakes "not yet dry" for "no cracking".
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: lick test passes = smooth and soapy, no grittiness; ribbon test = roll a 6 mm coil out to 15–20 cm without breaking or transverse cracks, and a 3 mm coil that still bends into a ring indicates high plasticity; shrinkage test = 4 cm ball air-dried 24 hours, fine surface checking only — deep cracks mean excessive shrinkage and call for temper; settling = equal volumes of soil and water, stir, stand 1–2 hours and read the layers (coarse sand at the bottom, silt in the middle, fine clay on top).
  5. Observations to record: per sample — deposit ID and spot / all three test results / settling fractions / estimated workable quantity / sampling date.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = all three tests pass (smooth, unbroken coil, fine checking only); rework = noticeable grittiness, wash and retest; scrap = deep shrinkage cracks that persist after tempering at 10–20% (that deposit is for coarse ware or brick only).
  7.
