Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) coil breaks at once → plasticity short, check sand content from the settling test first, then consider blending in a more plastic clay; (2) deep shrinkage cracks → excess shrinkage, retest with 10% and 20% washed quartz sand (0.5–1 mm) temper; (3) settling layers unreadable → not stood long enough or water too turbid; (4) heavy grittiness on the lick test → high-sand deposit, use as temper or brick clay only.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one complete three-test plus settling record; L2 = records for three deposits that allow ranking them by data; L3 = a second person retests the same sample from this card and reaches the same conclusions (if not, the criteria in this card are still too soft and need rewriting).

docs.title: 8.3 Wood Ash, Limestone, and Other Basic Feedstocks
docs.text:
Wood-ash composition (qualitative description + engineering uses): mainly potassium carbonate, calcium and magnesium carbonates, phosphates, silicates, and traces of sodium. Hardwood ash and softwood ash differ in their potassium/calcium ratio; grass-straw ash is silica-rich. Ash is the only alkali source obtainable at scale in this stage.

Lye (ash water) leaching:

  • Ratio: ash:water = 1:3 to 1:5 (by volume, measured with the Chapter 3 standard wooden bucket).
  • Process: suspend the ash in a wooden trough or hide bag to steep 2–4 hours (rule of thumb, must be field-calibrated), stir twice, let settle, pour off the clear liquid; a second leach can raise the concentration.
  • Criterion: a slippery feel = strong alkalinity (the feel test is qualitative — it judges presence, not concentration).
  • Egg-floating concentration grades (completed in v2: upgrading "slippery" into comparable grades): put a fresh egg into the lye — sinks to the bottom = weak (about the 5% grade and below); hangs half-suspended upright = medium (about 5–10%); floats with the exposed top about the size of a thumb = strong (about the 10–15% grade) (an empirical correspondence for potassium carbonate solutions, must be field-calibrated: mix your own solutions of known grades and measure this egg's corresponding postures — egg size affects posture, so each team calibrates with its own eggs). Use the medium/strong grades for soapmaking and the weak grade for leaching and re-leaching; record egg posture and use together, batch by batch, to build the team's "egg-posture–use" table. Eggs washed after use remain edible (brief lye soaking is harmless).
  • Uses (at this stage): cleaning greasy tools and degreasing hides; small trials of hemp retting to assist degumming; the alkali source for later saponification soapmaking (formal saponification in Chapter 23).
  • Warning: lye corrodes skin and eyes; rinse after handling; keep it off wounds; its containers are dedicated and marked (Section 8.4 pigment marking).

Limestone identification (this chapter only identifies and stocks it; calcining is in Chapter 13):

  • Appearance: gray-white, fine-grained, dense, usually bedded; hardness about 3 (a bone flake barely scratches it; quartz scratches it easily).
  • Acid test (natural acid source): drop sorrel-leaf juice or soured fruit pulp on a freshly scratched face; fizzing = carbonate (calcite). Powder that fizzes slowly may be dolomite — note the distinction when registering.
  • Distinguishing from quartzite: quartzite is hardness 7 and quartz cannot scratch it; limestone takes a white scratch from quartz and fizzes.
  • Registration: site location, estimated quantity, apparent purity (how many impurity vein lines), into the resource map.

Other basic feedstock registration checklist (location, estimated quantity, verification test, intended use): salt (salt springs, salt earth, sea salt — taste test and evaporation residue); sulfur (yellow crystalline blocks in volcanic areas; blue flame and acrid fumes when burned — register, do not mine; handled in Chapter 23); trona (white frost on alkaline lakes); bitumen/petroleum seeps (black, sticky, flammable); quartz sand (abrasive and Chapter 14 glass feedstock; grain criteria: rounded grains, silt-free, 0.1–0.5 mm); ochre ore (8.4); graphite (black shiny scratch mark; register).

[Card 08-01 Lye Extraction and the Floating-Egg Scale] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: wood ash (hardwood ash preferred — higher potassium-to-calcium ratio, stronger lye; softwood ash is weak — never mix and record them as one); water; one fresh egg (for the floating test; wash and reuse); a dedicated, clearly marked lye vessel (red stripe, see 8.4). Ash must be stored dry; once it cakes from damp, extraction yield drops.
  2. Tools required: standard wooden measure (Chapter 3, for the volume ratio), wooden trough or hide bag for steeping, stirring stick, a dedicated marked lye container. Calibration source: ratio measured by volume with the same measure every time; strength graded by the floating egg, no instrument.
  3. Sequence and control points: ash into vessel → add water at the volume ratio → steep 2–4 hours → stir twice midway → stand → decant the clear supernatant → second extraction if a stronger liquor is needed. Control points: steeping time and stir count; decant only after standing — liquor carrying grit etches unevenly and clogs.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: ash-to-water 1:3 to 1:5 by volume; steep 2–4 hours (empirical, calibrate against your ash on site); stir twice. Floating-egg scale (upgrades "feels slippery" to a comparable grade): fresh egg in the liquor — sinks = weak (below about 5%); stands half-suspended = medium (about 5–10%); floats = strong. The hand-feel test only tells presence, not strength, and cannot replace the egg scale.
  5. Observations to record: per batch — ash type (hardwood / softwood / mixed) / volume ratio / steeping time / stir count / egg grade / intended use (cleaning, degreasing, retting, soap-making feedstock).
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = egg grade meets what that use requires; rework = grade too low, run a second extraction or steep longer and retest; scrap = no soapy feel and the egg sinks flat (ash spent or not wood ash — start over with fresh ash).
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) lye too weak → check ash type first (softwood ash is low in potassium), then steeping time; (2) turbid liquor → insufficient standing or unfiltered grit; (3) large strength difference between two extractions from the same batch → incomplete records, go back and record ash type and time; (4) corrosive injury → lye burns skin and eyes; rinse after handling, keep away from wounds — this belongs at the head of the card, not in a footnote.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one batch plus egg-grade record; L2 = one hardwood and one softwood batch with the grade difference documented; L3 = a second person makes the same grade from this card alone, and both judge the egg consistently.

[Card 08-04 Plant Acid: Extraction and Use in the Carbonate Test] (eight fields)

Scope note: this card covers only extracting an acid liquor for the limestone test, all of it supported by the body text. The "fruit-mash acidification" in the original index entry has no established process in the text, so it is not written here — better a gap than an invention. A proper vinegar process would need its own chapter.

  1. Input materials: sorrel leaves (or any plant leaf with a clear sour taste) or soured fruit mash, either one; a freshly cut face on the rock being tested (it must be freshly cut — a weathered face will not fizz and will make limestone look like quartzite).
  2. Tools required: stone mortar (crushing), cloth (wringing), reed or thin bamboo tube (for dropping, more controlled than a finger), record tablet.
  3. Sequence and control points: gather leaves → crush in the mortar → wring the juice through cloth into a small vessel → drop one drop onto the fresh face with the tube → watch for fizzing. Control points: freshness of the cut face; drop size just enough to bead and not run off.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: fizzing = carbonate (calcite group, i.e. limestone); slow fizzing may be dolomite and must be recorded separately; no fizzing = not a carbonate. Distinguishing from quartzite requires both checks: quartzite has hardness 7 and quartz will not scratch it; limestone is scratched white by quartz and fizzes.
  5. Observations to record: per site — acid source (sorrel juice / fruit mash) / position of the cut / fizzing speed / whether the hardness test agreed.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = acid and hardness tests agree and clearly separate limestone from quartzite; rework = acid too weak (change source or concentrate) or face weathered (recut); scrap = the two tests contradict and no verdict is possible — do not list that site as limestone for now.
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) nothing fizzes anywhere → check acid strength first, then whether the face is weathered; (2) fizzes but slowly → possibly dolomite, record as "undetermined" rather than using it as pure limestone; (3) quartzite mistaken for limestone → the fizzing was read without the hardness test; always run both.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = acid and hardness record for one site; L2 = three sites, at least one judged non-carbonate, with records that reproduce the judgment; L3 = a second person judges the same batch from this card alone with the same conclusions.

docs.title: 8.4 Natural Pigments and Surface Treatment
docs.text:
Pigment mineral sources and color families:

Color Source Notes Red hematite (reddish-brown streak) streak tested by scratching on a coarse stone slab Yellow-brown limonite/goethite — Black manganese ore; carbon black (collected from resinous-fire smoke) carbon black is easiest to obtain and the most stable White chalk, kaolin distinguish from limestone: kaolin does not fizz with acid White (substitute) shell powder burned, then ground fine

Processing workflow: smash → dry-grind on a stone anvil → water-settling classification: stir the fine powder into water in a trough to cloud it, let stand briefly, pour the suspended upper layer into a second trough, and after settling keep the bottom — this yields the fine pigment fraction; repeat 2–3 times for finer grades. After settling, fineness passes when "rubbed between the fingers it feels grain-free."

Mixing: pigment slurry + binder (gum solution 8.5, animal fat, or egg white), starting from 2:1 by volume (rule of thumb, must be field-calibrated). Paint a stripe on a sample board (a planed board or stone slab) for every batch and number it; record recipe and date.

Uses (the three formal uses at this stage):

  1. Tool and container marking: ownership, numbering, hazards (red stripe on lye containers) — the first carrier of the information lineage.
  2. Test specimen numbering: one-to-one correspondence with the Section 8.6 record sheets.
  3. Wood surface treatment: many thin rubs of animal fat (waterproofing); hot-melt beeswax coating (in beekeeping regions); pine-resin coating (8.5); smoke-blackening (insect repellence, decoration).

docs.title: 8.5 Resins, Plant Gums, and Natural Binder Materials
docs.text:
Pine resin collection:

  • Living-tree cuts: with a stone-flake knife cut a slanted downward V-groove into the trunk, stopping 1–2 cm below the cambium; girdling is strictly forbidden (girdling kills the tree). ≤3 cuts per tree per season.
  • Collecting: fit a birch-bark gutter at the lower end of the cut and collect every 1–2 weeks; also gather hardened resin lumps from old tree scars.
  • Processing: warm fresh resin until it thins and use it at once; long storage volatilizes and hardens it — it can be restored with gentle heat (low fire, do not boil; near flames there is flash-fire risk).

Birch-bark tar (the first high-strength glue; pottery-free method):

  1. Roll birch bark (scrape off the hard outer rind, use the inner layer) into a tight solid cylinder 5–8 cm in diameter.
  2. Bury the bark cylinder upright in a dirt pit, tamp soil firmly around it, leave a small hole at the top, and bank a charcoal fire around the pit.
  3. After 1–2 hours of sealed pyrolysis (rule of thumb, must be field-calibrated), withdraw the fire; once cool, dig it out and scrape the glossy black tar from the cylinder's inner wall and core.
  4. Pass criterion: draws threads while warm, still slightly tacky and plastic when cold; brittle and hard = overburned; thin and runny = underburned.

Principle: oxygen-starved pyrolysis converts betulin and other constituents of birch bark into sticky tar; the dirt pit is the "pottery-free dry-distillation retort." Yield is low (a few grams to a few tens of grams per cylinder), but the cost per run is extremely low and it can be repeated indefinitely.

Hafting glue recipe (parts by volume): tar 2 + fine charcoal powder 1 + dry grass fiber or crumbled moss 0.5. Apply warm to the blade–handle mating faces, assemble and bind while hot; it sets on cooling.

Plant gums: dry gum lumps exuded by acacia and Prunus-type trunks, dissolved in water into a paste — low strength, used for pigment binding and light-duty joining; root-starch paste gelatinized in hot water — light adhesive for the pre-paper era.

Hide glue (gelatin precursor; stone-boiling bypasses the container bottleneck):

  • Feedstock: hide offcuts and scraps, minced fascia.
  • Process: fill a hide bag with water and the stock, drop in fist-sized fire-heated cobbles (stone-boiling), and swap stones to hold 60–80°C (by feel, "hot but not touchable for long") for 4–8 hours (rule of thumb, must be field-calibrated); reduce the liquid until it coats a spoon; it sets to a jelly on cooling.
  • Limitations: make fresh and use at once; spoils easily in hot humid weather; dried gel slabs store well and rehydrate for reuse (empirical method — register and verify). Scaling up awaits Chapter 11 pottery (direct boiling becomes possible).

Bond-strength test (rough quantification): standard lap specimens — two planed wood strips lapped 3×3 cm; after the glue cures 24 hours: first break by hand (three force grades: opens with a light pull / opens with a hard pull / will not open), then hang weights in increasing steps until it separates; record the separation load and the failure face (glue-line failure = weak glue; wood tear = glue stronger than the wood). n≥3 per recipe.

Storage: tar lumps wrapped in leaves and kept in a cool place; gum lumps stored dry; lye and glue kept in separate zones. [Card 08-03 Birch-Bark Tar and Hafting Glue] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: inner birch bark (outer crust scraped off, inner layer only); fine charcoal powder (sieved from the Chapter 6 bed); dry grass fiber or chopped moss (cut under 5 mm); soil (for sealing the pit). Peel and roll the bark fresh — dried inner bark goes brittle, will not roll tight, and yield drops sharply.
  2. Tools required: flake knife (scraping the outer crust), earthen pit (or a spent clay pot after Chapter 11), receiving vessel (bark roll or broad leaf). Calibration source: no thermometer — judge the fire by the color and consistency of tar seeping from the wall; pyrolysis time calibrated on site against roll diameter and weather.
  3. Sequence and control points: roll bark tight into a solid cylinder 5–8 cm across → stand it upright in the pit, backfill and tamp the soil → leave a small hole at the top → heap charcoal around the pit → pyrolyse 1–2 hours → pull the fire, let cool → scrape the glossy black tar from the inner wall and core. Control points: the backfill must be tamped (leaks burn the charge to ash) and the top hole must not be omitted (it is the vent; plugged, the roll can burst).
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: roll diameter 5–8 cm; pyrolysis 1–2 hours (empirical, calibrate on site); three acceptance signs — draws a thread when warm and stays slightly tacky and workable when cold = good; brittle and non-tacky = over-fired; runny = under-fired. Hafting glue (parts by volume): tar 2 + fine charcoal 1 + dry grass fiber 0.5, applied warm to the blade-handle interface, assembled and lashed while hot, set on cooling.
  5. Observations to record: per roll — bark quantity / diameter / pyrolysis time / yield in grams / consistency grade (threads / brittle / runny) / weather.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = draws a thread and stays tacky when cold; rework = under-fired and runny, return to the pit in 20-minute steps, checking between; scrap = over-fired, brittle and non-tacky (still usable as charcoal powder, so not true waste).
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) very low yield → check whether the roll was tight first, then whether the soil seal leaked; (2) tar brittle → fire too hot or too long (over-fired); (3) tar runny and will not glue → under-fired, return to heat; (4) joints crack after gluing → too much charcoal or fiber in the mix, or assembly was not done while hot; (5) ignition → tar is flammable near flame; clear a flame-free radius around the retort, the same discipline as the fire rules in 6.8.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one roll of acceptable tar plus consistency record; L2 = five consecutive rolls with comparable yield and grade, and at least one tool glued with the hafting mix that passes a load test; L3 = a second person produces the same grade from this card alone, with yields within 50% of each other (a wider gap points to technique or bark source differences).

docs.title: 8.6 How to Run Small-Scale Materials Tests
docs.text:
Five principles of testing:

  1. Single variable: change one factor at a time (recipe, water content, drying method, firing temperature).
  2. Control: every group must have a baseline group (the variable left unchanged).
  3. Repetition: n≥3 per group; take the median result.
  4. Standard specimens: unified dimensions — clay bar 12×2×2 cm, clay ball 4 cm, glue lap 3×3 cm, cord sample 50 cm.
  5. Full records: failed specimens are kept and recorded like any other; failure data carry the same weight as success data.

Standard specimen library: mark finished specimens with scribed numbers (bow-drill tip or stone-flake marks) + pigment color dots (8.4); store them dry on racks off the ground; re-inspect once a month (moisture uptake and warping, cracking, mold spots).

Record-sheet template (wooden tablet):

Field Example Number/date T-011 / before the rainy season of Restart Year 3 Objective compare the dry-crack rate of East Slope clay with 20% sand temper Materials East Slope clay batch 2, river sand sieved 0.5–1 mm Recipe clay 4 : sand 1 (volume, by bucket) Process parameters wedged 12 minutes; shade-dried 48 hours Environment overcast; humidity by feel "damp" Result 1 of 3 pieces with hairlines; dry shrinkage 7% (10 cm line → 9.3 cm) Conclusion hairlines acceptable; proceed to firing trial Next step make fire-baked test pieces at the same recipe

Worked example — preliminary design for "the local best pottery recipe": 3 clay sources × 3 sand ratios (0/10/20%) = 9 groups × 3 pieces = 27 pieces, with unified drying and bake trial (15 minutes on a charcoal bed), graded (no crack / hairline / cracked / shattered). This design yields the starting recipe for Chapter 11.

docs.title: 8.7 How to Record Recipes and Process Parameters
docs.text:
Record carriers (pre-paper stage):

Carrier How made Use Wooden tablet planed softwood board + charcoal pencil (a charred, pointed charcoal stick) day-to-day test records; can be scraped and rewritten Birch bark large sheets stripped and flattened; written in charcoal pencil duplicate copies, carrying Notched stone/wood symbols cut with a stone flake permanent key data (baselines, recipe numbers) Knots + pigment marks — memory aids; never the primary archive

Storage: dry and off the ground, rodent-proof; two copies stored in different places (one fire must not destroy the whole archive).

Measurement discipline (Iron Law: "add to taste" is forbidden):

  • All ratios use volume standards: self-made wooden buckets (verified against the Chapter 3 baseline), mussel shells (dedicated after their capacity is calibrated), the standard rod (per the Chapter 3 length units).
  • Water content is described by the "feel ladder + coil criteria" (8.2), never as "add some water."
  • Temperature is described by fire position + the state of a standard specimen (6.7), never as "burn for a while."

Record-field discipline: date, objective, materials (source + batch number), recipe, process, environment, result, conclusion, next step — a missing field voids the record.

Version management (implementing the Chapter 4 rules): a recipe change must take a new number (T-011 → T-011b) and never overwrite the old version; failed recipes are kept with the cause of failure noted.

Inheritance test: a novice independently reproduces the result once from the records; a dimensional deviation >15% counts as a gap in the records — review the process for holes and backfill the record. The final acceptance of an archive is not "it is all written down" but "someone else can follow it and succeed."

docs.title: Capability Boundary
docs.text: Can do: clay three-test screening and temper pre-studies; ash-alkali leaching and egg-floating grading; natural acid preparation (sorrel/vinegar); bitumen tar collection and glue compounding; pigment and marking systems. Explicitly cannot do: quantitative concentration (pH and a temperature scale wait until after Chapter 25); lye concentration by crystallization (awaits pottery). External dependencies: none.

docs.title: Master Parameter Table
docs.text: Parameter Value Class Ash:water leaching 1:3–5 (by volume) empirical Egg-floating grades sinks = weak / upright = medium / top exposed = strong ◎ comparative method, calibrated with this team's eggs Clay sand-content verdict settling clay layer >50% is excellent empirical Tar glue firing point leave the fire once it draws threads without breaking ◎ hand-feel technique

docs.title: Failure Modes and Diagnosis
docs.text: Symptom Candidate causes (by probability) Remedy Lye has no slippery feel ash got damp and lost its potassium / too much water switch to dry ash; re-leach with less water Egg-floating readings drift egg sizes differ / slurry temperature differs dedicate a calibration egg; read at the same temperature Glue cracks brittle tar boiled too hard blend in fat to soften; re-boil on a lower fire Clay "false plasticity" high sand content misjudged re-check with the settling method

docs.title: A. Existing Tools List
docs.text:
• Chapter 5 full stone tool set; Chapter 7 woodworking tools, bow drill, cordage, tripod; Chapter 6 full heat sources.
  • Chapter 3 measurement and recording instruments.

docs.title: B. New Tools in This Chapter
docs.text: Tool Specification Made from Clay test kit (standard bar mold, scribed rule) 12×2×2 cm Chapter 7 woodworking Settling trough gourd/shell/fire-carved wooden trough Chapter 7 Grinding slab + twin water-settling troughs stone anvil + wooden trough Chapters 5, 7 Lye leaching barrel wooden trough/hide bag + marking 7 + 8.4 pigment marking Tar pit (pottery-free dry distillation) dirt pit + bark cylinder Chapter 6 charcoal fire Stone-boiling bag hide bag + cobbles Chapter 6 heated stones Hafting glue, plant gums, hide glue see 8.5 this chapter's processes Standard specimen library and wooden-tablet archive see 8.6, 8.7 this chapter's systems

docs.title: C. Unresolved Dependencies
docs.text:
• Boil-proof containers (pottery, Chapter 11): lye concentration, hide-glue boiling, and saponification are all constrained; at this stage only leaching and stone-boiling are possible.
  • Quantitative concentration and temperature measurement: lye strength and fire temperature stay qualitative; pH and a temperature scale come in Chapters 25–27.
  • Lime calcining (Chapter 13) and mortar: this chapter only completes limestone identification and stock preparation.
  • High-purity reagents and glassware (Chapters 14, 26): the precision ceiling of all liquid chemistry is constrained by container material.

docs.title: Safety Boundary
docs.text:
• Wear dry-leaf glove pads for lye work and guard against splashes into the eyes; containers are always marked with a red stripe and never mixed with tableware.
  • Do not process pyrite or sulfur ore samples near fire (burning gives off an irritant gas).
  • While the tar pit smolders, no one may bend over the vent hole; do not open the pit before the fire is withdrawn and it cools.
  • Swap stone-boiling stones with wooden tongs or a hide pad; never grab hot stones with wet hands.
  • Keep the specimen library away from fire and rodent runs; discard moldy specimens and record it.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• L1 proof-of-principle: complete clay test bars passing the three tests; one successful birch-bark tar run that bonds a lap joint of wood securely.
  • L2 repeatable manufacture: 2 or more clay sites pass the three tests and are archived; tar succeeds 3 times running with bond-strength test data on file (at least 1 case at wood-tear grade); ash lye leaching reproducible; the 9-group "best recipe" pre-study completed with clear conclusions.
  • L3 sustainable production: tar feedstock (birch) registered and harvested within the cut quota; monthly-output and loss accounts kept for glue, pigments, and lye; the record system independently reproduced and verified by a second person on ≥1 item; specimen-library monthly inspection in execution.

docs.title: Next-Step Dependencies
docs.text:
• Chapter 9: tar glue goes straight into the hafting upgrade (connection level 4); pigment marking enters the tool-numbering system.
  • Chapter 10: moisture-proofing for basket grain storage; smoke and ash applications in storage.
  • Chapter 11: clay recipe and shrinkage data feed the first pottery jar directly; pottery repays this chapter's container bottleneck.
  • Chapter 13: limestone calcining and mortar.
  • Chapter 14: the quartz-sand registry feeds glass feedstock evaluation.
  • Chapter 23: the chemistry mainline — ash alkali, acids/bases/salts, saponification, purification.

docs.title: Chapter 9: The First Truly Reusable Tool Kit
docs.text: Part 2 · Survival, Fire, and Primitive Materials (final chapter of this part). The previous four chapters accumulated stone tools, fire, wood and cordage, clay and glue; this chapter combines them into a tool system that is reusable, repairable, and replicable: composite tools, tooling (drills, saws, grinding, clamping), workbenches and tool kits, plus multi-person collaboration and throughput systems. This part's acceptance goal: the basic capabilities of gathering materials, making tools, controlling fire, working wood, and recording processes.

docs.title: Chapter Objectives
docs.text:
• Complete the upgrade from "placeholder tools" to "proper composite tools": the four-way joint of hafting standard + glue + wedge lock + lashing.
  • Establish the first tooling: sand-abrasive drilling (stone/bone/wood), bow saw and cord saw, grinding platforms.
  • Establish the first set of fixtures and workbench (clamping is the precondition of repeatable precision).
  • Establish the "tools that make tools" bootstrap route, standard parts, and a repair system.
  • Establish multi-person task breakdown and the first basic tool kit.
  • Deliverables: one qualified tool kit per workstation + ledger + repair records.

docs.title: Minimum Prerequisites
docs.text: Item Requirement Source Tools full stone tool set, woodworking tools, bow drill, three cord grades Chapters 5, 7 Heat source fire pit, charcoal bed, charcoal Chapter 6 Materials tar glue, rawhide strips, sinew, tempered clay, pigments Chapter 8, 7.3 Records angle board, scribed rule, numbering system Chapters 3, 8

docs.title: 9.1 Combining Stone and Wood
docs.text:
Complete composite-tool specification table:

Tool Edge angle Handle length Haft angle Use boundary Stone axe 60°–80° 60–90 cm edge line perpendicular to the handle axis felling, splitting Stone adze 45°–60° 30–45 cm edge at 60°–75° to the handle smoothing, gouging Stone knife 20°–40° 15–25 cm straight handle or side slot cutting Stone chisel 30°–50° 15–20 cm coaxial gouging, prying; hammering forbidden Scraper 45°–70° 10–15 cm coaxial scraping smooth

Wooden caliper (completed in v2: the first "reading" measuring tool — a size comparator for the pre-iron age): nail or scribe a fixed straight stop (reference jaw) at one end of a hardwood strip; on the strip, scribe lines at the standard rod's "finger-width" graduations to position the sliding jaw — after the sliding jaw (a small straight-stop block) is pressed against the workpiece, press-scribe its edge line onto the strip and read the nearest graduation. Zero calibration: with both jaws closed, the sliding jaw's edge should press on the zero line — if it is off, shim thin wood slivers behind the back of the jaw to correct, then fix with a scorched brand on the hardwood strip + a dot of tar (wire waits for Chapters 17–18). Precision: finger-width graduations + eyeballed half-finger (about the 5–8 mm grade, rule of thumb) — stronger than "looks about right," one grade weaker than the Chapter 20 snap gauge; it is made precisely so that "the same size" has evidence before a snap gauge exists. Re-check zero weekly (wood swells and shrinks; tighten the schedule in the wet season).

[Card 09-03 Wooden Caliper Making and Zero Calibration] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: one hardwood strip (the beam); two straight-stop blocks (reference jaw and sliding jaw); thin wood slivers (for shimming the zero); tar (for fixing the setting).
  2. Tools required: marking tool (to scribe the standard rod's "finger" graduations), charcoal for branding the hardwood beam (scorch marks fix the lines), grinding stone (truing the jaw faces). Calibration source: the graduations are taken from the standard rod's finger-level sub-units (Chapter 3); graduations are never self-invented.
  3. Sequence and control points: nail or scribe the fixed straight stop at one end (reference jaw) → scribe finger graduations along the beam → press the sliding jaw against the workpiece and press-scribe its edge line onto the beam, reading the nearest graduation → zero calibration (with both jaws closed the sliding jaw's edge should press the zero line) → if off, shim thin slivers behind the back of the jaw → fix with a scorch brand plus a dot of tar → re-check weekly. Control points: no use before the zero is calibrated; tighten the re-check schedule in the wet season.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: precision = finger-width graduations + eyeballed half-finger (about the 5–8 mm grade, empirical value — must be calibrated to local conditions); zero re-checked weekly, tighter in the wet season; readings are comparative only (same size / half a finger off), never absolute.
  5. Observations to record: caliper number / beam wet-dry state / zero re-check date and deviation (in half-finger units) / workpiece number and reading / comparison against the template.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = the zero sits on the zero line and two readings of the same piece agree; rework = the zero drifts — re-shim and re-fix; scrap = the beam cracks or the graduations wear flat (remake from dry stock; old readings may not be carried over).
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) readings drift → check the zero first (moisture swelling is the first cause), then whether the jaw faces are rounded (they must be trued flat), last whether the measurement was taken on a sloped face; (2) two readings of the same piece differ by more than half a finger → first check whether the sliding jaw is pressed home (release it and it backs off), then whether the graduations are worn flat; (3) the zero will not stay calibrated → first check whether the shim is too thick (slivers, not a thick shim), then whether the jaw back is crushed (change the jaw); (4) it is always one grade off against the template → first check whether the graduations came from the standard rod (self-invented graduations always differ), then whether the measurement points match.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one caliper that can read "half a finger off" plus a zero re-check record; L2 = weekly re-checks for two consecutive months, with the readings used for hole-diameter judgments; L3 = a second person re-checks the same caliper from this card alone and the zero agrees.

Anti-vibration handle wedge (completed in v2): driven wedge locks loosen under long-term impact; use all three anti-loosening methods together — (1) double-wedge cross: drive one wedge with the grain and one cross-grain, interleaved (their expansion locks each other); (2) dip the wedges in glue (tar glue) before driving to fill the gaps; (3) one wrap of wire/cord as a collar at the handle end to hold down the wedge mouth. Weekly inspection: the moment a gap shows at the wedge mouth, re-drive it (clean grit out of the gap first — sand crushes wood fibers).

[Card 09-02 Anti-Vibration Double-Wedge Method] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: two hardwood wedges (one with the grain, one cross-grain; 7.5 specification: face angle 8°–12°, 2–3 mm blunt head); tar glue; cord (or wire after Chapters 17–18) for the end collar.
  2. Tools required: wooden mallet (driving), scraper (cleaning the gap), angle board (checking the wedge face angle), marking tool. Calibration source: wedge face angle checked against the angle board (the 45/60/90 hard grades plus the approximate grade); wedge dimensions per 7.5.
  3. Sequence and control points: clean the gap (grit must go — sand crushes wood fibers) → drive the first wedge with the grain → drive the second cross-grain, interleaved (their expansion locks each other) → dip the wedges in glue to fill the gaps → one collar wrap at the handle end to hold the wedge mouth down → weekly check. Control points: the two wedges must be one with and one across the grain (two in the same direction is just a single wedge).
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: wedge face angle 8°–12° (empirical value — must be calibrated to local conditions); blunt head 2–3 mm; wedges dipped in glue; one collar wrap at the handle end; inspection every week; drive a dry wedge into a wet hole (it locks as the hole dries and shrinks).
  5. Observations to record: tool number / directions of the two wedges (with grain, cross-grain) / wedge face angle (angle-board check) / dipped or not / collar turns / gap at the wedge mouth at each weekly check (present or not, width eyeballed).
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = both wedges interleaved and seated, no gap at the mouth, collar holding the mouth down; rework = a gap shows — clean it and re-drive (never just hammer it tighter without cleaning); scrap = the handle end splits at the mouth (fibers already crushed) — change the handle or shorten it.
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) the wedge backs out within days → first check whether only one wedge was driven (a single wedge always backs out), then whether both run the same way (one must be cross-grain); (2) it still backs out after re-driving → first check whether grit was cleaned from the gap, then whether the wedges were dipped in glue; (3) the wedge splits the handle end → first check whether the face angle left the 8°–12° range, then whether the blunt head has mushroomed; (4) the end collar loosens → re-wrap at the weekly check (the collar holds the wedge mouth down; it is not decoration).
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one tool completed with double-wedge cross, glue dip, and collar; L2 = an unbroken run of weekly check records with no gap at the wedge mouth; L3 = a second person re-wedges the same handle from this card alone with the same wedge directions and face angles, and the weekly check shows no gap.

Standard hafting procedure (four-way joint):

  1. Cut the slot: fire-carving sets the slot lines (6.5) → deepen with the stone chisel → dress the walls with the scraper. Slot width = blade thickness with 0.5–1 mm interference; slot depth = 2/3 of the blade height.
  2. Apply glue: tar glue (8.5 recipe), warmed, coating the full blade-slot mating faces.
  3. Seat the blade: set the blade and align the force line — the striking-force direction must pass through the midpoint of the cutting edge and the handle axis (verify with lines drawn on the bench top).
  4. Lash: with wet rawhide strip or sinew (7.3), wrap the slot mouth in a cross pattern, 5 turns above and 5 below; it self-locks as it dries and shrinks.
  5. Wedge lock: drive a hardwood wedge with the grain into the slot-mouth end face until it is fully expanded.
  6. Cure: rest 24 hours before issue.

Acceptance (three escalating stages): 20 air swings → 20 light chops into a wood block → 1 day of normal use. Pass criteria: lashing displacement <2 mm; blade does not shift, no glue-crack sounds; no continuous cracking in the glue line. Failures go back for rework: heat to soften the glue (tar re-melts and re-bonds) → re-lash.

Tool anatomy essentials: handle diameter 3–3.5 cm (palm-fit rule; standard part in 9.4); the axe's balance point near the head, the adze's near the edge; straight-grained handles, no knots on load-bearing faces. Ranked main causes of hafting failure: force line off > glue layer too thick > uneven lashing > slot too wide.

[Card 09-01 Four-Way-Joint Hafting] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: blade (stone axe / adze / knife / chisel / scraper, per the 9.1 table); handle stock (straight-grained hardwood, handle diameter 3–3.5 cm); tar glue (8.5 recipe); wet rawhide strip or sinew (7.3); hardwood wedge (7.5 specification).
  2. Tools required: fire chisel and stone chisel (slot), scraper (dress the walls), wooden mallet (driving the wedge), bench scribing (aligning the force line), angle board (checking the haft angle). Calibration source: slot interference referenced to blade thickness; the haft angle per the 9.1 table (axe edge line perpendicular to the handle axis, adze 60°–75°) checked with the angle board.
  3. Sequence and control points: (1) cut the slot (width = blade thickness with 0.5–1 mm interference, depth = 2/3 of blade height) → (2) apply glue (warm, coating the full blade-slot mating faces) → (3) seat the blade on the force line (striking force through the edge midpoint and the handle axis, verified with bench lines) → (4) lash (cross pattern, 5 turns above and 5 below the slot mouth) → (5) wedge lock (drive a hardwood wedge with the grain until fully expanded) → (6) rest 24 hours. Control points: force-line alignment; the glue layer must not be thick.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: slot interference 0.5–1 mm; slot depth = 2/3 of blade height; 5 lashing turns above and below; 24 h cure; three-stage acceptance = 20 air swings → 20 light chops into a wood block → 1 day of normal use; pass criteria: lashing displacement <2 mm, blade does not shift, no continuous glue-line cracking; handle diameter 3–3.5 cm (palm-fit rule).
  5. Observations to record: tool number / edge angle and handle length (against the 9.1 table) / measured slot width / glue-layer thickness (eyeball) / lashing turn count / force-line check result / cure time / result of each acceptance stage.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = all three acceptance stages pass and lashing displacement <2 mm; rework = glue line cracked or lashing loose — heat to soften the glue (tar re-melts and re-bonds) and re-lash; scrap = the handle cracks or the slot is too wide to re-glue (shorten the handle for other work, recycle the blade blank).
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order (ranked by the text's main causes): (1) force line off (the first cause of blades leaving the handle and of handles snapping) → re-align on the bench so the striking force passes the edge midpoint and the handle axis; (2) glue layer too thick (the glue holds the mating faces apart) → heat, scrape thin, re-coat; (3) uneven lashing → re-lash 5 turns above and below in the cross pattern; (4) slot too wide (interference beyond 0.5–1 mm) → shorten the handle for other work or change the handle; (5) a gap at the wedge mouth → clean the grit out and re-drive.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one four-way-joint composite stone axe passing air swings and light chops; L2 = 3 axes in a row passing all of the 9.1 acceptance; L3 = a second person hafts from this card alone, passing all three stages with lashing displacement <2 mm.

docs.title: 9.2 Simple Drills, Saws, and Grinding Tools
docs.text:
Sand-abrasive drilling (this chapter's core new process):

  • Wood: bow drill (7.6) + stone drill point, direct cutting. 5–15 minutes per hole in 2 cm hardwood (rule of thumb, must be field-calibrated).
  • Stone and bone: cutting is not feasible; switch to abrasion grinding — hollow drill (bone tube, bamboo tube) + wet quartz-sand abrasive: press the tube drill against the workpiece, drive rotation with the bow drill, feed slurry every few turns, and lift every 20–30 seconds to clear the cuttings. Piercing a 1 cm stone slab takes about 2–6 hours (rule of thumb, must be field-calibrated); when the hole breaks through, a ring-shaped boss appears on the back face of the workpiece — a light tap knocks it free, leaving a clean round hole.
  • Drill wear goes on the books: change the bone tube's end every 2–3 holes; quartz-sand consumption counted by the bowl.

Two sawing routes:

Tool Making Use and efficiency Bow saw toothed stone flake (5.5 blank, tooth pitch 2–3 mm) lashed into a bow-shaped wooden frame and tensioned reciprocating sawing of wood: a 5 cm wooden pole in 20–40 minutes (rule of thumb, must be field-calibrated); cuts flatter than axe chopping Cord saw cord + wet quartz sand slicing stone slabs, shell, bone: the cord with abrasive slurry saws back and forth; slow but the kerf is flat and straight — can blank stone preforms for grinding

Grinding platform and workflow:

  1. Abrasive stone grades: coarse (scratches visible to the eye) — medium (felt by a fingernail) — fine (no grain feel); fix the coarse and medium stones between stop blocks on the workbench (9.3) to form the "grinding bench."
  2. Flat-grinding sequence: scribe with allowance → coarse-grind off the allowance → medium-grind to shape → fine sand on the slab + leather polish.
  3. Flatness self-check: mate the two workpieces' faces against each other — coat with charcoal dust and press; high spots show black; or sight against the light for a transmission gap; a gap <1 mm passes (checked against the Chapter 3 reference straightedge).
  4. Angle control: check against the wooden angle board (45°/60°/90°) as you grind.

Grinding a complete stone axe takes 3–8 hours (rule of thumb, must be field-calibrated); grinding is a slow process — throughput is maintained by division of labor (9.5).

[Card 09-04 Grinding-Bench Work and Angle-Board Checks] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: three abrasive-stone grades (coarse: scratches visible to the eye; medium: felt by a fingernail; fine: no grain feel); water and quartz sand (fine sand sprinkled on the slab); leather (polishing); the stone blank to be ground.
  2. Tools required: stop blocks (clamping the coarse and medium stones between the bench stops to form the grinding bench), wooden angle board (45°/60°/90°, Chapter 3 bootstrap), charcoal dust (flatness mating check), reference straightedge (Chapter 3). Calibration source: angle by fitting against the angle board and sighting the light gap; flatness by charcoal-dust mating of two workpieces or by light-gap sighting.
  3. Sequence and control points: scribe with allowance → coarse-grind off the allowance → medium-grind to shape → fine sand on the slab plus leather polish; check the edge angle against the angle board between every pass. Control points: grinding striations consistent in direction and parallel to the edge (the evidence the angle has not changed); keep the original edge angle throughout.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: flatness criterion = light gap <1 mm; the three hard angle grades 45/60/90 (approximate grade ±2–3°); grinding one stone axe takes 3–8 hours (empirical value — must be calibrated to local conditions); edge angles per the 9.1 table (axe 60°–80°, adze 45°–60°, chisel 30°–50°, scraper 45°–70°).
  5. Observations to record: workpiece number / stone grade used / angle-board check after each pass / striation direction / light-gap width / hours per piece / stone wear depth.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = light gap <1 mm, edge angle matching the angle board, striations parallel and same-direction; rework = the edge angle wanders — go back to coarse grinding, re-open the edge, and check pass by pass; scrap = over-ground (blade too thin or under template size) — demote to practice stock or make a smaller piece.
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) the ground edge angle wanders → first check whether the angle board was used between passes (no angle-board check is the first cause), then whether the stone face has hollowed (stop blocks not clamped), last whether the hand wobbles; (2) the ground face is not flat and the light gap varies → first check the stone face flatness (charcoal-dust mating of two workpieces), then whether the stop blocks are loose; (3) slow going, only scratches and no stock removed → first check whether the wrong stone grade is in use (coarse grinding needs the coarse grade), then whether the water was forgotten (coarse sandstone is ground wet); (4) edge chipping → first check whether grinding runs against the edge (it must follow the edge), then whether downward pressure is excessive.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one ground piece with an angle-board check and a light-gap record; L2 = one piece completed on each of the three stone grades, with hours and wear on the books; L3 = a second person grinds a piece to the same edge angle from this card alone (the angle-board fit shows the same light gap).

docs.title: 9.3 How to Make a Simple Workbench and Fixtures
docs.text:
Workbench: low post table — top slab 5–8 cm thick (riven board, 7.2), height 50–70 cm seated / 75–90 cm standing, four legs mortise-joined (7.5) + wedge locks, with cross rails between the legs against wobble. Plane one long edge of the top straight as this workstation's first straight-line reference (the physical extension of the Chapter 3 baseline). Drive stop blocks and stop pins into the top (into drilled holes) as planing stops.

Fixture lineage (clamping is the precondition of repeatable precision):

Fixture Structure Applies to Wedge-clamp groove V-groove cut into the benchtop; workpiece sits in the groove, wedges driven in on both sides round stock, handle shaping Rope-windlass clamp Π-shaped wooden frame + rope wound and twisted tight (windlass rod inserted into the rope loop and twisted; the spring-back self-locks) planing boards — the primitive vise Forked-branch clamp forked branch fixed to the bench edge or a ground anchor holding round work for drilling Ground anchor + foothold bent stake driven slantwise into the ground; workpiece held underfoot rough work on large pieces Hot-tar spot glue small parts spot-glued to a stone slab; heat to release drilling small parts, edge grinding (keeps hands away from the drill point)

Layout and positioning: bench reference edge + square (Chapter 3) for cross layout lines; for batch parts use templates: trace a qualified part's outline onto thin board to make the template, then work new parts against it; a light gap <1 mm passes — this stage's realization of the template-replication method (Iron Law 2: precision must have a source).

Workstation layout: light from the side (frontal light casts misleading shadows); keep the grinding bench and the drilling station apart (slurry and sawdust foul each other); posture: work surface near elbow height; leave two-person space at the bow-drill station (7.6).

docs.title: 9.4 How to Make the Tools That Make Tools
docs.text:
Bootstrap principle: every tool must be re-makeable from "other verified tools + recorded processes"; once a tool can only be repaired and not re-made, the system has a single point of dependency (the Chapter 1 three-tier definition).

Tool mother-machine prototypes (three bootstrap lines):

  1. Bow drill + bench fork clamp = rotary power head: bits are interchangeable (stone point for cutting / bone tube for abrasive grinding) — the drill-press prototype.
  2. Grinding-stone platform + stop blocks = flat-surface machining prototype: the stop blocks set the angle; grind the bench's reference edge; the reference edge then re-verifies the grinding stones — grinding and measuring calibrate each other.
  3. Template + slot location = replication template: the template is generated from a qualified part, and new parts are made to the template, realizing "replicate one size" (Iron Law 2).

Standard parts (the first step toward interchangeability):

Standard part Unified spec Use Handle diameter 3–3.5 cm (palm-fit rule) any tool handle swaps with the same grip feel Axe handle length 75 cm spare-part interchange Drill shaft 25×2.2 cm shared by bow drill and tube drill Cord diameter grades 3/6/10 mm lashing and hoisting tiers

Repair system (every tool registered):

Fault Remedy Process source Dull edge regrind, angle unchanged 7.8 Small chip (<3 mm) pressure-flake and redress 5.5 Large chip recover the blade blank and re-flake 5.5 Loose lashing re-lash per the standard lashing diagram 7.4 Glue failure hot re-melt and re-bond (a tar property) 8.5

Spare-parts stock (rule of thumb; calibrated against weekly consumption): stone-flake knives ≥5, stone drill points ≥3, bone-tube bits ≥2, cord coils ≥20 m, tar glue ≥2 lumps, rawhide strips ≥10, one spare each of coarse and fine grinding stones. Stock below the floor triggers replacement manufacture — never wait for run-out.

docs.title: 9.5 From Solo Handwork to Multi-Person Collaboration
docs.text:
Task-breakdown example (axe making, 7 stations): quarry → rough flaking → finish flaking → grinding → handle-slot cutting → hafting (glue + lashing + wedge) → inspection. One person end-to-end: 1–2 days per piece; a flow line of 3–5 people makes several pieces per day (rule of thumb, must be field-calibrated — backfill the ledger with this team's measured figures).

Two-person operating rules:

  • Large-piece flaking: one steadies the core (wood clamp + side stance), one strikes; the steadier stands 45° behind the striker's flank.
  • Bow-drill deep holes: one presses the cap and holds alignment, one draws the bow for power.
  • Carrying: unified commands ("lift — walk — set"); for long stock, call ahead and answer behind.

Quality responsibility system:

  • Every tool is marked with the maker's number (8.4 pigment marking) → traceable, repairable.
  • The inspector is independent of the maker; acceptance follows the 9.1 table and is signed (carved mark).
  • Rework rate goes on the books: a station whose rework rate stays above 20% (empirical criterion) goes back for retraining.

Master–apprentice transfer (landing the information lineage):

  1. Turn procedures into mnemonics: compress each key procedure into a chant (select — flake — dress — grind — glue — lash — wedge).
  2. Demonstrate + reproduce: the apprentice independently makes 3 pieces; all must pass 9.1 acceptance to graduate (L3 personnel criterion).
  3. Archive-reproduction examination: periodically draw one person to reproduce a specified process from the 8.7 records; deviation beyond limits triggers a revision of the record.

Safety collaboration iron rules: a 3 m exclusion zone around flaking splash; before swinging tools (axe, hammer), call out to anyone behind you; no hands in the bow-drill cord zone; clear slurry off the grinding bench promptly against slips.

[Card 09-05 Seven-Station Flow Line and Workstation Layout] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: blanks (stone and bone, sorted into the 9.7 three-way material rack); per-station consumables (tar glue, rawhide strips, sinew, quartz sand); archive cards (9.10, one card per tool).
  2. Tools required: station kits (flaking: hard hammer, soft hammer, pressure flaker; grinding: grinding bench; slotting: fire chisel and stone chisel; hafting: glue, wedge, lashing stock; inspection: template, angle board, wooden caliper). Calibration source: inspection tooling is the 9.4 standard parts, and the criteria are the 9.8 three-grade system.
  3. Sequence and control points: lay out the seven stations — quarry → rough flaking → finish flaking → grinding → handle-slot cutting → hafting (glue + lashing + wedge) → inspection → every piece travels with its card → the inspector, independent of the maker, signs (carved mark) against the 9.1 acceptance table. Control points: the inspector must not also be the maker; every piece carries the maker's number.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: one person end-to-end 1–2 days per piece; a flow line of 3–5 people makes several pieces per day (empirical value — must be calibrated to local conditions, backfilled with this team's measured figures); a rework rate staying above 20% (empirical criterion) means retraining; graduation = 3 pieces made independently, all passing 9.1 acceptance.
  5. Observations to record: station number / operator number / time each piece clears each station / rework cause per station / daily output / rework rate / material batch number.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = every piece clears all seven stations, passes the three-stage 9.1 acceptance, and has a complete card; rework = a station's rework rate above 20% — stop that station for retraining before rescheduling; scrap = the card is missing or the maker number untraceable (not issuable — send it back to the first station to be re-marked).
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) output will not rise → find the bottleneck station first (longest clearing time), then check whether one person is covering two stations (two-person rules: large-piece flaking, bow-drill deep holes, and carrying each have their division); (2) rework clusters at one station → first check the maker numbers (clustering means that station needs review), then whether material batches cluster (a source problem), last whether the specification itself is unsuitable (revise the 9.1 table); (3) pieces and cards do not match → first check whether station sign-offs were skipped, then whether the maker number was ground off; (4) cross-traffic injuries → first check whether the travel path crosses the drill station's cord zone (the "6"-shaped circuit of 9.7), then whether anyone swung before calling out.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one piece carried through all seven stations with its card on file; L2 = 3 pieces in a row passing all 9.1 acceptance with the rework rate on the books; L3 = two or more members graduated (3 pieces each passing acceptance) plus rework-rate and daily-output data used for scheduling.

docs.title: 9.6 The First Basic Tool Kit
docs.text:
Kit list (one standard workstation):

Class Items Quantity Spec/Source Cutting stone-flake knives, scrapers 5, 3 Chapter 5 Chopping stone axe, stone adze (composite handles) 2, 2 9.1 Drilling full bow-drill set, stone points, bone-tube bits, bearing caps 2 sets, 5, 2, 2 7.6 + 9.2 Sawing/grinding bow saw, cord saw, coarse grinding stone, fine grinding stone, quartz-sand bag 1 each, 2 each, 1 9.2 Clamping rope-windlass clamp, wedge set, forked sticks 1, 6, 2 9.3 Joining cord coils (coarse/fine), tar-glue lumps, rawhide strips, sinew bundles 20 m/50 m, 2, 10, 5 Chapters 7, 8 Measuring wooden straightedge, 5 m rope scale, plumb bob, angle board, scribed rule, templates 1 each Chapter 3, 9.3 Recording charcoal pencils, wooden tablets, pigment marking box several Chapter 8 Maintenance tallow box, grinding-dust brush (grass bundle), spare-parts box 1 each 7.8

Storage: wooden tool chest (mortise-and-tenon + rope-lashed lid, self-made with the 9.3 workmanship), 30 cm off the ground against damp, with a dried-grass pack and an ash pack inside (desiccant, changed each season).

Inventory system:

  • Weekly: functional visual check (edges, lashings, glue, cords).
  • Monthly: regrind, re-lash, restock to the floors.
  • Quarterly: full-chest teardown check + ledger reconciliation (records, objects, and locations all agree).

Ledger fields: number, name, maker's number, manufacture date, repair record, status (in use / spare / awaiting repair / scrapped). The tool chest itself is managed under the same system — it is also a tool.

docs.title: Capability Boundary
docs.text: Can do: standardized manufacture of the five composite-handled tool types; four-way-joint hafting and anti-vibration wedging; wooden-caliper measurement (± half a finger); a complete basic tooling set of grinding bench, rope-windlass clamp, and workbench; seven-station flow-line division of labor. Explicitly cannot do: metal edged tools (Part 4); reading-type measuring tools (the wooden caliper only reaches "comparative" grade); large-batch interchangeability (no standard-parts system). External dependencies: none.

docs.title: 9.7 Tool-Kit Master List and Workstation Layout
docs.text:
Tool classification ledger (six classes): the 9.6 list is arranged by use; the ledger files them under six classes, one page per class; during inventory, go class by class without skipping:

Class Covers Ledger points Floor Cutting stone-flake knives, scrapers, toothed stone flakes record edge length and chip count; edge <3 cm is downgraded cutting class total ≥8 Gouging stone chisels, stone adzes, fire-carving tools record measured edge angles (checked against the angle board) ≥3 Grinding coarse/medium/fine stones, sand bags, leather strips record stone wear depth; past half-worn, stage a replacement ≥1 each coarse and fine + sand ≥2 bowls Drilling bow drill, drill shafts, stone points, bone tubes, bearing caps record piercings per tube (9.2 counting) drill points ≥3, bone tubes ≥2 Clamping rope-windlass clamp, wedge set, forked sticks, templates number every wedge individually (wedges are small and easily mixed up or lost) wedges ≥6, clamps ≥2 Carrying cord coils, carrying poles, grass-bundle wrapping stock record the cord's cumulative meters and aging state (7.3 criteria) cord ≥20 m

Write the workstation number and the inventory date in each page's header; check the records against the objects piece by piece; one missing item is logged "missing" the same day and triggers replacement manufacture (9.10). Never conclude an inventory with "mostly complete" — an inventory has only three possible outputs: complete, missing (list the missing items), broken (list the broken items).

Workstation floor plan (text version): four zones and one circulation line around the workbench:

  • Workbench at the center, reference edge facing the side light (9.3 lighting rule).
  • Grinding bench about an arm-and-a-half to the workbench's front left (within 2 m), wet-sand work, stone slabs on the floor against mud; between it and the workbench stand the shavings bucket and the water bowl — slurry does not cross zones.
  • Drilling station to the workbench's front right, with room for two (cap-presser + bow-puller); nothing suspended overhead, no foot traffic in the cord rebound zone.
  • Stock rack against the rear wall: blank stock stored horizontally in three divisions (stone/bone/wood); marked-out blanks laid flat in a single layer, never stacked.
  • Finished-goods rack by the door: inspected pieces and pieces awaiting repair in separate sections, with a wooden tag standing between them (carve the character for "awaiting" to mark repairs).
  • Circulation line: stock rack → workbench → grinding bench → drilling station → workbench → finished-goods rack, looping in a "6"; never crossing, never cutting through the drilling station's cord zone; when two people work simultaneously, each keeps to one line (one bench, one line), and swapping positions requires setting down the workpiece first.

Fixed-position tool management (shadow board): hang a thin board inside the tool-chest lid or on the workstation wall; after placing every tool in its storage spot, trace its outline (charcoal pencil); a tool's return must land inside its silhouette. Triple payoff: missing tools visible at a glance (an empty silhouette is a missing tool — no need to dig through the ledger); wrong-tool returns exposed instantly (a round head does not fit a square silhouette); newcomers know every tool's home without memorizing. Rule: the shadow board is checked once at each weekly inspection; any silhouette-object mismatch is logged as a missing item; a borrowed tool must leave a wooden tag on its silhouette spot (carved with the borrower's number). This is the prototype of fixed-position management — the ancestor of the later machine-tool rule "tool in position means work in position."

docs.title: 9.8 Fine Grinding of Stone Tools
docs.text:
9.2 gave the grinding framework; this section completes the criteria of the three finishing procedures up to the third tier.

Hole-diameter and perpendicularity criteria for tube drilling:

  • Diameter control: the tube's outer diameter is the hole's lower bound — with the sand layer wrapped around the tube, the finished hole comes out 0.5–1 mm larger than the tube (rule of thumb; field-calibrate: drill three holes with the same tube, measure the diameters with the wooden caliper, take the average, and transcribe "tube diameter + increment" into the ledger). For a hole of diameter d, pick a tube of outer diameter about d−1 mm.
  • Perpendicularity criterion: after breakthrough, insert a test rod (a thin stick whittled from 9.4 standard drill-shaft stock, diameter = hole diameter −1 mm); if the difference in its wobble between the two sides of the hole mouth is <1 mm, count it perpendicular (empirical criterion); or scribe a cross on the workpiece's bottom face beforehand and sight the offset of the hole's center from the cross intersection against the light — an offset <1 mm passes — this is the workstation-level internal control (stricter than final acceptance, leaving margin) for the L2 acceptance item "hole-position deviation <2 mm."
  • Three anti-drift methods: (1) first lightly chip a positioning dimple on the start face with the stone point (1–2 mm deep); (2) the cap-presser applies vertical pressure only, no lateral force (two-person division, 9.5); (3) stop every 5 minutes and re-check against the layout lines — if drift is found while the hole is still shallow, you can grind the hole oval and then bring it back round to correct; once past half thickness, discovery means scrapping or demotion to a small part.
  • Slurry: sand:water about 2:1 by volume (thick paste that coats the wall without running); double-sieve the sand — coarse-sieve grade (grains ≤1 mm) to break through, fine-sieve grade (grains ≤0.3 mm) to finish; switch to fine sand just before breakthrough.

Slot cutting (progressive-width method): slots ground into stone blanks (lashing slots, handle slots, decorative slots) must not be ground to full depth in one pass — three progressive passes:

  1. First pass: width to half of full width, depth to a third of full depth; press a charcoal-dusted wood strip the width of the slot against the slot floor — an even print of charcoal dots means the floor is flat and straight.
  2. Second pass: widen to 3/4, deepen to 2/3; gauge the width with the slot gauge (a hardwood strip of the same width + scribed lines on both sides).
  3. Third pass: to size; dress the slot walls with the fine grinding stone.

Rationale: grind the full width in one pass and the walls have no retreat — over-grinding cannot be undone. Check between every pass; the checking pieces are the wood strip and slot gauge above (the Chapter 3 self-made gauge method).

Polishing (three abrasive tiers + leather strip):

  1. Coarse tier: wet quartz sand (fine-sieve grade) with water, circular strokes, removing every medium-grind scratch — criterion: no directional scratches under side light.
  2. Medium tier: fine settled silt (from the still bottoms of river bends; slick and grit-free when rubbed) with water — criterion: a continuous reflective band seen at 45° against the light.
  3. Fine tier: dry leather strip (rawhide from 7.3, cut into 10 cm lengths) charged with tallow, pulled rapidly — criterion: the strip leaves no mark, and a fingertip drawn across meets no drag.

Ceiling criterion: stop when the polished face shows a blurred reflection of your finger outline. Beyond that, returns approach zero while hours double — a high-cost, low-return procedure — so polish to grade by use (edges fine tier, bodies medium tier, blanks unpolished); never polish for polishing's sake.

Finished stone-tool grading (three tiers): every piece is graded at completion, the tier number carved at the handle end (8.4 pigment marking):

Tier Criteria Use Tier 1 (service) all dimensions pass the template (light gap <1 mm), no visible edge chips, hafting passed the 9.1 three-stage acceptance issued for use Tier 2 (reserve) dimensional deviation 1–2 mm, or edge chips <1 mm shallow without affecting loading into the spare-parts box; replaces Tier 1 on retirement Tier 3 (practice stock) pieces failed mid-work: chips >2 mm, slots off-line, holes skewed teaching and hand-feel practice only; barred from the ledger tool roster

Promotion/demotion rules: a Tier 2 piece that after regrinding and re-inspection meets the Tier 1 criteria may be promoted to service; a Tier 1 piece damaged in use goes through the 9.4 repair table, then re-inspection and re-grading. Never let Tier 3 pieces mix into the Tier 2 box — practice stock leaking into the store is the number-one source of "unreliable spares."

docs.title: 9.9 Bone and Antler Workshop
docs.text:
Bone and antler are this stage's only tough materials — stone chips, wood splits; bone can bend, be ground, and be drilled. They are the exclusive source of needles, awls, hooks, and handles, and worth a dedicated workshop (workstation layout per the 9.7 four-zone system; the "bone" section of the stock rack is its store).

Bone degreasing by simmering: fresh bone carries fat; worked directly it turns rank and slippery, and glued faces never hold (fat blocks glue — 8.5 tar glue has no adhesion to oily surfaces).

  1. Saw into short lengths (method below) into a pottery pot (Chapter 8) or a pit lined with stone slabs as a boiler; cover the bone with water; after boiling, hold at a bare simmer 2–3 hours (rule of thumb; field-calibrate: lift a section and press the fracture face with a fingertip — an oily sheen means another hour; a dry, grabby feel means done).
  2. Change the water once midway (at the 1-hour-after-boil mark) to keep fat from re-coating the bone.
  3. Lift out and shade-dry 3–5 days (rule of thumb; criterion: the knock changes from dull to crisp) — fire-drying always warps and cracks: forbidden.
  4. Final degrease verdict: no oily sheen on the fracture face; after a 15-minute soak, no oil film on the water. Degrease quality directly determines later glue-bond and lashing life; record the stock batch number and let it travel with the record card (9.10).

Sawing (stone-knife groove + snapping): blanking bone does not use the cord saw for full cuts (slow and jittery); use "stress breaking":

  1. With the stone-flake knife (edge angle 20°–40°, the 9.1 table) score a ring groove around the break position, to 1/3–1/2 of the bone-wall thickness (empirical starting point; see the practice method).
  2. Line the groove with double-sieved fine sand to speed the scoring (the dry-use version of the 9.2 slurry principle).
  3. Bridge both ends, align the groove with the bench edge, and tap the bone lightly with a wooden mallet face or press it — it snaps cleanly along the groove.

Criterion: the fracture follows the groove (if not, the groove depth was uneven); diagonal cracking running >5 mm into the bone body demotes that piece to Tier 3. ◎ Hand-feel: the measure of a "light tap" is the hardest thing to put into words — practice method: take 10 scrap bone sections, start at 1/4 wall-thickness groove depth and deepen piece by piece, recording each fracture quality in the practice ledger, and find the critical groove depth for this team's usual stock (most animal bone falls between 2/5 and 1/2 of wall thickness, an empirical band); misjudgment compensation: rather score too deep than strike too hard — scoring deep costs a few minutes; striking hard costs the whole section.

Point and edge grinding (bone needle/awl/fishhook specification table):

Item Spec Grinding method Pass criterion Bone needle length 6–8 cm, diameter 1.5–2 mm, eye diameter 0.8–1 mm (rule of thumb) fine tier of the grinding bench, reciprocating to a point; the eye spun with a fine bone tube (a scaled-down 9.2 tube drill, half-depth from each face to prevent breakout) no cracks around the eye; the point thin enough not to split leather thread Awl length 10–15 cm, point section 3–4 cm coarse-grind to shape, fine-grind the edges, taper from four faces trial stab into hardwood: 2 mm penetration without snapping Fishhook inner bend diameter 5–8 mm, barb length 2–3 mm cut the blank from a bone plate (groove-and-snap) → grind the curve → grind the barb → sharpen the tip hang a stone weight of about 1× the target fish's weight, hang still for 10 seconds: no deformation, no springing straight Scraper blade bone plate length 8–12 cm, edge angle 45° bevel one face test scraping a hide: no curling, no scored grooves

The bone needle is this workshop's difficulty ceiling: a practiced hand makes 5–10 per day at about 50% yield (rule of thumb, must be field-calibrated and entered in the ledger) — schedule production from measured capacity, not from "how many we want" (9.5).

Antler tools (handle stock and mallet faces):

  • Handle stock: the straight main beam of antler (length ≥15 cm, diameter 2.5–3.5 cm) is a natural handle, the swollen burr at the base serving as the grip — eliminating slot-cutting and hafting; after drilling the edged piece, fix it with a fine bone pin dipped in glue (8.5), for small knives, awls, and scrapers. Criterion: no longitudinal cracks in the beam; fracture face dense, no honeycombing.
  • Mallet face: a cross-section of the antler base (4–6 cm thick) serves as a soft mallet, dedicated to pressure flaking (5.5) and to seating hafting wedges — it is softer than stone and will not shatter stone edges. After the face is ground flat (the 9.8 coarse polish tier suffices) it goes into the clamping/striking class of the ledger.
  • Heat bending: antler softened in hot water can be bent into hook shapes and crank handles (large fishhooks, crank-drill handles); after bending, bind with cord to hold shape and shade-dry 3 days to set (rule of thumb).

docs.title: 9.10 Tool-Life Ledger, Detailed Rules
docs.text:
9.4 gave the repair table, 9.6 the inventory fields; this section closes the loop on "the life of one tool" — the ledger is not a recording hobby; it is the only data source for replacement planning and process review.

One record per tool (record card): a tool gets its file the moment it enters service — one card per tool (wooden tablet, hung beside its silhouette spot on the shadow board):

Field What to record Example Number/name ledger number (Chapter 8 system) + tool name T-041 stone axe Made/batch manufacture date + stock batch number (stone/bone batch number) Autumn Day 3 / stone batch B-7 Grading 9.8 three tiers (recorded at entry to service and at every change) Tier 1 Regrind count each regrind/re-lash/re-bond counts once, with the date 3rd, Winter 1 Damage record symptom + cause judged on the spot (fill in a row against the failure-mode table) 2 mm edge chip / stock too wet and tough Status in use / spare / awaiting repair / retired in use Retirement date + reason (one of five: ground out / shattered / handle lost beyond re-bonding / snapped / lost) —

Record discipline: regrinds left unrecorded break the life curve, and replacement planning will systematically undercount; card and tool stay together; retired cards are bundled monthly into the archive box and must not be destroyed.

Monthly loss roll-up → replacement plan: on the last day of each month every workstation submits card copies, rolled up into the monthly loss table:

Roll-up item Source Use Retired/in-service counts by class card retirement column monthly loss rate = retired ÷ in-service at month start High-loss item ranking retirement causes classified sets replacement priority; revises the 9.4 spare-part floors Batch correlation card batch numbers one batch losing abnormally → a stock problem (trigger line)

Replacement plan, three lines: N retired this month → replace with N next month (same spec) → if N would take stock below the 9.4 floor, top up to "floor − on hand"; take the larger of the two. Replacement pieces enter the 9.5 flow-line schedule — never "make it when there's time."

Process-review trigger line for high-loss tools: when a tool type's monthly loss rate exceeds 1/3 of its in-service count (empirical trigger; revise from measured data after 3 months of running), a process review triggers — not simply making a few more:

  1. Check stock: are the retired pieces' batch numbers concentrated? — if so, change the stock source or revise the selection criteria;
  2. Check workmanship: are the retired pieces' maker numbers concentrated? — if so, review that station's rework flow (linking to the 9.5 rework-rate >20% clause);
  3. Check spec: losses uniform → the spec itself does not fit the station; go back and revise the 9.1 specification table.

Review conclusions go into the ledger's appendix; triggering without reviewing counts as the ledger system failing — data produced and not used is worse than no data. [Card 09-06 ] (eight fields) 1. Input materials: bone tube (outer diameter = target hole diameter −1 mm, wall ≥2 mm); quartz sand, double-sieved grades (≤1 mm to break through, ≤0.3 mm to finish); water. Substitute: bamboo tube for bone tube (wears about twice as fast; calibrate hole diameter the same way). 2. Tools required: bow drill (7.6; cord tension criterion: the plucked cord rings crisp); cap-pressing block; slurry bowl; test rod (thin stick, diameter = hole diameter −1 mm). Calibration: run dry; the tube end's wobble circle ≤1 mm means concentric. 3. Operating sequence: (1) positioning dimple (chip 1–2 mm deep with the stone point) → (2) coarse slurry in, medium bow speed → (3) lift the tube and clear the cuttings every 20–30 seconds → (4) check drift against the layout lines every 5 minutes → (5) switch to fine slurry before breakthrough → (6) after breakthrough, flip the piece and tap the core loose. Control point: force may only be vertical (the cap-presser's duty, 9.5). 4. Empirical parameters and calibration method: piercing a 1 cm stone slab takes 2–6 hours; slurry sand:water 2:1 by volume. Calibration: time three holes in the same stock, take the median, and enter the ledger; slurry consistency judged by "coats the wall without running." 5. In-process observation items: cuttings color when lifting the tube (white = normal stone cuttings; dark = touching some different lower layer); a warm hole wall = the sand has gone blunt (change immediately); drift (eyeballed against the lines) — enter in the record card's damage column. 6. Pass/rework/scrap: hole diameter = tube diameter +0.5–1 mm and perpendicular offset <1 mm = pass; drift found while the hole is shallow, ground oval and brought back round = rework; drift past half thickness or a chipped hole mouth >2 mm = scrap, cut down to a small part. 7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: not cutting → first check for blunt sand (change sand) → then check tube-end wear (regrind the end) → last check insufficient speed (tighten the cord). Hole drift → first check dimple depth → then check lateral force at the cap → last check a tilted stock face (shim level and re-clamp). 8. L1/L2/L3 evidence: L1 keeps the first-hole workpiece; L2 keeps the three-hole calibration record + caliper-measured hole diameters; L3 keeps the monthly hole-piece ledger + sand-consumption record (bowls per hole). [Card 09-07 ] (eight fields) 1. Input materials: degreased bone plate (after the 9.9 simmering, 1.5–2.5 mm thick, length ≥8 cm). Substitute: hardwood whittled needles (do not endure piercing; practice only). 2. Tools required: grinding-bench fine stone; leather strip (fine polish); fine bone tube (for drilling the eye); tallow. Calibration: check the grinding-stone face flatness weekly by the 9.2 mutual-grinding method. 3. Operating sequence: (1) cut the blank (groove-and-snap) → (2) coarse tier grinds the needle's taper → (3) fine tier grinds the point, rolling it on a fingertip as you go to check roundness → (4) grind the tail section flat and thin → (5) spin-grind the eye with the tube drill (half from each face, preventing one-face breakout) → (6) fine-polish the whole needle with the tallow-charged leather strip. Control point: the eye sits within the tail quarter of the needle, centered. 4. Empirical parameters and calibration method: needle diameter 1.5–2 mm, eye diameter 0.8–1 mm, a practiced hand makes 5–10 per day. Calibration: record the pass count of the first 20-piece batch to set personal capacity; judge eye diameter by test-inserting a fine splinter. 5. In-process observation items: while grinding the point, a "skreek" that sharpens means nearly done (resonance of the thin section); white rings around the eye are a crack omen — enter in the practice ledger. 6. Pass/rework/scrap: no cracks at the eye, needle straight (rolls flat without hopping), point thin enough that it does not split leather thread = pass; eye cracked but not through = grind away and re-drill (the needle gets shorter) = rework; snapped, eye collapsed, or body bent = scrap into the practice box. 7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: eye-edge cracking → first check single-face drilling (switch to half per face) → then check tube oversize → last check bone not degreased (return to 9.9 and re-simmer). Point splitting → first check the stone grade too coarse → then check the grinding direction (must grind along the bone's long axis). 8. L1/L2/L3 evidence: L1 keeps the first passing needle; L2 keeps the 20-piece batch yield record; L3 keeps the monthly output ledger + classified causes of lost needles (as the basis for scheduling and stock selection).
