docs.title: 27.1 Springs, Levers, and Mechanical Indicating Mechanisms
docs.text:
Springs (the power source of mechanical indication):

  • Leaf spring: tempered steel strip (Chapter 19), cut to shape for its use; elasticity test: deform under a known force, release, and recover; residual deformation < 5% passes (empirical value, must be field-calibrated);
  • Helical spring: steel wire close-wound on a mandrel to shape, then tempered to set (in the blue temper-color band); stiffness calibration: hang weights step by step and record the extension at each step, giving a straight "force–deformation" line — one stiffness card per spring;
  • Hairspring: thin steel strip coiled into an Archimedean spiral (mandrel + hand coiling), used for the pointer's restoring torque.

Lever and sector-gear magnification: two routes from small displacement to large reading: the lever ratio (two 1:10 stages in series give 1:100); the toothed arc–pinion (a sector tooth arc drives a pinion — angular magnification, a large ratio from the small gear). Fabrication key points: knife-edge pivots (Chapter 25 balance knife-edge technique); fitting the tooth arc tooth by tooth (Chapter 20 tooth-correction method); hairspring removal of return play (the gear backlash is preloaded one-sidedly against one flank by the hairspring — return difference is the instrument's number-one enemy).

The indicating-mechanism trio: pointer (thin duralumin/copper sheet; thin copper when no aluminum is available — low mass, low inertia), dial (equal-division ruling, Chapter 3), zero adjuster (eccentric cam or threaded fine-shift plate).

The mechanisms of this section are the "meter movement" shared by all four instrument classes of this chapter: the protection shells and lookup tables of 27.2, the sector-gear drive of the 27.3 pressure gauge, the counting digit wheels of the 27.4 flowmeter, and the reading scale of the 27.5 vacuum gauge all take this section's springs, levers, and hairsprings as their skeleton.

docs.title: 27.2 Temperature Instruments: The Glass Thermometer Calibration Chain and the Thermocouple
27.2.1 Removable Thermometers and Multi-Point Rounds (Version 1 content, retained)
docs.text: • Instrumenting temperature: alcohol thermometers mounted in metal protection shells (Chapter 17); shells and threaded fittings (Chapter 22 standard threads) standardized — the "removable thermometer" becomes the standard interface for furnaces, kettles, and piping; multi-point temperature measurement (furnace top / furnace waist / furnace bottom) and inspection routes (two meter readings per shift).

docs.title: 27.2.2 The Glass Thermometer Calibration Chain: Three Points Fix the Scale, Two Segments Divided Equally
docs.text:
Why three points: the capillary bore is uneven along its length; "linear equal division by column length" is only an approximation over short spans. Fix only the ice point and the boiling point, and mid-range deviation can reach several divisions with no way to detect it. Only by fixing three phase-transition points — cutting the range into two segments and dividing each equally — can mid-range deviation be detected and controlled.

The three fixed points (phase-transition reproduction, independent of any existing thermometer):

  1. Ice point 0 ℃: mix crushed ice (≥500 g) with a little clean water — ice not fully melted, water not crusted over; insert the sensing bulb without touching the cup wall or bottom, equilibrate ≥10 min; record the mark only once the reading has held unchanged for 1 min. Self-check: after adding more crushed ice the reading must not move (movement = the ice has melted out or warm water got mixed in).
  2. Local boiling point: a boiling-water bath, open, with no lid (a lid = raised vapor pressure, raised boiling point, reading voided). The local boiling point is not 100 ℃: t_b = 100 − (760 − P)/27 ℃ (P is the same-day barometer reading, mmHg; empirical formula, error on the ±0.3 ℃ level — verification: repeat on 10 consecutive days of different weather; if the range >0.5 ℃, check the bath water's purity and the bulb's position). Rough altitude rule: the boiling point drops about 1 ℃ per 300 m of elevation.
  3. Beeswax point 63 ℃: beeswax melts at 62–65 ℃ (nominal 63 ℃). Why beeswax as the third point: the phase-transition plateau — melting wax holds its temperature constant for several minutes, giving a wide reading window (rosin softens with no plateau; not used). The melting point drifts between sources; the system is: the workshop fixes one batch of beeswax as the "reference wax" (batch number entered in the ledger); the first batch's actual plateau temperature is reverse-measured once with an existing standard glass thermometer and put on file; from then on every calibration uses that batch, and when the batch runs out, the replacement batch must be reverse-measured again.

Operating sequence:

  1. Scribe the three capillary marks (fine-file cross marks or ink dots): ice-point mark → wax-point mark → boiling-point mark, each mark following the equilibration criteria above;
  2. Uniformity check: measure the two segment column lengths L₁ (ice-point mark → wax-point mark) and L₂ (wax-point mark → boiling-point mark); the column length per ℃ is L₁/63 and L₂/(t_b−63) respectively. If the two segments' per-℃ column lengths differ by >5% (empirical value, to be revised by statistics from the first batch of 20) → capillary bore unevenness exceeds limits; scrap that tube;
  3. Two-segment equal-division transfer: divide the 0–63 ℃ segment equally by the per-℃ column length L₁/63 and the 63 ℃–to–boiling-point segment by L₂/(t_b−63), transferring the graduations with the Chapter 3 equal-division ruling method (divider trial divisions); draw a special mark at the segment boundary (63 ℃) to remind that a reading spanning the two segments faces two different scale values;
  4. Re-check and spot check: re-measure each of the three points once; deviation ≤±1 division; separately compare in the same bath as the standard thermometer in warm water at about 30 ℃; deviation ≤±1.5 divisions (empirical value, must be calibrated).

Scale interval: 1 ℃ per division on the 0–63 ℃ segment, 2 ℃ per division above 63 ℃ (blanks with column length to spare: 1 ℃/division throughout — set per blank and written into the calibration card).

Range ceiling and the expansion chamber: at atmospheric pressure the alcohol column tops out around 78 ℃; to reach the boiling-point mark (99–100 ℃) the blank must be the top-expansion-chamber type (Chapter 14 lampwork: blow a φ6 mm expansion bulb at the top of the capillary, leaving a dry air cushion above the column before sealing), so that at 100 ℃ the column enters the expansion chamber instead of dead-ending. Blanks without an expansion chamber get only the ice point and wax point; above 80 ℃ the thermocouple takes over.

The temperature-standard hierarchy (pyramid): 1 standard thermometer (used only to calibrate other thermometers, never enters the workshop; quarterly three-point re-verification; scrapped on any knock) → working thermometers (monthly one-point spot check against the standard + quarterly boiling-point re-verification). The structure is isomorphic with the Chapter 22 length-standard pyramid.

[Card 27-01 Glass Thermometer Three-Point Calibration] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: ungraduated thermometer blank (top-expansion-chamber type, capillary with no column breaks, 1 per run); crushed ice ≥500 g; 50 g of beeswax from the reference-wax batch (batch number in the ledger); 3 L clean water; same-day barometer reading.
  2. Tools required: boiling-water bath pot ≥2 L (open); wax bath cup seated in a boiling-water double boiler (wax temperature stays under 100 ℃); dividers and scriber (Chapter 3; true the divider points to zero before use); fine flat file; timing water clock; standard thermometer (for reverse-measuring the wax batch and for spot checks).
  3. Operating sequence and control points: ① ice-water bath, equilibrate ≥10 min, mark the ice point — control point: record the mark only once the reading has held for 1 min; ② mark the wax point during the solid–liquid coexistence period of the wax bath (bulb fully immersed, equilibrate ≥5 min) — control point: the wax must be on its melting plateau; insert the thermometer as soon as it begins to clear overall; ③ mark the boiling point in the open boiling-water bath (t_b=100−(760−P)/27); ④ measure L₁/L₂ — control point: per-℃ column lengths of the two segments differing by >5% means scrap; ⑤ transfer the two segments, each with its own equal division; ⑥ three-point re-check + 30 ℃ same-bath spot check.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: beeswax nominal 63 ℃ (actual value per this batch's reverse measurement); scale 1 ℃/division (2 ℃/division above 63 ℃); re-check tolerance ±1 division; spot-check tolerance ±1.5 divisions (revised after statistics on the first batch of 20); boiling-point empirical-formula coefficient 27 mmHg/℃ (verified by the repeat range over 10 sunny days).
  5. Process observation and recording items: lengths of the three marks from the bottom of the sensing bulb (mm), L₁, L₂, same-day barometric pressure, wax batch number, re-check deviations, spot-check deviations — entered on the thermometer calibration card (the card travels with the thermometer).
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: accept = three-point re-check ≤±1 division and spot check ≤±1.5 divisions; rework = graduations transferred to the wrong segment (grind off the graduations and re-rule, the three marks untouched, then repeat step ⑥); scrap = two-segment column-length ratio out of tolerance (uneven tube), cracked sensing bulb, a column break that will not rejoin.
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: symptom "mid-range spot check off by 3 divisions" — first check for graduations transferred to the wrong segment (check whether the 63 ℃ segment-boundary mark lines up) → then check a locally wide bore section (add one temporary bath point above and below the deviating region to localize it) → then check wax batch drift (re-measure the wax plateau temperature with the standard thermometer).
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one qualified thermometer + calibration card; L2 = the standard thermometer's quarterly re-verification records + a monthly-check ledger for ≥10 working thermometers; L3 = the reference-wax batch ledger + scrap/downgrade records + a calibration-chain traceability chart (who calibrated whom, and when).

docs.title: 27.2.3 The Thermocouple: Wiring a Temperature Difference to a Pointer
docs.text:
The principle in one sentence: join two different metal wires into a loop; when the two junctions sit at different temperatures, a thermoelectric EMF appears in the loop — an iron–constantan (copper–nickel alloy) pair gives about 50 μV/℃ (empirical value; calibration method below), so a 100 ℃ difference gives about 5 mV, enough to drive a galvanometer pointer. The physical mechanism, the constantan recipe, and wire purification are developed in Chapter 30; this chapter handles only the instrument face of "sensor + meter movement + calibration."

How to build it: 1.5 m each of iron wire and constantan wire (φ 0.5 mm class, drawn per Chapters 17, 19); twist the measuring-end tips together 5 turns, then tin-solder or forge-weld them into a junction (the third metal introduced by the solder is isothermal end to end and does not affect the EMF — the law of intermediate metals, proven in Chapter 30). With no constantan, substitute copper wire: the signal is roughly half as large and reading sensitivity drops one grade; note "substitute wire" on the calibration card.

The rustic cold-junction compensation (empirical method): during calibration, bury the cold junction in ice water (0 ℃) and build the "temperature difference vs. divisions" lookup table; in the field the cold junction sits at room temperature, so true temperature = galvanometer indication + cold-junction temperature. Procedure: tie a small glass thermometer (a product of 27.2.2) to the cold-junction terminal; at every reading, read the tied thermometer first, then add. Tying requirement: wrap the sensing bulb and the two-wire junction tight with cloth strip — ◎ hand-feel: wrap until a light pull on the wires does not shift them, yet the wrap can still be undone at any time; practice method: after 20 practice wraps on scrap wire, immerse the whole assembly in a 40 ℃ warm water bath; if the converted indication difference between thermometer and thermocouple is ≤2 ℃, the wrap passes; compensation: water-bath comparison (replace the "tightness" hand-feel with a measurable bath temperature).

Calibration: reproduce the boiling point and the beeswax point as the two anchors; in a soybean-oil bath (stirred; liquid temperature restricted to below 250 ℃, keeping at least 30 ℃ of margin under the flash point), read in the same bath as the standard thermometer, one point every 20 ℃, and plot the "temperature difference vs. divisions" lookup table; iron–constantan is nearly linear from 0–400 ℃ and bends gradually above — use the table throughout; never a straight line.

Tier declaration: the reading mechanism (the galvanometer) belongs to Chapter 30's electrical instruments — until the galvanometer stability loop closes, this section is Tier 2 (it can be built and used; reproduction and acceptance not yet closed-loop); backfill and raise the tier once the Chapter 30 galvanometer reaches L2.

Ceiling: 500 ℃ for bare wire (oxidation loss); 750 ℃ class once fitted with the Chapter 14 quartz/porcelain protection tube (empirical value; calibration method: mutual cross-check with the Chapter 12 temperature cones in the same kiln).

docs.title: 27.2.4 The High-Temperature Band: Bringing the Temperature Cones Back In
docs.text: The Chapter 12 temperature cones map their numbers to bend-over temperatures, covering roughly 600–1400 ℃. This chapter formally brings them into the temperature-quantity system, forming a three-band linkage: glass thermometer (−20 to 110 ℃) → thermocouple (≤750 ℃, with protection tube) → temperature cones (600–1400 ℃). The 500–750 ℃ band is the overlap cross-check zone: cones + thermocouple go into the same kiln, are compared after firing, deviations go into the ledger, and a "cone number vs. thermocouple temperature" correspondence table is summarized every 10 kiln runs (empirical value, accumulated kiln by kiln). Division of labor: the thermocouple handles the process curve (heat-up rate, soak segments); the cones handle end-point acceptance (was the final temperature reached) — release of ceramic and metallurgical kilns is judged by cone bending; this is where the Chapter 12 system sits within this chapter's temperature chain.

docs.title: 27.3 Pressure Instruments: From the U-Tube to the Spring-Tube Pressure Gauge
27.3.1 Four Reinforcements for the U-Tube Manometer (on the Chapter 25 Basis)
docs.text:
Chapter 25 already built the U-tube manometer; this chapter does not rebuild it, only adds four reinforcements:

  1. Conversions in writing (at first occurrence): 1 atm = 760 mmHg = 10.34 m of water column; 1 mmHg = 13.6 mm of water column. Read low pressures (<0.3 atm) on a water column, high pressures on mercury;
  2. Liquid-temperature correction: when the indicating liquid is above 25 ℃, correct by 0.15% per 10 ℃ (empirical value; calibration method: measure the same pressure once with hot water and once with cold; the difference is this device's correction amount);
  3. Inclined-tube micromanometer: replace one arm with a glass tube inclined at 30°, ≥500 mm long, graduated along the tube — under the same pressure difference the slanted column length is 1/sin30° = 2 times the vertical height difference, magnifying the reading 2×; used for furnace negative pressure and duct pressure differences (the tens-of-millimeters-of-water-column class). Calibration method: compare five points at identical pressures against a vertical U-tube; a magnification ratio of 2.00±0.05 passes (empirical value, must be calibrated); if the inclination has been disturbed it must be recalibrated;
  4. Both arms the same diameter: the extra capillary pressure difference makes the level in a fine tube read low — use glass tubes of the same diameter in both arms so the capillary effects cancel; before every reading, tap the tube frame lightly to drive off wall bubbles.

docs.title: 27.3.2 The Diaphragm Pressure Gauge (Version 1 content, retained)
docs.text:
• Pressure gauge (mechanical reading): structure — a sealed leather diaphragm (Chapter 15 grease-impregnated leather) or a thin copper diaphragm takes the pressure; the diaphragm's center pushes a lever–sector-gear–pointer train; the dial is graduated point by point against a U-tube manometer (Chapter 25); range covers 0 up to several times working pressure; mark the overpressure red line in red paint.

The diaphragm type is easy to make and suits low pressures and low pressure differences of 0–0.5 atm; for higher pressures, longer life, and smaller size, the answer is the spring tube.

docs.title: 27.3.3 Manufacturing the Spring-Tube (Bourdon-Tube) Pressure Gauge
docs.text:
Principle: a bronze tube of flattened elliptical cross-section is bent into an arc of about 270°; the fixed end is open to the pressure medium, the free end sealed shut. Internal pressure pushes the elliptical cross-section toward circular — the surface areas of the outer and inner arcs are both unchanged, so a more circular cross-section necessarily increases the arc's radius of curvature; the tube straightens overall and the free end moves outward. At working pressure the free end displaces 2–4 mm (empirical value; calibration method: measure point by point under the deadweight method), amplified through link–sector gear–pinion–pointer (the 27.1 mechanism; total magnification on the order of 100×: a 2 mm displacement becomes a 200–400 mm arc travel of the pointer tip). Version 1's C list said "the Bourdon tube requires thin-wall tube drawing and welding upgrades" — Version 2's practical conclusion: Chapter 17 bronze tubing + Chapter 22 tin soldering are enough; silver soldering is unnecessary; strike it from the C list.

Dimensions and materials (empirical values, must be field-calibrated):

Part Specification Criterion Tin-bronze tube OD 6 mm, wall 0.8 mm, length 200 mm Wall thickness difference over three caliper points ≤0.1 mm; no pressure dents on the surface Cross-section after flattening flattened ellipse, major axis 7 mm × minor axis 3.5 mm Minor axis by caliper 3.5±0.2 mm; a scrapped sample sawn open shows no wrinkles in the section Arc bend radius 35 mm, included angle 270°, fixed-end straight segment 25 mm / free-end straight segment 15 mm Gap against the template ≤0.5 mm Range full scale = 1.5 × maximum working pressure (red line, Chapter 28) The red line falls near the 2/3 point of the scale

Manufacturing sequence:

  1. Cut to length, then anneal (Chapter 17: about 600 ℃, hold 30 min, slow cool; empirical value, calibrate per batch: under-annealed tube cracks during bending);
  2. Fill with rosin: fill the tube with molten rosin (prevents the section from collapsing dead during flattening and prevents wall wrinkling); wooden plugs in both ends;
  3. Die-press the ellipse: file a semi-elliptical groove into each of a pair of hardened steel dies (semi-major axis 3.5, semi-minor axis 1.75 mm; closed, the dies form the 7×3.5 ellipse); close the dies and press flat — ◎ hand-feel: press until the two die faces just meet at the seam, then stop; add no extra hammer force (over-pressing wrinkles); practice method: press 10 scrapped tubes, saw each one open, inspect the section for wrinkles; compensation: judge acceptance by caliper measurement of the minor axis, never by hand-feel;
  4. Heat to pour out the rosin, scrub the inner wall clean with hot lye water, then rinse with clean water — residual wax is the number-one source of hysteresis;
  5. Bend the arc: the ellipse plane lies perpendicular to the bending plane — criterion: the major axis of the tube-end cross-section points at the bending form's center; bend slowly in segments against the R35 form; springback is 5°–10° (empirical value; record this batch's springback angle on the first piece) — bend the compensation to final position; ◎ hand-feel: slow bending with even force, seated to the form in one continuous pass; one hard jerk-bend is forbidden; practice method: bend 10 scrapped tubes and check each against the template; compensation: judge the template gap with a 0.5 mm feeler gauge or a thick paper shim;
  6. Tin-solder the M10×1.5 fitting onto the fixed end (Chapter 22); tin-solder the free end shut and solder on the φ2 mm copper pin (to connect the link);
  7. Fit the movement (27.1): link effective length 30 mm, sector-gear–pinion angular magnification about 1:10, hairspring preloaded to remove backlash;
  8. Pressure test: pressurize by deadweight to 1.5 × full scale and hold 5 min — no leak at the fittings (soap-solution method), return to zero after unloading ≤1 division, zero point unchanged on second pressurization (a change = the tube has taken a permanent set);
  9. Dot-mark calibration on the white blank dial (the 27.3.4 five-point method) → fit the formal graduated dial → install the gauge glass → lead seal (wax + numbering stamp).

Quick reference: hysteresis (same-point difference between rising and falling pressure >1 division) → check in order: residual wax in the tube (boil it out) → worn link pin hole (replace the pin) → insufficient hairspring preload (add 1/4 turn); indication drift → micro-leak at a solder seam (soap-solution method).

docs.title: 27.3.4 The Deadweight Calibration Method: Bootstrapping the Pressure Standard
docs.text:
Principle: standard pressure = weight force ÷ piston area, P = mg/A. Mass traces to the Chapter 3/22 weights; diameter traces to the Chapter 22 micrometer — the pressure quantity bootstraps locally from mass × length, depending on no purchased standard whatsoever.

The deadweight tester:

  • Cylinder–piston: a bronze cylinder (drill–ream–lap, Chapters 20, 22) paired with a hardened steel piston, diameter 10.000 mm (micrometer, four points in two directions, range ≤0.01 mm) → area 78.5 mm²; fit-clearance criterion: with lubricant applied, the piston slides slowly down under its own weight (about the 30 s/100 mm class, empirical value; calibration method: verified against the mercury-column comparison point); wobble visually indiscernible;
  • Screw pressurizing pump: an M16×2 lead screw (Chapter 22) drives a small water cylinder (medium: water or castor oil); a tee on the cylinder branches to the gauge under calibration and to the piston column;
  • Weights: 500 g×2, 1 kg×2, 2 kg×1, 5 kg×1 (verified on the Chapter 3 balance); the self-weight of the piston and tray is weighed on the balance, chisel-engraved on the tray rim, and counted into the zero-point pressure.

Pressure-point table (d = 10 mm piston, area 78.5 mm²):

Applied load (incl. tray) Pressure produced Equivalent 2 kg 0.25 MPa ≈2.5 atm ≈1870 mmHg 4 kg 0.50 MPa ≈4.9 atm 6 kg 0.75 MPa ≈7.4 atm 8 kg 0.99 MPa ≈9.8 atm

Operation: bleed the gauge cavity and the cylinder → hang the weights → rotate the piston slowly and continuously (about one turn per 2 s, to kill friction) → tap the case lightly and read → five points rising, five points falling; at each point the rising–falling difference ≤1 division; five-point indication error ≤2% of range.

Cross-verification: connect the tester to a 1 m mercury U-tube, pressurize to a mercury difference of 500 mmHg; the applied load should be 0.53 kg (a difference >2% means check the piston area, the weights, or the mercury column reading) — cross-verify the deadweight tester once before each month's use; record the cross-verification value in the ledger.

docs.title: 27.3.5 Periodic Calibration of Boiler Pressure Gauges (the Chapter 28 Release Interface)
docs.text:
• Every in-service pressure gauge gets a monthly check (deadweight, five points); after calibration it is lead-sealed and hung with a calibration tag (this date / next date / calibrator);
  • Max-recording pointer: a passive pointer is added inside the gauge, pushed by the working pointer to the highest value and not returning — overpressure leaves its evidence; the first item of the Chapter 28 boiler release check is precisely "has the max pointer touched the red line";
  • A boiler without a valid calibration tag must not be fired (Chapter 28 release clause);
  • Three events — a knock, over-travel, a suspicious reading — mean it goes straight back for calibration (consistent with the 27.10 period grading).

[Card 27-02 Spring-Tube Pressure Gauge Manufacture and Deadweight Calibration] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: tin-bronze tube 6×0.8×200 mm (Chapter 17, quantity per gauge); rosin 20 g; one pair of elliptical press dies (hardened); R35 tube-bending form; tin solder and flux; 1 × M10×1.5 fitting; φ2 mm copper pin; movement parts (sector gear–pinion–hairspring–pointer–white blank dial, self-made per 27.1).
  2. Tools required: deadweight tester (27.3.4, d10.000 piston; cross-verify the mercury-column point before use); micrometer (Chapter 22; zero check + one gauge-block point before use); hand hammer and files; arc template (0.5 mm feeler gauge / thick paper shim); soap-solution brush (leak checking).
  3. Operating sequence and control points: ① anneal ② fill with rosin ③ die-press the ellipse — control point: stop when the die faces meet at the seam ④ remove the wax and wash clean — control point: rinse with solvent until no film remains ⑤ bend the 270° arc (ellipse major axis pointing at the form center; compensate the springback with a corrective bend) ⑥ solder the fixed-end fitting + seal-solder the free end and solder the pin ⑦ pressure test at 1.5 × full scale for 5 min (no leak / return to zero ≤1 division / zero unchanged on repressurizing) ⑧ fit the movement ⑨ deadweight five-point dot-marking (five points each rising and falling) ⑩ formal dial + lead seal + calibration tag.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: full scale = 1.5 × red line; 1 kg applied load ≈1.23 atm (d10 piston); five points = 0/25/50/75/100% of range; indication error ≤2% of range, return difference ≤1 division (empirical values; calibrate to local conditions — revise by statistics on the first batch of 10); springback angle 5°–10° (empirical value; calibrate to local conditions — record this batch's value on the first piece).
  5. Process observation and recording items: measured minor axis after flattening, arc template gap, pressure-test curve (pressure–time), five-point rising/falling deviation table, calibrator and next due date — entered on the pressure gauge calibration card.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: accept = five points ≤2% + return difference ≤1 division + pressure test passed; rework = hysteresis over limit (boil the residual wax out of the tube and reassemble; add 1/4 turn to the hairspring and recalibrate), dial dot-marks misplaced (change the dial and re-mark); scrap = permanent tube deformation (zero shifts on repressurizing), a seam that still leaks after two repair solders, damaged sector gear.
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: symptom "indication reads low" — first rule out the reference (the deadweight tester itself: recheck the mercury-column cross-verification point, 500 mmHg≈0.53 kg), then check in order of frequency: ① residual-wax hysteresis in the tube (look at the rising–falling difference) ② worn link pin hole (inspect the slop visually, feel for wobble) ③ insufficient hairspring preload (pointer jump >1/4 division when tapped lightly). Symptom "pointer does not move" (by frequency) — ① fitting blocked ② tube flattened/collapsed (no displacement during the pressurized leak test) ③ movement jammed (check per 27.1).
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = five-point deadweight record for one gauge; L2 = statistics ledger for the first batch of 10 + the monthly-check system put in writing; L3 = the deadweight tester's traceability file (weights/micrometer/mercury cross-verification records) + the calibration tag and max-recording pointer systems written up and linked to the Chapter 28 release.

docs.text:
[Card 27-01] Glass thermometer three-point calibration (card at end of 27.2.2) | [Card 27-02] Spring-tube pressure gauge manufacture and deadweight calibration (card at end of 27.3)

Both cards can be copied onto a single page and carry the full eight fields.

docs.title: Part A Acceptance Criteria
docs.text: L1: one thermometer with two fixed points + one pressure gauge with one deadweight point; L2: temperature three points + pressure three stages all pass through the calibration chain; L3: merged into Part B's calibration system.

docs.title: Part A Safety Boundaries
docs.text: Mercury thermometers banned (the cinnabar red line); mercury U-tubes follow the mercury discipline of Chapters 33/53; boiler gauges follow the Chapter 28 release clause.

docs.title: Part A Failure Modes and Diagnosis
docs.text: Symptom Candidate causes (by probability) Disposition Two thermometers read far apart uneven capillary / wrong fixed-point conditions Re-calibrate the ice point three times; cross-check within the batch and grade Pressure gauge loses pressure (during the hold) seepage / gauge zero drift Localize by staged pressure holds; re-zero and recalibrate Bourdon tube lag insufficient temper / uneven wall thickness Remake with a new tube; register a downgrade

docs.title: Part A Next-Step Dependencies
docs.text: Pressure gauge → Chapter 32 boiler release; thermometer → all temperature control in Chapters 26/34/35; calibration chain → Part B's 27.10 overview.

docs.title: Ch 27 Part B Flow Vacuum and Calibration Chain
Chapter 27 · Part B: Flow, Vacuum, and the Four-Quantity Calibration Chain (27.4–27.11)
docs.text: Continues from Part A. The "gauge-selection table" for the four quantity classes and the calibration-chain overview belong to this part.

docs.title: 27.4 Flow Measurement: The Reference Is a Bucket and a Clock; the Engineering Pieces Are Weirs and Pitot Tubes
27.4.1 Volume–Time Method: The Acceptance Reference for All Flowmeters
docs.text:
Principle: flow rate = standard volume ÷ fill time. Calibration chain: volume is fixed by the weighing method (mass traces to the Chapter 3/25 balances, density traces to Chapter 25), time traces to the Chapter 3 timekeeping reference — the source of the flow quantity is likewise mass × time.

  • Standard bucket: trust no "scale markings", only weighing — total weight after filling the bucket with water − empty bucket weight = net water weight; divide by the water density at the prevailing water temperature (for 10–25 ℃ take 1 kg/L, error <0.3%, acceptable to take directly; for greater accuracy use the Chapter 25 density table) to obtain the actual volume V; chisel-mark the bucket body and enter it in the ledger;
  • Timer: a drip water clock or a pendulum stroke counter (Chapter 3); acceptance method: over 10 consecutive full-bucket timings the range ≤2%; if out of tolerance, replace the timer;
  • Operation: at the same flow rate measure 3 buckets consecutively and take the median; for large flows (>100 L/min) use a 200 L large bucket or a two-bucket relay;
  • Order-of-magnitude sanity check: bucket 50 L, pipe flow 20 L/min → full bucket 2.5 min, timing error on the order of 1 s → flow error <1%; the bucket method is more than adequate. If the flow is 500 L/min, a full bucket takes only 6 s and the timing error starts at 5% — switch to a larger bucket or change to the weir method. Even a reference has an applicable range; that is the first lesson.

docs.title: 27.4.2 Tipping-Bucket Flowmeter (first-edition content, retained)
docs.text: • Flowmeter (positive-displacement): a fixed-volume bucket tips and is counted — the water fills the standard bucket, which then tips over and empties; each tip advances one notch; mechanical counter = ratchet and pawl (Chapter 21) + dial. Daily flow = tip count × bucket volume (accumulated automatically in the ledger). adds one item: the bucket volume is re-verified once per season with the volume–time method (buckets wear and foul); if the bucket volume changes by >2%, repair the bucket and update the ledger coefficient.

docs.title: 27.4.3 Weir Method: A Head–Flow Lookup Table for Open-Channel Flow
docs.text:
Applicable to: open channels, waterwheel supply flumes, drainage ditches — situations where the pipe cannot be capped and led into a bucket.

Structure:

  • The weir plate (3 mm thin steel sheet, or a wooden board sheathed with iron sheet) stands in the channel, with a 90° V-notch cut into it; the downstream face of the notch is filed into a 45° edge — ◎ hand-feel: lightly scraping the edge backward with a fingertip gives a "scratched" feel with no rounded bluntness; practice method: cut 10 notches on scrap board; compensation: the drip test — the water nappe should lift completely off the plate face by 2–3 mm without clinging to the wall; clinging flow = dull edge or insufficient chamfer;
  • Flow steadying upstream of the weir: a straight channel reach ≥10 times the maximum head upstream of the weir plate; the crest is ≥150 mm above the downstream water surface, and the cavity beneath the nappe's lower edge is vented to atmosphere (visually confirm bubbles churning under the nappe — an unvented clinging flow can make readings low by 10%-order; the empirical value must be calibrated by comparison before and after venting);
  • Water-level point gauge: the measurement point sits 200–400 mm upstream of the notch (3–4 times the maximum head, clear of the falling-water disturbance); the needle tip is lowered slowly until it touches the water surface (read when the tip and its mirror image just meet, visually; resolution 0.5 mm), or use a hook gauge; zero point = the needle tip just touching the apex of the weir V; re-zero before each calibration.

Calibration (self-made lookup table): empirical formula for a 90° triangular weir Q = 1.4·H^2.5 (Q: m³/s; H: head on the weir, m; coefficient range 1.34–1.42). The empirical formula serves design estimation only; acceptance must be by direct measurement: set 6 head steps (20/40/60/80/100/150 mm); at each step record the gauge reading H and the volume–time-method flow Q simultaneously (3 buckets per step, take the median), yielding a six-point lookup table; chisel a plate and hang it beside the weir; in use, look up the table and interpolate. Interpolation error between two steps ≤2% (verified by re-measuring an inserted step; empirical value, must be calibrated). Free-overfall criterion: the nappe lifts completely clear and no water backs up downstream of the weir — if the downstream water level submerges the notch, this table is void (submerged weirs have their own formulas, not covered in this book; when submergence occurs, switch to direct measurement by the volume–time method).

Order-of-magnitude sanity check: H=100 mm → Q = 1.4×0.1^2.5 ≈ 4.4 L/s ≈ 266 L/min; a 50 L bucket fills in about 11 s, timing error 2–3% — a critical step. Disposition: for this step switch to a 200 L large bucket, or time it as "measure the total over 5 minutes and take 1/5".

docs.title: 27.4.4 Pitot Tube: Reading Flow Velocity from Pressure Difference
docs.text:
Principle: the stagnation pressure at the impact opening (total pressure) = static pressure + dynamic pressure, with dynamic pressure = ½ρv². Connect the total-pressure opening and the static-pressure opening to the two legs of a U-tube respectively; the liquid-column difference is the dynamic pressure. For measuring water flow with water as the indicating liquid: ρgh = ½ρv² → v = √(2gh) (h = water-column difference, g=9.8 m/s²). Worked example: h=50 mm → v≈0.99 m/s; h=200 mm → v≈1.98 m/s. Do not take readings when the water-column difference is <25 mm (reading error is large); switch to the inclined-tube micromanometer (27.3.1).

Construction: two copper tubes, φ3 mm — the total-pressure tube has a φ1.5 mm impact opening at its tip and is bent into an L shape (opening facing squarely into the oncoming flow); the static-pressure tube runs parallel to the flow with 4 φ1 mm side holes (evenly spaced, ≥3 tube diameters from the tip). Simplified version: a single tube measures total pressure only, with static pressure taken from a hole in the pipe wall — easy to make, error of 5% order (empirical value; calibration method below).

Pipe installation: the Pitot tube passes through a stuffing box (Chapter 22 threaded joints + Chapter 15 grease-soaked leather packing) and is inserted to the pipe centerline; ◎ alignment hand-feel: loosen the stuffing box, rotate the probe slowly, and lock it when the U-tube reading is maximal (maximum reading = facing the oncoming flow); practice method: practice 5 times on a straight pipe section; compensation: rotating ±10° fore and aft changes the reading by ≤5%, which judges alignment acceptable.

Center-to-mean conversion: velocity is greatest at the pipe centerline; the cross-sectional mean velocity ≈0.8–0.85× the center value (turbulent empirical value). This-tube calibration: compare the whole pipe once against the volume–time method and derive this tube's "center coefficient" = mean/center; enter it in the ledger; recalibrate when the pipe diameter changes or the flow changes greatly. If the flow visibly appears laminar (slow flow in a small pipe), do not use this empirical value; calibrate separately with the bucket method.

Flow = mean velocity × cross-sectional area (inner diameter measured in two directions with the Chapter 22 micrometer). Measuring air flow: dynamic pressure is small (air at v=5 m/s has a dynamic pressure of only about 1.5 mm water column) — an inclined-tube micromanometer is mandatory; usable for duct velocities in the 3–10 m/s band; do not read below 3 m/s.

Pipe-flow worked example (order-of-magnitude sanity check demonstration): a pipe of 50 mm inner diameter, center-point water-column difference 128 mm → center velocity v=√(2×9.8×0.128)≈1.58 m/s; this tube's center coefficient 0.82 → mean velocity ≈1.30 m/s; cross-sectional area π×0.025²≈1.96×10⁻³ m² → flow ≈2.55 L/s ≈153 L/min. Cross-check: a 200 L bucket fills in about 78 s, timing error <1% — the whole chain is of reasonable magnitude and may be entered in the ledger.

[Card 27-03 Weir Flow Calibration] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: one weir plate (3 mm thin steel sheet or board sheathed with iron sheet); point gauge (needle tip + vernier, resolution 0.5 mm); standard bucket (volume fixed by weighing, 50–200 L, bucket number in the ledger); timer.
  2. Tools required: square (90° verification of the notch); fine file (45° chamfer of the edge); level and plumb line; Chapter 3 layout tools; full volume–time-method set (27.4.1).
  3. Operating sequence and control points: ① lay out – saw – file the notch to 90°±0.5° (check the light gap with a square) ② 45° edge on the downstream face — control point: drip test with the nappe lifting off the plate face ③ stand the plate plumb, crest ≥150 mm above downstream ④ gauge zero point — control point: needle tip just touching the V apex ⑤ set 6 head steps (20–150 mm), 3 timed buckets per step — control point: measurement point 3–4 times the maximum head from the weir ⑥ record the six H-Q points; chisel the table plate.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: Q=1.4H^2.5 is for estimation only (coefficient range 1.34–1.42; empirical value, calibrate to local conditions — the six measured steps are that local calibration); the lookup table defers to direct measurement; interpolation error ≤2% (re-measure an inserted step); upstream straight reach ≥10 times the maximum head; visual venting criterion; the weir table is qualified when the table-derived flow deviates from the bucket method by ≤5%.
  5. Process observation and recording items: gauge reading at each step, fill time per bucket, net bucket weight, water temperature, nappe state (lifted/clinging), table plate number and date — enter into the weir ledger.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: accept = six points monotonic + same-step re-measurement repeat ≤2% + interpolation verified + deviation from the bucket method ≤5%; rework = dull edge (after re-filing, re-calibrate the entire table); scrap = warped weir plate (straightedge light gap on the plate face >1 mm), or downstream submergence that cannot be remedied.
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: symptom "table-derived flow differs from the bucket method by 8%" — ① gauge zero point drifted (re-touch the V apex) ② measurement point too close to the falling-water zone (watch the surface disturbance) ③ nappe clinging to the wall (check venting) ④ table plate out of date (fouling and notch wear change the geometry) — troubleshoot in order; at each step, if present, correct it and re-measure.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = a record of two step points agreeing with the bucket method to ≤5%; L2 = six-step table plate + quarterly re-verification records; L3 = the weir ledger incorporated into hydraulic production scheduling and waterwheel output calculation (Chapter 38 account book), with quarterly re-verification continued for half a year.

docs.title: 27.5 Vacuum Measurement: One System, Three-Stage Gauge Selection
27.5.1 Why Gauge Selection Must Be Split by Pressure Regime
docs.text:
Every kind of vacuum gauge covers only two or three orders of magnitude: a mercury gauge is capped by a 760 mm tube length, and the McLeod gauge has a limited compression ratio. Using a gauge of the wrong range = reading a handsome false number — connect a low-range gauge to a high-vacuum system, read "bottom of scale" and believe the target is reached: this is the number-one accident source in vacuum work (silent failure; the first lesson of Chapter 33 vacuum processing). So establish the gauge-selection regime first, then discuss building gauges.

Pressure regimes and gauge-selection table ( addition):

Pressure regime Absolute pressure range Primary gauge Resolution Continuous/spot Rough vacuum 760–10 mmHg Open U-tube mercury vacuum gauge 1 mmHg Continuous Transition 10–1 mmHg Closed single-tube mercury gauge 1–2 mmHg Continuous Low vacuum 1–10⁻¹ mmHg Closed gauge for trends + McLeod gauge spot-check confirmation — Mostly spot High vacuum <10⁻¹ mmHg McLeod gauge (Chapter 33) + discharge-tube color indication Qualitative to semi-quantitative Spot

docs.title: 27.5.2 Open and Closed Mercury Vacuum Gauges
docs.text:
• Open type: one leg of the U-tube connects to the system, the other to atmosphere; the reading h = atmospheric pressure − system absolute pressure (i.e., the "degree of vacuum"); absolute pressure = that day's barometer reading − h. Advantage: easiest to build and maintain; limitation: h maxes out at the atmospheric pressure value, and the absolute pressure comes from "subtracting two large numbers" — dedicated to the rough-vacuum regime;
  • Closed single-tube type (Torricelli type): a single tube sealed at one end is filled with mercury and inverted to stand in a mercury trough; above the mercury column top at the sealed end is itself an approximate vacuum (residual pressure of negligible order), and the system connects on the trough side — the reading is the system absolute pressure, read directly over 0–760 mmHg, with no same-day barometric correction needed. Manufacturing key points: fill with mercury free of bubbles (thin funnel + iron-wire guide for slow pouring; tap the tube section by section to expel bubbles); perform the inversion inside a tray; interpretation: a bubble column appearing at the tube top = failed filling, refill;
  • Mercury purity: an oil film fouling the mercury shifts surface readings by 0.5–1 mmHg order — alkaline wash, water wash, filtering through chamois or pinhole paper until the surface is mirror-bright (acceptance criterion);
  • Reading apparatus: both gauges are fitted with a vernier reading scale sliding along the tube (Chapter 22 vernier concept), resolution 0.5 mm; read the mercury surface at the crown of the convex meniscus, with the eye level with the crown to eliminate parallax; before each reading tap the tube stand lightly to drive bubbles off the walls;
  • Safety (hard rule): all mercury operations inside a white-porcelain/iron tray (spills seen at once); spilled mercury is immediately covered, mixed with sulfur powder, and collected (forming mercury sulfide reduces vaporization); mercury bottles stored under water seal; work in a ventilated place. Mercury poisoning symptoms are delayed in onset (silent failure); the occupational-protection regime is developed in Chapter 39 — this chapter only establishes the operating rules.

docs.title: 27.5.3 McLeod Gauge (referenced by Chapter 33)
docs.text: A compression-type vacuum gauge: take a known-volume sample of the system gas, compress it with a mercury column to a known small volume, read the mercury-column difference after compression, and back-calculate the original pressure from Boyle's law (P₁V₁=P₂V₂). Range roughly 10⁻¹–10⁻³ mmHg; spot readings (one compression, one reading). Structure and glassworking fabrication are in Chapter 33; this chapter only sets the regime: all readings below 10⁻¹ mmHg are governed by the McLeod gauge; mercury gauges serve only as evacuation-process indicators.

docs.title: 27.5.4 Gauge-Switching Procedure During Evacuation (Putting the Gauge-Selection Regime into Practice)
docs.text:
1. Start of pumping: connect the open mercury gauge; the liquid-column difference climbs from 0;
  2. When the liquid-column difference nears the local atmospheric pressure value (within 40 mmHg remaining) → switch to the closed gauge (absolute pressure read directly) — the open gauge has entered the unreliable "large-number subtraction" zone;
  3. When the closed gauge's liquid column falls below 10 mm (reading uncertainty >10%) → switch to McLeod gauge spot readings; the closed gauge serves only for trends;
  4. High-vacuum regime: McLeod gauge spot readings + discharge-tube color cross-check (Chapter 33); when the two disagree, the McLeod gauge rules;
  5. Leak prevention in gauge-changing actions: grease the joints (Chapter 33 vacuum grease) or add a small U-shaped mercury-seal trap; if the system pressure rises back >10% within 5 min after a gauge change, shut down and check the joints (empirical value; calibrate to system volume: for small-volume systems substitute an absolute criterion of 5 mmHg).

[Card 27-04 Vacuum Gauge Selection and Handover] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: the vacuum system to be measured (joints M10×1.5 or ground-glass, Chapter 33 specs); that day's barometer reading; mercury ≥500 g (washed to mirror-bright); two glass tubes φ8×900 mm (Chapter 14).
  2. Tools required: open U-tube and closed single-tube mercury vacuum gauges (self-made per 27.5.2); McLeod gauge (drawn from Chapter 33, draw number entered in the ledger); mercury tray and sulfur powder; pinhole filter paper/chamois (filtering mercury); steel rule or vernier (reading column heights, Chapter 22).
  3. Operating sequence and control points: ① judge the pressure regime — control point: an unknown system always starts on the open gauge; connecting the McLeod gauge directly to draw conclusions is forbidden ② connect the open gauge to the system and record h; absolute pressure = that day's barometer − h ③ when h has <40 mmHg remaining, switch to the closed gauge ④ when the closed liquid column is <10 mm, switch to McLeod gauge spot readings ⑤ grease/mercury-seal the joints at the gauge change — control point: a >10% rise-back within 5 min after the change means stop and hunt leaks ⑥ record the gauge used, the readings, and the gauge-change times for each stage.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: regime thresholds 40/10 mmHg (empirical value; corrected after one McLeod-gauge cross-check in the boundary zone); closed gauge reads absolute pressure directly; open-gauge conversion formula; 10% rise-back as the leak criterion (changed to an absolute criterion according to system volume).
  5. Process observation and recording items: gauge-change sequence, each gauge's readings and times, joint method, anomalies (bubble column at the tube top, dull mercury surface) — enter into the operating ledger of that vacuum apparatus.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: accept = the two gauges connected simultaneously once in the handover zone with converted-reading difference ≤2 mmHg, and no missed judgments throughout; rework = leaking joints (re-grease or replace the mercury seal, then re-test); scrap = bubble column at the closed gauge's top (refill the mercury), mercury too dirty to wash (replace the mercury).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: symptom "McLeod gauge contradicts the closed gauge" — ① compression done too fast, entraining bubbles (re-measure) ② closed gauge mercury dirty (mirror-bright criterion) ③ the system itself fluctuating (pump stopped, temperature rising — watch the trend) ④ slight joint leak (rise-back method). Symptom "cannot pump down further" — ① the selected gauge has reached its lower limit (switch to the McLeod gauge to confirm the vacuum; not a pump fault) ② system leak (Chapter 33 leak-detection method) ③ pump fault (Chapter 33).
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one complete gauge-change sequence record; L2 = gauge-selection placards at all vacuum work sites + handover-zone mutual-verification records; L3 = the gauge-selection regime linked with the Chapter 33 McLeod gauge draw ledger, with quarterly mutual verification continued.

docs.title: 27.6 Four-Quantity Calibration Chain Overview ( addition)
docs.text:
The four instrument classes each form their own chain, and every chain traces back to a reference chapter already in this book:

Quantity Local reference Transfer Working Traceability endpoint Temperature Ice point / local boiling point / reference wax batch — three phase-change points Standard thermometer (quarterly three-point re-verification) Working thermometers, thermocouple lookup tables Chapter 3 equal-division scribing + Chapter 25 barometer (boiling-point correction) Pressure Deadweight tester (P=mg/A) Mercury-column mutual verification (monthly) Bourdon-tube pressure gauges, diaphragm gauges, U-tubes Chapter 3/22 weights + Chapter 22 micrometer (piston area) Flow Standard bucket + timer (volume–time method) Weir H-Q lookup table, bucket-volume coefficients Weirs, tipping-bucket flowmeters, Pitot tubes (center coefficient) Chapter 3/25 mass (volume fixed by weighing) + Chapter 3 timekeeping reference Vacuum Atmospheric pressure value + mercury column length Open/closed mercury gauges McLeod gauge spot readings (built in Chapter 33) Chapter 3 length + Chapter 25 barometric reference

This table is the first-hand material for the "27.11 are the instruments adequate" judgment: whenever any instrument reports a number, one must be able to answer along this table "whom you calibrate toward, and who calibrates toward you."

docs.title: 27.7 How to Build Instruments That Can Be Repeatedly Calibrated (first edition 27.3, retained)
docs.text:
The three requisites of calibrability; missing any one makes it a "toy," not an instrument:

  1. Comparable: the instrument has standard interfaces (pressure port, thermometric well, weight hanger) and can be connected at any time to reference standards (U-tube, standard thermometer, standard weights);
  2. Adjustable: two independent mechanisms for zero adjustment and slope adjustment (zero offset adjusted at the zero, full-scale deviation adjusted at the slope);
  3. Disassemblable for inspection: modular movement (pointer mechanism separate from the pressure-sensing element; replace the diaphragm without replacing the dial).

Calibration procedure: the five-point method (one point each at 0/25/50/75/100% of range) — the reference standard supplies the true value; read the instrument and record the deviation; if the deviation is linear, correct it by adjusting the slope; if nonlinear, draw a "correction curve," paste it on the back of the instrument, and correct readings from the curve. After calibration, apply a lead seal (wax + numbered stamp); once opened it is void and must be recalibrated.

docs.title: 27.8 From Mechanical Amplification to Optical Reading (first edition 27.4, retained)
docs.text:
When mechanical amplification reaches its limit (the mechanism's own deformation eats up the amplification gains), switch to optical amplification:

  • Mirror-and-scale method: an arc-shaped graduated scale placed beside the pointer plus a small plane mirror at the pointer's side (Chapter 24) — at reading, eye, pointer, and mirror image lie on one line, eliminating parallax; equivalent to raising the reading resolution by one grade;
  • Optical lever (king of micro-displacement): a mirror mounted at the point of micro-motion to be measured (e.g., thermal elongation of a metal rod, beam deflection); the light spot aimed at the mirror is reflected onto a distant scale, deflected at twice the mirror's angle — each additional 1 chi of mirror distance adds another grade of magnification; hundredfold magnitude is easily achieved (empirical value, must be field-calibrated). The "tiny quantities" left open in Chapter 25 — thermal expansion coefficients, magnetic deflection, beam deflection — all become measurable;
  • Telescope scale reading (Chapter 24 telescope + graduated scale): read at distance without walking up (high-temperature/hazardous positions), combining parallax elimination with fine scale graduation.

docs.title: 27.9 Measurement Error, Sensitivity, and Resolution (first edition 27.5, retained)
docs.text:
Three concepts often conflated; they must be kept distinct:

Concept Definition Criterion question Resolution The smallest perceptible scale interval "How large is the smallest division?" Sensitivity The indication change caused by a unit change of input "Add one unit — how many divisions does it move?" Error (accuracy) The deviation between indication and true value "Compared with the reference standard, how large is the difference?"

High sensitivity does not mean accuracy: a pointer amplified 100-fold, if its zero point drifts, gives readings that are splendid and entirely wrong. Errors are handled in two classes:

  • Systematic error (one-directional, repeatable): correct by calibration — correction curve / zero adjustment / interchange method (unequal balance arms);
  • Random error (two-directional, scattered): take the median of multiple measurements and report "median ± range"; if the range does not narrow with repetition = an uncontrolled variable exists; return to Chapter 25 Section 25.7 for troubleshooting.

Three instrument-health questions (weekly): Is the zero point right? Is it repeatable (do two readings at the same input agree)? Is the return difference large (difference between up-scale and down-scale readings)?

docs.title: 27.10 How to Establish Instrument Calibration Records (first edition 27.6, retained and expanded)
docs.text:
Each instrument gets one calibration card, containing: instrument number/name, reference standard number, all past calibration data (five-point deviation table), correction method (slope adjustment or curve), ambient temperature, calibrator, next calibration date.

Interval tiers (empirical value, must be field-calibrated): working instruments calibrated monthly; transfer-grade instruments calibrated quarterly; reference standards mutually cross-checked semi-annually (reusing the Chapter 22 pyramid). Three events — impact, overrange (driven to full scale), anomalous reading — trigger immediate sending for calibration. Each quarter, transcribe a copy of the complete calibration archive for off-site storage (fire protection, Chapter 4).

** additions: four new ledgers (each in its proper place, transcribed into the Chapter 43 master ledger): thermometer calibration cards (three-mark positions, wax batch number); pressure gauge deadweight five-point records + calibration placard register (basis for Chapter 28 release); weir H-Q lookup table plates and the bucket-volume coefficient book (quarterly re-verification); Pitot tube center coefficients and cone–thermocouple lookup tables (summarized every 10 kiln firings). For every parameter marked "empirical value, must be calibrated," the moment the calibrated value is settled, transcribe it into the ledger; the next batch of people need only look it up, not recall it.**

docs.title: 27.11 How to Judge Whether the Instruments Suffice to Support the Next Technology (first edition 27.7, retained)
docs.text:
Judgment procedure (four steps):

  1. Write out the measurement requirements of the next technology: which quantity to measure, over what range, and what error is allowed (example: steam-engine trials need pressure at the 0–5 water-column level ±5%; a generator needs voltage comparable and current comparable in grade);
  2. Check against the existing instrument list: is the range covered? Is the error up to standard? Do the interfaces match? — only when all three questions pass is it sufficient;
  3. When insufficient, two roads: upgrade the instruments (this chapter's route) vs. modify the process to route around (example: if high pressure cannot be measured, lower the trial pressure and run an extrapolated comparison within the measurable region — prefer lowering the specification; blind trial is forbidden);
  4. Register the conclusion: "Instrument prerequisites for the Chapter 28 steam trials = ×××, ×××; achieved on day ×" — the release slip for starting a technology.

This section turns "instruments" into explicit nodes on the dependency graph: passing the instrument gate before any chapter begins work is the institutional floodgate that prevents technological leaps in the latter half of the book. supplement: the release prerequisites for vacuum-class work must include "McLeod gauge in place" (Chapter 33) and gauge-selection placarding (27.5); otherwise Chapter 33 vacuum processing may not begin.

docs.title: Capability Boundary (Part B)
docs.text: Can do: weir/Pitot-tube flow, open mercury vacuum gauge, the four-quantity gauge selection and calibration-chain overview. Cannot do: the McLeod gauge itself (Chapter 33); precision spirit levels; pressures in the high-pressure band (before the heavy-liquid gauge is unlocked).

docs.text:
Ordered from "most common → hardest to detect":

Symptom Candidate causes (by probability) Verification Remedy Thermometer mid-section off by 3 divisions (most common) Mis-scribed segment; locally thick bore; wax batch drift In order: segment-boundary marks → add bath points above and below → re-test the wax with a standard thermometer Re-scribe; scrap after localizing the fault; back-measure again with a new batch Thermometer drifting 1–2 divisions overall Aging drift of the bulb volume; broken column or broken thread Cool fully and re-check the broken column; same bath as the standard Downgrade to a teaching piece; scrap Thermocouple reading low Loose cold-junction binding (cold end actually too warm); oxidized junctions 40 ℃ water-bath comparison; inspect the junctions Re-bind; re-solder the junctions Thermocouple chain drifting as a whole (irregularly) Galvanometer zero drift (Chapter 30 mechanism); third-metal contamination at the wire junctions Disconnect the sensor and short the galvanometer to check the zero; placarding regime Mercury-surface reading off by 1 mmHg order Dirty mercury (oil film) Mirror-bright surface criterion Alkaline wash – water wash – filter Kiln temperature "believed sufficient but actually under-fired" (hardest to detect) Thermocouple chain reading systematically low with no cross-check Compare in the same kiln against temperature cones Establish a "cone–thermocouple" lookup ledger; the bent cone is the authority

docs.title: Process Card Index
docs.text:
[Card 27-01] Glass thermometer three-point calibration (card at end of 27.2.2, Part A) | [Card 27-02] Spring-tube pressure gauge manufacture and deadweight calibration (card at end of 27.3, Part A) | [Card 27-03] Weir flow calibration (card at end of 27.4) | [Card 27-04] Vacuum gauge selection and handover (card at end of 27.5)

All four cards can be copied onto a single page and carry the full eight fields; the first two sit at the ends of their sections in Part A, the last two in this part.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• L1: one helical spring stiffness card completed; one glass thermometer three-point calibrated with back-test ≤±1 division; pressure gauge vs U-tube five-point comparison deviation <1 division; optical lever measuring the thermal elongation of a metal rod; the weir producing two H-Q points agreeing with the bucket method to ≤5%; one complete vacuum gauge-change sequence (open→closed) completed.
  • L2: at least 1 instrument of each of the four classes — temperature, pressure, flow, vacuum — in service with continuous monthly calibration records; the Bourdon-tube pressure gauge calibrated by five-point deadweight (indication ≤2% of range, return difference ≤1 division); the weir lookup table complete at all six steps with interpolation verified ≤2%; the Pitot tube's own center coefficient on file; the thermocouple lookup table complete (including cold-junction binding water-bath verification); return difference <half a division after hairspring anti-backlash work (empirical value, must be calibrated); the boiler pressure gauge calibration placard regime joined in writing with the Chapter 28 release clause.
  • L3: the four-quantity calibration chain (27.6 master table) fully operating: quarterly re-verification of the standard thermometer, monthly mercury mutual verification of the deadweight tester, quarterly re-verification of the weir table, vacuum gauge-selection placarding linked with the Chapter 33 McLeod gauge — records continuous for half a year with no gaps; the first "instrument release slip" issued for Chapter 28; instruments locally repairable (tube replacement / spring replacement / diaphragm replacement / re-scribing dials) with the off-site archive copy (Chapter 4) in place.

docs.title: Labor Hours, Manpower, and Consumables
docs.text: Item Manpower Labor hours (empirical value) Three-point calibration of one thermometer 1 person 0.5 days (including wax-point and ice-point equilibration waiting) One thermocouple + lookup table (oil bath, point by point) 2 people 1–2 days (depends on the galvanometer being in place) One Bourdon-tube pressure gauge (flattening – arc bending – movement assembly – calibration) 2 people 3–4 days One deadweight tester (cylinder lapping and piston fitting) 2 people 5–8 days Pressure gauge monthly calibration (deadweight five points, per gauge) 1 person 0.5 h/gauge·month One triangular weir (plate + point gauge) + six-step lookup table 2 people 2–3 days One Pitot tube + this-tube center coefficient 1 person 1 day One closed mercury vacuum gauge (including washing the mercury) 1 person 0.5 days Monthly full calibration (four instrument classes) 1 person 1 day/month Consumables: mercury, rosin, beeswax, bronze tube, tin solder, abrasive, soybean oil — Enter into the Chapter 38 account book

docs.title: Safety Boundary
docs.text:
• Pressure gauges are never used beyond range (driven to full scale means it has failed and is sent for calibration); the red line mark is the shutdown line;
  • Deadweight tester and pressure-withstand testing: during loading, keep head and hands out of the space directly above the cylinder and directly in front of the dial; observe from behind a barrier; when the medium is oil, guard against slipping and fire;
  • Three hard rules for mercury work: all operations inside a tray, spills immediately covered with sulfur and collected, storage in water-sealed bottles — mercury poisoning is delayed in onset; records of abnormal exposure go into the Chapter 39 occupational file;
  • Oil-bath calibration (thermocouples) is limited to 250 ℃ (a margin of at least 30 ℃ below the flash point); keep fire-extinguishing sand beside the oil bath;
  • Weir and open-channel work: guard against slipping and drowning; operate the point gauge crouched and steady on the upstream side; no work on rising water after rain;
  • For the optical lever's lamp flame/condensed light, guard against fire; replace a cracked mirror at once (reading distortion);
  • For spring making, the tempering step follows the Chapter 19 quench-and-temper safety rules.

docs.title: A. Existing Tool List (partial)
docs.text: Tempered spring steel (Chapter 19); threads and gears, prototype comparator (Chapters 20–22); thermometers / U-tubes / flow methods (Chapter 25); magnifiers and mirrors (Chapter 24); knife-edge technique (Chapter 25); record-keeping archive regime (Chapters 4, 25); equal-division scribing and timekeeping (Chapter 3); weights and balances (Chapters 3, 25); barometer and mercury (Chapter 25); temperature cones (Chapter 12).

docs.title: B. New Tools Added in This Chapter
docs.text: Leaf springs/helical springs/hairsprings and stiffness cards; lever–sector-gear pointer mechanism and hairspring anti-backlash; detachable thermometer interface standard; diaphragm pressure gauge; tipping-bucket flowmeter and mechanical counting; the three requisites of calibrability and the five-point calibration method + lead seal; mirror-and-scale method, optical lever, telescope scale reading; the three-way vocabulary of error/sensitivity/resolution and the handling of systematic/random errors; calibration cards and the interval-tier regime; instrument release slips (27.11 judgment procedure). ** four-quantity deepening**: temperature — three-point calibration chain, reference wax batch regime, top expansion chamber blank, thermocouple cold-junction binding compensation and cone–thermocouple lookup; pressure — inclined-tube micromanometer, spring-tube (Bourdon-tube) pressure gauge, deadweight tester (pressure-bootstrap reference), boiler calibration placard and maximum-record pointer; flow — standard bucket with volume fixed by weighing, weir method and H-Q lookup table, point gauge and venting criterion, Pitot tube and center coefficient; vacuum — open/closed mercury vacuum gauges, four-regime gauge-selection table, gauge-change leak-prevention procedure; four-quantity calibration chain overview (27.6).

docs.title: C. Unresolved Dependencies
docs.text:
• Mercury thermometers and high-temperature glass (glass-liquid thermometry above 110 ℃, vacuum-fill process);
  • Noble-metal thermocouples (platinum) — continuous thermometry above 750 ℃ still relies on the semi-quantitative Chapter 12 temperature cones;
  • Pirani / ionization vacuum gauges — continuous reading below 10⁻¹ mmHg (after the Chapters 30–33 electrical instruments);
  • Deadweight calibration above 10 atm (cylinder and weight strength) — for now transitioned via dual-gauge mutual calibration + mercury-column comparison;
  • Constant-temperature and vibration-isolated environments (building and overall industrial level).

docs.title: Next-Step Dependencies
docs.text:
• Chapters 28–29: pressure gauges (including calibration-placard release), thermometers, dynamometry, and flowmeters are the quantitative eyes of heat-engine development; the "instrument release slip" and "no ignition without a calibration placard" regimes directly serve trial safety;
  • Chapters 30–31: the galvanometer (pointer mechanism + new sensing principle) is the electrical descendant of this chapter's mechanisms; the physical side of thermocouples and the constantan formula are developed in Chapter 30; after the galvanometer reaches L2, this chapter's thermocouple section is backfilled and upgraded;
  • Chapter 33: the McLeod gauge and vacuum grease are supplied by Chapter 33; the gauge-selection placard regime is a start-of-work prerequisite for Chapter 33 vacuum processing;
  • Chapter 34: the optical lever and precision temperature control are prerequisites for observing crystal growth;
  • Chapters 37–39: the four-quantity calibration ledgers merge into spot checks and the skill matrix; occupational protection for mercury work belongs to Chapter 39;
  • The Part 10 environment editions: the instrument maintenance regime is the universal prescription for keeping industrial capability under harsh conditions.

docs.title: Chapter Objectives
docs.text:
Build heat-engine capability: understand the heat–pressure–work conversion chain, master the key properties of water vapor, and build the first low-risk atmospheric (Newcomen-type) steam engine (the Newcomen route—it tolerates coarse tolerances and is the bootstrap entry point), while giving an upgrade route toward Watt-style improvements.

The first lesson of this chapter is safety, not efficiency: the energy stored in a steam system can kill instantly. Early experiments use only low-pressure demonstration devices; never perform high-pressure experiments with unverified homemade vessels.

docs.title: Capability Boundary
docs.text:
Can do: an atmospheric (Newcomen-type) steam engine (boiler at gauge pressure near zero) running self-sustained while driving a pump; riveted boilers released after a two-times hydrostatic test; quantitative safety-valve setting.

Explicitly cannot do: high-pressure steam (the four unlock conditions are in Section 28.8; until all four are met it remains "knowing ≠ being able to build"); the separate condenser and slide valve (Watt-style; depends on precision boring and valve-machining upgrades; preliminary study and unlock conditions in Section 28.14); locomotive and marine use and high-speed rotation (requires a governor).

External dependency: dedicated stokers (Iron Law 7: continuous-process watches are staffed by two people)—without an established stoker corps, the steam engine must not be fired.
