docs.text:
• The generational ramp of yield and cleanliness (the Section 36.8 table);
  • Generational upgrading of metrology and analytical instruments;
  • Double-sided boards and through-hole metallization (the electroless copper line on hole walls — the generational boundary declared in 36.14);
  • Greater power and population specialization (the population topics of Part 10's environment editions).

docs.title: Safety Boundary
docs.text:
• All chemical red lines inherited from Chapters 26, 35; fire patrols in the burn-in bench's continuously powered zone;
  • Glass/ceramic shards from teardown decapping are handled as sharps; burn protection at the bonding thermocompression station;
  • Repairing high-voltage equipment (grid side) follows Chapter 32's two-person procedure.

docs.title: Acceptance Standards
docs.text:
• L1: The test master runs in-furnace; failure files are established and the first ten three-level analyses are completed.
  • L2: Flip-flop-level (ramp level 2) yield reaches target; the burn-in screening regime operates; at least three of the first five equipment classes are in active service.
  • L3: The monthly operating account is auditable for six consecutive months; a supply-cutoff drill has been run at least once; two-person backup across the seven workstations is fully institutionalized — the electronics industry becomes a sustainable organ of the settlement.

docs.title: Next-Step Dependencies
docs.text:
• Chapters 50–53: how electronic capability is arranged and combined in different environments (the island's communication-first priority, the desert's remote-controlled irrigation, the permafrost's low-temperature reliability, the rainforest's moisture-proof packaging);
  • The loop back to the general outline: this chapter is the contemporary apex of the "information lineage" among the six great lineages — the thousand-year leap from oral experience to electronic computation closes its loop here.

docs.title: Chapter 37: Ecological Carrying Capacity, Population Balance, and Labor Organization
Chapter Objectives
docs.text:
After reading this chapter, a settlement should be able to produce four documents:

Document Content Use Carrying-capacity estimate document The supportable population range computed by the three-ceiling method Decides "whether more people can be taken in, whether a new furnace should be lit" Off-farm balance table Agricultural surplus → number of artisans supportable → technology-step ceiling Decides "which chapter's technology to build up to now" Shift and watch schedules The minimum shift establishment for each continuous process Keeps the blast furnace, long kiln, and steam engine from stopping for lack of hands Skill matrix and responsibility boundaries Skill grades for the ten posts, resource red lines, change control Keeps the technology chain from breaking because any one person is lost

docs.title: Capability Boundaries
docs.text:
Can do:

  • Given at least one complete farming-season record, estimate carrying capacity to an order of ±30–50%.
  • Compute the off-farm artisan quota (historical range 5–15%) and lay out the minimum shift schedule that satisfies the continuous processes.
  • Define the minimum skill sets, training periods, and assessment evidence for the ten posts.

Cannot do:

  • Predict sudden population changes from epidemic, conflict, or migration in and out. This chapter can only partially hedge with the redundancy coefficient (Section 37.2.4); it cannot predict.
  • Give a reliable estimate without farming-season records. In that case every result can only be marked "provisional figures", with error up to ±100%, and is forbidden for furnace-lighting and capacity-expansion decisions.
  • Replace the safety procedures of the individual process chapters. This chapter governs "how people are arranged and how accounts are kept", not "how the furnace is fired".

External dependencies (counted on the C list):

  1. Yield records for at least one complete farming season (including under-yielding plots and their causes) — this is the foundation of every estimate.
  2. A health roster of the whole settlement (who can work a full day under the blazing sun and who cannot).
  3. An inventory of leftovers from the start (metal tools, containers, clothing, medicine stocks) — this sets the buffer for the first two years.

docs.title: Pre-Work Verification
docs.text:
Checklist style. If any criterion fails, the corresponding estimate must be downgraded to "provisional figures", and the cover of the estimate document must state which item is missing.

# Verification item Criterion (confirm you have X in hand, and the standard is Y) 1 Population roster Every person registered with name, age, health status; the "full laborers" (recommended definition: aged 15–55 with no long-term injury or illness) can be counted 2 Grain stock count Everything weighed or converted by volume measure, error ≤10%; registered in three columns: "edible, moldy, seed stock" 3 Arable land register Areas measured by survey-rope pacing (Chapter 3 method), in three columns: "under cultivation, fallow, reclaimable"; each plot carries a soil note 4 Forest land register Area and round-trip labor hours to the nearest cutting site; at least 3 quadrats of 10 m×10 m with tree-species and DBH (diameter at breast height) records 5 Water source records Dry-season minimum flow estimate (Chapter 2 method) + water actually drawn by people and livestock over 3 consecutive days 6 Fuel account Day-by-day weighing records of household firewood for 7 consecutive days; specific fuel consumption of furnaces and kilns already built copied from each chapter's acceptance ledger 7 Farming-season records For at least one season: sown area, actual harvested weight of unprocessed grain, under-yielding plots and their causes 8 Weights and measures One set of length, volume, and mass standards for the whole settlement (Chapters 3 and 22), cross-checked on the spot once between the account office and each workshop's handlers

docs.title: 37.1 Energy Flow and Per-Capita Consumption Benchmarks
docs.text: Balance starts from "what one person consumes in a year". Every number in this section is an empirical value that must be field-calibrated, each with its calibration method attached. Until calibration is done, the ranges may be used only for order-of-magnitude judgment and must not be used for production scheduling or furnace-lighting decisions.

docs.title: 37.1.1 Per-Capita Annual Consumption Benchmark Table
docs.text:
Item Empirical range Applicable conditions Field calibration method Food ration (unprocessed grain) 200–300 kg/person·year, of which cereals 180–250, legumes 20–40 Normal labor intensity; children counted at 0.5, the elderly at 0.7; heavy labor (miners, forging smiths, loggers) raised 20–30% Current grain stock ÷ number of people ÷ months it can sustain × 12; cross-check against the actual-harvest account; if deviation >20%, re-weigh the grain stock Household firewood 2–4 kg/person·day Temperate zones; take the lower bound for cooking only, the upper bound for winter heating; workshop fuel is accounted separately and must never be mixed into this line Pick 3 typical households and weigh the wood they actually burn day by day for 7 consecutive days; take the median Fiber (hemp/cotton/wool) New fiber 2–4 kg/person·year Garments held: 3–4 pieces per person, each lasting 4–8 years Inventory the garments in use and the year's mending hours; back-calculate the annual replacement quantity Salt 3–5 kg/person·year Includes pickling and preservation; fatigue, cramps, and a sudden drop in appetite are salt-deficiency signals Record actual issues in the account; check the stock difference monthly Housing materials Service life of earth-and-timber houses 10–20 years Annual maintenance ≈ 1/10–1/15 of the material for one new room Inspect houses before and after the rainy season; register repair labor and materials

◎ Judging whether a grain bin is full or hollow (tapping the bin and listening to detect mold and voids) is a hand-feel step. Practice method: practice 20 times on grain bins that have already been weighed, then estimate blind. Misjudgment compensation: insert a probe tube into each bin to take a mid-layer sample for weighing, and spot-check 10% of the bins.

docs.title: 37.1.2 Workshop Specific Fuel Consumption (Separate Account)
docs.text:
Workshop fuel is not spread into per-capita figures; each furnace keeps its own account. A furnace or kiln with no specific-consumption record must first burn one run and record one run before production scheduling is discussed.

Furnace/kiln Empirical specific-consumption range Calibration method Source chapter Batch pottery kiln 0.3–0.8 t firewood per firing Weigh the wood loaded for the whole kiln, or convert by wood-bundle volume Chapters 11–12 Iron-smelting fuel ratio Charcoal : iron = 4–8 : 1 (by weight) Record charcoal charged and iron produced per furnace run Chapter 18 Charcoal yield 1 kg charcoal ≈ 4–6 kg firewood Weigh everything in and out of the kiln Chapter 6 Lime kiln 0.3–0.5 t firewood per t lime Keep accounts kiln by kiln Chapter 13

Specific consumption for the glass melting furnace, steam engine fuel, and the like is accounted in the corresponding chapters; this table does not fill it in on their behalf.

docs.title: 37.1.3 Energy Flow Directions
docs.text:
Farmland ─→ food ration + seed stock (10–15%) + fodder + reserves
Forest ─→ household firewood + workshop wood/charcoal + construction and implement timber (all three draw on the same standing stock)
Water ─→ drinking and cooking + irrigation + workshop cooling and washing
Human labor ─→ farm work + gathering and transport + workshop labor + night watch shifts (one person's hours are a hard constraint)

Two corollaries feed directly into what follows: first, every furnace lit is in fact drawing on two budgets at once — the forest and the agricultural surplus; second, human hours are a balancing item just like grain — this is why the shift scheduling of Section 37.4 exists.

Draft-animal conversion: one draft ox consumes 8–12 kg of hay per day (or grazes 4–6 h), and its annual feed equals 0.3–0.6 ha of grassland or cropland by-products; this must be counted when reckoning cultivated area and supported population.

docs.title: 37.2 The Three-Ceiling Method for Carrying Capacity
docs.text:
Carrying capacity is not one number; it is the thinnest of three chains:

Supportable population N = min(food ceiling N₁, fuel ceiling N₂, water-and-building-materials ceiling N₃) ÷ redundancy coefficient k (1.3–1.5)

docs.title: 37.2.1 Food Ceiling N₁
docs.text:
Formula: N₁ = arable area S (ha) × yield y (kg/ha·year) × multiple-cropping index × net retention ratio ÷ per-capita ration r (kg/person·year, weighted by population structure).

Empirical yield ranges (unprocessed grain):

Farming method Empirical yield range Applicable conditions Slash-and-burn 500–1000 kg/ha·season Cropped 2–3 consecutive years, then fallowed 8–15 years (Chapter 50 scenario) Unfertilized dry farming 600–1200 kg/ha Slopes, no irrigation, no compost Dry farming with composted rotation 1000–2000 kg/ha With compost and legume rotation (Chapter 10) Irrigated rice 2000–4000 kg/ha·season Plains, controllable water source, ample draft power

Calibration: leave 3 harvested quadrats of 10 m×10 m in each field class, thresh and weigh them separately; scale the quadrat result up to the whole field, then cross-check against the season's total harvest; if deviation >20%, switch to the total-harvest basis and discard quadrat extrapolation.

Net retention ratio: deduct 10–15% for seed stock and 10–20% per year for storage losses (rats, insects, mold); the edible net ≈ harvest × 0.65–0.80.

docs.title: 37.2.2 Fuel Ceiling N₂
docs.text:
Formula: N₂ = (forest area × annual growth × 0.7–0.8) ÷ (per-capita household firewood + workshop fuel converted to a per-capita share).

  • Empirical annual growth: temperate mixed forest 2–5 m³/ha·year (air-dry weight about 1.2–3.5 t/ha·year); tropical secondary forest is higher, but the part that cannot be hauled out in the rainy season must be deducted (Chapter 50).
  • The 0.7–0.8 coefficient: reserve 20–30% of the growth for construction timber, implements, and forest enclosure; burning the entire growth as fuel is not allowed.
  • Fuelwood coppice runs on a rotation cycle of 10–20 years: required fuelwood stand area = annual wood consumption × rotation cycle, and each year wood is taken from only 1/cycle of the area.
  • Calibration: set 3–5 quadrats of 10 m×10 m and measure the DBH increment year by year; without year-by-year records, fell 1–2 sample trees, weigh them, and count the growth rings to back-calculate the annual increment per hectare.

◎ Eyeballing "which stand has been thinned by cutting" (stand-structure hand feel) is a hand-feel step. Practice method: practice 10 times against quadrats that have already been measured. Misjudgment compensation: stump counts inside the quadrat + a measured DBH distribution; in a thinned-out stand the DBH distribution shifts left as a whole.

docs.title: 37.2.3 Water and Building-Materials Ceiling N₃
docs.text:
• Water: drinking and cooking 20–50 L/person·day; peak irrigation demand per the field accounts of Chapter 10; workshop cooling and washing counted separately per the specific consumption of Chapters 26 and 28. Criterion: if the dry-season minimum flow < the sum above → the ceiling binds on water, and only the irrigable part of the arable land is counted.
  • Building materials: register every extraction point for clay, sand, stone, and straw. Criterion: if round-trip extraction hours exceed 1/3 of the day's working hours, that source is deemed unsustainable — recalculate the cost using the farther source, or lower the building standard.

docs.title: 37.2.4 Redundancy Coefficient k = 1.3–1.5
docs.text:
Redundancy rationale Magnitude (empirical values) Bad-year fluctuation (drought, flood, insects) ±30% Annual reserve set aside 10–15% of output Storage and transport losses 10–20% Downtime from illness and injury 5–10%

Setting the value: two full seasons of records and no major disaster → 1.3; less than one season of records or frequent disasters → 1.5; interpolate between according to circumstances. k may not go below 1.3 unless the settlement already has back-verification records for three consecutive seasons.

docs.title: 37.2.5 Worked Example (for instruction; the numbers are hypothetical)
docs.text:
Suppose a settlement has 300 people: arable land 80 ha, composted rotation, y taken as 1500 kg/ha, net retention 0.70 → net grain 84 t; weighted r = 250 kg → N₁ = 336 people. Forest 400 ha, annual growth 2.5 t/ha, coefficient taken as 0.75 → usable 750 t/year; total per-capita wood (household 1.1 t + workshop-converted 0.75 t) = 1.85 t → N₂ = 406 people. Water: sufficient in the dry season → N₃ does not bind. min = 336, k taken as 1.4 → N = 240 people < the current 300 people. Conclusion: this settlement is already overloaded, and its options are only three — reclaim land and/or compost to raise yields, seal furnaces to cut workshop wood, or split off part of the people to establish a separate outpost. This example shows what the three-ceiling method is for: what it often tells you is not "how many more people can be taken in" but "what must be cut right now".

[Card 37-01 Carrying-Capacity Estimate Card] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: population roster, arable and forest registers, weighed grain-stock records, 7-day fuel weighing records, farming-season harvest records; volume measures and scales (Chapter 3; cross-checked against standard weights before use).
  2. Required tools: survey rope and ranging poles (Chapter 3), 10 m quadrat rope, scales, account book. Calibrate before use: compare the survey rope's length against a standard rule; if error >0.5%, replace the rope; check the scales' zero point and full scale with known weights.
  3. Operating sequence and control points: ① Check the 8 pre-work verification items and mark missing ones on the cover; ② compute N₁, N₂, N₃ item by item, each on its own line; ③ take the min, then divide by k, obtaining a range rather than a single value; ④ Reverse check: if the current population exceeds 80% of the ceiling, put production cuts, land reclamation, or furnace closure on the agenda and write this into the estimate document's conclusion field; ⑤ Transcribe into the ledger, noting the data cutoff date.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: y, annual growth, net retention ratio, and k take their values from the tables of Section 37.2, with the raw quadrat and weighing data attached; filling in numbers from impressions is not allowed.
  5. Process observation and recording items: the location of each quadrat, the weighing date, and the handler; the first page of the estimate document states the "data cutoff date" and the "missing-items list".
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = each of the three ceilings has an independent measured source and the arithmetic can be recomputed; rework = a ceiling used the range default instead of measurement (re-measure that item and recompute); scrap = estimates substituted for weighing records (the whole card is voided and the inventory redone).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: result clearly too large → first check whether seed stock and storage losses were not deducted → check whether workshop wood was mixed into the household-firewood line → check whether dividing by k was forgotten; result too small → check whether the quadrats happened to be placed in under-yielding fields → check whether inaccessible slopes were counted as forest → check whether r was marked up twice.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = an estimate document containing the arithmetic and the missing-items list; L2 = the estimate document + back-verification records of one farming season's actual harvest and actual fuel consumption (deviation ≤50%); L3 = two consecutive seasons of back-verification + ledger update records + resource red-line patrol records (Section 37.6.4).

Blank record sheet (for copying the card):

Item Year 1 Year 2 Population N / full-laborer count Arable land S (ha) / measured yield y Net grain output Y (t) N₁ formula and result Forest area (ha) / measured annual growth Household wood + workshop wood (t/year) N₂ formula and result Dry-season minimum flow / N₃ result min ÷ k = supportable range Conclusion (take in people / hold steady / overloaded) Missing-items list

docs.title: 37.3 Agricultural Surplus Rate and Off-Farm Artisan Balance
37.3.1 Surplus Rate and Off-Farm Quota
docs.text:
Formulas:

  • Surplus grain S_sur = net grain output Y − N×r − seed stock − reserve increment
  • Fully off-farm people supportable D = S_sur ÷ r
  • Off-farm ratio = D ÷ N

Empirical range: the long-term off-farm ratio of stable traditional agricultural societies is 5–15%; in good years with irrigation plus compost it can briefly reach 20%; in bad years it is 0 or negative. Any long-term plan laid out at an off-farm ratio >15% must present measured evidence for irrigation or compost (Chapter 10), or it is deemed overload overdraft.

Two corrections:

  • Artisans eat more: rations for heavy-labor posts (miners, forging smiths, loggers, kiln workers) are raised 20–30% (Section 37.1.1); in the balance, count these people at r×1.25.
  • Half off-farm counts as half: part-time artisans who return to the fields for the busy season and enter the workshops in the slack season count as 0.5 of a quota.

docs.title: 37.3.2 Population Size → Technology-Step Reference Table
docs.text:
The table below turns "how many people does a settlement need to reach which chapter" into arithmetic. "Stable support" in the table means the materials, fuel, watch-keeping, and succession of that step can be sustained long-term; "having made one piece once" does not count (that is L1).

Settlement size Off-farm headcount (on the 5–15% range, midpoint 10%) Technology steps it can stably support What it cannot support A village of 50 people 3–5 people (mostly seasonal part-timers) Parts 2 and 3: stone tools and woodworking (Chapters 5–9), pottery, brick, and tile (Chapters 11–13), compost agriculture and grain storage (Chapter 10), small glass items in a batch crucible furnace (Chapter 14) A continuously run blast furnace (one non-extinguished blast furnace alone requires a 7-person establishment, see Section 37.4.2), machine tools, steam engines, electricity of any kind A settlement of 300 people 15–45 people Parts 4 and 5: bloomery smelting and small blast furnaces fired seasonally (Chapters 16–18), steel and tool forging (Chapter 19), a single machine tool and standard parts (Chapters 20–22), glassware and basic chemistry (Chapters 14, 23–26), simple instruments (Chapter 27) Year-round non-extinguished metallurgy, continuous power beyond the waterwheel, the power grid (Chapter 32), electronic devices A market town of 2000 people 100–300 people Most of Part 6: year-round blast-furnace production, machine-tool work crews, a single steam engine (Chapter 28) and water and wind power (Chapter 29), an electromagnetism laboratory (Chapter 30), a single generator and in-plant distribution (Chapter 31), carbon-filament lamps and trials of simple vacuum devices (Chapter 33) Grid-scale power supply (Chapter 32), semiconductor-grade purification (Chapter 34), integrated circuits (Chapter 35) — these require division of labor at the ten-thousand-person scale and a stable chemical industry

Three principles for reading the table:

  1. The step is set by the thinnest ceiling. Even if a 50-person settlement finds a complete set of drawings, it cannot field a 7-person blast-furnace establishment — what is missing is not knowledge but off-farm people and surplus grain.
  2. The threshold of Chapter 35 is organizational, not technical. Going from 2000 people to the ten-thousand scale adds not "smarter artisans" but a higher grain commercialization rate, transport, and the account-office system.
  3. The environment editions move the thresholds. The four environments of Chapters 50–53 each rewrite this table: the fuel ceiling is tighter in the rainforest, the food ceiling tighter in permafrost, water and minerals tighter on islands. Re-run the three-ceiling method of Section 37.2 for each environment; do not copy this table as-is.

docs.title: 37.3.3 Busy-Season Pullback
docs.text: Most artisans are still relatives of farm households and will be pulled back to the fields for the 20–40 days of the busy season. Production rule: any workshop plan spanning the busy season is pre-scheduled at a reduction factor of 0.5; continuous processes (blast furnace, long kiln) must either shut down for maintenance before the busy season or lock the stay-behind shift schedule in advance and buy out the labor with double rations.

docs.title: 37.4.1 Watch-Keeping Classification and Labeling Principle
docs.text:
Throughout the book, processes are labeled in three classes by watch-keeping demand, and every chapter's process cards use the same vocabulary:

Class Criterion Examples Single-person process Interruptible; stops when hands stop; no hazard accumulation Woodworking, textiles, the account office, card copying Two-person process Heavy labor requiring rotation, or a need for mutual safety supervision Underground mining (Chapter 16), sledgehammer forging (Chapter 19), logging (Chapter 7) Crew process Continuous and non-interruptible; shutdown means scrap or an extremely costly restart Blast furnace, long-kiln firing section, steam engine running, large glass melting furnace

The classification is a hard constraint: a single-person process needs only one person scheduled; solo work is forbidden on two-person processes; a crew process must not be lit until its establishment is complete.

docs.title: 37.4.2 Blast-Furnace Shift Schedule (Must Not Go Out)
docs.text:
Once a blast furnace is lit, molten iron and furnace condition must never be left unattended overnight. Minimum establishment: 3 shifts per 24 hours × 2 people per shift + 1 float spare = 7 people, with cross-shift responsibility held by the furnace head (a grade-3 forging smith; see Section 37.5).

Shift Hours Post A Post B Handover contents Morning shift 06–14 Charging worker (weighs material per the ledger's batching sheet) Tuyere worker (watches flame color, logs blast conditions) Batching progress, iron-tapping and slagging records, the three anomaly columns Mid shift 14–22 Same as above Same as above Same as above Night shift 22–06 Same as above Same as above Same as above + hourly tuyere records

Rules: no solo night shifts; each handover takes 15 min of face-to-face checking with dual signatures; the spare rests by day and covers vacancies at any time. The smaller the furnace, the less you should skimp on these 7 people — skimping ends with a frozen hearth at three in the morning, and the cost of reopening exceeds three months of wage grain.

docs.title: 37.4.3 Shift Schedule Templates for the Long Kiln, Steam Engine, and Glass Melting Furnace
docs.text:
Facility Continuous-run duration People per shift 24-hour establishment Notes Long kiln (firing section) 20–60 h 2 (stoking + fire-watching and temperature taking) 3 shifts × 2 = 6 people Before the firing section starts, wood must be stockpiled beside the kiln and weighed Steam engine running The entire run 1 driver + 1 fireman 6 people Add 1 electrical-watch recorder when coupled to a generator Large glass melting furnace Melting–forming 24–72 h 2 in the melting section; 4–6 in the forming section 6–10 people depending on furnace size In the forming section gathering rotates; one person gathers ≤2 h at a stretch

◎ The hand feel of gathering glass and of reading the fire is not covered in this chapter; follow the practice methods of the corresponding chapters (Chapters 12, 14, 18, 19). This chapter only fixes "how many people per shift and how many hours per rotation".

docs.title: 37.4.4 Fatigue and Night Shifts (Iron Law 7)
docs.text:
Empirical values: past 12 h continuously on duty, or from the 4th hour of a night shift onward, error rates rise significantly; the night-shift scrap rate runs 1.5–3 times the day-shift rate. Calibration: tally scrap counts by shift (record field of Card 37-02); three weeks yields the settlement's own ratio.

Control rules:

  1. Night shifts are always two-person; solo watching of a furnace, kiln, or machine is forbidden.
  2. Key parameters (batching ratios, gate openings, steam-pressure limits) require two-person recheck with signatures.
  3. Mandatory 8 h of rest after a night shift; running straight into the day shift is not allowed.
  4. No more than 4 night shifts per person per week; the account office checks the schedule for violations.

[Card 37-02 Shift Schedule Card] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: the skill matrix (Card 37-03), the minimum establishment of each continuous process (Sections 37.4.2/37.4.3), the ration quota table (Section 37.1), the time basis from moon phase or sundial (Chapter 3).
  2. Required tools: the time basis (Chapter 3 sundial or water clock, cross-checked against the noon shadow before use), a schedule board with chalk or cards, an account book. Accuracy requirement: shift-change error ≤15 min.
  3. Operating sequence and control points: ① List the continuous processes to be lit this ten-day period and their minimum establishments; ② schedule the night shifts first (starting from the hardest hours), then the day shifts; ③ check three lines per person: ≤4 night shifts per week, ≤12 h continuously on duty, 8 h rest after a night shift; ④ List the spare crew on a separate page; ⑤ Post publicly and copy to the account office and the mess kitchen (those with occupation-based ration uplift draw rations against the schedule).
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: shift length 8 h (empirical value); verify the settlement's actual work-rest pattern by "scrap rate tallied by shift"; if one shift's scrap rate stays more than 50% above the mean, check fatigue before checking the process.
  5. Process observation and recording items: dual signatures on every shift handover, hourly records (whichever applies: tuyere/kiln temperature/steam pressure), scrap counts by shift, absences and who filled in.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = establishment complete, no one violating the three lines, handover records complete; rework = a solo night shift or overtime double shift occurred (re-lay the schedule within the same ten-day period and recheck that shift's output); scrap = running without records (all output of that period is treated as an unfinished process and may not be accepted, per Iron Law 6).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: night-shift scrap rate rising → first check whether the watch was solo → check that person's night shifts this week → check whether a handover signature is missing → only then check the process parameters; workshops paralyzed during the busy season → check whether the 0.5 reduction factor was pre-scheduled → check whether the stay-behind shift was locked.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one filled-in schedule; L2 = one month of schedules actually run + handover records + scrap tallies by shift; L3 = three months of records + a documented instance of the spare filling in + the account office's signed violation checks.

Ten-day period: __ Morning shift 06–14 Mid shift 14–22 Night shift 22–06 Spare Day 1 A__ B__ Day 2 … Scrap count (by shift) —

docs.title: 37.5.1 Skill Grade Definitions
docs.text:
Grade Definition Discriminator 0 Cannot do — 1 Operates under guidance Can complete the steps with a grade-3 person present 2 Operates independently and can judge scrap Works a shift alone and can pick out defective pieces by the criteria 3 Can take apprentices and propose parameter changes Has passed assessment and has apprenticeship and change records

Redundancy iron rule: every key post (miner, kiln worker, forging smith, electrician, medic) must have ≥2 people at grade 2. A post with only one person loses a technology chain to a single accident — this is a veto item in L3 acceptance.

docs.text:
Post Minimum skill set Source chapters Training period (empirical) Assessment evidence Miner Ore identification and sampling, the underground two-person rule, ground support, waste-rock sorting Chapter 16 0.5–1 year Completing a section of level-drift support independently + sampling records Kiln worker Reading temperature by flame color ◎, kiln loading, firing-curve control, judging scrap pottery and brick Chapters 11–13 1–2 years A ledger showing ≥80% pass rate over 3 consecutive firings Forging smith Reading the heat ◎, forging to shape, quenching and tempering, judging scrap by fracture Chapters 18–19 2–4 years Test-bar fractures + tool-life tracking records Woodworker Material selection and cutting out, mortise-and-tenon joinery, repair of devices and fixtures Chapters 7, 9, 21 1–3 years A load test of one load-bearing timber member Mason Bricklaying, lime mortar mixes, arches and foundations Chapter 13 1–2 years Plumb and mortar-joint inspection records for a section of wall Chemical worker Distillation, purification by crystallization, reagent accounting, hazardous-substances procedures Chapters 8, 23, 26 2–3 years Purification batch records + purity test criteria Electrician Windings and insulation, wiring, the "spins but no power" troubleshooting chart, electric-shock first aid Chapters 30–32 2–3 years A record of independently troubleshooting one electrical fault Medic Bleeding control, fracture immobilization, burn treatment, isolation, dosage accounting This chapter fixes only the post and the minimum first-aid set; details are in Part 9 of this book 1–2 years First-aid drill assessment + the medicine account Bookkeeper Cross-checking weights and measures, ledger keeping, materials and energy accounting, schedule verification Chapters 3 and 22 + this chapter 0.5–1 year Monthly reconciliation records with books matching physical goods Teacher Literacy, card copying, the apprenticeship procedure, assessment records Chapter 4 + this chapter 1 year onward Records of apprentices passing assessment

◎ The practice methods and misjudgment compensations for hand-feel skills such as reading temperature by flame color and reading the heat are in the corresponding process chapters; this table registers only whether the person has passed assessment.

Apprentice cost: apprenticeships run 0.5–4 years, and an apprentice's output counts as 1/3–1/2 of a skilled worker's. When balancing off-farm headcount, reserve an extra 0.3–0.5 apprentice quota for every grade-2 post, or three years on there will be no one to take over.

[Card 37-03 Skill Matrix Card] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: the population roster (with age and health), each chapter's process cards and assessment criteria, past ledgers (who did what, pass rates).
  2. Required tools: matrix grid paper or a wooden board with chalk, and an account book. No precision instruments, but assessment evidence must correspond to physical objects (test bars, defective pieces, records).
  3. Operating sequence and control points: ① List names by post; ② grade each person 0–3 on each skill item, accepting evidence only, never word of mouth; ③ flag red the posts where "only 1 person has reached grade 2" and arrange apprenticeship at once; ④ Re-evaluate once per season, writing the reason for every promotion or demotion; ⑤ Transcribe into the ledger.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: training periods take the ranges from the table in Section 37.5.2; correct for the settlement's actual speed after back-verifying "the number of months until the first apprentice reaches grade 2".
  5. Process observation and recording items: assessment date, examiner, and evidence number for each person at each grade; apprentice pairings and progress.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = at least 1 person at grade 2 in each of the ten posts and ≥2 people at grade 2 in the key posts; rework = a post with no one at grade 2 (remedial training within the season; in the meantime that post's process runs one grade down and requires a grade-3 person present); scrap = grades assigned without evidence (the whole sheet is re-evaluated).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: a technology chain breaks → check the number of grade-2 people in that post → check whether the apprenticeship is on the books → check whether the assessment evidence has been lost; inflated grades → have that person work one day's shift alone and tally the accuracy of their scrap judgments.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = a matrix sheet filled in with grades; L2 = the matrix + archived assessment evidence for each grade; L3 = two seasons of re-evaluation records + apprenticeship on the books for every post + the dual grade-2 redundancy achieved in the key posts.

docs.title: 37.6.1 Resource Use Rights and Maintenance Duties
docs.text:
Resource Use rules Maintenance duty Records Mine Going underground against the annual extraction quota, logged as two-person entry The on-shift miner does support and ventilation; major drift repairs are chartered through the account office Underground entry register, sampling records Forest Firewood taken against the annual cutting-area quota (Section 37.2.2); closed forest areas are off-limits Whoever cuts hauls and replants; young-stand tending rotates within the logging crew Cutting-area register, replanting survival counts Water source Intake and outfall separated upstream/downstream; settling-basin dredging rotates Beneficiary households rotate; during epidemics a well closure has a designated keeper Water account and dredging records Roads and bridges Beneficiary workshops share the labor The sharing list is agreed at the start of the year, supervised by the account office Road-repair labor account Workshop furnaces and kilns Daily upkeep by the users Overhauls chartered as projects; spares carry a separate maintenance account Furnace and kiln operating ledgers Warehouse Two people, two locks Monthly inventory by the account office; discrepancies >5% must be resolved within the month Monthly inventory records

Principle: a shared resource with unclear responsibility will certainly be overused — the forest dies first, then the mine drifts and the roads. Every rule line must come down to "who, for how long, recorded where".

docs.title: 37.6.2 Accident Response Authority
docs.text:
1. The right to stop work: anyone facing a risk of death or disabling injury may halt the process on the spot. No blame attaches to stopping; the review looks for institutional faults; blame attaches only to concealing risks.
  2. Three things within 24 h of an accident: treat the injured (the medic post), preserve the scene (do not move key physical evidence), and make a written record (time, people, process, parameters, injuries).
  3. Before production resumes, the process must pass a change check (Section 37.6.3) confirming the accident cause has been dealt with.

docs.title: 37.6.3 Change Control: Who May Alter Process Parameters
docs.text:
• Altering a parameter = the dual signatures of the holder of that process card (grade 3) and the workshop supervisor; neither suffices alone.
  • Five entries in the ledger: date, old parameter value, new value, reason, and the verification results of the first batch of 3 samples.
  • For an alteration without dual signatures, the entire batch's output is treated as an unfinished process and may not be accepted (Iron Law 6).
  • Right of rollback: if verification fails, anyone may demand restoration of the old parameters; the rollback is recorded the same way.

docs.title: 37.6.4 Historical Failure Mode of Over-Cutting
docs.text:
The typical death chain: in year 1 firewood is cut nearby and fuel looks plentiful on the books → by year 3 the cutting radius has doubled and haulage hours eat the net fuel gain → by year 5 the tree line has retreated into the watershed and erosion smothers the fields → metallurgy and firing are cut off, the artisans disperse back to their villages, and the technology step falls back two parts.

Red-line criteria (any one triggered forces forest closure and production cuts):

Red line Threshold (empirical value; must be calibrated year by year) Annual increase in cutting radius >20% Firewood haulage hours ÷ total fuel-procurement hours >40% Young-stand share of the fuelwood forest <30%

Red-line patrols run once per season and are entered in the ledger; when a line is triggered, cut workshop wood first (seal the furnaces), not household wood.

docs.title: 37.7 Internal Exchange and Labor Accounting (completing C7)
docs.text: The settlement's internal "who owes whom" must be computable: labor chits — non-farming posts (workshops/guards/teaching) are issued labor chits per standard workday, redeemable against rations and common supplies (the redemption rate is set quarterly by the council and entered in the ledger); a barter account — cross-post barter (smith ↔ potter) is priced in both parties' labor chits and entered in the account, eliminating the distortion of "favor debts"; inter-workshop transfer notes — materials moving between workshops must carry a three-column note (item and quantity/issuer's work number/receiver's work number), reconciled monthly against the materials account of Chapter 38. Criterion: any "debt" can be stated on one page with its principal and its booking date. Labor chits are not money (no accruing interest, no use outside); the boundary is fixed to prevent financialization.

docs.text:
Ordered by "most common, hardest to detect". Overestimating carrying capacity is the classic silent failure: invisible in the first year, it surfaces in the second or third as a growing cutting radius and shrinking rations.

docs.title: Safety Boundary
docs.text:
This chapter contains no direct high-temperature or high-pressure processes, but the following three items are part of its process steps; not executing them counts as not completing this chapter:

  1. The solo-night-shift ban: every furnace, kiln, and machine carries at least two people on night shift; violators have that shift's output processed under the scrap rules of Card 37-02.
  2. The underground and felling two-person rule: the original procedures of Chapters 16 and 7 apply, and this chapter's scheduling must not split up the pairs.
  3. The fatigue red line: ≤12 h continuously on duty, 8 h rest after a night shift, ≤4 night shifts per week; the account office checks violations every ten days and posts them publicly.

Electric-shock first aid is a mandatory assessment item for the electrician post; accident response authority and the 24 h three items are in Section 37.6.2.

docs.text:
A list (executable directly in this chapter):

Item Criterion Ration and firewood calibration 7-day weighing records archived, medians entered in the ledger Three-ceiling estimate Card 37-01's eight fields filled, arithmetic recomputable Off-farm balance and step comparison The Section 37.3 arithmetic entered in the accounts, with the courage to write an overload conclusion into the estimate document Continuous-process schedule Card 37-02's three-line checks passed and posted publicly Skill matrix and apprenticeship Card 37-03's grades backed by evidence, red-flagged posts scheduled for apprenticeship Resource red lines and change control Section 37.6.4 thresholds patrolled seasonally; the five change entries registered

Item Notes One complete farming-season record Without it, every estimate is a provisional figure Population health roster Determines the full-laborer definition Salvage inventory The two-year buffer of the starting B/C items Epidemic, conflict, abrupt climate change Unpredictable; only partially hedgeable with k and reserves

docs.title: Next-Step Dependencies
docs.text:
• Chapter 38, the materials-and-energy ledger: turns this chapter's per-capita annual benchmarks and furnace/kiln specific consumptions into a day-by-day running account — this chapter gives "per person per year"; the ledger gives "per furnace, per kiln, per day".
  • Chapter 39, maintenance and spare parts: extends "who keeps watch" into "what gets repaired and what gets stocked"; the spare crew in this chapter's schedules will be tied to the spares account.
  • Whole-book backstop: the "materials, records, succession" three columns of the L3 acceptance for every process card in Chapters 1–40 all cite this chapter's three cards and its ledger system — without this chapter, every preceding chapter stops at L2.

docs.title: Chapter Objectives
docs.text:
On completing this chapter, the settlement should establish and maintain four ledgers, one summary table, and one wall board:

Deliverable Content Question it answers Materials ledger (Card 38-01) Four-column daily flow: receipts / consumption / stock / in-transit How many more smelts will the material last? Unit-consumption summary table (38.2.1) Per-product main material, fuel, transport, wear-and-tear unit costs What must be stocked for the next smelt? Energy master ledger (Card 38-02) All fuels converted to firewood-equivalents; human and animal power listed separately Can the woodland sustain this? Wear-and-spare-parts ledger (38.5) Consumable life, amortization, reorder points What will fail within six months? Three-color warning board (38.6.3) Months of reserve for key materials, updated monthly Cut production now, or expand?

docs.title: Capability Boundaries
docs.text:
Can do:

  • After 3 full months of per-smelt records, calculate main-product unit consumption to ±20–30% and identify which factor drove the change.
  • Use three-color lines to flag supply-cutoff risk 1–2 months ahead; use unit-consumption trends to catch process drift and ore-grade decline early.
  • Convert fuel, transport, and wear into one unit (firewood-equivalent and person-days) to compute the "full cost per ton of main product," testing any new-furnace decision.

Cannot do:

  • Predict when an ore vein will run out. Grade can only be monitored month by month; the inflection point is unpredictable.
  • Replace the improvement duties of the process chapters. This chapter only keeps accounts, never cuts consumption; to reduce unit costs, go back to the relevant chapter and change the process.
  • Smooth out fluctuations. Wet-wood seasons, new kilns, and ore-source changes swing unit costs ±20–30%; record them as they are — averaging for appearance is forbidden.
  • Produce data from nothing. Without per-smelt weigh-ins, the ledger is an empty form; recording without weighing is recording imagination.

External dependencies (entered in the C list):

  1. Chapter 37 per-capita annual baselines (ration grain, household fuelwood) — the base of the household account.
  2. Measured unit consumption from every furnace and kiln (Chapters 6, 11–14, 16–19, 28; from each chapter's L3 acceptance ledgers); uncalibrated items may only use this chapter's ranges.
  3. Settlement-wide unified weights and measures (Chapters 3, 22) and the ledger-archival institution.

docs.title: Pre-Start Verification
docs.text:
Checklist form. Any item unmet demotes the corresponding account to "provisional," not usable for furnace-start or production-planning decisions.

# Verification item Criterion (confirm you have ××, standard is ××) 1 Weights and measures One scale and one volume measure each; bookkeeper and workshops cross-check on site: mass error ≤2%, volume ≤5%; fix before recording 2 Per-capita baselines Chapter 37 grain and fuelwood medians calibrated and copied into the ledger; uncalibrated items marked "provisional" throughout 3 Furnace/kiln register Every active furnace registered with five items: name, source chapter, monthly output, unit-cost status (measured / uncalibrated), staffing establishment 4 Bookkeeping office ≥1 person at Level 2 (passed the Chapter 37 bookkeeper assessment: cross-checking, recording, monthly stocktake — all evidenced) 5 Ledger books Printed from Card 38-01, one set per workshop; requisition-stub numbers continuous, no gaps 6 Warehouses Two-person two-lock system in place (37.6.1); fuel, ore, finished goods, and consumables stored in four separate zones, each with a stock placard 7 Production plan Next 3 months' furnace schedule and output targets in writing; the bookkeeper computes the "monthly consumption baseline" from them 8 Opening stocktake All stock weighed or counted, error ≤10%, recorded as the opening account; every later entry measured from this origin

docs.title: 38.1.1 The Death Chain of Product-Only Accounting
docs.text:
Project a settlement that records products but never consumption, over 5–10 years (each step an empirical value; the generic shape of a historical failure mode):

Stage Books (products only) What actually happens off-book True system state Year 1 300 kg iron produced; only "output" and "grain trades" recorded Firewood cut and charred within 1 km; wood treated as free, never entered Healthy Years 2–3 Output raised to 1 t/yr; books look better Cutting radius expands to 3–5 km; wood-hauling hours already 20–30% of total fuel-acquisition labor (37.6.4 yellow line) Hidden overdraft Years 4–5 Output barely maintained Radius 8–10 km; acquisition hours per kg of charcoal exceed forging hours per kg of iron; furnaces forced to intermittent operation Inverted returns Years 6–8 Iron-for-grain exchange rate worsens quarter by quarter Forest line retreats to the watershed; erosion hits fields (37.6.4 chain); farthest kiln abandoned, smiths drift back to farming Eve of supply cutoff Years 8–10 Bookkeeping ends with the workshop Metallurgical supply cut off; timber and stone repairs substitute for iron; technology drops two tiers (cf. 37.3.2) Collapse

Reading point: every link looked "normal" in its own year. The fuel forest isn't eaten in a year — it's eaten one extra li of walking per day over three years, and only the ledger can see that extra li. The two signals that should have raised the alarm in Years 2–3 (hauling-hours share, acquisition hours per kg of charcoal) are buried precisely where nothing is recorded.

Interception points of the various ledgers on this same chain:

Stage Ledger signal readable at that stage Intercepting action Year 1 Opening stocktake has no "firewood" page — fuel was never entered Open Card 38-01; start wood and charcoal pages immediately Years 2–3 Transport master ledger: wood-hauling person-days rise to 20–30% Cap the cutting radius; plan fuelwood rotation (37.2.2) Years 4–5 Energy master ledger: acquisition hours per kg charcoal > forging hours per kg iron Freeze expansion; fuel-saving furnace retrofits back in the relevant chapter Years 6–8 Monthly energy ledger over woodland budget >20% for consecutive months Recompute N₂; seal furnaces and cut output per 37.6.4

All four interception points fall two to six years before "iron-for-grain deterioration." The earlier the ledger opens its pages, the more reversible the collapse.

docs.title: 38.1.2 The Ledger's Three Questions
docs.text:
Materials bookkeeping has one discipline: every product entry must simultaneously answer three questions.

Question Corresponding ledger Line item Unit What was burned for it Energy ledger (38.3) Wood, charcoal, lamp oil, as firewood-equivalent kg firewood-equiv. What was hauled for it Transport ledger (38.4) Movement of ore, charcoal, wood, products t·km and person-days What tool wore out for it Wear ledger (38.5) Amortization of crucibles, furnace lining, files, bellows leather piece-uses and hours

Plus the first question, "how much main material did it use" (materials ledger, 38.2). Four questions together = the four ledgers of 38.2–38.5.

Three-question worked example (a 1.5 kg iron hoe, mid-range values from this chapter):

Question Reading Source Main material used Iron ore 30 kg; iron-material consumption already inside the 25–40% yield factor 38.2.1 What was burned Charcoal 27 kg ≈ 110–160 firewood-equiv. (production basis) 38.2.1, 38.3.2 What was hauled Ore 30 kg × 5 km + charcoal 27 kg × 3 km ≈ 0.2–0.5 person-days 38.4.2 What wore out Furnace-lining and forging-tool amortization 0.02–0.05 person-hours + refractory clay 0.1–0.7 kg 38.5.2

Reading: the full cost of a new hoe ≈ 0.5–1.2 person-days (smelting labor computed separately in 38.3.4); regrinding an old hoe costs only 0.05–0.15 person-days. The book-keeping case for maintenance before replacement sits in that one line — the same entry goes into the wear ledger (38.5) and the maintenance plan (see Next Dependencies); it counts only when the two agree.

The ledger's second identity: a diagnostic instrument. Month-over-month unit-cost rise is the earliest signal of process drift or ore-grade decline — earlier and cheaper than fracture inspection or the scrap pile (38.6.2, third check). Using the ledger only as a record spends half its value.

docs.text:
This table collects empirical values from earlier chapters; all are empirical values requiring field calibration; before calibration they may serve magnitude judgment only, never production scheduling (same rule as Chapter 37). Each row's calibration method is directly executable.

Three table-reading rules: ① for workshops with multiple furnaces/kilns, keep unit costs per furnace per kiln as separate rows — workshop-wide averages mask differences, and the hungriest furnace is the one the account must catch; ② production planning and reserves use the upper bound of the range; efficiency testing uses the lower bound — write the two uses separately; ③ the replacement moment is "the day 3 continuous furnace measurements are complete"; replacement goes through 37.6.3 dual signatures.

Settlement materials opening-page list (minimum pages at account opening):

Category Materials requiring pages Pages (reference) Household Grain, salt, household firewood, lamp oil 4 Fuel Dry wood, green wood (separate pages), charcoal 3 Ores Iron ore, copper ore, roasted ore, limestone 3–4 Auxiliaries Refractory clay, sand, soda or plant ash 3 Products Iron ingots, pottery, brick, lime, glassware per active product Consumables Crucibles, files, saggars, rope 4 External purchases & relics Salt (if bought), relic metals and medicines 2

Criterion: any material a furnace needs to start must have a page first — no page, no furnace start; record opening quantities the day pages are opened. Open pages top-down: the household account first — bookkeeping on an empty stomach doesn't work.

◎ Estimating charcoal-pile and wood-stack weight (visual volume → kg) is a hand-feel step. Practice: compare against 5 pre-weighed charcoal piles, 20 trials. Misjudgment compensation: weigh a 10% random sample of piles; if error >15%, switch that month entirely to scale weighing.

docs.title: 38.2.2 The Unit-Cost Formula: Where the Ranges Come From
docs.text:
Unit cost is not a memorized number — it is the reciprocal product of stage factors:

Ore consumption = 1 ÷ (grade × beneficiation recovery × smelting recovery × yield factor)

Worked example: grade 0.20 × beneficiation recovery 0.75 × yield 0.32 → ore consumption = 1 ÷ 0.048 ≈ 20.8 kg/kg, at the low end of the 20–40 range. Two uses: first, when unit costs worsen, check factors in order — grade from Ch. 16 batch sampling records, recoveries and yield from this chapter's per-smelt ledger; whoever changed, fix that. Second, before switching ore sources, pre-compute unit cost with the new grade and decide.

docs.title: 38.2.3 The Four-Column Ledger Format
docs.text:
One page per material, daily flow, four fixed columns:

Date Summary (workshop / furnace no. / batch) Receipts (kg/L/pieces) Consumption (kg/L/pieces) Stock In transit Dual signatures (ex.) Mar 2 Charcoal kiln No. 3 output Charcoal +420 — 640 — A / B (ex.) Mar 4 Smelter No. 1, 7th smelt, draws stock — Ore −260, charcoal −180 460 — C / A

Hard bookkeeping rules:

# Rule Criterion 1 Stock = yesterday's stock + receipts − consumption In-transit never enters stock; a negative stock column is a recording error — same-day investigation 2 Units only kg, L, pieces "One shoulder-load, one cart, one pile" forbidden; convert before entry 3 Dual signature per entry Handler and custodian each sign one cell; single-signed pages are invalid 4 Requisition stub numbers continuous Gaps reported to the bookkeeper same day; replacements marked "replacement"; no alterations — errors crossed out and re-signed 5 All receipts weighed or counted Estimated entries treated as scrapped (Card 38-01 field 6) 6 Month-end reconciliation with physical stock Process and shortage three-check per 38.6

Three-way reconciliation (ledger↔ledger, ledger↔goods, ledger↔voucher):

Comparison Frequency Tolerance Over-tolerance action Workshop sub-ledger ↔ bookkeeper master Every 10 days 0 (only transcription errors allowed) Reconcile same day; hunt gaps and omissions Ledger stock ↔ physical stock Monthly (Card 38-03) ≤5% Three checks (38.6.2) This chapter's unit costs ↔ chapter acceptance ledgers Quarterly ±20% Any deviation: check definitions and batches — never let both sides adjust independently

In-transit column definition: quantities ordered or shipped but not yet received into stock. Criterion: the three-color warning (38.6.3) reads only the stock column; in-transit is for scheduling receiving labor only — never treated as available for furnace starts.

Full-month example (charcoal page; figures illustrative):

Date Summary (workshop / furnace / batch) Receipts Consumption Stock In transit Dual signatures Mar 1 Opening carry-forward — — 950 — A / B Mar 4 Kiln No. 3 output +420 — 1370 — A / B Mar 6 Smelter No. 1, 7th smelt draws — −180 1190 — C / A Mar 9 Forge draws charcoal — −60 1130 — D / A Mar 12 Kiln No. 3 ignited (in transit) — — 1130 +400 A / B Mar 15 Smelter No. 1, 8th smelt draws — −180 950 400 C / A Mar 22 Kiln No. 3 output received into stock +400 — 1350 0 A / B Mar 26 Forge and glass shop draw — −270 1080 0 D / B Mar 31 Month-end carry (receipts +820, consumption −690) — — 1080 0 stocktake dual signature

Mid-month reading (example): by the 15th, 420 kg consumed; month-end projection 840 kg vs. the 750 kg monthly plan — 12% over. No color line tripped yet, but per criterion projected monthly deviation >10% goes into the ten-day report; >20% launches a cause hunt (38.6.2 third check: change register → ore grade → lining wall thickness). Don't wait for the month-end stocktake to react.

docs.title: 38.2.4 The Reorder-Point System
docs.text:
General formula:

Reorder point = consumption during replenishment lead time + 2 furnace (kiln/batch) safety reserves

Key material Replenishment lead time (empirical, calibrate) Lead-time calibration Reorder-point example Charcoal 7–14 days (cut, load, burn, cool) Time 3 full cycles, take the longest Daily charcoal use × 14 + 2 kiln charges Refractory clay 3–10 days (dig, haul; aging adds 7–20 days) Same Monthly use ÷ 30 × cycle + 2 relines Crucibles 20–40 days (form, dry, fire) Same Monthly crucible use ÷ 30 × 40 × 1.5 Iron ore 3–7 days (mine, beneficiate, deliver) Same Daily ore use × 7 + 2 furnace charges Soda / plant ash 10–30 days (collect, sieve, dry-store) Same Monthly use ÷ 30 × 30 × 1.5

Stop-line criterion (linking to Chapter 18's L3 raw-material reserve clause): if charcoal, ore, or refractory stock falls below 2 furnace-charges, stop the line and replenish. "Scrounging while running" is forbidden — a half-smelt that runs dry costs more than no smelt: furnace-temperature collapse, a frozen hearth; restart costs per 37.4.2.

Worked example (illustrative): daily charcoal use 200 kg; measured longest lead time 10 days; one furnace charge = 180 kg → charcoal reorder point = 200 × 10 + 2 × 180 = 2,360 kg. The day book stock falls below 2,360 kg, the bookkeeper issues a replenishment order to the kiln crew and marks a yellow dot on the ledger header; below 2 × 180 = 360 kg (hard 2-charge line) → stop line and replenish.

docs.title: 38.2.5 Volume-to-Weight Conversion Table
docs.text:
Where per-entry weighing is impossible (whole stacks, whole kiln charges), entry by volume-to-weight conversion is allowed using the coefficients below; re-weigh 10% monthly as a spot check — error >10% reverts that material to full weighing.

Material Bulk density (empirical, calibrate) Measuring convention Loose charcoal pile 180–250 kg/m³ measured pile height × base area Loose wood stack 300–450 kg/m³ (stacked volume) stack length × width × height Iron ore (loose) 1.5–2.5 t/m³ depends on lump size and clay content; re-standard after washing Clay (loose measure) 1.3–1.6 t/m³ — Lime (powder, out of kiln) 0.9–1.2 t/m³ —

Calibration: pick 3 typical piles per material, measure volume then weigh the whole pile for a local coefficient; re-standard after any ore-source or kiln change. Converted entries must carry the marker "converted" in the summary column; month-end stocktakes spot-check converted batches first.

[Card 38-01 Materials Ledger Card] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: ledger pages (Ch. 4 recording materials: bound book or waxed board), requisition stubs, ink and charcoal pencil, opening-stocktake record (verification item 8).
  2. Required tools: scale (Ch. 3/22; check zero and full scale against a standard weight before use, >2% error = out of service), volume measures (≤5% error), three-color board (painted plank). No higher-precision instruments needed.
  3. Operating sequence and control points: ① opening stocktake by weight establishes the account, marked "data origin date"; ② every receipt and issue entered same day, dual-signed, stock balance computed same day; ③ in-transit listed separately, never in stock; ④ missing requisition stubs reported same day; ⑤ Card 38-03 stocktake executed every month-end; ⑥ calibrated unit costs copied into the summary table immediately with date.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: unit-cost ranges from table 38.2.1; replaced after per-smelt measurement (four-point weighing: charge, output, bloom, ingot); reorder points computed per material per 38.2.4 and written on each ledger page header.
  5. Process observation and recording items: the summary column must state "which furnace, which batch"; anomalies (wet wood, fines fraction, returned material) go in remarks; daily stock balance checked against the previous row.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = daily closure, monthly closure, stocktake gap ≤5%, continuous vouchers; rework = gap 5–10% resolved within the month, replacement stubs marked, originals retained with strikethrough; scrap = reconstructing entries from memory or entering estimates (page voided, physical stock recounted and rebuilt).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: books≠goods → check omissions first (missing stubs, unentered returns) → check scales (calibration) → check pilferage (38.6.2); negative stock → check receipt/issue direction reversal → check unit mixing (kg vs. loads, pieces vs. kg); erratic unit costs → check whether the summary column mixes furnaces/batches.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one month of original four-column flow records; L2 = 3 months of stocktake records with gap ≤5% + at least one product's measured unit cost; L3 = one genuine three-color trigger with disposition record + books≠goods holds after a change of bookkeeper + all calibrated values copied into the archive.

Blank ledger page (copy from card):

Date Summary (workshop / furnace / batch) Receipts Consumption Stock In transit Dual signatures

Ledger binding rules: one page per material, one book per workshop, master ledger at the bookkeeping office; sub-ledgers go to the office every ten days for reconciliation.

docs.title: 38.3.1 The Firewood-Equivalent: An Accounting Unit, Not a Physical Constant
docs.text:
Definition: 1 firewood-equivalent (FWE) = the heat content of 1 kg of air-dried pine wood (15–25% moisture), roughly 3,500–4,000 kcal (1 kcal ≈ 4.19 kJ; ≈ 14.6–16.7 MJ).

Field calibration (no calorimeter — use the comparison method; stove efficiency cancels out in same-condition tests): same stove, same pot, same damper setting — boil the same quantity of water (suggest 5 kg, from 15 ℃) separately with the test fuel and with reference pine wood; 3 trials each, take the median. Conversion coefficient = reference-pine consumption ÷ test-fuel consumption. Example: to boil the same pot, pine costs 0.90 kg, a hardwood costs 0.75 kg → coefficient = 0.90 ÷ 0.75 = 1.2 FWE/kg. Auxiliary method (stove-efficiency estimate): keep boiling after the roll and weigh the evaporated water; heat delivered = evaporated water × 539 kcal/kg; divide by theoretical heat content for efficiency — useful when improving stoves. Local variation ±15% is allowed, but the whole settlement must use one conversion table, copied onto the energy ledger's flyleaf with a version date.

Two hard rules:

# Rule Reason 1 Heat-equivalent and production-equivalent are used separately: charcoal yields 1.7–2.1 FWE/kg as fuel, but costs 4–6 kg of wood to make Heat-equivalent tests the furnace's heat balance; production-equivalent tests woodland pressure — charcoal is not gathered for free 2 Green wood must be converted: wood at 40–60% moisture enters the books at 0.5–0.7 FWE/kg Unconverted, the books inflate 30–50% and the fuel ceiling N₂ (37.2.2) is overstated

◎ Judging wood dryness (heft and knock: dry wood rings crisp, green wood thuds) is a hand-feel step. Practice: 20 trials on batches of known moisture. Misjudgment compensation: weigh 3 sticks, oven-dry at the stove for 24 h, weigh again — the loss is the moisture content; any batch with >10% error is booked as green wood.

docs.title: 38.3.2 Energy Conversion Table
docs.text:
All empirical values requiring field calibration; the calibration method is uniform: weigh-in/weigh-out for fuels, daily records for humans and animals.

Energy source Unit Heat (kcal) Heat FWE Production/keeping cost Use boundary Pine wood (air-dry) kg 3,500–4,000 1.0 Felling, splitting, drying 0.7–1.5 person-hr/10 kg Reference unit; all furnaces and cooking Hardwood kg 4,000–4,500 1.1–1.2 Same; splitting +30–50% labor All furnaces Green wood (40–60% moisture) kg 1,800–2,600 0.5–0.7 2–6 months drying Must convert on entry; direct use in smelting furnaces forbidden (Ch. 18) Charcoal kg 6,800–7,500 1.7–2.1 Production costs 4–6 kg wood (Ch. 6) Metallurgy, glass, forging only; must not be diverted to household use when short Straw and leaves kg 3,000–3,500 0.8–0.9 Farm by-product Cooking and drying; bulky — never mixed into kiln-fuel accounting Peat (if sourced) kg 3,000–4,000 0.9–1.1 Digging + 1–3 months drying Sulfur-bearing; use cautiously in metallurgy Lamp oil (plant oil, fat) kg 8,500–9,500 2.2–2.5 Pressing 0.2–0.4 person-days/kg Lighting only; burning in furnaces forbidden Pine resin, pitch (if any) kg 8,000–9,000 2.2–2.5 Collection 0.1–0.2 person-days/kg Kindling, waterproofing, preservation only; no bulk furnace use Human labor person-day Effective mechanical work 0.15–0.3 kWh (130–260 kcal) not converted Ration 1–1.5 kg grain; +20–30% for heavy work (37.1.1) Mechanical work and heat are not interchangeable, see below Animal power head-day Effective mechanical work 2–3 kWh not converted Hay 8–12 kg/head-day (37.1.3) Separate line in the transport ledger (38.4)

Why human and animal power are not converted into FWE: one person-day of effective mechanical work equals only 0.04–0.07 FWE of heat — but the reverse fails: burning 100 kg of wood produces no 1-person-day of hauling. Before the steam engine (Ch. 28), mechanical work has only four sources: humans, animals, water, wind. Mechanical work and heat are two separate budgets; mixing them simultaneously overstates fuel and understates human labor (Ch. 37: person-hours are the balancing variable).

docs.title: 38.3.3 The Monthly Energy Master Ledger
docs.text:
Convert the whole settlement's monthly fuel movements into firewood-equivalents and compare with the woodland budget of 37.2.2. Table form (illustrative figures):

Line item Physical quantity Conversion factor Firewood-equiv. (kg) Notes Pine wood (air-dry) into store 12 t 1.0 12,000 Felling crew weighed in Green wood into store (~50% moisture) 3 t 0.6 1,800 Converted after measured moisture Charcoal into store 2.5 t 5.0 (production equiv.) 12,500 Woodland-pressure basis Lamp oil drawn 40 kg 2.3 92 Lighting only Total monthly outlay — — 26,392 = 26.4 t

Reading: against the 750 t annual available wood of the 37.2.5 example settlement (monthly average 62.5 t), this month used 42% — within budget; but charcoal alone is 47% of the 26.4 t — woodland pressure is driven by metallurgy, cross-checking the 38.3.4 computation. The two bases must never share a column: this table uses production-equivalent for woodland pressure; for in-furnace heat balance, charcoal switches to heat-equivalent (2.5 t × 1.9 = 4,750 FWE) in a separate column. Hard criterion: monthly energy ledger over woodland budget >20% for two consecutive months → mandatory recompute of N₂ (37.2.2).

docs.title: 38.3.4 Worked Example: The Full Energy Cost of One Ton of Iron
docs.text:
Teaching computation; figures are mid-range assumptions to be replaced by local ledgers. Assumptions: ore grade 20%, beneficiation recovery 0.75, in-furnace fuel ratio 6:1 (by bloom weight), yield 0.32, ore carted 5 km by wheelbarrow, charcoal kiln on site (wood not hauled), charcoal hauled 3 km.

Physical quantities first: bloom = 1,000 ÷ 0.32 ≈ 3.1 t; ore consumption = 1 ÷ (0.20 × 0.75 × 0.32) ≈ 20.8 t; charcoal = 3.1 t × 6 = 18.8 t (in-furnace) + 15% screening loss 2.8 t + forging heating 1.4 t = 23 t; wood = 23 t × 5 kg-wood/kg-charcoal = 115 t.

Stage Physical quantity Firewood-equiv. (t) Person-days (range) Basis and calibration ① Mining Ore 20.8 t — 21–42 Hand-pick mining 0.5–1 t/person-day (Ch. 16; calibrate: 3 days of real production) ② Crushing and beneficiation Ore 20.8 t — 7–21 Crush and sort 1–3 t/person-day ③ Woodcutting Wood 115 t 115 77–164 0.7–1.5 t/person-day incl. splitting, drying, stacking (calibrate: 5 person-days of real output) ④ Charcoal burning Charcoal 23 t counted in ③ 29–77 0.3–0.8 t charcoal/person-day (Ch. 6 kiln records) ⑤ Ore haul 5 km 10.4 t·10 km — 69–130 Wheelbarrow 80–150 kg/person-day·10 km (38.4.1) ⑥ Charcoal haul 3 km 6.9 t·10 km — 46–86 Same ⑦ Furnace floor Bloom 3.1 t charcoal counted 43–109 0.2–0.5 t/furnace-day × 7-person crew (37.4.2) ⑧ Forging densification Ingots 1 t charcoal counted 20–50 20–50 kg/person-day (Ch. 19) ⑨ Lining relining amortized 1/10–1/30 per lining generation 0.1–0.5 0.7–4 One lining generation yields 10–30 t iron; relining 20–40 person-days + refractory clay 2–5 t + drying wood 2–5 t Total — ≈115 (92–139 when charcoal yield swings 4–6) 314–684 —

Order-of-magnitude self-check (per file G02 §5): charcoal 23 t ÷ bloom 3.1 t ≈ 7.4:1, upper edge of the 4–8:1 range (incl. screening loss and forging heat) — pass. Wood 115 t ÷ (temperate forest growth 2.5 t/ha × 0.75 harvestable share, 37.2.2) ≈ 61 ha of woodland's sustainable annual yield — that is the true price of one ton of iron. With back-hauling instead of carts, or the kiln off-site, person-days climb past 1,000.

Three immediate conclusions:

Conclusion Basis Decision implication The ironworks must sit where ore, charcoal, and water meet ⑤⑥⑦ are 50–60% of total person-days Site-selection procedure per Chapters 16, 18 Doubling output = doubling woodland pressure 61 ha·yr/t Recompute N₂ (37.2.2) before any new furnace; against the 37.2.5 example settlement (400 ha woodland, 750 t/yr), 1 t/yr of iron already consumes 15% of annual yield Fuel is the largest single cost item in iron First in both FWE and person-days Fuel-saving technology (furnace insulation, waste-heat preheating of blast) pays better than mining more ore

[Card 38-02 Energy Ledger Conversion and Computation Card] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: conversion table (38.3.2 copied onto the flyleaf), monthly materials ledger (Card 38-01), per-furnace unit-cost records, weighing water and a measure (for approximate heat-value calibration).
  2. Required tools: scale (calibrated per Card 38-01), graduated measure and water-boiling stove (boiling method), ledger book; no higher-precision instruments needed.
  3. Operating sequence and control points: ① calibrate the local firewood-equivalent first (boiling method, median of 3); ② the conversion table is settlement-wide and unique — copy onto the flyleaf with version date; ③ all green-wood batches converted before entry; ④ fill physical quantity / FWE / person-days per stage in the blank table; ⑤ attach computation basis per stage; ⑥ compare results against next month's actual consumption; deviation >30% → re-examine stage factors.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: every stage factor from the right-hand calibration column of the 38.3.4 table; filling from impression is forbidden.
  5. Process observation and recording items: wood moisture batch number, charcoal kiln firing number, assumption row (grade, recovery, yield) listed separately; changed assumptions → recompute.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = three columns complete, every row justified, order-of-magnitude check passed; rework = any stage substituted a range default for measurement (measure and recompute within a month); scrap = green wood unconverted, or human/animal power mixed into FWE (whole card recomputed).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: result clearly too small → check screening loss and auxiliary consumption → check yield numerator/denominator; too large → check whether the wrong grade batch was used → check whether woodcutting hours double-count hauling (hauling is ⑤⑥); FWE doesn't match materials ledger → check whether both ledgers use the same conversion-table version.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one completed computation sheet (range values allowed); L2 = computation sheet + one month of actual-consumption back-check (deviation ≤30%); L3 = two consecutive seasons back-checked + conversion table under version control (changes via 37.6.3 dual signature).

Blank computation sheet (copy from card; target product: __ t):

Stage Physical quantity Firewood-equiv. Person-days Basis Mining Crushing/beneficiation Woodcutting Charcoal burning Ore haul Charcoal haul Furnace floor Forging Lining amortization Total

docs.title: 38.4.1 Hauling-Capacity Table
docs.text:
All empirical values requiring field calibration; uniform calibration: three real loaded trips per mode, recording load, one-way distance, round-trip time — take the median.

Mode One-way load Daily range Capacity (kg/person-day·10 km) Boundary Notes Human back-carry 25–40 kg 20–25 km round trip 25–40 Roadless hills, emergencies Long-term back-hauling = a siting error Shoulder poles 40–60 kg 15–20 km 40–60 Paths Shoulder gear is a woodworking product (Ch. 7–9) Wheelbarrow 80–150 kg 15–20 km 80–150 Graded dirt roads; out of use in mud season Vehicle wear into the 38.5 ledger Pack animal 60–100 kg/head 20–30 km 60–100 (per head incl. drover) Mountain trails Feed cost listed separately (38.3.2) Animal cart 300–600 kg 15–25 km 300–600 (per cart crew: one person, one animal) Dry roads Vehicle maintenance in its own account Water (if navigable) 0.5–5 t/boat 30–60 km calibrate per boat crew Downstream and flat stretches Where navigable, water precedes all land transport

Road-condition derating factors (multiply table capacity):

Condition Factor Criterion Grade >10% or gravel surface ×0.5–0.7 rests required on grades >200 m Mud season ×0.4–0.6 wheelbarrow out of service when ruts hold >50 mm of water Snow and freeze ×0.6–0.8 snow >100 mm → switch to sled; capacity re-calibrated

Derating entry rule: the transport master ledger's "mode" column notes the month's road condition; condition changes never rewrite history — they change next month's budget.

docs.title: 38.4.2 Entering Transport Costs
docs.text:
Two line items: t·km (displacement) and person-days (consumption). Formula for the transport column of any product's unit cost:

Transport person-days = unit physical quantity (kg) × distance (km) ÷ 10 ÷ capacity (kg/person-day·10 km)

Ore, charcoal, wood, and finished goods are carried in four separate accounts — merging them into "misc haulage" is forbidden: distances and capacities differ, and merging destroys diagnostic power (failure-modes table, row 5). Table capacities already include the return trip (empty return counted at half); one-way carriers (downstream rafts) account recovery costs separately — table values do not apply.

Monthly transport master ledger form (illustrative; capacities from 38.4.1):

Category Monthly tonnage Mean distance (km) t·km Person-days (or cart-crew days) Mode Ore → smelter 18 5 90 60–113 wheelbarrow Charcoal → forge 6 3 18 12–23 wheelbarrow Wood → settlement (household + workshop) 14 2 28 5–9 cart-crew days animal cart Iron ingots → market 0.6 10 6 4–8 wheelbarrow

Two readings: first, the wood-hauling share = (5–9) ÷ (felling 9–20 + hauling 5–9) ≈ 20–50% — the range straddles 37.6.4's 40% red line, so this month's measured hours set the reading; above 40%, or rising >10 points in a year, the forest is sealed and output cut. Second, ore haul at 60–113 person-days is ~50% of all transport, confirming that step ③ of 38.4.3 ("move the furnace to the ore") deserves priority evaluation. Also links to the 37.2.3 building-material criterion: any material whose round-trip sourcing exceeds 1/3 of the working day is re-assessed as unsustainable.

docs.title: 38.4.3 Transport-Radius Criterion: When Does a Mine Stop Paying
docs.text:
Three-step estimate (for 1 kg of iron):

Step Computation Criterion and outcome ① Ore-haul person-days Ore consumption (20–40 kg) × distance ÷ 10 ÷ capacity — ② Compare with mining person-days Against 38.3.3 ①② (≈0.7–3 person-days/t ore, converted per kg) Hauling > mining → haul roasted concentrate instead (roasting per Ch. 16), cutting tonnage 30–60% ③ Compare with furnace-moving cost On-site primary smelting increment (build furnace, haul charcoal to ore) vs. raw-ore haul increment Ore haul + charcoal haul person-days > on-site increment → move the furnace to the ore

Empirical thresholds (calibrate to local capacity): for lean ore (>20 kg ore/kg iron), economic ore haul distances — back-carry 3–5 km, wheelbarrow 8–15 km, animal cart 20–40 km. Beyond threshold, evaluate in order: haul roasted bloom only → move furnace to ore → abandon the site (back to Ch. 16 site evaluation).

Another standing red line (37.6.4; executed through this chapter's transport ledger): wood-hauling hours ÷ total fuel-acquisition hours > 40% → seal the forest and cut output — this red line's reading comes precisely from the four-way transport accounts of this section.

docs.title: 38.5.1 Consumable Life Table
docs.text:
All empirical values requiring field calibration. Master method: tag every item with an item-history card, record its start date and each use; at scrap, record cause and cumulative output. After 3 months of operation, replace this whole table with settlement-measured values, copied into the archive.
