docs.title: 38.5.2 Wear Amortization
docs.text:
Formula:

Amortization per unit product = (replacement labor + replacement material) ÷ lifetime output

Example: a copper-smelting crucible's replacement = 6–10 person-hours of making + 15–25 kg clay and sand; life 10 melts × 8–15 kg copper per melt → per melt, 0.6–1 person-hour + 1.5–2.5 kg clay/sand → per kg of copper, 0.04–0.13 person-hours and 0.1–0.3 kg clay/sand. This figure enters the 38.2.1 summary's "consumables amortization" column.

Three amortization rules:

# Rule Reason 1 Amortize by measured life, not by this table's ranges indefinitely the table is a starting point; after 3 months without measurement the item counts as uncalibrated 2 Spare-parts stock = daily consumption × replenishment lead × 1.5 same structure as 38.2.4 reorder points; execution belongs to the maintenance system (Next Dependencies) 3 Scrapped items retained until the monthly stocktake stocktake-gap evidence; disputed scrap criteria are settled by the physical item (Iron Law 6: a pass without evidence is not a pass)

Item-history card (tag) format:

Number Item name Batch no. Start date Use record (date / conditions) Scrap date Scrap criterion Cumulative output

Registration rules: one tag per item, the tag travels with the item; at scrap the tag is torn off and pasted into that month's stocktake sheet; items of one batch (crucibles from one kiln load) share a batch number so whole-batch life can be compared — a uniformly short batch points to workmanship; individually short items point to service conditions.

Disposition priority before scrapping (executing Iron Law 4: "tool damage must state whether it is repairable"):

# Disposition Example 1 Repair file re-cut; drill regrind (counted per 38.5.1) 2 Downgrade fine file → coarse file; cracked-but-not-leaking crucible → preheat crucible; old lining brick → kiln supports 3 Material recovery scrapped iron back to the forge (Ch. 18); broken belt → sling (recounted) 4 Scrap with sample retained history card pasted to the stocktake sheet; item into the retention basket

Criterion: skipping 1–3 straight to scrap requires a written reason in the history card's "scrap criterion" field.

docs.title: 38.6.1 Stocktake Procedure
docs.text:
Step Action Criterion 1 Open the stocktake after month-end books close; two-person count (custodian + bookkeeper) single-person counts invalid; rushing the count before close = scrapped (Card 38-03 field 6) 2 Weigh or count everything 10% re-weigh sample; re-weigh discrepancy >2% → re-weigh the whole batch 3 Gap rate = physical − book 4 Shortage three-check (38.6.2) in order: records first, physical evidence second, people last 5 Update the three-color board (38.6.3) color changes posted at the mess hall and workshops 6 Stocktake sheet dual-signed and archived copied into the ledger with counter and date

Yellow-tier ten-day mini-sheet (one row per ten days during yellow tier; key materials only):

Ten days Material Physical count Ten-day use Monthly projection Reserve months Color Signature

Rule: ten-day use × 3 is for early warning only and never replaces the monthly stocktake; two consecutive ten-day periods darkening the color triggers a red-tier assessment early — do not wait for month-end.

docs.title: 38.6.2 The Shortage Three-Check
docs.text:
Check Criterion (what counts as a hit) Disposition 1. Missing records requisition stub gaps, unentered returns, proxy signatures, vague summaries that don't match batches replacement marked "replacement"; the handler does bookkeeping practice that month and later pages are re-checked 2. Pilferage shortages concentrated in concealable small items (salt, lamp oil, iron nails, copper, finished tools) with patterned timing audit the two-person two-lock records; personnel handled separately; fix the warehouse system first, accountability second 3. Process drift books complete but unit costs rise month over month — nothing stolen; the process is eating more check 37.6.3 change register (unsigned changes?) → per-batch grade records (Ch. 16) → lining wall thickness (38.5.1)

The check order is fixed: records first, physical evidence second, people last. Inverting the order turns process drift into a theft case — after which nobody records honestly again; that kills the ledger institution faster than any fuel cutoff.

docs.title: 38.6.3 Three-Color Warning Lines
docs.text:
Reserve months = physical stock ÷ trailing 3-month average monthly consumption (rolling update; last season's stale average is forbidden).

Color Reserve months Action (fixed on the board; no on-the-spot debate) Green ≥2.0 months normal production; meet reorder points (38.2.4); bookkeeper's monthly stocktake Yellow 1.0–2.0 months no new orders; increase cutting and purchasing; non-critical furnaces limited; key materials move to ten-day counts Red <0.5 month (~2 weeks) cut production to survive: seal non-essential furnaces (per each chapter's shutdown procedure; metallurgy per Ch. 18); protect household fuel and critical maintenance only; draw reserves per the pre-agreed plan; the recovery order is pre-written on the board's reverse

Dual criterion for key furnace materials: charcoal, ore, and refractory carry, besides the months line, a hard furnace-charge line — stock < 2 furnace-charges = stop line and replenish (38.2.4, linking to Ch. 18 L3). The months line governs slow variables (household wood, salt, grain); the charge line governs fast variables (furnace materials); each triggers independently, neither substitutes for the other.

Color-change record sheet (pasted on the board's reverse):

Date Material Color change (→) Reserve months at trigger Action Responsible Back-to-green date

Rule: a color change without a record = an unhandled event (L3 veto item); returning from red to green requires dual signature from the bookkeeper and the works supervisor — preventing "paper green" by borrowing against in-transit quantities.

Red-tier shutdown order (agreed in advance; on a red day, execute in order — no debate):

# Seal first Reason 1 Glass furnace, non-ferrous smelting most fuel-intensive; product can wait 2 Brick and tile kilns construction can defer; use stocked brick 3 Lime kiln (retain one) agricultural and sanitary lime must not stop 4 Iron smelting furnace seal and hold warm per Ch. 18 shutdown procedure; preserve the furnace body 5 Cooking and heating never sealed — household fuel is the last reserve (37.6.4)

Recovery runs in reverse order; the shutdown order is written on the board's reverse and archived with the color-change records.

[Card 38-03 Monthly Stocktake Card] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: current month's sub-ledgers from every workshop, full requisition stub book, last month's stocktake sheet, three-color board, scrap-retention basket, standard weights for spot re-weighing.
  2. Required tools: scale (cross-checked once before starting, >2% error = out of service), board chalk or colored earth. No higher-precision instruments needed.
  3. Operating sequence and control points: ① stocktake only after month-end close; ② two-person count + 10% re-weigh sample; ③ compute gap rate; >5% triggers the three-check this month; ④ three-check order fixed: missing records → pilferage → process drift; ⑤ update and post the three colors; ⑥ dual-sign and archive, copies to the works supervisor and the council.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: gap line 5% (37.6.1); sample share 10%; three-color thresholds 2.0/1.0/0.5 months — after one year of operation, re-validated against local cutoff and color-change history; revision via 37.6.3 dual signature.
  5. Process observation and recording items: gap rate per warehouse, three-check hits, color changes with trigger dates, whether the board-reverse recovery order still matches physical reality.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = every warehouse counted, gap ≤5% or three-check concluded, board updated and posted; rework = gap 5–10% unresolved within the month (due by the 10th of next month, else escalated to scrap); scrap = rushing the count before close, or a single-person count (that month's books re-counted).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: same warehouse gap >5% two months running → check the scale → check two-person two-lock execution → check handler rotation; color change with no action → check whether actions are truly fixed on the board → check whether the council overrode the lines; yellow accelerating to red → check whether the consumption baseline misuses a slack-season average.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one completed monthly stocktake sheet; L2 = 3 months gap ≤5% + one complete three-check record; L3 = one genuine color change with full plan-based disposition + threshold revision dual-signature slip + archived ledger.

Blank monthly stocktake sheet (copy from card):

Warehouse / material Book Physical Gap rate Three-check result Color this month Disposition Dual signature

Stocktake sheets are transcribed per warehouse, one page per warehouse, bound and archived at year-end.

docs.title: Safety Boundaries
docs.text:
No high-temperature or high-pressure operations in this chapter, but the following four items are part of the procedure — failing to execute them equals failing the chapter:

  1. Charcoal-store fire prevention: fresh charcoal air-cooled 24–48 h before storage; charcoal store ventilated, no open flame, ≥20 m from dwellings; daily patrol (smoke, scorched smell). A charcoal-shed fire burns more than charcoal — it burns the data origin of the entire fuel account.
  2. Stocktake yard safety: piles no taller than a person, nobody stands on pile tops; two-person carries; ladder holder required for high retrieval.
  3. Custody/bookkeeping separation: the custodian and the bookkeeper must not be the same person (two-person two-lock, 37.6.1); violations rework that month's books.
  4. Red-tier actions put people first: red-tier furnace sealing follows the Ch. 18 shutdown procedure; "rescuing stock" through rule-breaking rush-smelting is forbidden; when fuel runs short, household wood is protected first (37.6.4) — cold, hunger, and smoke dust kill the workforce faster than supply cutoffs (Iron Law 7).

docs.title: Chapter 39 Maintenance, Spare Parts, Life, and Quality Traceability
Chapter Objectives
docs.text:
After finishing this chapter, a settlement should be able to produce four documents and run them at the workstations:

Document Contents Purpose Equipment spot-inspection sheets Daily/weekly/monthly/annual four-tier inspection sheets; every item states "what to check, how to check, condemnation criteria" So that wear, corrosion, and fatigue are seen before they become accidents Spare-parts ledger Class A/B/C three-tier spare-part classification, minimum stock quantities, and inspection records of the stocked parts themselves When a part must be replaced, a part is on hand—and it is a good one Life calibration table the Section 39.4 empirical life table + measured columns for this settlement, heat by heat and piece by piece Upgrades "empirical values" into "this settlement's numbers," supporting production scheduling and spare-part minimums Failure-analysis archive three-tier batch numbers, the failed-sample library, five-step-method analysis sheets, and process-card version change records The same kind of bad part fails only once; knowledge lives in the archive, not in personal memory

docs.title: Capability Boundaries
docs.text:
Can do:

  • Establish the three institutions—spot inspection, spare parts, quality traceability—and tie them to the Chapter 37 shift roster and the Chapter 38 ledger.
  • Use the five senses (look, listen, touch, smell, compare) plus simple tools (feeler gauge, steel rule, wax chips, kerosene and chalk powder, magnet, scale) to find observable precursors of wear, corrosion, and fatigue.
  • Use ledger measurements to calibrate every line of the Section 39.4 empirical life table into the settlement's own life data.

Cannot do:

  • Nondestructive testing: ultrasonics, magnetic particles, penetrant dye, and X-rays are all unavailable (they depend, respectively, on the electronics industry and high-pressure equipment; no route exists before Chapter 33). Internal cracks and subsurface inclusions can only be handled by the kerosene-chalk method for surface-opening cracks plus post-hoc fracture-face reading; unopened internal defects cannot be found.
  • Precise life calculation: the stress–cycle curve of fatigue life (the S-N curve) requires controlled-load testing of hundreds of specimens; this stage has no such capability. This chapter does not predict "how many more hours this shaft can turn"; it does two things only: keep hours in the ledger, and condemn on precursors.
  • Online monitoring: there are no continuous-recording instruments. Temperature is measured only "at the moment of inspection"; clearance only "at the moment of shutdown." Degradation between inspections is hedged by shortening periods, not by instruments.

External dependencies (counted in the C List):

  1. A continuous small-scale supply of lubricating grease and oil (animal fat, vegetable oil, graphite—Chapters 8, 15). Without grease there is no steady-wear period for a sliding pair; bearing life is cut by half or more.
  2. ≥1 year of local humidity, freeze–thaw, and acid-mist exposure records—the foundation for calibrating corrosion rates; without this line, all anti-corrosion periods are temporary numbers.

docs.title: Pre-Start Verification
docs.text:
Checklist format. If any item is unmet, the corresponding institution runs on a "temporary period" first and marks it in the sheet header; life figures must not be extrapolated from it.

# Verification item Criterion (confirm you have X in hand; the standard is Y) 1 Equipment register Every furnace, kiln, machine tool, waterwheel, and bellows has a number (e.g., JC-01, Machine No. 1) and a current-status mark (in use / awaiting repair / mothballed) 2 Existing tool archive The Chapter 19 cutting-tool archive is on the books: every piece has a number, material batch number, and regrind count; unarchived tools are marked "unverified items" 3 Operating ledger Each machine has accumulated operating hours (or heats, kiln firings) on record; if none, this table starts from zero 4 Weights and measures Feeler gauge (Chapter 20), steel rule, scale, and calipers mutually cross-checked (Chapters 3, 22); wax chips prepared (thin slices of beeswax or mineral wax) 5 Accounts-office linkage The Chapter 37 accounts-office monthly stocktake is running, and the spare-parts store can be hooked into the stocktake 6 Maintenance responsible person Every machine has a named inspection owner on the shift roster, skill Grade 2 (Section 37.5) or above; the annual inspection must be chaired by a Grade 3 7 Anti-corrosion materials Grease, oiled paper / waxed-cloth wraps, and dunnage in stock; stock quantities per the Section 39.3 Class-C consumables table 8 Failed-sample shelf A shelf or cabinet has been set aside (dry, sheltered from rain, adequate load capacity); the tagging rules are in Section 39.6.3

docs.title: 39.1 Three Ways Machines Die: Wear, Corrosion, Fatigue
docs.text:
All failures of human-made artifacts are classified, in this chapter's framework, as three ways of dying. If you cannot tell the modes apart, you will treat fatigue as wear and "tighten up the clearance," or treat corrosion as fatigue and "fit a new shaft"—and the new shaft breaks again three months later. Learn to identify first; talk about inspection and spares after.

Death mode Mechanism Typical sites Development speed Inspection focus Wear gradual loss of surface material from a friction pair journal–bearing, saddle–guideway, nut–lead screw, piston–bellows wall, cutting edges chronic: months to years clearance, accuracy, wear debris, sound Corrosion chemical or electrochemical dissolution of the surface furnace and kiln steel parts, ironwork in acid-mist areas, sweaty fingerprints, dissimilar-metal contact faces, items in storage slower but never stops: it rusts even while shut down surface products, weight loss, remaining cross-section Fatigue crack initiation and growth under alternating stress, sudden fracture shafts, springs, chains, slings, gear tooth roots, bellows links latent without signs, breaks in an instant cracks, sudden deformation change, dead sound, the hours ledger

docs.title: 39.1.1 Wear: The Chronic Death of Friction Pairs
docs.text:
Wear occurs on a pair of surfaces; it is not a disease of a single part: as the journal wears thin, the bearing bore wears large, and the clearance is the sum of both wears. Development has three stages: the run-in period (a new pair's initial wear, clearance rises slightly—normal), the steady period (extremely slow wear, ninety percent of life), and the accelerating period (clearance large enough for impact loading, wear avalanches). The entire meaning of inspection is to intervene before the accelerating period.

Visible precursors (field observation methods):

  1. Clearance growth: with the machine stopped, rock the part radially by hand—from "just perceptible" to "obviously loose" (the Chapter 20 acceptance for a scraped bearing is about 0.05–0.1 mm; empirical value, must be field-calibrated). Quantify with feeler blades or the lead-wire crush (place a lead wire between journal and bearing, turn half a revolution, remove, and measure its thickness).
  2. Accuracy decline: on the machine tool, turn the same test bar in the same chuck, and the diameter difference between the two ends (taper) grows month by month; re-measure the lead screw's thread-cutting tooth-by-tooth error table (Chapter 20, Section 20.9). A pitch error exceeding 1.5 times the original table means the guideways or lead screw are worn beyond limits.
  3. Wear debris in the oil: draw oil from the bearing housing's oil port and pick up the sludge with a magnet—in the steady period it comes out as gray-black fine mud; shiny flakes or obvious iron filings mean the accelerating period has begun. Quantification: once a month, take the magnet-picked sludge from the same spot, shade-dry and weigh it, and enter it in the ledger.
  4. Sound change: a sliding pair goes from "sh-sh" to "clack-clack" (clearance impact). There are no rolling bearings in this framework, but gears behave the same way, going from a continuous hum to knocking.

◎ Judging clearance by ear is a hand-feel step. Practice: on the same machine, listen 10 times each just after overhaul, in the steady period, and just before the limit is exceeded, to build your own "scale of sounds." Misjudgment compensation: whenever sound is in doubt, always return to the lead-wire crush to measure clearance—hand feel is only for screening "this needs measuring now," never for waiving measurement.

docs.title: 39.1.2 Corrosion: The Death That Never Stops
docs.text:
Corrosion runs on two tracks. Chemical corrosion: acid mist, salt fog, and high-temperature oxidation directly dissolve the surface—the ironwork of the distillation workshop (Chapter 26), all steel on islands and salt works (Chapter 52), the high-temperature scale on furnace-door steel. Electrochemical corrosion: a water film plus two metals in contact (copper–iron, or iron from different heats) forms a galvanic cell, and the contact seams rot fastest—riveted seams, copper gaskets on iron shells, sweaty fingerprints (salt) leaving rust.

Visible precursors:

  1. Surface products: iron's red-brown rust layering and peeling, copper's green patina, white bloom on lead-gray parts, varnish-like tackiness in wood-ash (potash) areas. Condemnation looks at depth, not area: after scraping off the rust scale, measure the remaining cross-section with calipers; a stressed part with >10% section loss is condemned (empirical value, must be field-calibrated; calibration method: load-test three same-batch pieces at different rust depths, with the Chapter 19 scratch sequence as auxiliary confirmation that the material itself is unchanged).
  2. Weight loss: the coupon method—3–5 thin iron sheets from one batch, numbered and weighed (precision 0.1 g, Chapter 22), hung at four points: beside the furnace, in the acid-mist workshop, in the storeroom, and in the open air. Each month remove them, pickle off the rust (soak in dilute acetic acid, rinse in clean water, dry), and reweigh. This yields each workshop's monthly corrosion rate (g/dm²·month), convertible into a penetration speed. Any workshop whose coupon loses >0.05 g/dm² per month (empirical value) halves the inspection period for its ironwork.
  3. Cross-section loss and seizure: a bolt rusted solid and twisted off inside its hole is the costliest corrosion failure. The precursor is rust nodules on the threads and "it won't turn"—when it won't turn, hard twisting is forbidden; first soak with oil (kerosene or hot grease) for 24 h, then work it back.

Three anti-corrosion methods (write them into the inspection sheet): grease-and-wrap preservation for idle items (grease the whole piece + wrap in oiled paper); off-floor, off-wall storage on wooden dunnage (a damp storeroom floor is the number-one killer of stocked parts); leather or greased separator layers at dissimilar-metal contacts.

docs.title: 39.1.3 Fatigue: Sudden Death Without Warning
docs.text:
For parts under alternating load (a rotating shaft takes one bending cycle per revolution, a spring one tension–compression cycle per stroke, a chain one impact per engagement), cracks initiate at surface stress concentrations (keyway corners, section steps, old scratches), grow slowly, the remaining cross-section shrinks and shrinks, and then in one instant comes brittle fracture—almost no deformation before breaking. This is the fundamental difference between fatigue and wear or overload. So fatigue inspection is not about "measuring clearance" but about "finding cracks" and "counting hours."

Visible precursors:

  1. Surface cracks—the kerosene-chalk method: clean the suspected spot, brush with kerosene and let it soak 10–15 min, wipe dry, brush on a coat of chalk slurry (lime slurry works as a substitute); kerosene seeps out of the crack, showing a dark hairline. This method only finds cracks open to the surface; depth is unknown—find one and condemn; do not gamble.
  2. Sudden deformation change: early fatigue often shows as slight bending first. The belt suddenly drifts, gear meshing suddenly bottoms at the tooth roots, a seal suddenly wears off-center—check the shaft that carries them: run a dial indicator against the shaft through one full turn (Chapter 27); radial runout >0.2 mm (empirical value, must be field-calibrated) → stop the machine and inspect.
  3. Sound deadening: a sound piece rings bright with a long sustain; a cracked piece sounds hoarse and muffled with short sustain. ◎ Strike-listening is a hand-feel step. Practice: strike a known-good shaft and its fractured counterpart 20 times each, and compare. Misjudgment compensation: any audible suspicion goes straight to the kerosene-chalk method; never close the case on hearing alone.
  4. Fracture-face reading (afterward, for failure analysis): a flat, smooth fracture face with arc-shaped "beach marks" spreading from one edge point = fatigue (beach marks are the growth rings of the crack advancing cycle by cycle); a rough, fully crystalline, glittering face = brittle fracture; a dull, fibrous face with obvious necking = ductile overload fracture. The fracture-reading conclusion goes directly into step 5 of Card 39-02.

Fatigue's management tool is the hours ledger, not instruments: accumulate operating hours for each machine (blast furnace by heats, chains by tonnes hoisted); as a part approaches the lower bound of its life interval in the table, double the inspection period (monthly inspection escalates to a ten-day inspection). This is the other half of the reason the Section 39.2 daily inspection exists—the daily check both looks for wear and keeps time for fatigue.

docs.title: 39.2 The Inspection Institution: Tiered Inspection Sheets
39.2.1 Four-Tier Periods and Responsible Persons
docs.text:
Tier Period Performed by Time Scope Daily before start-up each shift operator (Grade 1 suffices) ≤10 min the four acts—look, listen, touch, record: oil level, abnormal noise, temperature, obvious damage Weekly once a week workshop master or Grade-2 worker half a day all daily items + hand-feel clearance + magnet pick of wear debris + cutting-tool archive check + walk-through of stocked parts Monthly same day each month as the accounts-office stocktake Grade-2 worker + accounts office 1 day all weekly items + quantitative measurement (feeler gauge, lead-wire crush, coupon weighing, test-bar turning) + spare-parts stocktake Annual yearly shutdown chaired by a Grade 3, all hands take part 3–5 days teardown inspection, accuracy re-measurement (guideway scraping point counts, remaking the lead-screw error table), furnace-lining major-repair assessment, life-table calibration summary

Principle: periods may only be shortened, never lengthened; the grounds for shortening (abnormal precursors) are recorded at the foot of the sheet. Lengthening a period must go through the Section 39.7 change-control dual signature.

docs.title: 39.2.2 Object Inspection Sheet (what to check / how to check / condemnation criteria)
docs.text: Object What to check How to check Condemnation criteria Furnace/kiln lining cracks, spalling, erosion depth after shutdown and cooling, lamp-light the inner wall and scribe each zone with a steel rod (slag line, tuyere zone, hearth bottom); compare against the new lining's baseline scribe marks crack wider than 5 mm or deeper than 30 mm; slag-line erosion deeper than 1/3 of wall thickness; either one reached → patch the furnace or relinish the lining. Empirical life 3–8 campaigns (see Section 39.4), recorded heat by heat Tuyere ceramic tubes end burn-through, blockage, cracking shut off blast, pull out, inspect visually; measure the end's inner diameter bore enlarged >1/3 (burn-through) or cracked to the point of air leakage → swap in the spare tube (the Chapter 18 keep-2-spares rule) Bellows flap seals, valve plates, housing cracks press the valve plates by hand to check seating; hold a candle near the seams and watch for the flame being sucked in (air leak); listen for creaking of the housing (wood cracking) flaps hardened and cracked, seating gap >1 mm → replace flaps (Class-C spare); monthly: feel the bushes' temperature rise (a water-cooled part should be near water temperature); annual: shut the water, drain, inspect the timber bush clearance >3 mm (empirical value, must be field-calibrated) → replace the bush; blade erosion deeper than 1/4 of timber thickness → replace the blade; timber condemned per Chapter 13 timber construction Gears tooth-face pitting, broken teeth, backlash inspect tooth faces visually (pits merging into patches = pitting advancing); roll against red-lead powder to read the contact pattern; measure backlash with the feeler gauge a single tooth broken → replace the wheel (wooden wheels can take a single-tooth insert, Chapter 21); pits covering >1/3 of the tooth face, or backlash >0.5 mm (empirical value, must be field-calibrated) → replace the wheel or flip it for reversed use Building roofs rain leaks, displaced tiles, rotten rafters before the rainy season, go up and check room by room; in rain, map the damp stains from inside more than 3 adjoining rafters rotted, or load-bearing sag exceeding 1/100 of rafter length → replace rafters per Chapter 13 Drainage ditch silting, foundations soaking within 2 h after rain, check for standing-water points; when a ditch's depth is halved, dredge it workshop floor staying damp for more than 3 days → check drainage and the underlayer, to prevent equipment foot rot and rust

docs.title: 39.2.3 The Five-Sense Inspection Method
docs.text:
Look (cracks, rust color, wear debris, drift) → listen (abnormal noise, dead sound, strike sustain) → touch (temperature, vibration, looseness) → smell (scorched odor = lubrication failure; sour odor = corrosion environment worsening) → compare (against last month's numbers, against spare parts, against identical machines). Comparison is the chief of the five senses: a single reading becomes information only when placed into a ledger series. The daily sheet accepts only numbers or "no abnormality seen + signature"; writing the bare word "normal" and being done with it is forbidden—this is precisely the root disease named in the first row of the failure-modes table.

[Card 39-01 Equipment Inspection Card (with period-table template)] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: the equipment register (every unit numbered); grease (Chapters 8, 15); chalk or lime wash and kerosene (for oil-stain crack reveal); paper forms or a chalkboard.
  2. Required tools: feeler gauges and lead wire, steel rule, calipers (Chapter 22, cross-checked before use), wax sheet, magnet, small hammer, lamp. Accuracy needed: 0.1 mm-class calipers suffice; home-made feeler leaves are each checked for thickness against the calipers.
  3. Operating sequence and control points: (1) work through the register unit by unit — the four daily actions (look, listen, feel, record) are never skipped; (2) every quantitative item (clearance, weight loss, counts) must carry a number; (3) any over-line item gets an "out of service" board on the spot and is reported to the workshop head; (4) the form's footer records "items whose period was shortened this round, and why"; (5) the monthly inspection runs on the same day as the counting-house monthly stocktake, with the spares column checked on the same form.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: scrap thresholds are in the 39.2.2 table, all marked "empirical, calibrate in the field"; calibration method: at the annual inspection take the distribution of measured values in this settlement, set each threshold between "the worst unit still passing" and "the earliest unit to fail," then copy each value into the ledger and update this card.
  5. Process observation and recording items: daily entries are a number or "no abnormality," plus a signature; an over-line item records four columns — phenomenon, value, action, reporter; the weekly check records abrasive-debris weight; the monthly check records coupon weight loss.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = every item recorded within its period and every quantitative item carries a number; rework = a missed day (make it up that week, marked "make-up"; more than 2 misses in a month sends that unit's responsible person back to training); record scrap = two consecutive periods with no entries (the unit is treated as unmaintained and must be re-assessed before use).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: inspection done and the failure still happened → first check whether quantitative items were written as "normal" → then whether periods were extended verbally → then whether over-line items were boarded and handled → then whether the responsible person was a lone Level-1 stand-in with no second check.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = at least one unit with four consecutive weeks of inspection forms; L2 = one month of records for every registered unit plus one monthly quantitative ledger; L3 = a year of records + an annual accuracy re-verification report + at least one case where inspection caught degradation early (caught = taken out of service, stripped, and the defect confirmed).

Inspection period-table template (copy per unit, one sheet each):

Unit no.: __ Responsible: __ Daily Weekly Monthly Annual Oil level / grease quantity (number) Abnormal noise (location) Bearing temperature (wax-sheet result) Clearance (mm, lead squeeze / feeler) — Abrasive debris on magnet (dry weight, g) — Oil-stain crack reveal (yes/no) — Running hours / furnace cycles cumulative Over-line item handling (four columns)

docs.title: 39.3 The Spares System: Three Tiers and Minimum Levels
docs.text: The spares system answers one question: when something breaks in hand, how long is the downtime? The answer comes from tiering plus minimum levels together. More spares is not better — stock ties up materials and hours and rusts on the shelf; nor is waiting for breakage to rebuild — per Chapter 19, one chisel from stock to tool runs the full carburize-quench-temper chain, one to several days. Tiering exists to spend money and hours on the parts whose downtime costs most.

docs.title: 39.3.1 Three Spares Tiers
docs.text:
Tier Definition Examples Minimum rule A (critical single item) single-point failure: one broken piece stops a line, no on-site substitute blast tuyere tubes, bellows flaps and valve plates, waterwheel bearing shells, transitional master lead screw, crucibles, precast lining bricks ≥2 per machine (1 in use, 1 spare), extending Ch. 18's "2 tuyeres in stock" and Ch. 19's "≥2 critical blades" rules B (common interchangeable) shared across machines; one failure degrades but does not stop the line bolts, pins, keys, wedge irons, bushings, wooden gears, bearing scraping blanks, belt joints ≥2–3 per spec; interchangeable items pooled C (consumables) continuous consumption, managed by burn rate files, whetstones, wax plates, grease, oil paper, charcoal (workshop ledger), hemp line, leather scraps minimum = daily use × replenishment lead (days) × 1.5 safety factor

Calibration of the minimum formula: lead time measured by the Chapter 38 ledger — from "reorder triggered" to "spare in store," log days per occurrence and take the upper quartile; the 1.5 safety factor is empirical, raised to 2.0 in lean or harvest-busy seasons (37.3.3 derating). Stock below minimum triggers a rebuild order — never wait for exhaustion (generalizing the Chapter 9 institution).

docs.title: 39.3.2 Minimum-Quantity Table (empirical, field-calibrate)
docs.text: Spare Tier Minimum Calibration Blast tuyere tubes (per furnace) A ≥2 log burn-through rate per furnace (bore widening mm/smelt); stock 3 smelts' worth Bellows flaps / valve plates (per box) A ≥2 sets log flap hardening cycle (months) per shift Waterwheel bearing shells (per wheel) A ≥1 pair + 1 wooden blank annual measured clearance-growth rate Crucibles (glass / copper) A ≥2 checked against 39.4 melt-life and production plan Furnace lining bricks and refractory mud (per furnace) A half a reline log patch-mud consumption per furnace; reline size back-computed from measured lining erosion Critical blades (chisels, saws, drills, each type) A ≥2 Ch. 19 institution; corrected by regrind cycle and requench yield Files (coarse/fine, each spec) C 2–4 per 39.4 filing-hours life ÷ weekly filing hours Wax plates C ≥10 measured monthly use Grease C ≥30 days' worth summed monthly weigh-ins across lube points Belt leather and joints B 1 belt's worth belt life (39.4) + tension-adjustment margin Whetstones (coarse/fine) C 1 each + blanks monthly weigh-in wear

docs.title: 39.3.3 Inspecting the Spares Themselves (a shelf is not a safe)
docs.text:
Spares rotting on the shelf is the stealthiest failure: the part is fetched for an swap and found rusted solid or moldy — the whole minimum-level institution has failed. Stock inspection is folded into the monthly check:

Check Method Scrap / disposition Metal corrosion visual + touch per item; oiled items checked for intact film surface rust removed and re-oiled; rust into the base metal judged per 39.1.2 Leather mold/stiffness visual mold spots; finger-flex for elasticity brush off mold, re-grease; crack network on flex → downgrade to C Wooden items (bearing blanks, gears) cracks, insect bores, moisture (cool-damp feel = absorbed water) dry in shade and re-weigh; warp >1 mm/100 mm → downgrade Ceramic items (tuyeres, crucibles) crisp ring on tap (◎ listen; compensation: soak and watch for bubble streams) dull ring or visible crack = scrap — it would shatter in service Grease rancidity smell: acid; touch: sticky, separated downgraded to non-bearing rust protection Storage conditions ≥200 mm off ground on sleepers, off walls, ventilated, rain-proof violations corrected that month, entered in the monthly sheet

[Card 39-03 Spares Ledger Card] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: equipment register, Chapter 38 ledger (consumption flow), 39.3.2 minimum table, monthly stock-inspection records.
  2. Required tools: ledger book, scale, calipers; cross-checked per Chapters 3, 22 before use.
  3. Operating sequence and control points: ① one row per spare: number, tier, minimum, on hand, location; ② every issue and receipt entered immediately — "use first, record later" forbidden; ③ rows below minimum flagged red, triggering a rebuild work order copied to scheduling (Ch. 37); ④ monthly stocktake reconciles books and goods; gap >5% investigated that month (Ch. 37 warehouse rules); ⑤ stock-inspection results entered in the "stock status" column.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: minimums and lead times per 39.3.1; validated quarterly against actual cutoff/overstock events — a cutoff = minimum too low; overstock >1 year = minimum too high or storage poor.
  5. Process observation and recording items: issue date/use/issuer; receipt date/making batch (per 39.6 batch number); stock-status monthly column.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = books match goods, no below-minimum rows, all stock inspections passed; rework = below-minimum rows appeared (rebuild that week; halve the affected machines' inspection intervals meanwhile); scrap = books-goods gap >5% unresolved (all spares treated as unverified that month, individually re-inspected before issue).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: a spare found broken at swap time → was stock inspection actually run? → check oil-seal and sleeper conditions → check whether it was uninspected at intake; always one spare short → is the rebuild order entering production scheduling? → is the measured lead time underestimated?
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one filled ledger; L2 = one month books-match-goods + one cutoff/overstock back-check with correction; L3 = one quarter's ledger + minimums corrected by event back-check + zero missed stock inspections.

Spares ledger template (copy from card):

Number Name Tier Minimum On hand Location Last issue Rebuild order no. Stock status (monthly)

docs.title: 39.4 Life Table: All Empirical Values, Field-Calibrate
docs.text:
This table is the book's master expected-life ledger for consumables, gathering scattered data and filling gaps. Every row is an empirical value — inferred from historical magnitudes, not settlement-measured; every row must be replaced in the "measured" column by settlement ledger data at annual inspection. General method: record each retired item as "install/start date + cumulative running hours (or firings, cycles) + scrap reason"; after one year, each row's settlement distribution is the measured life.

Item Empirical life Unit Pre-scrap signs (linking 39.1/39.2) Main variables Bloomery/small blast furnace lining (rammed refractory) 3–8 campaigns campaign (between major relines) slag-line erosion >1/3 wall, cracks >5 mm slag basicity, temperature, ramming quality (Ch. 18) Furnace hot-patch mud 1–3 smelts smelt patch falls away exposing red patch mix and drying Pottery/lime kiln body 30–100 firings firing roof spalling, firebox arch spreading heating/cooling rates (Ch. 12) Crucibles (glass/copper) 5–20 melts melt wall down to 2/3 original, glassy skin weeping melt temperature, alkalinity (Ch. 14) Blast tuyere tubes 3–10 smelts smelt bore widening >1/3 blast pressure, slag-line position Scraping blades 20–40 regrinds count blade shortened to hard-to-grip; hardened layer ground away regrind overheating (Ch. 19) Files 40–100 filing hours h tip polish >1/3; won't cut wrought iron filing hard stock, rust, no brush cleaning Leather drive belts 1–3 years year tension adjustment exhausted, still slipping; delamination slip heating, damp (Ch. 15) Hemp rope (static lashing) 1–2 years year fuzzed and stiff; yarns breaking in strands damp, UV Hemp rope sling 50–200 hoists hoist one broken strand = downgrade/no hoist; two = scrap shock loading, sharp edges Leather seals (bellows flap, piston ring) 3–12 months month hardening; fit gap >1 mm action frequency, grease (Ch. 12, 15) Wood bearings (oiled hardwood) 0.5–2 years year clearance >3 mm; journal wearing wood dust water/dust environment, lubrication Cast-iron/bronze bearing shells 3–10 years year same but several times slower completeness of the metallurgical chain Springs (valve, bow-saw) 10⁴–10⁶ cycles cycle oil reveals crack lines; free length short >10% stress amplitude, rust onset (Ch. 19) Drive chain 1–5 years year elongation >2% pitch; dull running lubrication, shock Machine oil (grease) change every 30–90 days day oil blackened and dry; magnet picks much iron dust ambient dust

Wood vs. metal bearing trade-off (a decision basis, not a quality verdict):

Item Wood bearing (oiled hardwood, Ch. 21) Metal bearing (cast-iron/bronze shell, Ch. 17, 19) Life 0.5–2 years 3–10 years Replacement cost half a day; wooden blank self-made scraping fit 1–3 days + metallurgical chain Failure mode gradual loosening, visible wear dust — ample warning also gradual but with high seizure risk (heat welding) Fit waterwheels, low-speed drives (<~1 m/s peripheral, empirical) machine tools, steam engines; metal always where >60 ℃ line applies Spares strategy wooden blanks stocked (tier B); swap on failure scraping blanks stocked; rescrape and reuse

◎ Judging "wood or metal for this shaft" by touch (feel heat, listen) is insufficient — the criterion always returns to the 60 ℃ line and the speed ledger.

[Card 39-04 Spare-Part Life Card (Life-Table Calibration and Retirement Registration)] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: the original 39.4 life table (empirical column); the item-number file (commissioning date, cumulative usage); Card 39-03 spares ledger (issue and restock flow, rebuild lead time); scrap tickets (item number, reason, scrapping person, signed at Level 2 and above); the Card 39-02 stub for any item retired for an abnormal cause.
  2. Required tools: ledger book (one row per item, the replacement table copied onto the flyleaf); scale and calipers (wear, wall thickness, elongation measurement), steel rule and scriber, a time base (sundial or water clock, Ch. 3, for accumulated running hours). Calibrate before use: zero and full-scale check on the scale, zero the calipers, cross-check per Chapters 3 and 22 — out-of-tolerance instruments are withdrawn.
  3. Operating sequence and control points: ① on entry into the register fill item number, commissioning date, and unit of measure at once, taking the unit row by row from the 39.4 table (furnace campaign / furnace / kiln firing / crucible melt / lift / cycle / year / day / h) — never mixing them; ② at every retirement fill cumulative usage + scrap reason + scrapping person on the spot, scrap authority resting at Level 2 and above; ③ merge same-type items into one row and give the settlement's measured range (shortest value to median); ④ recompute the whole table on the annual inspection day, replacing the empirical column with measured values on every row that has them and noting the replacement year; ⑤ items retired for abnormal causes — fatigue fracture, early corrosion — are flagged "abnormal" at the row end and force-routed to Card 39-02 for the five-step analysis and into the failure-sample library (39.6.3); ⑥ copy the measured rebuild lead time (upper quartile) into the minimum-formula field of Card 39-03 and recompute the minimum.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: take every life range from the 39.4 table — furnace lining 3–8 campaigns, kiln body 30–100 firings, crucible 5–20 melts, tuyère clay pipe 3–10 furnaces, file 40–100 filing hours, sling 50–200 lifts, leather seal 3–12 months, wood bearing 0.5–2 years, metal bearing shell 3–10 years, spring 10⁴–10⁶ cycles, drive chain 1–5 years, machine oil changed every 30–90 days. General calibration: record three columns per item (commissioning date + cumulative usage + scrap reason); after one year each row's local distribution is the measured life. A row with too few samples must not be replaced by a single item's value — note the item count beside the measured column and keep the empirical range.
  5. Process observation and recording items: item number, commissioning date, unit of measure and cumulative usage, scrap date and reason, scrapping person, whether the retirement was abnormal, whether it entered the sample library, number of retired items of that type with measured median, and the measured rebuild lead time in days.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = every retirement carries the three-column record, the measured column states item count and year, and the Card 39-03 minimum has been recomputed from the measured rebuild lead time; rework = commissioning date or cumulative usage missing (pull the item-number file within the deadline; if still missing, leave the empirical column and mark the row "file gap"); scrap = filling the measured column from impression or guesswork (the whole column is voided, the table reverts to empirical values, and the annual calibration is redone).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: spares always one short → first check whether the measured column still carries empirical values → then whether the rebuild lead time used unmeasured days → then whether the minimum was computed with the 1.5 safety factor (39.3.1) → only then add stock; same-type items dying early over and over → check whether abnormal retirements were missed for Card 39-02 → run the 39.2 three checks (oil, alignment, load) → check whether the 60 ℃ line was crossed; measured lives uniformly shorter than the empirical range → check for mixed units (firings vs. campaigns, lifts vs. years).
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one page of the life table with the three-column record complete for every retirement; L2 = at least 3 rows carrying the settlement's measured column (with item count and year) + one record of the minimum recomputed from measured rebuild lead time; L3 = a full year's table calibration + the trace of measured values replacing empirical ones + one dual-signed registration of a minimum changed on measured life (37.6.3) + the quarterly count showing every abnormal retirement transferred into the sample library.

Blank life-table page (copy and use, one row per item):

Item Item no. Commissioned Unit of measure Cumulative usage Scrapped Scrap reason Scrapping person Abnormal (to Card 39-02) Measured here (count / median)

docs.title: 39.5 Scrap Criteria and Retirement: Scrap Is a Resource, Not Garbage
39.5.1 Scrap Authority and Tagging
docs.text: Scrap authority sits with Level-2 workers and above, registered through Card 39-03 (item number, reason, scrapping person). A scrapped item is handled on the spot, one of three ways: tagged "downgraded," tagged "material," or tagged "sample" — untagged piles are forbidden and processed per the 39.6 failure mode. Any item retired for abnormal causes — fatigue fracture, early corrosion — is force-entered into the failure-sample library (39.6.3) for one five-step analysis; an abnormal retirement is itself a free information product.

docs.title: 39.5.2 The Downgrade Chain
docs.text:
A worn precision part is not waste; it is a crude-use part. Each link of the chain states its criterion and destination:

Item Level 1 (primary duty) Down one Down again End point Master lead screw thread-cutting master off-pitch ordinary drive screw grinding mandrel / scraping-bar core to furnace (steel sorting bin) File precision file dull → coarse file, wood sawing blank → scraper blank (good steel, Ch. 19) to furnace Scraper scraping rough chipping, rust removal — to furnace Bearing shell (metal) precision fit rescraped for coarse equipment — to furnace Crucible glass melting low-alkali melts / annealing cover broken → refractory grog aggregate (Ch. 11) furnace-founding filler Lining bricks — broken grog backfilling — furnace-founding filler Hemp rope sling lashing mats, fire-lighting fuses fuel (clean rope only; oiled rope burned separately, never in the cooking stove) Leather seal / drive washers, handle wrap polishing wheel fat boiling (Ch. 15)

Two downgrade disciplines: first, downgraded items are hole-punched or notched (e.g., a 3 mm hole in the tail = down one level) to prevent them flowing back to precision posts — a downgraded part mistakenly returned to the master machine is a leading precision accident; second, the downgrade destination is entered in the ledger, and the materials store sorts into four pools ("steel / iron / grog / wood" — an extension of the Ch. 19 grading store), with high-carbon steel items (old files, springs) entering the steel pool separately — they are precious carburizing stock at remelt.

docs.title: 39.5.3 Remelt and Recovery
docs.text: Retired metal ultimately returns to the furnace: iron into the Ch. 18 re-smelting flow; steel (blades, springs, files) broken up as high-carbon stock for Ch. 19 carburizing and charging. Remelted items must carry their source batch number (39.6) — a batch repeatedly remelted accumulates impurities and elemental uncertainty; the Ch. 19 archive system requires no more than 2 remelts before a stock loses blade eligibility, becoming casting stock from the third. The rule runs without instruments: batch numbers and the ledger are the whole apparatus.

docs.title: 39.6 Quality Traceability: Batch Numbers, the Failure-Sample Library, and the Five-Step Failure Analysis
docs.text: Before Chapter 37, knowledge lived in two heads: the old smith remembered the last ore batch differed; the bookkeeper remembered last month had more scrap. One death, one illness, one forgetting — and the knowledge is gone. Quality traceability has a single purpose: make the information from every failure outlive the person. The review review named the root disease: "storing only successful recipes, never failure conditions, material differences, or damaged samples." This section's batch system makes "differences traceable"; the sample library keeps "the physical evidence alive"; the five-step method makes "conclusions reusable."

docs.title: 39.6.1 Three-Level Batch Numbers: Furnace–Batch–Item
docs.text:
Level Definition Numbering (example) Use Level Definition Numbering (example) Use Furnace no. output of one smelt / one kiln firing / one crucible date + same-day sequence: L261029-02 = 2nd smelt of Oct 29 locks raw-material batches (ore, charcoal, sand) and furnace-condition records Batch no. a post-processing batch under a furnace no. suffix on furnace no.: L261029-02-T3 = 3rd anneal batch of that furnace's output locks process parameters (carburizing time, annealing curve, temper color) Item no. lifetime number of a critical single item post code + sequence: GD-014 = 14th blade from the forge post locks the item's full history of regrinds, inspections, downgrades, scrap (linking the Ch. 19 tool archive)

Execution rules:

  1. Travelling transfer: batch numbers chalked/soapstone-marked on the item or tied as a wooden tag; the next process copies the number before starting. Three places must agree (on the item, on the travelling tag, in the ledger).
  2. Parallel recording of material differences: every furnace number must record its ore batch and charcoal batch (source pit / kiln load) and the day's weather (rain-wet feed directly changes smelting behavior); Ch. 14 glass additionally logs the sand and soda batches. Raw-material batches themselves are numbered — ore by pit + pile, charcoal by kiln load.
  3. Traceability drill: each quarter, one finished product is drawn and traced backwards from item number to ore and charcoal batches within half a stick of incense (about 1 hour). A broken trail = a broken traceability chain; the item is treated as unverified. This drill is the institution's acceptance test — traceability is proven by exercise, not by ledger thickness.

docs.title: 39.6.2 The Failure-Sample Library: Every Failed Part Is a Teaching Aid
docs.text:
Every scrapped and accident item whose failure was abnormal (early fracture, unusual corrosion, the first piece of a batch scrap, failed trials) enters the library, not the bin. Four zones: fracture (broken parts), corrosion, wear (out-of-tolerance items), scrap zone (batch scraps keep 3 samples: best, worst, middle). Every item carries a four-field tag:

Field Content Symptom broke / cracked / went soft / rusted through; when and where found Parameters at the time batch number, shift record summary (temperature band, medium, load), material batches Autopsy conclusion fracture reading (39.1.3), file and scratch tests (Ch. 19), weight and caliper measurements Disposition was the process card revised, to what version, by whom

The library's enemy is becoming a junk pile: untagged items are counted quarterly; two consecutive quarters untagged = back to the furnace as material — an untagged sample is not knowledge; it is clutter. On intake, a one-line index is transcribed (item / date / batch / one-sentence conclusion) for teaching apprentices — the failure-sample library is the best physical teaching aid of the apprenticeship system (toward Ch. 43); one real fracture beats ten verbal descriptions.

docs.title: 39.6.3 The Five-Step Failure Analysis
docs.text:
Step 1: Preserve the scene. Do not move the item, do not wipe the fracture faces, do not mate the broken halves (mating crushes the fracture marks); sketch the scene first (position, orientation, scattered pieces); cover the fracture with a dry cloth against hand-sweat rust. When injury occurred, merge scene preservation with the Ch. 37 "24 h three tasks."

Step 2: Gather all parameters. Back-trace by batch number: material batches and differences (this batch's ore/charcoal/sand vs. the last), shift and handover records, recent inspection-sheet values, weather and season, the item's full history (item archive: regrinds, downgrades, remelts). Incomplete parameters are themselves part of the conclusion — note "inspection record missing" as a candidate cause.

Step 3: Rank hypotheses by probability. Common before rare; mark each as verifiable or not: ① human execution deviation (card not followed) ② material differences (checkable by batch comparison) ③ wrong process parameter (the card itself wrong) ④ equipment degradation (inspection chain) ⑤ environment (weather, season) ⑥ material defect (the batch's metallurgical history). Jumping straight to ⑥ to blame the material is the lazy answer when nothing else was checked.

Step 4: Single-variable verification. Change one variable at a time; lock everything else to the card; run controls (same material batch, same station, old vs. new parameters, 3 pieces each). This is Ch. 26's experimental discipline applied to maintenance. Verdicts rest on physical evidence — test bars, fracture faces, scratch sequences — never on "it looks fine now."

Step 5: Archive the conclusion and revise the process card. The conclusion is three lines: root cause, evidence, fix. The fix lands on the card as a revision — header version +1 (e.g., Card 19-03 v2 → v3); the old version is not destroyed but archived with the superseded reason (linking the Ch. 43 archive); register on the Card 39-02 stub and circulate card swaps to all holding stations. If the root cause is in the equipment rather than the process, revise the inspection sheet or spares minimum — with the same version trail.

[Card 39-02 Failure Analysis Card (Five-Step Flow Sheet)] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: the failed item (preserved), travelling batch tags, shift and inspection records, material batch ledger, item archive.
  2. Required tools: magnifier (Ch. 24), steel rule and calipers (cross-checked), standard file and hardness reference set (Ch. 19), scale, kerosene and whiting powder, paper. Dry-brush fracture faces before examination; water washing forbidden.
  3. Operating sequence and control points: ① sketch the scene and number scattered pieces; ② fracture read before touched: judge beach marks / coarse grain / fibrous and draw; ③ back-trace batch numbers to ore and charcoal lots; missing links logged as "chain broken"; ④ hypothesis list ranked by probability, each marked verifiable / not-yet-verifiable; ⑤ single-variable verification requires controls — verification without a control group is void; ⑥ three-line conclusion + card revision number registered + swap signed.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: the hypothesis order (human → material → process → machine → environment → material defect) is an empirical sequence; calibration: each quarter tally the settlement's concluded root-cause distribution — if "material defect" exceeds 30%, re-check whether the first four hypotheses were敷衍'd.
  5. Process observation and recording items: scene sketch, fracture drawing, parameters and 3-piece results per verification group, revision number and swap recipients.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = five steps complete, controls present, conclusion lands as a card revision; rework = steps skipped or no controls (redo step 4 and re-close); scrap = conclusion unarchived or old cards uncollected (analysis voided; case reopened).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: same failure recurring → did the last conclusion actually change the card? → did swapped cards reach the stations? → were controls run?; analysis stuck at "bad material" → check whether hypotheses 1–4 were individually excluded with a trace.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one completed five-step sheet; L2 = one case closed with a controlled test and a card revision; L3 = a year's analysis binder + fully tagged sample library + a no-recurrence record (any recurrence triggers re-examination of the prior analysis).

Failure analysis sheet template (copy from card):

Step Record ① Scene sketch and piece numbering ② Fracture reading (form / origin / drawing) ③ Batch back-trace (to ore/charcoal lots; where the chain broke) ④ Hypothesis ranking (1–6, verifiability) ⑤ Single-variable verification (parameters / 3 controlled results) ⑥ Three-line conclusion + card revision no. + swap signatures

docs.title: 39.7 Change Control: Dual Signatures, First-Article Inspection, and Rollback
docs.text:
This section lands Ch. 37's 37.6.3 change control in maintenance and quality contexts. Any change to a process parameter, inspection interval, scrap threshold, or spares minimum is a change, subject to the same rules:

  1. Dual signature: changing a parameter = the process-card holder (Level 3) + the works supervisor, both required; five items entered in the ledger (date, old value, new value, reason, verification result), linking to Ch. 37.
  2. First-article inspection after any change: the first 3 pieces are 100% inspected (not sampled) — against the corresponding chapter's acceptance criteria item by item (test bar, fracture, scratch sequence, full dimensions); all 3 must pass before normal production resumes; one first-article piece is retained in the sample library's scrap or control zone.
  3. Rollback conditions (any one restores the old parameter, with a registered rollback): a first-article failure; one same-type failure within 30 days of the change; abnormal life shortening after the change (inspection finds precursors early — e.g., clearance growth at twice the historical rate); new scrap appearing in adjacent processes.
  4. Rollback also requires dual signatures, and rollback is not case closure — the root cause returns to Card 39-02 for a fresh five-step analysis. Anyone holds the right to request a rollback (Ch. 37); suppressing such a request is itself an accountability violation.

Change control is accepted by drill too: each quarter, draw any parameter's current value from the ledger — its "why is it this value" registration chain (original card + every change's five items + verification result) must be findable within one hour. Not findable = change control lost; the whole line is treated as unverified process.

docs.title: Safety Boundaries
docs.text:
Most actions here occur stopped and cold, but the following are part of the procedure — failing to execute them equals failing the chapter:

  1. De-energize stored-energy parts first: unload or lock springs, tensioned belts, and slings before disassembly; fatigue-fracture fragments flying out and spring ejection are this chapter's two direct injury sources.
  2. Entering furnaces for inspection: furnace ≤60 ℃ (wax-plate verified) and ventilated ≥15 min before entry, two-person rule (Ch. 37); CO is odorless — entering by feel is a violation.
  3. Roof and height checks in pairs, roped or railed; wet roofs after rain are off-limits.
  4. Scrapped slings cut up on the spot to prevent回流 misuse; scrapped items punched/notched before leaving hand.
  5. Chronic-exposure recording: inspections also log exposure hours for dust (swarf, charcoal), noise (forging, riveting), and acid mist (Ch. 26 shops), filed monthly — this is the raw data of occupational health, handed to Part 9 (toward Ch. 49) for filing. Maintenance workers themselves are a high-exposure group; this line may not be skipped.

  • Ch. 43 Archives and transmission: long-term preservation of card versions, ledger transcriptions, and the sample-library index — every binder this chapter produces must outlive a generation in the Ch. 43 archive.

docs.title: Chapter 40: Alternative Routes, Degraded Operation, and Disaster Redundancy
Chapter Objectives
docs.text:
After reading this chapter, the settlement should produce four documents:

Document Content Use Alternative route register Four-column registration for every alternative route (performance loss / resource cost / applicability boundary / final bottleneck) + trial-production evidence When a main resource is missing, know what to switch to, how much is lost, how long it can run, and where it counts as safe Degraded-operation plan set Trigger criteria for every critical line (linked to the Chapter 38 three-color lines) and switchover action lists In a crisis, switch by the book, not by improvisation Annual degraded-operation drill record Once a year, actually stop one line for 24 h per the plan: five-column record plus rectification and closure Proves the plan is not a paper exercise Six-disaster recovery cards and stand-in boards Reserves, bypasses, and recovery order for drought / flood / fire / epidemic / mine disaster / critical equipment failure; stand-in arrangements for critical posts Recover by the card after disaster: save people first, then food and fuel, machines last

docs.title: Capability Boundaries
docs.text:
Can do:

  • Build a substitution matrix for the five classes of critical resources — fuel, ore, power, materials, processes — registering every alternative in four columns, with temperature, lifespan, precision, and hazard boundaries stated item by item (Section 40.2).
  • Write a "drop one tier and still run" plan for every critical production line: trigger criteria, switchover time limit ≤48 h, exit conditions (Section 40.3).
  • Establish reserve lists, bypasses, and post-disaster recovery priorities for the six disasters, and test them with annual drills (Sections 40.3.3, 40.4, 40.5).

Cannot do:

  • Cannot declare a nonexistent alternative feasible. If the territory holds no peat, no coal, no copper ore, the corresponding matrix cell can only say "no route" — "theoretically obtainable in trade from afar" does not fill the cell. Iron Law 5: never claim complete substitution on the grounds that a thing exists in theory.
  • Cannot predict when a disaster arrives. Every reserve and plan in this chapter only shortens "minimum post-disaster downtime"; redundancy is not immunity.
  • Cannot replace the Chapter 39 maintenance system or the safety procedures of the process chapters. This chapter governs "after it breaks, in what order to switch and into what"; it does not govern "how to keep it from breaking."
  • Cannot guarantee an undrilled plan works. Any plan that has not been through one drill is treated as a draft and does not count toward acceptance.

External dependencies (counted on the Class-C list):

  1. Chapter 38 ledgers with ≥1 quarter of continuous stock flows — the sole data source for the three-color lines.
  2. Chapter 39 spare-parts ledger and inspection records — the basis for the "critical equipment failure" disaster entry.
  3. Chapter 37 skills matrix and work schedules — proof that every degraded route "has someone who can run it."
  4. Chapter 2 resource survey records of grade, reserves, and round-trip haul distances for substitute resources.

Four-column format (the only core table format in this chapter, applied uniformly to all alternative routes throughout the book):

Column Must answer Passing standard (adjectives alone are not allowed) Performance loss How much is lost after substitution Give numbers: furnace temperature down how many °C, precision down how many grades, lifespan down how many tenths, labor up how many times Resource cost What extra it costs Give unit consumption and labor: extra fuel, manpower, and haul distance per ton of product Applicability boundary Where it counts as safe Give upper limits: temperature, load, lifespan limit, contact media, hazard properties (sulfur, CO, brittle fracture) Final bottleneck What the downgrade ultimately is Name the level "below which there is no substitution," and which chapter the whole technical chain falls back to when it is lost
