tourniquet time-marking ≤3 min; immobilization ≤5 min Quarterly race records validate 44.10.2

docs.title: Failure Modes and Diagnosis
docs.text:
Ordered by most common and hardest to detect. Wound infection is this chapter's typical silent failure: at the time of suturing it "looks fine", and only on day 3 does it reveal itself as throbbing pain and fever.

Symptom Candidate cause Verification method Treatment Prevention Throbbing wound pain + fever on days 2–3 post-op Infection (contaminated wound sutured by mistake, insufficient irrigation, retained foreign body) Treatment sequence: first remove the tightest 1–2 stitches to check for tension necrosis → lift the dressing to check redness, swelling, exudate → check for foreign body → if fluctuance, drain per Section 44.9.3 Remove sutures and open, drain, record daily; fever + red streaks = escalate (Section 44.9.2) Grade Ⅱ: immediate suturing forbidden; minimum irrigation volumes Tourniquet limb distal end purple-black and without sensation Forgotten application time (most common fatal error) Check the hand/forehead and tourniquet markings Release immediately and switch to pressure; once the necrotic boundary is clear, assess per Section 44.8 Write the time in two places at application; the time must be reported at every transport handoff Suture line white, black, and dry Suturing too tight and too dense; ischemic necrosis of the skin edges Direct inspection + perfusion observation Remove tight stitches to relieve tension; excise once the necrotic boundary is clear Minimum margins and intervals; do not suture high-tension wounds Red streaks running from the wound toward the trunk Lymphangitis; spreading infection Visually check the direction of travel; take the temperature Beyond-boundary escalation: open drainage fully, immobilize, record Open drainage for contaminated wounds Wound exudate turning yellow-green and foul Deep retained foreign body or liquefying necrotic tissue Explore with tweezers; fingers forbidden Widen, drain, extract; record daily Minimum irrigation volumes; observation after conservative debridement Casualty still down after rescue and the rescuer also dizzy Rescuer unprotected; second poisoning Re-check the environment with the flame test Both withdraw together, then reassess The Section 44.7.1 sequence must never be inverted Shivering and purple lips after flushing a large burn Flushing-induced hypothermia Watch shivering and lip color Stop flushing, dry, keep warm, rewarm Above 10–15%, rotate flushing by region Blister fluid turbid and yellow Infection inside the blister Direct inspection Nick at a low point to drain, remove crusts, leave open Keep the blister roof; apply nothing extraneous Sharp pain increase after splinting, distal swelling Straps too tight or padding slipped Nail-bed refill test Loosen one notch and re-tie; reposition the padding Never skip the 30 min recheck Weeks after injury: lockjaw, spasms triggered by sound and light Tetanus (often misdiagnosed as dental disease) History: contaminated deep wound Isolate in a dark, quiet place; accompany and record; state honestly that there is no solution Contaminated wounds left open unsutured; thorough irrigation

docs.title: Process Card Index
docs.text:
[Card 44-01] Hemostasis (card at end of 44.2) | [Card 44-02] Debridement and suturing (end of 44.3) | [Card 44-03] Splinting (end of 44.5, summary form)

Cards 44-01 and 44-02 carry the full eight fields and copy onto one page; card 44-03 is still in the old summary form and is outside this batch.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria L1/L2/L3
docs.text: Level Criteria Test conditions Evidence kept L1 The first-aider can recite the lineage table's three first-minute actions and the four hemostasis steps; completes 10 stitches on the skin frame with self-assessment; correctly fills out one sample injury record sheet Pre-work verification: items may be missing among the 11 but must be flagged Drill sign-in sheets, self-assessment forms, sample record sheets L2 Passed the 30-stitch suturing practice assessment (interval difference ≤2 mm, no inversion, knots hold 500 g × 1 min); one full-process drill on record: simulated casualty from discovery to transport, with tourniquet time-marking, splint race, and three-person flat lift each meeting the line once (lines of Section 44.10.2) On drill day, boiling, instruments, and kit all present; two judges score against the cards 30-stitch assessment record sheets, drill scoring sheets, physical kit sign-off L3 The first-aid kit monthly inventory audit system is running (accounting office, Chapter 38 ledger); drill records on file for two consecutive quarters; injury record sheets bound and archived and linked to later chapters (validation data for the Chapter 45 disinfection procedures, base accounts for the Chapter 46 medicine ledger, data source for the Chapter 47 case register); ≥2 people at the medic post reach level 2 (redundancy Iron Law, Section 37.5) Spot-check drills still meet the line with different people and in different quarters Two quarters of drill ledgers, monthly audit records, injury record register, skills-matrix review copies

docs.title: Work Hours, Manpower, and Consumption
docs.text: Item Staffing and duration (empirical) Notes Medic-post training 1–2 years (Section 37.5.2); the 30-stitch assessment is the entry line Apprentice cost counted as 1/3–1/2 of a skilled worker's output 30-stitch assessment 2 h per session × 1 candidate + 2 examiners Skin frames and leather supplied from slaughter by-products Quarterly drill Half day × everyone (≥10 people × 4 h) Continuous-process posts must attend; scheduled into the Section 37.4 shift gaps First-aid kit initial outfitting 20–30 person-hours; materials per Section 44.10.1 Boiling and sewing are the bulk Monthly audit Accounting office 0.5 person-hour/kit Thread spot checks, alcohol ignition test Routine dressing changes 0.5–1 person-hour/severe casualty/day Records included Amputation (if performed) 4 people present 1–2 h + post-op care 1 person × 14 days All boxes of the Section 44.8.3 checklist ticked

docs.title: Safety Boundary
docs.text:
Hard gate restated (implementation of the Part declaration): wherever the criteria section of a medical card in this chapter marks a situation "beyond the boundary", all action stops; treatment is reduced to warmth / fluid replacement / analgesia / accompaniment / records (see the Chapter 44 Part declaration).

The following items are part of the process steps (Iron Law 7); failure to execute them is deemed failure to complete the treatment:

  1. Rescuer self-protection comes first: no reaching in while the source is live, no entering while toxic gas lingers, no approaching a machine not yet stopped — the second casualty cannot save the first; the Section 44.7.1 sequence must never be inverted.
  2. A tourniquet without a marked time = deemed not hemostased; the application time must be reported at every transport handoff.
  3. Wash hands with soap solution before treating any open wound (Chapter 23); on any day the instruments have not been boiled, no suturing and no incision.
  4. Nothing by mouth for the drunk or the unconscious (aspiration).
  5. Night transport requires at least two people carrying torches (Chapter 6), with the route scouted first.
  6. For large-area burns, warmth takes priority over flushing: shivering means stop flushing.

docs.title: A/B/C Three Lists
docs.text:
List A (executable directly in this chapter):

Item Criterion Lineage table copied and posted at every workshop All 12 rows present, positioned within sightlines of the work position Drills of the four procedures: hemostasis, debridement, immobilization, burns Quarterly drill results entered in the ledger 30-stitch suturing practice and assessment Criteria per Section 44.3.6; record sheets archived Injury record sheets in use One sheet per case, dual-signed, archived within 24 h First-aid kit establishment and monthly audit List per Section 44.10.1 complete; accounting office audits

List B (requires outputs from earlier chapters):

Item Prerequisite Boiling sterilization Chapter 6 fire + Chapter 11 ceramic cauldron Iron instruments Chapters 18–19 smelting and forging Suture thread, cloth, bandages Chapter 15 textiles Splints and stretchers Chapter 7 woodworking Alcohol and soap Chapter 23 basic chemistry Protective filter lenses Chapter 14 glass Medic-post establishment and scheduling Chapter 37 Record paper and ink Chapter 41

List C (external dependencies and irreducible items):

Item Notes Antibiotics, vaccines, biologicals Excluded by the General Outline; restored by external industry Transfusion, general anesthesia No route; restored by external systems Tetanus antitoxin No solution, stated honestly (Section 44.9.4) Mechanical ventilators, oxygen No route; manual airway opening is the ceiling Legacy medicines and dressings Consumed without replacement; entered in the Chapter 38 accounts

docs.title: Downstream Dependencies
docs.text:
• Chapter 45, infection control, disinfection, and sterilization: this chapter's "boil ≥15 min" is the baseline; Chapter 45 provides the three-tier cleaning/disinfection/sterilization procedures and the batch sterilization system for dressings; this chapter's quarterly infection-rate statistics are the validation data for the Chapter 45 procedures.
  • Chapter 46, medicines and dosage trials: the dosing and effect registration of alcohol analgesia, oral rehydration, and traditional dressings are upgraded into a system here; whether invasive local anesthesia enters the procedures is decided by that chapter's acceptance.
  • Chapter 47, case records and epidemiological investigation: the injury record sheet (Section 44.10.3) is the direct predecessor of that chapter's case register; CO clusters, wound infection rates, and tetanus cases are all its epidemiological clues.
  • Chapter 49, occupational medicine and prevention: every row of this chapter's lineage table must ultimately be moved upstream into "prevention" in Chapter 49 (ventilation, eye protection, wet methods, exposure records) — treating one scald saves one person; changing one ventilation procedure saves a generation.

docs.title: Chapter 45: Infection Control, Disinfection and Sterilization, and Sanitary Engineering
Chapter Objectives
docs.text:
After reading this chapter, a settlement should be able to produce four documents and four facilities; missing any one means this chapter is not finished:

Deliverable Content Use Three-tier cleaning–disinfection–sterilization system Tiered handling procedures for instruments and utensils + observable criteria Making sure "what enters a wound" and "what washes dishes" are never held to the same standard Drinking-water treatment line Water source tiering + isolation distances from pollution sources + the sedimentation–sand-filtration–boiling production line Cutting the largest transmission route, water to mouth Sewage and vector-control facilities Latrines, composting yard, refuse points, rat-proofing and fly-proofing devices Sending excrement back to the field, not back into bellies Epidemic isolation plan + sanitary inspection registers Activation criteria, isolation-hut procedures, five-item inspections, case registration Stopping the twentieth case after the first one

docs.title: Capability Boundaries
docs.text:
What can be done:

  • Establish the three-tier cleaning–disinfection–sterilization system, with a hand-checkable observable criterion at every tier (protein-coagulation indicators).
  • Build the drinking-water treatment line (sedimentation, sand filtration, boiling) and work out the fuel-cost account for boiling.
  • Build the sewage system (three latrine types, seepage prevention, dead-animal disposal) and the ten-day inspection regime for vector control.
  • Establish the isolation procedures and the five-moments handwashing system, and keep the case register — this is Chapter 47's only raw data.

What cannot be done (declared honestly):

  • Pathogen identification. We do not know the enemy's name, only that it lives in feces, lives in water, and dies in heat. This chapter therefore does not distinguish "is this dysentery or cholera"; it sets its defenses purely in symptom language (vomiting and diarrhea, fever, rash).
  • Vaccines, antibiotics, and biological agents — the G01 exclusion table explicitly provides no manufacturing route; the recovery conditions (microscope + aseptic technique + strain collection + assay system) are bounded in Chapters 44–46. Without these four things, this chapter's system is the settlement's entire firepower against epidemic disease; there is no second line of defense.
  • Direct testing of effectiveness. Whether disinfection or sterilization has "killed everything" cannot be assayed; only indirect criteria exist (indicators, timing, case counts). Every criterion here is a lower-bound proof, not a full proof.

External dependencies (counted in the C list):

  1. Microscopes and pathogen-testing systems (cannot be manufactured on this route; see G01).
  2. Scale production and concentration testing of disinfectants (alcohol, soap, and lime have small-scale routes in Chapters 23 and 13; scaling up is in Chapter 46).
  3. Chemical testing of water quality (turbidity can be replaced by a visual criterion; chemical contamination cannot).

docs.title: Pre-Work Verification
docs.text:
Tick-box format. If any item fails, the corresponding facility runs at a downgraded level and the missing item is written down. First fix two measurement baselines: 1 pace = one adult's natural stride, measured on 5 people and take the median (about 0.6–0.8 m), with a marked pole kept on hand; 1 cubit = elbow tip to middle-fingertip, measured on 3 people and take the median (about 0.45–0.5 m). Every pace and cubit figure in this chapter must be converted to meters and marked on a pole before use; everyone measuring by feel is forbidden.

# Verification item Criterion (confirm you have X on hand; the standard is Y) 1 Boiling capacity Fire (Chapter 6) + ceramic pot or metal kettle (Chapters 11, 18); with the pot filled and boiling, the water level can be sustained for a continuous 20 min (lidded, hot water can be added) 2 Containers ≥2 watertight ceramic or wooden vats: left standing overnight, the water level drops <5 mm 3 Filter media Fine sand, coarse sand, and pebbles, one load each obtainable; charcoal (Chapter 6), half a load obtainable 4 Cleaning agents Soap (Chapter 23) registered in stock, or wood ash (stove ash, Chapter 8), one basket collectable every ten days 5 Measures and timekeeping A scale or equal-volume measures (Chapters 3, 22); a timekeeping means (water clock, incense stick — used only after field calibration by timing how long one stick takes to burn down) 6 Settlement plan One map marking dwellings, water sources, latrines, livestock pens, refuse points, and wind direction (Chapter 42 drafting method; drawn on board or paper, either will do) 7 Population roster Every person can be called by name, with a current-status column for "who has diarrhea now, who has fever" 8 Fuel account Actual daily-life fuelwood consumption recorded for the past 7 days (Chapter 38) — the boiling plan must pass through the account; see 45.2.6 9 Wind-direction record Observations of cooking-smoke direction over 3 consecutive days, giving the prevailing wind direction 10 Prior cases A retrospective record of "who was ill, with what symptoms" over the past quarter (even if only oral accounts)

docs.title: 45.1 Cleaning, Disinfection, Sterilization: The Three-Tier Distinction
docs.text: The general principle in one sentence: cleaning removes soil, disinfection kills most living microbes, sterilization kills everything, spores included. The tiers progress in order and cannot be skipped: without cleaning, disinfection and sterilization both lose most of their force — organic matter (blood, feces, food scraps) wraps up the living things inside it, and neither heat nor chemicals can reach in. The procedure is therefore always: wash first, then disinfect, and sterilize only when needed.

docs.title: 45.1.1 Three-Tier Definition Table
docs.text: Tier Definition Means (on this route) Applies to Hand-check criterion Cleaning Physically removing soil and most microorganisms with water and cleaning agents (soap, ash water, sand) Scrubbing under running water, soap washing, ash-water washing, sand rubbing The first step for all utensils, floors, clothing, and bodies No stain visible to the eye; the water film on the vessel wall is even and does not bead (beading = an oil film remains); a finger run through the crevices comes away without black grime Disinfection Killing most vegetative microorganisms; spores not guaranteed Boiling for several minutes, alcohol wiping, fumigation smoke, sun exposure Tableware, chamber vessels, a patient's surroundings, clothing, hands Temperature (or concentration) and contact time both met (see each means' subsection); missing either, treat as not disinfected Sterilization Killing every microorganism, spores included Intermittent steaming (3 days in a row); flame burning (surfaces of small metal items — not sterilization) Deep surgical instruments, childbirth instruments A record of 3 consecutive days of steaming + the indicator coagulated (45.1.3) High-level disinfection Killing vegetative forms and most viruses; unreliable against spores Held at a rolling boil ≥20 min Ordinary instruments and tableware; deep procedures are forbidden when this tier cannot be reached Indicator coagulated + timing met + water level never fell below the instruments

docs.title: 45.1.2 The Means, Taken One by One
docs.text:
Boiling — the mainstay of this route. Instruments submerged one finger-joint below the surface, held ≥20 min from the start of the full rolling boil (an experience value; calibration in Card 45-02). The fire of Chapter 6 plus the ceramic pot of Chapter 11 executes it, with no prerequisites. Honest boundary declaration: 20 min of boiling is high-level disinfection — it kills vegetative forms but is unreliable against tetanus, botulism, and gas-gangrene spores (boiling water at atmospheric pressure does not sterilize); "absolute sterility" cannot be proven by any test available here — so for every instrument that enters a wound, add two disciplines on top of the full boil: taken fresh at the moment of use, never touches the ground, never kept overnight; anything that touches the ground or sits overnight is reworked and reboiled without exception.

Intermittent steaming — the upgraded answer to spores. Steamer-basket style: bamboo or wooden baskets seated on a ceramic pot, steamed over a fierce fire ≥30 min a day, 3 days in a row, the load held at room temperature between steamings. Principle: the first steaming kills the vegetative forms; surviving spores germinate into vegetative forms during the holding period, and the second and third steamings kill them one after another — using time to force "invisible spores" into "visible vegetative forms that can die." Applies to: cloth-wrapped dressings and batch processing of heat-tolerant instruments. Criterion: at each steaming, the indicator block at the center of the cloth bundles in the basket coagulates (45.1.3) + the timing is met.

Flame burning. Small metal items (needles, probes) heated in an open flame until red-hot, then used once cooled. Only for small cross-sections; burning knives and scissors anneals them and ruins the edge (Chapter 19) — forbidden; they still go through boiling.

Alcohol (distilled spirits, Chapter 23) — a disinfection-tier agent only, never a sterilization-tier one. Two limits declared honestly: first, it does not work on spores; second, concentration is critical — experience range 60–75% (by volume). Too high (>80%) and surface proteins coagulate at once, laying a shell over the layers beneath; too low and it cannot kill all the way through. Rough field test (when the alcohol cannot be gauged): light a spoonful — if it will not light = too weak (about <40%), unusable as a disinfectant, reassign it to other uses; if it lights with a blue-white flame and little water is left in the spoon afterward = roughly up to standard. This test judges only the lower bound, never the exact value; when conditions allow, take the middle fraction of the Chapter 23 distillation and register the concentration grade. In use, keep the surface wet ≥1 min; if it evaporates fast, reapply. Never pour it into a deep wound — the tissue damage outweighs the benefit; wound irrigation follows the Chapter 44 procedures.

Fumigation smoke — an experience-based means, limits declared honestly. Smoke suppresses surface flora somewhat, but it cannot be quantified, cannot be verified, and penetrates poorly. Auxiliary only (in the terminal treatment of an epidemic house, together with ventilation and sun exposure); it must not replace boiling and steam; whenever written into the system it always ranks last.

Sun exposure. Direct sun on a clear day ≥4 h (experience value), turned over once; overcast hours do not count toward the total. Applies to: bedding mats, quilts and clothing, sleeping mats — the only routine treatment for bulky items, and a fixed step after isolation is lifted.

docs.title: 45.1.3 Indicators: Fitting an Observable Eye onto "Did the Temperature Get There"
docs.text:
Without a thermometer, neither "how long has the water boiled" nor "did the steam get through" can rest on impressions. This route's self-devised criterion is the protein-coagulation indicator: a fingertip-sized piece of starch paste or egg paste, tied up in cloth, boiled or steamed together with the instruments. Starch gelatinizing and egg paste coagulating proves the temperature at that point crossed the protein-denaturation line of about 70 °C. The evidence chain for sterilization temperature is three items as one: the indicator coagulated + the timing (counted from the full rolling boil) + the water level never fell below the instruments.

The reasoning and the limits of this criterion must be written out (the standing rule for self-devised observable criteria): coagulation proves only that "the denaturation temperature was reached at some point," not that "it reached 100 °C," and still less that "it held for 20 min" — the other two are supplied by watching for "the whole pot rolling in big waves" and by the clock. The indicator witnesses that the temperature arrived; the clock witnesses that the duration was served; release only when both witnesses are present. Either one absent, treat as sterilization not achieved (that tier = high-level disinfection; deep procedures may not claim sterility). The indicator must be tied at the center of the instrument bundle (the hardest place for heat to reach); an indicator tied on the outer layer does not count even if it passes.

◎ Judging whether the egg paste has coagulated "through to the core" is a hand-feel step. Practice method: boil egg-paste blocks in a pot of plain water, taking blocks out when the water is about to boil, at the first boil, 10 min into the full rolling boil, and 20 min into the full rolling boil; observe the cross-section color and the depth of coagulation; practice 20 times to build a comparison memory. Misjudgment compensation: keep the physical indicator block from every sterilization batch, labeled with its ledger number (Chapter 43); a batch whose coagulation is poor is reworked as unsterilized — releasing it because "it looks about right" is not allowed.

[Card 45-02 Boiling Sterilization and Indicators] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: instruments to sterilize (must first pass the cleaning tier: no visible soil, water film not beading); clean water (one finger-joint above the instruments); indicator block of egg slurry or starch paste (finger-sized, tied tightly in cloth, bound at the centre of the instrument bundle); firewood.
  2. Tools required: lidded clay pot (Chapter 11 acceptance item: water level drops <2 mm in 24 h, survives three boiling cycles without cracking); timing means (water clock or incense stick, the burn time of one stick measured and marked first; water clock checked against the sundial at noon); hearth (Chapter 6).
  3. Sequence and control points: Read the urgency criteria first: (1) boiling-water or steam scald → flush with clean cold water ≥15 min immediately (44.4.3; steam scalds estimated one grade deeper, 44.4.5) — the full flush time comes before any other action; (2) indicator fails to coagulate, or timing is interrupted → that whole batch is treated as unsterilized on the spot and may not be released (hard gate; no "looks about right" exemption); (3) deep procedures (joint cavity, body cavity, delivery) that cannot reach this tier → the procedure is not performed (45.1.1). Main sequence: (1) wash the instruments through the cleaning tier; (2) into the pot, water one finger-joint above them, indicator bound at the centre of the bundle; (3) fierce fire to a full rolling boil (the whole surface turning big bubbles, not small bubbles at the rim); (4) count ≥20 min from the full rolling boil; during it add only hot water to hold the level — adding cold water voids the timing and you start over; (5) open the pot and take the indicator first: coagulated right through = temperature reached; (6) instruments taken fresh at the moment of use, never on the ground, never overnight; anything dropped or kept overnight is reworked and reboiled.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: ≥20 min from the full rolling boil, water one finger-joint over the instruments; the indicator marks the protein denaturation line at about 70 °C — it proves only that the denaturation temperature was reached, not that 100 °C was reached, still less that it was held 20 min; the latter two are supplied by "whole pot at a rolling boil" and by the clock. Steam-intermittent method: ≥30 min of steam daily for 3 consecutive days. All empirical; with no way to culture, the "indicator + timing + water level" three proofs are what sterilization means in this chapter.
  5. Observations to record: date, batch number, instrument names, timing start and end, indicator number and coagulation result, operator — into the sterilization ledger (Chapter 43); keep the physical indicator from each batch labelled with its number.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = all three proofs present (indicator coagulated + timing from the full rolling boil + water never fell below the instruments) and recorded. Rework = timing interrupted or water fallen below the instruments (top up and recount from zero); dropped or left overnight after boiling (reboil). Scrap = indicator not coagulated (reboil the whole batch; if it fails twice, check the lid for steam leaks and whether the first boil was mistaken for the full boil). Hard gate: for any instrument entering a wound, 20 min of boiling is high-level disinfection only and is unreliable against tetanus, botulism and gas-gangrene spores — never claim sterility; where the sterilization tier is required, use the steam-intermittent method (3 consecutive days).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order (by frequency): (1) instruments were boiled, the wound is still infected (links to the 44.9.2 escalation criteria) → first check whether they touched the ground or sat overnight after boiling → check whether timing started from the first boil by mistake → check whether they ever passed the cleaning tier (organic matter shielding); (2) knives and scissors rust after boiling → wipe dry at once and wipe on a thin film of oil, scald the film off in boiling water before use; (3) indicator tied on the outside yet judged "pass" → rebind at the centre of the bundle and reboil; an outside indicator does not count.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one complete sterilization batch with records and the physical indicator kept; L2 = 3 consecutive batches with every indicator coagulated and complete timing records, including one executed instance of "left overnight after boiling, therefore reworked"; L3 = quarterly ledger statistics with no missing entries + one apprentice brought through to execute independently to standard + the interface by which this chapter's instrument-related infections feed the Chapter 44 infection-rate statistics.

docs.title: 45.2 Water Source Protection and Drinking-Water Treatment
docs.text: The review subject table's warning for this section is "mistaking clear water for safe water". Clear water and safe water are two different things: sand filtration strains out the turbidity you can see, not the living things you cannot. This section's production line is therefore three stages in series — sedimentation to cut turbidity, sand filtration to raise quality, boiling to kill — the first two stages save fuelwood for the third, and the third is the real line of defense.

docs.title: 45.2.1 Water Source Tier Table
docs.text: Tier Type Normally drinkable straight after filtering? Treatment required Protection required I Springs with an outflow; deep wells (water surface ≥3 m below ground and the well wall sealed) Yes Add boiling when the water turns turbid in the rainy season Fencing, a cover, daily patrol upstream of the intake point II Shallow wells No Filter + boil Well platform 0.3 m above ground, with a curb, a well cover, and a dedicated communal bucket III Rivers and lakes (draw from flowing stretches) No Must filter, must boil Intake upstream of the sewage outfall, ≥50 paces (about 35 m) between them IV Stagnant ponds and water pooled in hollows Drinking forbidden Washing, livestock, and irrigation only Dumping any filth into them is forbidden

docs.title: 45.2.2 Pollution-Source Isolation Distance Table
docs.text:
Experience values, and they must be field-calibrated; the calibration method is the soul of this table — the salt tracer: dissolve 5–10 kg of table salt at one go into a suspect seepage pit (a latrine, livestock-pen drainage), then for 7 days taste the intake water and the downstream well water day by day (the taster must boil the water and let it cool through, use a dedicated spoon, one mouthful a day). The water turns distinctly salty = the groundwater is connected; abandon that pollution source or that well at once. The saltiness itself is harmless, but a connection proves the fecal water has a road to travel — this is precisely the developing fluid that makes "the invisible fluid leak" show itself.

Pollution source Distance from intake point Additional conditions Latrines, seepage pits ≥30 paces (about 20 m; measured with the marked pole, no eyeballing), and always on the downstream side of the groundwater flow Livestock pens, composting yards ≥30 paces Drainage ditches carry the runoff away; no spreading flow Refuse dumps, ash heaps, animal-slaughtering waste points ≥30 paces Enclosed, so rain cannot wash them into the runoff Laundry, vegetable-washing, and bathing wastewater Carried away in open ditches Must not discharge upstream of the intake stretch

Common knowledge on the direction of groundwater flow (how to judge it without instruments): groundwater generally moves toward low ground, following the surface slope and the lie of the valleys; wet ground and the places that seep first after rain are downstream. When two sites are in doubt, defend on the assumption that they "may be connected," and always take the upper limit of distance.

docs.title: 45.2.3 The Treatment Line: Sedimentation → Sand Filtration → Boiling
docs.text:
• Sedimentation: turbid water into a vat, left to stand ≥4 h (overnight is better). Criterion: half a spoonful of the upper clear layer held to the light shows no suspension, and stirring raises nothing from the bottom. In the rainy season, high-turbidity water first passes an assisting-settling vat of wood ash or alum (if available, Chapter 23) — with no agent, extend the settling to a full night.
  • Sand filtration: cuts turbidity and traps most suspended matter, saving fuelwood for the boil. Sand filtration does not sterilize — after filtering, whether to boil is still decided by the water source tier; this sentence must be copied onto the wooden placard beside the filter vat.
  • Boiling: the main force against microbes. A full rolling boil is enough (no need to boil it long); cooking water is taken care of along the way with the cooking.

docs.title: 45.2.4 Principle and Maintenance of the Sand Filter Vat (Slow Filtration)
docs.text:
Layer order top to bottom: fine sand 40–50 cm → coarse sand 8–10 cm → pebbles (jujube-sized) 8–10 cm → outlet (wrapped in cloth). The charcoal sits in a separate small vat placed upstream (charcoal layer 15–20 cm; regenerated monthly: baked over an open flame until smokeless), its job being to strip odor and part of the impurities — charcoal does not sterilize, declared honestly. The place where slow filtration truly works is the brown sticky "filter skin" that forms on the top 2–3 cm of the fine sand after a few weeks of running: it is alive, the water level must be kept ≥5 cm over the sand surface, and the filter bed is never left exposed to air and never allowed to dry out. Cleaning only scrapes the top 1–2 cm; turning over the whole vat is forbidden — carrying the filter skin down to the bottom is putting everything it intercepted back into the water.

Empirical criterion for the filtration rate: after you stop adding water, the water level at the vat surface drops ≤1 finger-width (about 2 cm) per quarter-hour (15 min). Dropping too fast = short-circuiting or a broken layer; slowed to half = the top layer is due for scraping. Output capacity: a vat of 0.4 m inner diameter filters 150–300 L a day, drinking water for 50–100 people; a 200-person settlement needs 3–4 vats in parallel, or one big wooden-cabinet filter basin.

◎ Judging the scraping depth of the filter layer is a hand-feel step. Practice method: on a scrapped vat, practice scraping until you have the feel of "sand color going from black-brown to light yellow," checked against depth measured with a marked wooden rule 10 times. Misjudgment compensation: record the scraped depth of every scraping in the ledger; stop at once past 3 cm and hunt for the source of the turbidity.

[Card 45-01 Sand Filter Vat Construction and Maintenance] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: 1 watertight clay or wooden vat (50–100 L capacity; water level drops <5 mm overnight); fine sand (a wet handful holds its shape and crumbles when the fist opens; mud check: sand in a bottle, water added, shaken, still cloudy after a quarter-hour means wash the sand until clear); one load of coarse sand; one load of pebbles (date-sized, washed); half a load of charcoal (pea-sized pieces, dust sieved out); two layers of old cloth. Quantity scales with vat diameter: a 0.4 m vat needs about 60 kg of fine sand.
  2. Tools required: straight rule and measuring rod (Chapter 3, checked against a standard rule before use); wooden tamper (for tamping layers); wooden board (regulations and filtration-rate criteria copied on it, hung beside the vat); ledger book (Chapter 43).
  3. Sequence and control points: Read the urgency criteria first: (1) output fast and turbid (suspected short-circuiting or a broken layer) → take that vat out of service at once and do not drink its output; throw in a handful of fine charcoal powder to confirm (black water out within minutes = short-circuiting proven); (2) diarrhoeal or vomiting cases in the settlement, or any doubt about the source → boil everything per 45.2.6, without exception; filtered water is not drunk straight. Main sequence: (1) load from the bottom up — cloth-wrapped outlet → pebbles → coarse sand → fine sand; spread each layer flat and tamp it against the vat wall (a loose wall edge means short-circuiting); settle with water and top up the sand to the mark; (2) from then on keep the fine-sand surface under ≥5 cm of water — it must never be left dry or exposed; (3) discard the first 50 L (washing out sand dust); (4) feeding rhythm: fill in one go, stop when only a finger of water is left above the sand, never draw to the bottom. Control point: cleaning scrapes only the top 1–2 cm; never turn the whole bed over — turning the filter skin to the bottom puts everything it had trapped back into the water.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: fine sand 40–50 cm, coarse sand 8–10 cm, pebbles 8–10 cm, pre-filter charcoal bed 15–20 cm; filtration rate — after filling stops, the level drops ≤1 finger (about 2 cm) per quarter-hour (scale scratched on the vat wall, read once at each daily fill); output 150–300 L per vat per day (0.4 m inner diameter); scraping cycle 2–3 ten-day periods, or when output halves; charcoal vat regenerated monthly by baking over open flame until no smoke. All empirical; revised against the output ledger and turbidity spot checks.
  5. Observations to record: date of loading and thickness of each layer, volume discarded on first filtration, date and depth of every scraping, turbidity spot checks (full bowl against the light showing no suspended matter, carving on the bowl bottom readable through the water), filtration-rate readings — all into the ledger (Chapter 43).
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = output clear in a full bowl against the light, bottom carving readable, filtration rate within limits. Rework = turbid output (filter skin not yet formed in the first ten-day period — extend the discard period; if short-circuiting, re-tamp along the wall and reload); very slow output (scrape the top 1–2 cm; if the scrape exceeds 3 cm, stop and trace the source of the turbidity). Scrap = the vat cracks and leaks, or the sand bed turns black and foul throughout (wash and reload the whole bed, run first-filtration as for a new vat). Hard gate: filter output never replaces boiling under any circumstances; the all-boil policy of 45.2.6 is unaffected by the state of the filter.
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order (by frequency): (1) output fast and turbid → first check the gap between vat wall and sand (short-circuiting) → check whether the layer order is inverted → check whether the fine sand was loaded with mud still in it; (2) output very slow → surface clogging (normal; scrape 1–2 cm) → check whether it was fed too hard (switch to small amounts, often); (3) water smells of mud → first filtration insufficient, discard another 50 L; (4) charcoal smell exhausted → regenerate the pre-filter charcoal vat.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one vat built and producing water; L2 = 7 consecutive days of output meeting the turbidity standard + a record of filtration rate recovering after one scraping; L3 = filter skin established (≥1 month of stable running) + scraping and regeneration regime on the books + one apprentice brought through to load a vat independently to standard.

docs.title: 45.2.5 Engineering Protection of the Well
docs.text: The well is the settlement's most expensive water asset. The four-piece protection set: well platform (0.3 m above ground with a curb, keeping surface runoff out of the well), well cover (kept shut whenever water is not being drawn), communal bucket (a dedicated drawing bucket whose rope never touches the ground — private buckets and private ropes are strictly barred from the well; one dirty bucket bottom contaminates the whole well), and drainage ditch (leading the flow away beyond the curb, discharging downstream). The household on duty self-checks the platform each time it draws water; the hygienist inspects every ten days (45.9).

docs.title: 45.2.6 The Fuel-Cost Account of Boiling (connects to Chapter 38)
docs.text:
"How much firewood is burned for every mouthful of boiled water" must be computed before the policy is set. The arithmetic and the order-of-magnitude check:

  • Heating 1 L of water from room temperature (about 20 °C) to a full rolling boil takes about 335 kJ; fuelwood's heating value is about 14–16 MJ/kg, the open-fire stove's efficiency about 8–15%, so the useful heat is 1.2–2.2 MJ/kg.
  • Experience value: 1 kg of fuelwood boils 3–6 L of water (take the low end for a three-stone open fire, the high end for a stove with a firebox and stove ring). Calibration: burn it for real — a fixed charge of wood boils a fixed charge of water; weigh the wood and keep the account, and one ten-day period gives you your own stove's number.
  • Each person drinks 2–3 L a day; boiling everything converts to 0.4–1.0 kg of firewood per person-day (experience value). Set against Chapter 37's daily-life fuelwood of 2–4 kg per person-day: full boiling in an epidemic raises the fuel burden 15–30%.
  • Reasonable-range check: a 200-person settlement drinks about 600 L a day, converting to 100–200 kg of wood a day — roughly the wood of half a firing of an intermittent pottery kiln (Chapter 12). This order of magnitude says: full boiling is an epidemic-emergency policy, not a steady-state policy, and it must pass through the Chapter 38 energy ledger in advance.

Policy trade-off table (written into settlement law, copied in the cookhouse):

Situation Drinking-water policy Basis Normal times, Tier I source (spring/deep well) Drink after filtering; cooking water boiled along with the cooking The fuel account cannot carry full boiling long-term Normal times, Tier II–III sources Must boil after filtering The risk of shallow wells and river water is always there Rainy season, turbid water, vomiting-and-diarrhea cases appearing, epidemic period Boil everything, no exceptions Defend against the worst case; the fuel account draws on reserves Firewood-saving measures Kettles set on the firebox embers after the fire; clustered cooking and burning, one fire with several kettles Saves about half, but the account must still be kept

docs.title: 45.3 Sewage and Excreta Management
docs.text: Feces is a resource and a bomb: composted back onto the fields it is one link in Chapter 10's fertility chain, but the same pile harbors the settlement's entire population of intestinal enemies. This section's task is to give feces a one-way, controllable road: from the squat point to the composting yard, no step along the way may meet water, food, or hands.

docs.title: 45.3.1 The Three Latrine Types
docs.text:
Type Construction Applies to Key rules Pit latrine + wooden cover Pit dug 1–1.5 m deep; the squat point spans wooden beams, tightly closed with a wooden cover General purpose, starter choice One ladle of ash or dry earth over it after every use; when the fill comes within 0.3 m of the pit mouth, seal and bury it and dig a new pit Composting latrine (twin-pit alternation) Two pits side by side, each used 6 months; one in use while the other is sealed and maturing Settlements short on fertility and rich in labor May be cleared out only after ≥6 months sealed and the pile has heated (see the 45.3.3 maturation criteria); mature feces goes only onto field crops already standing, never onto vegetable plots eaten raw (worst-case defense) Chamber-bucket system Buckets indoors (for the old, weak, sick, and disabled; the rainy season; epidemics), collected daily by a designated person Supplementary type Buckets are lidded; after collection and emptying, rinsed with ash water and dried in the sun

Three rules of squat-point design: a narrow squat opening (less exposed surface), a tight cover (the wooden lid weighted with a straw bundle or a stone, so flies cannot enter), and a raised earth platform around it with a drainage ditch dug (rainy-season surface runoff must not pour into the pit).

docs.title: 45.3.2 Seepage Prevention and Siting
docs.text:
• Pit bottom ≥1 cubit (about 0.5 m, measured with the marked pole) above the water table. Criterion: seepage on the pit walls in the rainy season, or water visible at the pit bottom = the distance is insufficient; stop use at once, seal and bury, and move the site.
  • Ram the pit walls with clay (the rammed-earth method of Chapter 13) to reduce lateral seepage.
  • Three siting checks: ≥30 paces from the intake point (the 45.2.2 table), on the downstream side of the groundwater flow, on ground above the rainy-season water line.
  • Run one salt tracer (45.2.2) before a new pit enters service — half a day of digging buys the settlement ten years of peace of mind.

docs.title: 45.3.3 Fly and Maggot Control and the Compost Maturation Criteria
docs.text:
Three moves against flies and maggots: cover (a tight lid flies cannot enter), ash (wood ash is both drying and alkaline — eggs cannot hatch, maggots cannot grow), and diligence (a weekly clean-out carried to the composting yard; no feces left overnight at the squat point). Criteria: on inspection the squat point shows no maggot clumps, no fly swarms, and no residue at the squat opening.

Compost maturation criteria (they decide when feces turns from bomb back into resource): ① sealed ≥6 months; ② the core of the pile heated early in the sealing period — push a wooden stick into the pile core and pull it out half a day later; a stick tip hot to the touch (too hot to keep hold of, about ≥50 °C) is evidence of heating; ③ when the pit is opened, no foul smell and a dark-brown crumbly texture. Missing any one of the three, keep it sealed.

◎ Judging the pile-core temperature as "too hot to keep hold of" is a hand-feel step. Practice method: mix stove-side warm water and boiling water into basins of different temperatures and practice the stick check against them 20 times. Misjudgment compensation: leave a stick in the pile for half a day, then press an egg-paste block against the tip; the egg paste visibly thickening is proof enough of the temperature — the 45.1.3 indicator idea reused in this spot.

docs.title: 45.3.4 Rainy-Season Plan and Dead-Animal Disposal
docs.text:
Three things for the rainy season: before the rains, check each pit's fill level and seal-and-bury early anything over half full; overhaul the squat-point platforms and the drainage ditches; during flooding, latrines in the low ground are closed and everything switches to the chamber-bucket system.

Dead-animal disposal (any death of unknown cause is handled as the worst case): no eating, no skinning or selling, no throwing into water bodies. Deep burial: a pit ≥2 cubits deep (about 1 m, marked pole); lime scattered over the carcass (Chapter 13), earth backfilled and tamped; ≥50 paces (about 35 m) from the intake point and ≥30 paces from dwellings. The burial site is registered in the ledger, and is neither disturbed nor cultivated for half a year. Handlers soap-wash and change clothes afterward (45.8).

docs.title: 45.4 Vector Control (Flies, Mosquitoes, Rats, Lice)
docs.text: The order may never be inverted: environmental management first, physical means second, chemical means last. Using agents (smoke, poisoned bait) without removing the breeding grounds is bailing water out of a pool that keeps being refilled.

docs.title: 45.4.1 Environmental Management: Cut Their Food and Their Nests
docs.text:
• Standing-water removal (against mosquitoes): mosquito larvae develop only in still water; any still water stored more than 7 days is a hatchery. Every ten days, empty everything on the standing-water container list: broken jars, broken urns, scrap barrels, bamboo troughs, urn-lid hollows, tree holes, millstone hollows, roof water channels. What can be flipped is flipped over, what can be filled is filled with earth, and what must stay in use is covered or given fish (fish eat mosquito larvae, no chemical harm).
  • Refuse out of the house (against flies and rats): kitchen waste leaves the house every day — composted or deeply buried, never left lying overnight; refuse points are enclosed and cleared every three days.
  • Feces kept sealed (against flies): all of 45.3 is the main force of fly control.
  • Ditches kept clear: dead-water stretches are mosquito nurseries; keep the drainage ditches flowing.

docs.title: 45.4.2 Physical Means
docs.text: Target Means Key points Mosquitoes Cloth tents (fine close-woven mosquito nets), gauze screens on doors and windows A canopy over the sleeping place ranks above smoke — the canopy is a barrier; smoke only drives mosquitoes off, it does not kill Flies Covers (food shields, latrine lids), hanging sticky strips Cooked-food stalls must be shielded Rats Rat-guard bowls under chest legs (a shallow water-filled ceramic bowl under each of the granary chest's four legs — rats cannot climb past a bowl of water; or smooth ceramic bowls set upturned as foot pads), board snap-traps, bamboo cages Granary boards tightly jointed, door bottoms sheathed in sheet iron; the bowl water kept shallow and wide, for the sake of small children Lice Clothing and bedding scalded and boiled (connects to 45.1), sun exposure, combs and fine-tooth combs Always checked after crowded cohabitation; in a louse epidemic, shaving heads and beards is an engineering measure, not a humiliation

docs.title: 45.4.3 Limited Chemical Means (caution tier)
docs.text:
• Smoke against mosquitoes (mugwort, weed smoke): repulsion first of all; fumigate the room before sleep, people leave first, and ventilate before re-entering. Declared honestly: it repels and does not kill, its effect has no criterion to measure, and it may not stand as the only means.
  • Rat bait poisoning: set out at night, gathered at dawn; numbered and registered; one designated person responsible; placement avoids children's activity areas and livestock pens; dead rats are picked up with fire tongs and deeply buried (the 45.3.4 standard), bare hands forbidden. Bait stock enters the dangerous-materials account (the Chapter 23 chemical-work procedures).

docs.title: 45.4.4 Ten-Day Inspection Table
docs.text:
One fixed day every ten days, the hygienist leading a two-person team, carrying the table and scoring item by item (0 = fail, 1 = corrected on the spot, 2 = pass), entered in the ledger and posted at the council hall:

Target Checkpoints Pass criteria (a score of 0 triggers a rectification order) Standing-water containers Broken jars, urns, barrels, troughs; tree holes Not one item of still water standing more than 7 days; everything flippable flipped, everything coverable covered Ditches Silt plugs, dead stretches Water running free, no dead stretches Latrines Cover, ash, maggots and flies, pit fill level Cover tight, squat opening clean, no maggot clumps, depth remaining ≥0.3 m Refuse points Out of the houses, enclosed No spillage, no overnight kitchen waste Granary Rat signs (droppings, gnaw marks, new holes) No new rat signs; rat-guard bowls full of water

docs.title: 45.5 Food Hygiene
docs.text: The cookhouse is the mouth shared by the whole settlement, and the mouth that can fell the most people in one stroke. Five rules:

docs.title: 45.5.1 Raw–Cooked Separation
docs.text: Two boards, two knives, marked by carved notches: one board for raw meat, one for cooked food (notches carved into the side of the board; never swapped). Criterion: after the cooked-food board has cut raw meat, raw fish, or raw offal, it must be washed and scalded with boiling water before it cuts cooked food again; bowls and basins follow the same rule — a vessel that has held raw meat does not hold cooked food.

docs.title: 45.5.2 Tableware Boiling Cycle
docs.text: Communal cookhouse tableware is boiled once a day (≥5 min at a full rolling boil); during epidemics, and in any household with a case of diarrhea, boiled at every meal. Personal bowls and chopsticks are washed and used by their owner, marked with a carved name; a patient's tableware is dedicated, boiled separately after use, and never mixed into the communal boiling vat.

docs.title: 45.5.3 Kitchen-Worker Rules (the first personnel rule)
docs.text: Those with diarrhea do not enter the kitchen — the first personnel rule of this whole chapter. The other three: anyone with a festering hand wound does not touch cooked food; kitchen workers must soap-wash after the privy (the five moments of 45.8 bind kitchen workers equally); kitchen workers' aprons and cloths are changed, washed, and sun-dried every day. Self-reporting symptoms before a kitchen shift is a duty; a worker who conceals diarrhea and keeps on cooking is dealt with under Chapter 37's Section 37.6.2 accident response authority — any diner may halt their food-serving eligibility on the spot.

docs.title: 45.5.4 Leftover Reheating System
docs.text: Leftovers are reheated until steam billows from the center and a rolling boil holds for 2–3 min before they are handed out (without a thermometer, "big rolling bubbles" is the standard; rather too hot than not hot enough). Congee, meat, and beans left from a previous meal or overnight are all reheated before distribution; anything off in smell or taste is scrapped and deeply buried, not fed to the livestock (worst-case defense: spoiled food is a risk to livestock too, and losing livestock is the heavier loss).

docs.title: 45.5.5 Communal-Meal Poisoning Walkthrough: How One Banquet Fells Half a Settlement in 12 Hours
docs.text:
Walkthrough table (for teaching; every row is a checkpoint that could have intercepted it):

Time Event Checkpoint that could have intercepted it Afternoon of the day before Beasts slaughtered and ingredients made ready; the meat left overnight at room temperature in a big basin (night temperatures cannot check the breeding of living things in the filth) Ingredient-prep rule: only dry goods and vegetables the day before; the meat slaughtered that same day Morning of the day Meat cut on the raw board, then unwashed and unscalded, the same board and knife cut the cold platters Two boards two knives, raw–cooked separation (45.5.1) Before noon Big-pot quick frying; meat chunks at the pot's center ladled out before they boiled through Communal meat rule: big-pot meat at a rolling boil ≥30 min Noon The feast opened in the open air, flies gathering on the food; leftovers back into basins and kept till evening Food shields (45.4); leftovers buried at once (45.5.4) That night into the next morning Within 12 h, dozens vomiting and purging; many households down at once — all three checkpoints failed, nothing left to intercept The next day Half the settlement's labor down together: fields missing the farming season, furnaces without their watch (the Chapter 37 shift schedule broken), the caregiving hands sick themselves The institutional cost is cashed in here

The conclusion is written permanently on the cookhouse wall: The communal meal is the hygiene system's stress test. Of the three checkpoints — prep, raw–cooked, reheating — any one holding cuts this outbreak off; when all three fail, felling half the settlement is not an accident, it is the standard ending.

docs.title: 45.6.1 Dwelling Ventilation: In Low, Out High
docs.text: The same geometry as the Chapter 12 furnace and kiln draft: air comes in low and goes out high. Dwelling practice: an intake under the door or at a low window, an outlet vent high on the gable. Criterion: hang a paper strip at the outlet mouth; wind makes it flutter; the flutter stops = the ventilation is dead — check whether the intake is blocked. In winter it must not be sealed up entirely — for the fixed vent, better small than absent; the paper-strip criterion applies all the same.

docs.title: 45.6.2 Winter Heating and Carbon Monoxide Prevention (connects to Chapter 6 Section 6.8 and Chapter 28)
docs.text: Three iron rules: charcoal basins and fire basins do not go into bedrooms; after the fire is banked and the coals pressed down, the flue and the vents must be checked; several people waking at once with headache, nausea, and dizziness = a CO alarm — everyone out of the house and the doors open immediately. Symptoms easing after ventilation confirms it; no one re-enters until the fire is dead out. Flame color is a daily watch item: a stove flame gone yellow and sullen = not enough air; ventilate first, then add fuel. This rule joins onto the Chapter 44 CO first-aid procedure (44.7).

docs.title: 45.6.3 Damp and Mold
docs.text:
• Beds ≥0.3 m off the ground (raised on frames or stacked blocks) so the ground's damp cannot climb into the bedding.
  • Straw mattresses sun-dried monthly and turned every ten days; mold criteria: black spots, a moldy smell, damp straw stems that snap at one bend — seeing any one of the three means the whole mattress is replaced, and moldy straw is burned without leaving the compound.
  • Rainy-season clothes that cannot be sun-dried are not piled up to dry inside the dwelling (wet clothes hung in the house = damp circulating indoors); drying in the stove room's leftover heat comes first.
  • Ground damp-proofing and raised foundations follow the Chapter 13 building procedures.

docs.title: 45.6.4 Daylight and Dwelling Density [Background]
docs.text: Historical experience: dwellings crowded, dark, and unventilated for the long term go with the spread of consumption (wasting lung disease) — this route cannot verify the mechanism; it is adopted as background knowledge, and its engineering meaning is carried out as usual: window area no less than 1/10 of the floor area (experience value, measured with a rule); windows turned south to win the sunlight; not many people sleeping in one room, bunks at least one arm-length apart; the sick and the old housed in sun-facing rooms first. Tagged [Background] = it does not enter the acceptance criteria; it does enter design and allocation.

docs.title: 45.7.1 When It Starts
docs.text:
Nearly all of isolation's cost is concentrated at one point: "starting late." Activation criteria table (fixed in writing; no debating it on the spot):

Signal Criterion Action Single severe case High fever that will not break + rash, or violent vomiting and purging without stop Isolate that day; do not wait for a second case Clustering ≥2 cases with the same symptoms within 5 days and linked (same stove, same well, same house, same table) Isolate that day; report to the hygienist Waterborne outbreak Vomiting-and-purging cases appearing at several points within one day and night Isolate + seal the suspect water source and switch to the backup (the 45.2.1 tiers) Epidemic confirmed Any of the above + cases rising day by day Start the full Card 45-03

Activation authority is devolved: any hygienist may start on the table, ratified afterward; the council may not veto it with "let us watch two more days" — the same logic as Chapter 37's Section 37.6.2 accident response authority: stopping draws no blame, concealment does. Empirical walkthrough (an order-of-magnitude statement, not a precise forecast): most epidemic diseases run a generation in 3–5 days; every day the start is delayed past the first case roughly doubles the next generation's cases — the price of "watching two days" is four times the patients.

docs.title: 45.7.2 Setting Up the Isolation Hut
docs.text: Element Standard Criterion Location On the downstream side of the settlement's prevailing wind (by the daily drift of the cooking smoke), ≥20 paces from dwellings Marked on the plan (Chapter 42) Layout One person, one room; with several cases, rooms and utensils are still divided Name on the door plaque Personnel 1 dedicated meal-deliverer, fixed and not swapped; someone freshly recovered from the same disease is preferred Roster on file Utensils Bowls, chopsticks, and cloths dedicated, marked with red cord; boiled separately after use, never into the communal boiling vat Marks intact Entry and exit The deliverer sets the food down and leaves, does not enter; soap-washing + a change of clothes afterward (45.8) Dual signatures at delivery and at release Fecal waste The patient's feces covered with ash and hauled separately to a dedicated composting spot, never into the public seepage pits or the public latrines Dedicated bucket, marked

docs.title: 45.7.3 Contacts and Release Criteria
docs.text: Contacts (same house, same stove, caregivers) are registered on a roster and watched for 7 days (experience value; corrected against this settlement's measured interval from first onset to next onset, entered in the ledger). Release from isolation: after the fever is gone and every symptom has cleared, isolation continues another 2–3 days (experience value) — with no test available, better one day of isolation more. Settlement-wide release from epidemic standing: 7 days after the last case with no new case. On the day a release is granted, the patient's clothes and bedding are boiled in water, the bedding mats are sun-exposed, and the house is ventilated for 1 day before it is used again (smoke only as an auxiliary, 45.1.2).

docs.title: 45.7.4 Handling Bodies and the Boundary of Mourning
docs.text:
The bodies of the epidemic dead are handled by dedicated personnel: the mouth, nose, and limbs wrapped, spillage avoided while moving, soap-washing and a change of clothes afterward; buried ≥1.2 m deep with lime scattered, ≥50 paces from the intake point. During an epidemic, mourning is reduced: shared vigil meals are suspended, the collective grand encoffining is suspended; a name plaque records the dead and the rites are performed after the epidemic — write this sentence out plainly: this is the system, not heartlessness: one funeral can set off twenty, and twenty funerals can push a settlement from a lean harvest to the loss of a generation. The date of the rites to be performed later is announced publicly the moment the epidemic begins — leaving grief an outlet, putting a gate on gathering.

[Card 45-03 Epidemic Isolation Activation Card] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: the activation criteria table (45.7.1, copied on the back of the card); one isolation hut (an empty house, or a shed put up in half a day: Chapter 7 carpentry + Chapter 13 rammed earth); the patient's dedicated bowls, chopsticks, and cloths (marked with red cord); soap and ash water; the case register; the settlement plan.
  2. Tools required: the plan and the wind-direction records (the Chapter 42 mapping method + pre-work verification item 9); a timekeeping means (water clock or sundial, Chapter 3).
  3. Operating sequence and control points: ① check against the activation table — if any row matches, start that day; no council, no waiting; ② pick the hut: downstream of the prevailing wind, ≥20 paces from dwellings, entrance and exit of its own; ③ one person one room, utensils dedicated and marked; ④ appoint 1 dedicated meal-deliverer (the recovered preferred), rule: set down and leave, soap-wash and change clothes afterward; ⑤ register the contact roster, watch 7 days; ⑥ open a page in the case register (name, date of onset, main symptoms, dwelling, intake point, cook-stove, contact history — the Chapter 47 data source); ⑦ the patient's feces hauled separately, never into the public latrines or pits; ⑧ the course of illness recorded daily; release by the 45.7.3 criteria.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: isolation hut ≥20 paces (marked pole); observation 7 days and 2–3 days more before release (experience value, corrected by this settlement's measured generation interval and transcribed into the ledger); meal delivery twice a day, 1 dedicated person.
  5. In-process observation items: the activation date and the first-case date (the difference between the two gets its own column); the daily palm-to-forehead and palm-to-chest temperature-feel comparison (Chapter 44), the counts of vomiting and purging; dual signatures of the deliverer and on the release date.
  6. Accept / rework / scrap criteria: Accept = started on the signal day or the next + registration complete + the deliverer never swapped. Rework = a late start (start retroactively; the ledger states the days of delay and the reason, as teaching material for the next drill). Scrap = a patient left isolation with no follow-up (follow up and register at once, post a settlement-wide notice to watch, and the responsible person files a written self-criticism).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: the family resists → act under the Section 37.6.2 pre-authorization; the council endorses but does not withdraw the start; several cases and one hut is not enough → requisition a storehouse and partition it, utensils marked per person; the deliverer falls ill → replace at once and isolate the original deliverer, and retroactively record their contact list.
  8. L1/L2/L3 evidence: L1 = a record of one full-process drill; L2 = one real or exercise start, started ≤24 h, registration complete; L3 = full-course epidemic records + the case register with no ten-day period missing + the minutes of the post-epidemic review meeting (delay analysis included).

docs.title: 45.8.1 The Five-Moments Table (mandatory settlement-wide, doubled in an epidemic)
docs.text: # Moment The specific acts it covers 1 After the privy Always wash on leaving the latrine; if there is no soap, ash water 2 Before attending a birth The birth attendant washes hands and forearms to the elbow, dried where possible with a boiled cloth 3 Before treating a wound Connects to Chapter 44: clean hands are the step before the first step of debridement 4 After touching a patient After delivering meals, giving care, handling feces, handling bodies 5 Before eating Including before preparing food; kitchen workers are held to the stricter 45.5.3

docs.title: 45.8.2 Washing Method and Cleaning Agents
docs.text:
Method: running water is best; without it, the three-ladle method — the first ladle rinses off the loose soil; soap and work up a lather, rubbing to a silent count of 100 slow strokes (about half a quarter-hour), working the webs of the fingers, the palms, and the backs of the wrists; the second and third ladles rinse it off. A family washing from one shared basin is forbidden — washing to the end out of one basin hands the first person's filth to the whole family. Cleaning agents come in two tiers: soap (Chapter 23) first; ash water as the substitute — 1 part wood ash to 5 parts water, stirred and settled (Chapter 8), and the clear liquid on top is what you use.

◎ Judging ash-water strength by feel (the clear liquid feels slippery like thin soapy water) is a hand-feel step. Practice method: mix one basin at 1:5 and one at 1:10 and use them against each other 10 times. Misjudgment compensation: judge by the emulsification test — ash water stirred with a little grease that emulsifies and whitens passes; if the oil beads still separate after stirring, it is too weak — add ash and mix again.

docs.title: 45.8.3 Wound and Secretion Etiquette
docs.text: Wounds are covered with clean cloth and not left bare; wash hands after every dressing change (dressing procedures connect to Chapter 44); coughs and sneezes are covered with the inside of the arm, not the hand — the hand has food to hold and things to pass; the patient does not share the washing basin, the towel, or the bowls; sputum and mucus go into the ash crock — never spat on the ground, never upstream into the ditches.

docs.title: 45.9 The Hygienist Post and the Inspection System
45.9.1 Hygienist Duty List
docs.text:
The hygienist is a post, not volunteer work; graded and assessed under the Chapter 37 Section 37.5.2 skill matrix (the hygiene branch of the medic post); a 300-person settlement is allotted 1–2 (of whom ≥1 reaches grade 2):

  1. Run, score, and post the ten-day vector inspection (45.4.4) and the weekly five-item inspection (45.9.2).
  2. First report of epidemics: start isolation on the 45.7.1 table, exercising the pre-authorization.
  3. Keep the case register — the sole data source of the Chapter 47 epidemiological investigation; a ten-day period missing is dereliction of duty.
  4. The sterilization ledger and the indicators (Card 45-02), the filter-vat ledger (Card 45-01).
  5. Hygiene teaching: the five moments, the communal-meal three checkpoints, the three CO iron rules — re-taught to everyone once a quarter.

docs.title: 45.9.2 Weekly Sanitary Inspection Table (five items, scored)
docs.text:
One fixed day each week; a 0/1/2 three-point scale, 10 points in all; below 6 issues a rectification order (deadline and re-inspector named):

Item What is checked Pass criteria Water source Well platform, well cover, communal bucket, upstream of the intake Curb unbroken, cover tight, communal bucket dedicated, no filth within 50 paces upstream Latrines Cover, ash, maggots, fill level, location The 45.4.4 standards Kitchen Two boards two knives, tableware boiling, kitchen-worker symptom self-report, food shields All four checks pass; a worker with diarrhea on duty that day is an immediate 0 Refuse Out of the houses, enclosed, hauled No spillage, no overnight kitchen waste Standing water Water-holding containers, dead stretches of ditch No still water standing more than 7 days

docs.title: 45.9.3 Monthly Ranking and the Case Register
docs.text: The ranking is folded into the Chapter 37 organizational interface: households (or districts) are ranked by inspection score each month and posted; two months running at the bottom, the council calls them in for rectification — honor and rectification orders are used, not ration penalties (a ration penalty would turn concealment into the rational choice). The case register's fields are fixed: number, name, age, date of onset, main symptoms, dwelling, intake point, cook-stove, contact history, outcome. The register is transcribed once a month and archived (Chapter 43); it is the whole of the raw data for Chapter 47's diagnostics and epidemiological investigation — if this chapter does not register, Chapter 47 has nothing to consult.

docs.title: Master Parameter Table
docs.text: Parameter Experience value Field calibration method Section Pace/cubit conversion 1 pace about 0.6–0.8 m; 1 cubit about 0.45–0.5 m Measure 3–5 adults and take the median; mark the pole Pre-work verification Instrument boiling ≥20 min from the full rolling boil, water one finger-joint above The three proofs — indicator + timing + water level (Card 45-02) 45.1 Intermittent steam sterilization ≥30 min steaming a day × 3 days running The basket-center indicator coagulates at every steaming 45.1 Alcohol disinfection concentration 60–75% (by volume) The flame test judges the lower bound: will not light = <40%, do not use 45.1 Sun exposure Clear-day direct sun ≥4 h × both sides Keep the record; overcast days do not count 45.1 Pollution source to intake point ≥30 paces (about 20 m), downstream side of the groundwater Marked-pole measure + salt tracer to verify the connection 45.2 Intake-to-outfall spacing ≥50 paces (about 35 m) Marked-pole measure 45.2 Fine sand layer thickness 40–50 cm Measured with a rule while loading, entered in the ledger 45.2 Slow-filtration rate After water stops going in, the level drops ≤1 finger-width (about 2 cm) per quarter-hour Scale marked on the vat wall, read once a day 45.2 Filter vat daily output 150–300 L per vat (0.4 m inner diameter) Keep account of the output 45.2 Charcoal vat regeneration Once a month, open-flame bake until smokeless Judged by smell + recorded 45.2 Water boiled per kg of fuelwood 3–6 L Burn and weigh; one ten-day period fixes your own stove's number 45.2 Epidemic full-boiling wood use 0.4–1.0 kg/person-day Entered in the Chapter 38 energy account 45.2 Ash cover after the privy One ladle each time; the ash bucket stands always beside the squat point Ten-day check of the squat opening 45.3 Pit latrine fill-and-seal line Feces surface 0.3 m below the pit mouth = seal and bury By eye + pole measure 45.3 Pit bottom to the water table ≥1 cubit (about 0.5 m) Marked pole; pit walls seeping in the rainy season = not enough 45.3 Twin-pit alternation cycle Each pit used 6 months, sealed ≥6 months The commissioning date carved on a hung placard 45.3 Compost maturation Sealed ≥6 months + the pile core reached ≥50 °C Stick inserted half a day and drawn out hot; the egg paste on the stick as compensation 45.3 Dead-livestock burial depth ≥2 cubits (about 1 m), ≥50 paces from water Marked pole; the burial site registered 45.3 Standing-water removal line No still water stored more than 7 days Ten-day check, emptied clean 45.4 Tableware boiling Normally once a day (≥5 min); every meal in an epidemic Cookhouse records 45.5 Big-pot meat Rolling boil ≥30 min Timed 45.5 Leftover reheating Rolling boil 2–3 min after steam billows from the center Observed 45.5 Window area ≥1/10 of floor area [Background] Measured with a rule 45.6 Bed off the ground ≥0.3 m Measured with a rule 45.6 Isolation hut from dwellings ≥20 paces, downstream of the prevailing wind Marked pole + calibrated on the plan 45.7 Contact observation 7 days Corrected by this settlement's measured generation interval 45.7 Release from isolation 2–3 days more after all symptoms clear; epidemic standing ends 7 days after the last case with no new case The register 45.7 Epidemic-dead burial depth ≥1.2 m, lime scattered, ≥50 paces from water Marked pole 45.7 Handwashing rub A silent count of 100 slow strokes, working the finger webs, palms, and wrists Spot checks 45.8 Ash water ratio ash:water = 1:5 (by volume) Emulsification test as compensation 45.8 Inspection frequency Weekly five items, ten-day vector check, scored 0/1/2 The tables on file 45.9

docs.title: Failure Modes and Diagnosis
docs.text:
Ordered by "most common, hardest to detect." These failures are mostly silent failures: on the day of the contamination all is well; two or three days later they surface as case counts — so the first diagnostic instrument is not a test, it is the case map.

Symptom Candidate causes How to verify Disposition Prevention Vomiting and purging erupting at several points within one day and night Water source contamination (well, filter line, storage vats) The water-source-to-case map correlation: mark every affected household one by one on the settlement plan and lay the intake points over it — a markedly higher density of households on one well convicts the water source Seal the suspect source and switch to the backup; the whole settlement moves to full boiling (45.2.6) The isolation distance table + the well cover and communal bucket + a salt tracer before commissioning Cases spread evenly, every cook-stove hit A shared water source, or a communal meal within 48 h When the map method above shows no difference between wells, trace whether there was a shared meal or common food within two days Re-run the whole line of the communal-meal three checkpoints + full boiling The 45.5.5 walkthrough table re-taught every quarter Sand filter output fast and turbid A layer breached by the flow (short-circuiting): a gap between vat wall and sand, or the layers loaded upside down Throw a handful of fine charcoal powder into the vat: black water out within minutes = short-circuiting confirmed Out of service; tamp along the wall and reload, or empty the vat and reload the layers in order Tamp every layer while loading (Card 45-01) Sand filter output extremely slow The top layer clogged (normal wear) Read the filtration-rate scale: halved from first loading = the scraping line is reached Scrape the top 1–2 cm; docs.title: Safety Boundaries
docs.text:
Hard gate restated (the Part declaration made concrete): wherever the criteria sections of this chapter's medical cards say "beyond the boundary," all hands stop at once; the only treatments left are warmth, fluid replacement, pain relief, accompaniment, and record-keeping (see the Part declaration in Chapter 44).

This chapter's safety boundaries carry the same weight as the processes themselves (Iron Law 7); failing to execute any of the following counts as not finishing this chapter:

  1. The bodies of the epidemic dead and of dead livestock are handled by dedicated personnel, wrapped, with soap-washing and a change of clothes afterward — bare-handed handling and skipping the wash afterward are this chapter's highest-risk acts.
  2. The three CO iron rules (45.6.2), joined to Chapter 44's 44.7: several people with a morning headache means everyone out of the house; treatment before diagnosis.
  3. Rat bait out at night and gathered at dawn, numbered and registered; dead rats picked up with fire tongs and buried deep, bare hands forbidden.
  4. Lime work with eye and hand protection (the Chapter 13 procedures); ash water and lime slurry must not reach the eyes — if one does, flush at once with great quantities of clean water and transfer to the Chapter 44 chemical-in-the-eye procedures.
  5. Smoke work: people leave the house first and return only after ventilation; never performed in the same room as a patient.
  6. The salt-tracer taster: the water must be boiled and cooled through, a dedicated spoon, one mouthful a day, and the test registered when it is done.
  7. Rat-guard bowls hold shallow water and are not set in young children's activity areas.
  8. The boiling pot and the steam baskets are worked by grade-2 skill holders (the Chapter 37 grading); scalds are handled per Chapter 44.
