Differential interface (to Chapter 51): When registering a Section 47.3.4 chronic wasting lung disease (consumption-like) case, the case's dust work-years file must be checked—those with ten or more years of dry crushing / dry grinding work years are first registered as silicosis and immediately removed from dust posts, then registered and managed as consumption-like; the two diseases are handled differently: consumption requires infection control, silicosis requires exposure cutoff.

Engineering controls (four items, ordered by effectiveness):

  1. Wet work—the most effective item. Change ore breaking, screening, and dry grinding to wet grinding: sprinkle the work surface with water until soaked through. ◎Water-quantity hand-feel criterion: grab a handful of material and squeeze it into a ball that holds, does not fall apart on dropping, and no dust cloud visible where the hammer lands—then it is wet enough. Practice method: on the waste-rock pile run a dry-vs-wet comparison of 20 hammer blows each and observe the dust plume under the hammer; misjudgment compensation: take "floating dust still visible in the air one breath after the hammer lands" as failing—sprinkle again; decide not by hand feel but by the dust plume.
  2. Enclosure and settling—processes that truly need to be dry (such as dry screening) get three-sided baffles with the opening downwind; dust travels upward: open high windows to exhaust dust, take in air low (same standard as Section 45.6.1's low-in-high-out); workstations are not placed in the falling path of the dust plume.
  3. Wind-direction position—open-air crushing points are placed at the settlement's downwind end per the prevailing wind, at ≥100 paces from dwellings and the cookhouse (same class as the arsenic site, see Section 49.2.4).
  4. Workstation layout onto drawings—the three items above are completed into a workstation plan (Chapter 42): dusty workstations, wind-direction arrows, and spacing dimensions drawn clearly; new workshops are accepted against the drawing, not on a craftsman's "find an empty spot and start hammering."

Personal protection: Multiple layers of wet cloth over mouth and nose. Honest declaration: wet cloth blocks only coarse dust, not respirable fine dust—it is the last layer, not a permit. For dry work continuing while wet work is down, work hours are halved and registered. After work, wash hands and face and change out of work clothes before eating or returning to the residential area (same discipline as lead posts, below).

Exposure registry points: Per post, weekly "dry-work hours" (target is zero; if any, record the true number); the annual-examination slope-walk test and morning-sputum records go into the examination file (Section 49.3.3).

docs.title: 49.2.2 Lead
docs.text:
Where it comes from: Galena smelting (Chapters 16–17), lead-copper alloy (Section 17.8 route three), lead-glaze pottery (Chapter 14 glaze materials), lead-tin solder, lead-white pigment (paints), lead ware casting and repair. Lead's main route into the body is hand-to-mouth: lead dust on the hands enters with food, smoking, or licked fingers—the existence of this route determines that most of the control measures below are hygiene institutions rather than masks.

Acute manifestations: Lead colic—paroxysmal cramping pain around the navel, constipation for days, nausea; a metallic-sweet taste in the mouth. Chronic manifestations (four signs at the annual examination, all observable):

Sign How to check (criterion) Wrist-drop Both arms extended straight forward, palms down, held for 30 breaths (about 1 min): if the wrist cannot stay flat and the fingertips hang drooping = positive (early radial nerve palsy) Gum lead line Lift the upper lip and look in a mirror at the gum line: a blue-black line-like deposit = positive (more visible with poor oral hygiene) Anemic earthy-gray complexion Gray-earth face, pale palpebral conjunctiva, easy fatigue—compare against same-village same-age people, not on a single impression Mees' lines White transverse lines on the nails, appearing at the same height on multiple nails (more typical of arsenic, see Section 49.2.4; also seen in lead) = positive

Engineering controls: ① A high window or draft hood above the lead-melting pot, so lead fume is drawn upward; ② never overheat pouring—a smoking lead pot is overheated; reduce the blast and cool it; smoke is the visible proxy of lead vapor; ③ lead powder and lead white are always ground wet (same method as Section 49.2.1); ④ lead work areas are separately enclosed, children barred, livestock excluded.

Personal protection and hygiene system (the main force for this source): ① Soap washing before shifts, before meals, and after the toilet (Chapter 45 soap); ② no smoking, no eating, no snacks in the work area—written into the workshop wall rules; ③ dedicated work clothes, never worn back to the residential area, with a changing spot at the work-area door; ④ leather gloves with cloth liners (Chapter 15), replaced as soon as torn.

Two hard red lines: ① Pregnant women are barred from the post, and lead-post rotation for women of childbearing age is strict—lead crosses the placenta and the milk to damage the offspring's brain development, harming a child no one can see; ② children are barred from lead work areas (children's hand-to-mouth frequency and absorption rate are higher than adults'; the same exposure dose harms them several times over).

Exposure registry points: Weekly lead-melting hours; spot checks of the hand-washing system (the foreman randomly checks 3 people's after-work hands each week, entered into the file); the four annual-examination signs go into the examination file.

docs.title: 49.2.3 Mercury
docs.text:
Where it comes from: All mercury operations of the Chapter 33 electronic-device line—mercury displacement pump evacuation, McLeod gauge readings (raising and lowering mercury), the mercury storage jar, plus leftover mercury from starting point B; upstream is cinnabar roasting and distillation to make mercury (Chapters 16, 12). Characteristic: mercury evaporates continuously at room temperature, and the vapor is colorless, odorless, and unalarming—an open cup of mercury is an exposure source running day and night. Chapter 33 has already set the mercury-discipline red lines; this chapter folds them into the six-source system and adds the two missing rings, examination and waste.

Acute manifestations: When mercury is heated, or spilled and unrecovered: same-day choking cough, chest tightness, fever—a chemical-pneumonia-like picture; report to Chapter 48 the same day and leave the mercury room.

Chronic manifestations (three signs at the annual examination):

Sign How to check (criterion) Intention tremor Water-bowl test: carry a full bowl of water level for ten steps; spilling beyond a rim-width ring = positive; or write your own name three times and compare stroke wobble against last year's specimen Personality change Family inquiry (fixed question: "This year, are you worse than last year in irritability, insomnia, and causeless timidity?")—a subjective item, used as a hint only, never a verdict Gingivitis with drooling Red swollen gums that bleed easily, much saliva—distinguish from the lead line: mercury is inflammatory red, lead is a deposited blue-black line

[Background] Pre-industrial fur felting used mercury nitrate; "the mad hatter" (tremor and great personality change) is a historical record of an entire trade poisoned—a trade can be collectively broken by one process line using mercury. The mechanism cannot be verified on this route, but the engineering implications are enforced as usual.

Engineering controls: ① Shallow-tray work—all mercury operations are performed inside a large shallow tray; any spill lands in the tray (Chapter 33's original red line); ② a dedicated mercury room—mercury work shares no building with food and lodging, assembly, or the cookhouse; single room, single door, high cross-ventilation window; ③ sealed storage—the mercury storage jar is kept tightly closed with a layer of water over the mercury face as a seal (the water interrupts evaporation); close it as soon as use ends; ④ the McLeod gauge's raising and lowering mechanism moves slowly, preventing mercury impact and splashing (Chapter 33).

Personal protection and discipline (Chapter 33's mercury discipline incorporated in full): soap washing after operations; no eating, drinking, or smoking in the mercury work area; work clothes never carried out; spilled mercury is immediately covered with sulfur powder and collected (full emergency text in Section 49.6 and Card 49-03).

Toxin account interface (Chapter 38): reconcile the mercury balance monthly: last month's stock + newly made (or newly drawn) − current stock − amount deep-buried = loss. Empirical criterion: if loss > 2× the monthly ledger average, check floor seams, table seams, and jar seals—the mercury account is the exposure account: mercury missing from the books has all gone into the air. (Chapter 33 standard: each electron tube consumes 5–20 g of mercury, entered item by item.)

Exposure registry points: weekly mercury-operation hours, number of spills and recovered amounts (item by item), monthly loss.

docs.title: 49.2.4 Arsenic
docs.text:
Where it comes from: the arsenic-copper line (Section 17.8 route two: arsenopyrite / arsenical copper ore reduced with copper ore in one furnace); the more hidden source is companion arsenic—copper, tin, and gold ores often occur together with arsenic minerals; when dressing separation is incomplete (Chapter 16), arsenic follows the concentrate into the furnace, and the roasting fumes contain arsenic. This chapter adds one universal rule: at any new ore site's first roast, judge the fumes by smelling for garlic odor 100 paces downwind; any garlic odor means manage it as an arsenic ore—before you confirm the ore's name, defend against the worst case (same standard as Chapter 45's general rule).

Acute manifestations: garlic odor on the breath and in the fumes (observable, smellable); after exposure, vomiting, diarrhea, cramping abdominal pain.

Chronic manifestations (three signs at the annual examination):

Sign How to check (criterion) Mees' lines Monthly nail check: white transverse lines on the nails move outward as the nail grows; appearing at the same height on multiple nails = positive (arsenic's most typical sign)—on appearance, permanent transfer out of arsenic work (Section 17.8 original text) Palmoplantar keratosis Feel and press palms and soles: callus-like spots and punctate bumps beyond the normal callus zone = register Peripheral neuropathy Questioning + examination: stocking-distribution numbness of hands and feet (a wooden feeling in the sock-wearing area); compare pinprick perception of the instep against the forearm = register Pigmented spots Raindrop-like dark spots on the skin, mostly on the trunk = register and trace for the record (the Chapter 42 drawing method can trace and keep them)

Engineering controls: ① A dedicated site—the arsenic roasting and pouring site sits ≥100 paces downwind of the residential area (Section 17.8 original text), exclusive, never mixed with other trades; ② the roasting shed opens on three sides toward the downwind side, fumes venting straight up high, not pooling; ③ dedicated people, dedicated clothes, dedicated tools, no sharing work clothes with the copper shop; ④ enhanced dressing of companion-arsenic ores (Chapter 16 water separation) cuts arsenic at the source.

Hygiene system (Section 17.8 original text incorporated): after roasting, wash clothes and skin; after operations, do not directly touch food or children; work clothes never carried out.

Exposure registry points: roasting batches and hours; the monthly nail-check record page (each month record "no transverse lines" or "transverse lines, which nails, where").

docs.title: 49.2.5 Acid Mist and Chemical Fumes
docs.text:
Where it comes from: the green-vitriol dry-distillation sulfuric acid line, the nitric acid retort, the hydrochloric acid three-jar absorption line (Chapter 23); distillation and chlorine work (Chapter 26); metal pickling, bluing, passivation (Chapter 23); saponification and the oils line. Two kinds of fumes: acid mist (escaping from acid surfaces and exothermic reactions; a white mist with a suffocating sting) and chlorine (Chapter 26; yellow-green, heavier than air, pooling in low spots).

Acute manifestations: choking cough, suffocating feeling, tearing and burning eyes (acid mist); yellow-white burn marks on skin, burning eye pain (acid splashes); heavy chlorine exposure causes same-day pulmonary-edema-like shortness of breath (Chapter 47's three signs of shortness of breath are the escalation line; emergency transfer to Chapter 48).

Chronic manifestations (three items at the annual examination):

Sign How to check (criterion) Dental acid erosion Look in a mirror at the biting edges of the upper and lower front teeth: transverse grooves in the enamel, thinning and translucency of the edges = positive (a directional sign of acid mist; dentists do not exist—the mirror is the examination instrument) Chronic bronchitis Morning cough for over a month, worse in winter and lighter in summer; record year-over-year comparisons Diminished smell Three standard odor items (vinegar, ammonia water (a soap-line byproduct), pine smoke) tested against each nostril, compared at the annual examination

Engineering controls (Chapter 23 standards incorporated and extended): ① Enclosure + off-gas absorption bottle—any apparatus producing acid mist or chlorine connects the tail of its condenser to an ash-lye absorption bottle to capture the off-gas (Chapter 23 original text: HCl is neutralized by ash lye, with no white mist emission; chlorine likewise passes through ash lye); ② apparatus stands in the open or in a four-side cross-ventilated shed, the operator positioned upwind or crosswind; ③ the retort lid is sealed with clay leaving an observation hole; never open the lid to look; ④ on smelling a suffocating white mist, withdraw immediately; ventilate first, then handle; ⑤ emergency rinse station—every acid work point has a bucket of clean water (lidded against dust) + a dedicated rinse pot; on an eye splash, rinse 15 min (Chapter 44 interface); ⑥ acid-mixing discipline: add acid into water, never the reverse (Chapter 23).

Personal protection: apron plus sleeve guards (Chapter 15 leather); eye protection (simple flat glass pieces, Chapter 14); a wet cloth over the mouth blocks droplets only, not gas—gas is handled by ventilation and positioning, not by covering.

Exposure registry points: weekly acid-work hours; splash events recorded item by item (amount, body part, response, healed or not).

docs.title: 49.2.6 Carbon Monoxide, Heat, and Noise
docs.text:
Three sources out of the furnace zone and forging zone, merged into one section, but their control logics differ: CO relies on ventilation and the two-person rule, heat on rotation and salted water, noise on distance and work hours—noise has no safe exposure below a threshold; there is only dose control.

Where it comes from: the incomplete-combustion products (CO) of kilns (Chapter 12), blast and forge furnaces (Chapter 18), and the boiler house (Chapter 28); heat radiation at the furnace face and the forge; noise from hammering and the bellows (the bellows exhaust whistle is often overlooked—it is a continuous sound source).

Acute manifestations and response (to Chapter 48):

Source Acute manifestations Field red line CO Headache, dizziness, nausea, ringing ears → fainting Ventilate before rescuing: the rescuer must not rush into the furnace zone barehanded to carry someone out—double death in a CO zone is the classic accident. First open doors and windows for forced cross-flow ≥5 min, tie a rope, keep two people outside as watchers, then rescue; wet cloth blocks smoke and dust, not CO Heat Heat exhaustion: heavy sweat, weakness, dizziness, calf cramps; heat stroke: hot dry skin without sweat + confusion = Chapter 48 emergency grade At heat exhaustion, leave the furnace at once and drink salted water in the shade; heat stroke transfers to emergency care immediately, no "waiting it out" Noise After a blast (a single enormous report close to forging), tinnitus and deafness lasting over half a day Register on a single case; ear protection added permanently

Chronic manifestations (three items at the annual examination): CO chronic—regular morning headaches, year-round fatigue, worse in the season of closed winter windows (furnace-zone heating and insufficient dwelling ventilation share the source; check Section 45.6.1 dwelling ventilation at the same time); heat chronic—heat-intolerance exhaustion, summer output and appetite declining year by year; noise—the 5 m whisper test: subject facing away, the examiner 5 m away whispers three words for repetition; failure to repeat = register (compare against last year; the curve matters more than a single test).

Engineering controls: ① High windows for cross-flow in the furnace zone, low air intake (CO and hot air share the same upward path); ② two-person watch in enclosed furnace zones—single-person watch of an enclosed boiler house or a furnace-kiln basement is listed as forbidden (Chapter 37 scheduling interface); ③ continuous furnace-face work capped at ≤45 min per rotation (empirical value; calibration method: take "short of breath while speaking + sweat not stopping" as the relief signal, measure how long this settlement's own furnace workers take to reach that signal, take 70% of it as the cap, transcribe to the ledger); ④ in summer the furnace-face shift moves up to dawn and dusk (Chapter 37); ⑤ the furnace face gets a shaded rest spot and a salted-water drinking point (oral rehydration standard quoted from Section 47.3.3: 1 L water + 3.5 g salt; in hot weather, the full daily amount at the furnace face); ⑥ forging and bellows stations are concentrated at the workshop's downwind end, with hammer and bellows positions ≥3 paces apart and the rest spot another ≥5 paces back (the Chapter 42 workstation drawing fixes these three points).

Personal protection—wax earplugs (◎): beeswax mixed with cotton flock, kneaded into plugs, inserted into the outer ear. ◎Wearing hand-feel criterion: after insertion, your own speaking voice sounds distinctly muffled. Practice method: each forging apprentice makes, wears, and removes plugs 20 times each, inspected by the foreman; misjudgment compensation (measurable compensation): when worn properly, a loud shout at 1 pace (about 0.7 m) is needed to get a response—if ordinary speech is heard clearly, they are not in properly; ask not the hand feel but the response. Declaration: wax plugs reduce sound, they do not block it; real dose control rests on work hours and distance.

Exposure registry points: furnace-face hours, hammering hours, and bellows hours listed separately each week; the annual-examination whisper test and morning-headache inquiry.

docs.title: 49.3 Occupational Exposure Registry and Examination System
docs.text: Section 49.1 said it: chronic damage is silent; only the paper can sound the alarm. This section is that paper: one file per post, one examination per person per year, and tracing back from death—three rings connected to Chapter 51's record system.

docs.title: 49.3.1 Post Exposure File (One File per Post)
docs.text:
Field What to record (criterion) Common mistake Post name The settlement-wide uniform name (check against the post list table) One post, several names; the file cannot match the person Exposure source Six-source annotation (multiple allowed: forger = noise + heat + CO) Writing only "a bit dirty" Weekly hours Hours recorded per source: e.g. "hammering 12 h, furnace face 8 h" Recording "always at the furnace" Protection status Two check columns: engineering items (wet method / absorption bottle / ventilation, present or not) + personal items (gloves / earplugs / soap-wash spot check) Checking only personal items—the missing engineering layer stays hidden Start date / examination date Year-month-day; the schedule flags the examination 3 days before it falls due (Chapter 37) An expired examination nobody knows about

Post list master table (create files against it; extend likewise for new posts):

Post Exposure source annotation Corresponding subsection of this chapter Mining, crushing, screening workers Silica dust (+ noise) 49.2.1, 49.2.6 Grinders (abrasives, pigments, glazes) Silica dust 49.2.1 Smelters, casters (copper, lead, iron) Lead fume, CO, heat, dust 49.2.2, 49.2.6 Glazers, lead-tin solderers, pigment workers Lead 49.2.2 Mercury pump / McLeod gauge operators (tube works) Mercury 49.2.3 Arsenic-copper roasters Arsenic (+ fumes) 49.2.4 Acid workers, distillers, chlorine workers Acid mist and chemical fumes 49.2.5 Stokers, boiler workers CO, heat 49.2.6 Forgers, bellows workers Noise, heat, CO 49.2.6

docs.title: 49.3.2 Occupational Disease Registration: Chapter 47's Thirteen Columns Plus an Exposure Column
docs.text:
The registration system is not a new stove. On Chapter 51's case registry, add three columns: exposure source (checked against the post annotations in the table above), work years at that source (years, precise to year + month), and protection status (whether engineering and personal items were in place at the time of onset). Chapter 47's three disciplines (same-day entry, record the original wording not the disease name, sign your name) are all carried over—occupational disease registration is the subset of Chapter 51 case records sliced along the "occupational exposure" dimension; the standards must match, so that cases from the workshop and cases from the kitchen can enter the same weekly report.

Weekly report linkage: Section 47.6's weekly report adds one line, "cases related to occupational exposure" (defined as: new cases with a non-empty exposure column). Zero weeks draw a 0 too.

docs.title: 49.3.3 Annual Examination Observation Items Table (This Route's "Occupational Examination")
docs.text:
Once a year, every craftsman touching the posts, in pairs checking each other plus a hygienist's review. Every item has an observable criterion—an examination without criteria degenerates into check-boxes.

# Observation item Method and criterion Points to exposure source Positive-result response 1 Nails Monthly check (arsenic posts) / annual check (lead posts): white transverse lines, level across, multiple nails Arsenic (typical), lead Arsenic: permanent transfer (17.8); lead: removal from exposure + recheck (49.3.5) 2 Gums Lift the lip, look in a mirror: blue-black line (lead) / red swelling, easy bleeding, drooling (mercury) Lead, mercury Lead line: removal from exposure + recheck; gingivitis: mercury-room hours cut 3 Wrist Arms extended 30 breaths, wrist-drop test Lead Out of the lead post + recheck; second positive = transfer 4 Tremor Water-bowl ten-step test + name-specimen comparison Mercury Out of the mercury post + recheck; second positive = transfer 5 Breathing 100-brisk-step sentence-speaking test on flat ground + slope-walk test + morning-sputum inquiry Silica dust, acid mist Cut dry-work hours to zero; late stage: register work limits 6 Hearing 5 m whisper, three words repeated (annual exam same method, same time of day, measured in a noise-reduced setting) Noise Add ear protection + cut hammering hours; year-by-year curve filed 7 Tooth edges Mirror: transverse grooves on the front teeth's biting edges Acid mist Check the absorption bottles and standing positions; engineering correction takes priority over the person 8 Skin Palmoplantar keratosis, punctate trunk spots (trace and keep the drawing) Arsenic Transfer out of the arsenic post 9 Nerves Stocking-distribution numbness inquiry + pinprick comparison Arsenic, lead Removal from exposure + recheck 10 Body weight Monthly weighing (Chapter 47 standard: monthly loss >5% means register) Wasting damage from all sources Wasting + dust work years = register as early-stage silicosis with work limits 11 Headache Regular morning headache inquiry (worse in winter) CO Check dwelling and furnace-zone ventilation (check Section 45.6.1 at the same time)

The examination is not a diagnosis—this sentence goes into the table header. A positive means two steps: removal from exposure (transfer or work limit) + recheck the next month. If the recheck is still positive or worse, transfer per procedure and notify Chapter 41 scheduling. Transfer is not punishment—Iron Law Seven: what a transfer preserves is the craftsman himself and the transmission of his craft (moving to trainer, inspection, or drawing posts; Chapter 43 master–apprentice system interface).

docs.title: 49.3.4 Post Rotation: Spreading Out the Cumulative Dose
docs.text:
Rotation is the active means of reducing any one person's cumulative work-years dose; three rules are fixed:

  1. Dry dust posts: cap on continuous dry-work tenure of 5 years (empirical value; calibration method: correct against this settlement's annual-examination slope-walk-test positive rate—as the positive rate rises, the cap drops; transcribe to the ledger).
  2. Mercury pump operation: two fixed people rotate; no one person serves alone for consecutive months (Chapter 33's two-person system, filed).
  3. Forge hammer and bellows: swap every half day (doubles as skill backup).

Rotation presupposes skill redundancy: ≥2 qualified people per post (Chapter 37 skill matrix)—the rotation system in turn forces apprenticeship, which is precisely the direct payoff of the Chapter 47 master–apprentice system on poison posts.

docs.title: 49.3.5 Tracing Deaths Back: Connecting to Section 47.7's Death Registry
docs.text:
The Section 47.7 death registry adds two columns: the deceased's trade in life and exposure file number. The monthly death rate lists "occupation-related deaths" separately (defined as: exposure file on record and the cause-of-death syndrome matching that source's chronic manifestations, e.g. a chronic-wasting death with 15 years of dust work). This is not blame assignment; it is tracing back—same standard as Section 47.2.3's no-blame review system: every occupation-related death must yield one engineering or institutional change (switch to wet method, add an absorption bottle, cut hours), and the review minutes go into the Chapter 47 ledger. The twenty-year-scale "death of a trade" can only be seen year by year here.

[Card 49-01 Occupational Exposure Registration Card] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: register pages (Chapter 41 paper, criterion: ink does not blur overnight); a copy of the post-list master table; soap and wash stations (Chapter 45); exposure-file pages (one page per post on opening, one per person per annual examination). Per-use quantity: one page per post, one page per person per year.
  2. Tools required: day-counting means (Chapter 3, cross-checked first); one mirror (Chapter 14 glass, criterion: shows facial features clearly without distortion); scale (Chapter 22, monthly weighing); pace rope or marked pole (Chapter 3, fixing the 100-pace and 5 m distances). Calibration before use: mirror clean with no rust spots; scale zero checked; rope and pole length-compared.
  3. Sequence and control points: ① open post files from the post list with all four fields filled (the two protection-status columns checked separately; a missing engineering column means degraded operation); ② enter the start date on the first day on the job; ③ at week's end the foreman enters each source's hours and the hygienist draws lots to check three people's personal protection; ④ the annual examination walks the observation table item by item, recording each finding verbatim ("one transverse groove on the right index fingernail, 2 mm from the nail root"), never a criterion-free "normal"; ⑤ a positive item gets the two-step response (off exposure + recheck next month) and the transfer order is registered; ⑥ death cases backfill the trade and exposure-file number columns, triggering a review; ⑦ the examination data are transcribed year by year into a curve table, one row per person and one column per year—this table is the L3 deliverable.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: furnace face continuous ≤45 min (measured as 70% of the time to "short of breath talking + sweat not stopping"); dry-dust post tenure cap 5 years (lowered as the annual positive rate rises, transcribed to the ledger); whisper test at 5 m with three words (same method, same time of day, retested); water-bowl ten steps (spilling past a rim-width = positive); noise posts ≤2 h cumulative per person per day, CO posts ≤30 min continuous per person; monthly weight loss >5% is registered (Chapter 47 convention). All empirical values are revised annually against examination data and transcribed to the Chapter 47 ledger.
  5. Observations to record: weekly hours per source, spot-check results, the eleven annual-examination findings, transfer orders and recheck results, the two death-tracing columns (trade + file number), and each person's yearly curve point.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = no empty field among the four + every examination item carries a criterion-based finding + signed; rework = protection status ticked only on the personal column, or the examination written off as "normal"—recover the engineering column and the verbatim findings and mark as a supplementary entry; scrap = an entire examination page rewritten from memory (original kept on file marked "void," rewrite marked "re-recorded").
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order (most frequent first): ① post hours suspiciously identical (copied from last week) → foreman measures and reports at week's end + hygienist cross-checks the schedule (Chapter 37); ② examinations written off as "normal," items skipped → check item by item against the table and assess the examiner; ③ positives left unhandled → the transfer order must close with a recheck column, spot-checked at reviews; ④ protection status ticked only on the personal column with the engineering column missing → fill it in and mark the post degraded on the spot; ⑤ the examination curve skips a year → put the examination date in a fixed column of the schedule.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one post-file page + one real annual-examination page; L2 = every exposed post on file, 20 posts spot-checked with ≥90% current-month completion, positive items closed with a transfer order and recheck; L3 = the examination curve table plotted for two consecutive years, occupational deaths traced closed-loop, and one occupational hygienist brought up to examine independently.

docs.title: 49.4 The Four Waste Disposal Chains
docs.text: The second sentence of the review stands here: "The result of missing a disposal chain is reverse destruction: drinking water, farmland, and craftsman health are damaged in sequence." The disposal chain has four links: on-site classification → transport to a fixed point → endpoint disposal → ledger records; missing any one link fails the whole chain—disposal without records equals no disposal (after the next rain, no one knows what was buried where). The four chains follow; tailings and dust wastes go into the mining variant of the slag chain (Section 49.4.5).

docs.title: 49.4.1 Furnace Slag and Mine Slag (Chapters 16, 18)
docs.text:
On-site three-way classification (completed the same shift the slag comes out of the furnace; criteria checkable):

Class How to tell Destination Iron-bearing slag Magnet test (same as Chapter 16's magnetic dressing): pass crushed slag over a magnet; what sticks up plentifully is iron-bearing slag Pile in centralized storage as remelt feedstock reserve (potential feed for Chapter 18's lean-material re-reduction) Lean slag (building grade) Magnet does not attract it; light color, light weight, no metallic luster; powder rubbed between the fingers has no garlic odor (arsenic check, Section 49.2.4) Crushed for road base, aggregate in lime mortar (Chapter 13), rammed foundations Heavy-metal slag (mainly lead and arsenic) Slag out of lead, copper, and arsenic furnaces is classed here without question, no per-piece judgment (defend against the worst case) Into the Section 49.4.3 heavy-metal chain, forbidden in building materials

Four siting rules for the pile yard (Chapter 37's siting method applied to slag yards): ① ≥100 paces from the nearest water-intake point (more than three times Chapter 45's 30 paces for latrines—reason: slag volume is large, it contains metal, it sits for decades); ② not on a runoff line, not occupying a stream bank (rainy-season runoff washing the slag pollutes everything downstream); ③ downwind of the settlement's prevailing wind; ④ ground higher than the intake section, not in the same hollow. Once the site is drawn, it enters the slag-yard drawing (Chapter 42); stakes mark the boundary.

Yard operation: slag is piled by class with clear separation; an interception ditch around the perimeter diverts surface runoff away (same method as Chapter 45 drainage ditches); every cartload of slag is registered by source furnace, date, class, and quantity (estimated weight to ±20%, an empirical value; calibration method: fill a fixed-volume basket three times, weigh, take the average, and thereafter count by basket).

docs.title: 49.4.2 Chemical Waste Liquids and Acid Residue (Chapters 23, 26)
docs.text:
Treating waste with waste (core process: use waste to treat waste): waste acid is never poured out—the acid line's spent acid and pickle liquor are mutually neutralized with ash lye (wood-ash water, Chapter 23).

Step Operation Criterion 1 Collection Waste acid into a ceramic vat (dedicated vat, dedicated label), never mixed with the lye vat Vat labeled "waste acid," wooden lid (never open-topped) 2 Mutual neutralization Ash lye added slowly to the waste-acid vat, stirred with a wooden rod Indicator method (Chapter 23): drip in purple-cabbage juice while stirring—red means still acid; keep adding lye until it turns purple near the original color: that is the endpoint; a warm vat wall is normal; too hot to touch means slow down 3 Settling Let stand half a day Mud residue settles at the vat bottom 4 Splitting clear liquid from residue The supernatant goes into the waste-liquid pit (dedicated pit, clay bottom, connected to no ditch); the mud is shoveled out into the chemical-sludge landfill pit (same pit spec: clay bottom, capped with compacted soil, marker post) The pit locations enter the slag-yard drawing 5 Records Entered item by item into the Chapter 42 account Waste acid amount (estimated volume), lye used, date

Two prohibitions: ① Vessel-cleaning water must not enter the drinking-and-drainage system—water used to wash the acid vat is treated as waste acid into the waste-liquid pit; not one drop enters the household drainage ditch (the Chapter 45 ditch that runs toward the waters below the intake section); ② the saturated ash lye from chlorine absorption bottles is likewise disposed of as chemical waste liquid, not dumped into the stream just because it is "already neutralized"—chloride salts into farmland kill seedlings.

docs.title: 49.4.3 Heavy-Metal Slag and Mercury-Bearing Waste (The Red-Line Chain)
docs.text:
Three-bucket system: lead slag, mercury waste, and arsenic slag (and all slag and flue dust of the arsenic-copper line) each get one dedicated bucket, color-banded and lettered (lead: white band; mercury: black band; arsenic: red band—the color code enters the settlement-wide wall rules). Mixing buckets is forbidden; mixing into ordinary slag is forbidden—one bucket of lead slag mixed into building slag scraps the whole batch of building material and forces re-sorting; this is this section's only capital-level red line; violators are handled under Chapter 41's red-line disciplinary procedure.

Waste Treatment before leaving the bucket Deep-burial spec Mercury waste (spill collections, scrap mercury, mercury sludge) Mixed with sulfur powder until it turns black (conversion to mercury sulfide, same as Chapter 33's spill response); conversion criterion: no silver-white beads visible Pit depth ≥1 m, bottom compacted, capped with compacted soil Lead slag Mixed with lime (Chapter 13), moistened and encased Same as above Arsenic slag and flue dust Mixed with lime, moistened and encased Same as above

Four deep-burial rules: ① the pit location is recorded on the slag-yard drawing by paces and bearing (from the marker stake: pace count + bearing per the Chapter 3 orientation method, drawn in per the Chapter 42 drawing method); ② a marker post is erected with carved letters ("lead / mercury / arsenic + year"); ③ deep-burial spots are permanently barred from cultivation—no food crops may be planted (safety boundary item 5); ④ check year by year: at the annual slag-account reconciliation, verify against the drawing that the stakes are intact.

Toxin account closed loop (Chapter 38 interface): each of lead, mercury, and arsenic gets a balance page: in (mined / purchased) = out (in use + deep-buried + book loss). Mercury's loss monitoring line is in Section 49.2.3; lead and arsenic follow the same method—an abnormal book loss means check the pile yard, the bucket labels, and the burial spots.

docs.title: 49.4.4 Workshop Wastewater and Settling in Stages
docs.text:
General rule: workshop wastewater and household drinking water are separate systems. Chapter 45 has already ruled that household drainage ditches must not discharge upstream of the intake section; this chapter tightens it: workshop wastewater (slurry water, pickle water, quench water, furnace-zone wash water) does not enter the household drainage ditch; it gets its own separate system.

Three-stage settling ponds (in series from high to low):

Stage Function Spec (empirical + calibrated) Stage 1 · grit chamber Coarse sand and grit sink to the bottom Depth ≥0.8 m; a baffle at the inlet face slows the flow Stage 2 · settling pond Fine silt and suspended solids settle Volume 1.5× stage 1; the overflow between the two ponds passes at a high level Outlet · clarified water Overflows to a downstream non-intake section The outlet has a gravel filter layer (same method as the Chapter 45 filter line)

The desilting cycle is not fixed in days: empirical criterion = clean when silt reaches one third of the pond depth; measure this workshop's own days-to-full (survey with a rod once a month in the first season), then enter the measured cycle into the Chapter 43 maintenance table. Wastewater from heavy-metal workshops (lead, mercury, arsenic) does not enter the three-stage ponds—it goes alone into a dedicated pond; when that pond silts up, mix with lime and deep-bury per the Section 49.4.3 lead-arsenic slag method.

docs.title: 49.4.5 Tailings and Dust Wastes (The Mining Variant of the Slag Chain)
docs.text:
The hazard of dressing tailings (the fine slurry left after water separation) and of dust collected by dry dust removal lies not in a single toxicity value but in quantity and re-dispersal: a dry tailings beach at the first wind becomes a secondary exposure source inhaled by the whole village.

Step Operation Criterion Wet stacking The tailings slurry is directed to the tailings yard, the surface kept wet and dark If the surface dries white, channel more water or sprinkle—wet stacking is a rule, not a suggestion Retaining wall A stone retaining wall (Chapter 13 masonry) on the downhill side holds back slump slides Check for cracks before the rainy season Covering Decommissioned yard sections get ≥0.2 m of soil cover The soil layer is continuous with no tailings showing through Vegetation Sow Chapter 10's soil-binding fast-growing grasses or shrubs Green-up the next season is the survival criterion Windy-season patrols One patrol every ten days in wind season Any dust seen means sprinkle at once; patrols enter the slag-yard ledger

[Card 49-02 Waste Slag Classification and Disposal Card] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: a magnet (for iron-bearing slag; source Chapter 16, usable if it lifts iron filings ≥ its own weight); a small vial of purple-cabbage-juice indicator (freshly made per the Chapter 23 method; criterion: turns red with vinegar, green with ash-lye water—run both controls before use); sulfur powder and lime (Chapter 13) in quantity; fixed-volume slag baskets (marked once the volume is set).
  2. Tools required: the slag-yard drawing (Chapter 42); a pace rope; a wooden stirring rod; three ceramic vats (waste acid / lye / neutralized, each labeled); an iron shovel. Calibration before use: basket volume set by the water-weighing method (three trials averaged); pace rope and graduated rod compared for length.
  3. Operating sequence and control points: ① same-shift three-way magnet classification of furnace slag (iron-bearing / lean / heavy-metal); ② slag from lead, copper, and arsenic furnaces goes into the heavy-metal bucket without per-piece judgment; ③ waste acid and ash lye mutually neutralized in four steps, the indicator endpoint decided by color, never by "close enough"; ④ mercury waste mixed with sulfur until no silver-white beads remain; lead and arsenic slag mixed with lime and moistened; ⑤ deep burial per the four rules (1 m, compacted, marker post, paces-and-bearing on the drawing); ⑥ tailings wet-stacked, covered with soil, sown with grass; ⑦ entered item by item into the Chapter 42 toxin account and the slag-yard ledger (source, class, quantity, endpoint, date, handler).
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration method: slag quantity by basket (basket volume water-calibrated to ±5%); neutralization endpoint by indicator color change; desilt at one third (first-season measured days, then to the Chapter 43 cycle table); deep-burial pit depth ≥1 m; cover soil ≥0.2 m. All are empirical values; revise with this settlement's own measurements and transcribe to the ledger.
  5. Process observation record items: class and basket count of each slag cart, indicator endpoint color, deep-burial post number and bearing-paces, tailings surface wet/dry, windy-season patrol records.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = classification completed same day + account matches reality (monthly reconciliation) + post positions match the drawing; rework = classification lots mixed (re-screen with the magnet, register the rework); scrap = heavy-metal slag already used in building material—the whole batch of material is barred, recalled and re-sorted, the event goes to review.
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: account-vs-reality gap (the slag account will not reconcile) → check for illegal dumping (the next failure mode) and estimate drift (re-verify basket volume); neutralization endpoint misjudged → re-drip the indicator against both controls; burial spot lost → drawing and post locate doubly; if the post is lost, seek by the drawing.
  8. L1/L2/L3 evidence: L1 = one complete three-way slag sort + one mutual neutralization + one sample slag-yard drawing; L2 = the four disposal chains running one month straight, monthly reconciliation matching, the three buckets and deep-burial posts in place; L3 = quarterly slag account closed + toxin account balanced + the tailings yard greened + 1 slag-yard manager trained.

docs.title: 49.5 The Backfire Simulation: How a Settlement Poisons Its Own Water in Five Years
docs.text:
This chapter's "outbreak investigation." Section 47.4's five-step method investigates patients; this section turns the same method on the environment—the slag yard is the chronic version of the disease source, and the pin map is its X-ray. The simulation's base case is fictional; every hinge comes from the chains written above.

Base case: the Baishui settlement, 150 people. In year two it builds a copper-lead smelting shop and sites the slag yard on the gentle slope upstream of the stream—reasoning: "close to the shop, saves the slag-carting labor" (not one of Chapter 37's four siting rules followed). Rain in two seasons year-round. The simulation runs from the shop's founding:

Year What happened Signal visible at the time Gate that could have intercepted it (which link failed) Year one Lead slag and lean slag heaped together on the slope, no interception ditch; rainy-season leachate ran down the slope into the stream Nothing—this is the very shape of chronic poison: in year one nothing can be seen Gate 1 · siting (Section 49.4.1's four rules); Gate 2 · classification and interception ditch Year two The stream occasionally smells off; the downstream catch halves; upstream households say "the water tastes heavy" Biological signal: fewer fish are the earliest sentinels—earlier than people Gate 3 · slag account (the mixed heap not caught by reconciliation); Gate 4 · environmental sentinels unwatched Year three Downstream irrigated fields have weak seedlings, yield down two tenths; scattered abdominal pain and earthy-gray faces among downstream children, taken as "worms stirring" Children = the most sensitive sentinels: clusters of child abdominal pain and earthy-gray complexion precede adult occupational cases Gate 5 · children's cases not asked about address and water direction (Chapter 47's four-question table lacks "which fields' grain do you eat") Year four Downstream adults: growing numbers of fatigue, constipation, and colic cases; on the registry "scattered," no one reads them together The cases are already on the books—what was missing was pinning the cases onto the map by water direction Gate 6 · pin map not done (Section 47.4.2, overlay the water-source edge) Year five The hygienist, per this section's method, makes a slag-yard-vs-cases pin map + salt tracer: 10 kg of salt into the slag yard's seep pit; on day 4 the downstream intake point tastes salty—connectivity confirmed; the slag yard is sealed, fields moved, the water source changed With every gate breached, the bill is in the table below ——

One-line gate review: had any single link of the disposal chain held, the simulation stops in that year. Siting holds (year one), classification holds (year one), reconciliation holds (year two), asking children's cases about water direction holds (year three), the pin map holds (year four)—five gates, each a procedure already written above. The backfire is not fate; it is a list of skipped procedures.

docs.title: 49.5.1 The Slag-Yard–Case Association Investigation Method (Connecting to Chapter 51's Pin Map)
docs.text:
1. Pin map with three overlaid edges: use the Section 47.4.2 pin-map method as-is, but the three edges become the water system (stream course and intake points) / slag yards and burial spots (Section 49.4 drawings) / case households. Reading the clustering pattern: cases banding along the downstream water system while upstream households are clean = an environmental source is indicated; cases clustering only in workshop trades = an occupational source is indicated (Section 49.3's exposure files are the differential basis).
  2. The trade four-question table (a revision of Section 47.4.3's four-question table, run per case): what trade (exposure file) / usual water source / which bank do you live on (upstream / downstream) / which fields' grain do you eat (irrigation water direction). All four questions recorded; the common factor shows itself.
  3. Salt tracer to verify connectivity (Chapter 45's original method): 5–10 kg of table salt dissolved into the slag yard's seep pit at once; then for 7 days taste the intake point daily (boiled and cooled, a dedicated spoon, one mouthful a day); turning salty = groundwater connectivity; seal the slag yard. This is the only field developer of "invisible leachate," using no reagents at all.
  4. The child-sentinel rule: child abdominal pain + earthy-gray complexion + anemia-like clustering, check the environment before the trade—children do not enter workshops; their exposure comes only from water and food; the child curve is the environmental line, the adult trade curve the occupational line; draw the two lines separately.

docs.title: 49.5.2 The Remediation Cost Account (One Page for the Council)
docs.text:
Option Cost (empirical values) Timing Year one: build the yard per the siting method + classification + interception ditch 2 people × 5 days + 20 person-hours for the ditch At shop construction Year five remediation: seal and relocate the yard + change the water source (activate the Section 45.2.1 backup) + reroute irrigation + take downstream fields out of food crops (Chapter 10) + add the lead items to the whole-population examination 30–50 person-days + one season's harvest + trust in the drinking water Five years later Twenty years on: children's developmental damage and the loss of craftsmen Not convertible—Iron Law Seven's account has no depreciation line ——

How to use this page: only when the Chapter 38 ledger carries "disposal cost" and "epidemic cost" as parallel columns does the council have something to compare. The review called this "the part of rebuilding most prone to biting back at itself"—on the books, it is also the easiest part to compute clearly.

docs.title: 49.6 Emergency Plans (Field Response Sequences for Acute Events)
49.6.1 Universal Response Sequence (All Acute Poisonings and Exposures)
docs.text:
1. Leave the exposure (first action, person before property): move people upwind to fresh air; for skin exposure, dry-sweep / dry-wipe first, then flush with large volumes of clean water (lime classes: sweep before flushing—water activates the burn);
  2. Ventilate and isolate the scene: open doors and windows, stop fans, hang a maintenance tag; clear out unrelated personnel and post one person at the entrance;
  3. First aid (Chapter 44 procedures connect in): breathing and pulse response, burn flushing, eyes rinsed with clean water ≥15 min with the eyelids everted;
  4. Record: time, people, substance, response, symptoms—entered into the Chapter 47 case book the same day; poison-involved events also into this chapter's exposure file.

docs.title: 49.6.2 Three Specialized Plans
docs.text:
[Card 49-03 Mercury Spill Emergency Card] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: sulfur powder (a registered material; dry and free of lumps—damp sulfur is useless); a lidded dedicated ceramic jar (marked red "mercury," i.e. the mercury bucket of the Section 49.4.3 three-bucket system); stiff card and brush; mercury-spill ledger page and occupational exposure-file page (Chapter 41 paper). Per-use quantity: one ledger page and one exposure-file entry per spill.
  2. Tools required: sulfur dispenser (paper packet or shaker); soap wash station (for washing up after withdrawal); timing means (Chapter 3, for the 10 min wait); cordon sign and one person to hold the entrance. Calibration before use: sulfur crumbles freely between the fingers (not caked); the jar lid seals and the marking is legible; the timer is checked against the clock.
  3. Sequence and control points: Do first, in this order, no step skipped: ① get people out before touching the material—throttle that area's vent, send everyone not needed 10 min away, leave one person holding the entrance; ② gather the visible beads with the stiff card, pushing inward from the outer edge (no patting, no blowing, no sweeping); ③ sprinkle sulfur thickly over every visible bead and every floor seam; ④ after 10 min gather the sulfur-mercury mixture with the stiff card into the lidded red-marked jar; ⑤ sprinkle the seams with sulfur a second time; ⑥ give that area one week of boosted ventilation and rotate the personnel (two-person rotation, no one person month after month); ⑦ register time / location / estimated amount / who cleaned, enter the spill ledger and copy it into the exposure file (Section 49.3), and the same day into the Chapter 47 case register if symptoms appear. Never do: sweep with a broom or pat the spill (airflow shatters mercury into microbeads and the evaporating surface explodes); never vacuum, never blow air, never flush it into a drain; never gather it bare-handed; never put the sulfur-mercury mixture into ordinary slag or burn it; never "carry on as usual" after a spill with no registration and no rotation; no eating, drinking, or smoking in the mercury work area. When you must withdraw: a second spill at the same post within one year stops that post's work and triggers a process review (Chapter 33 linkage); if an indoor spill cannot be isolated or its vent throttled, withdraw everyone from the area, seal it, and wait for the sulfur; if the cleaner shows red swollen gums with excess saliva, spills past a rim-width in the water-bowl walk, or grows irritable or sleepless, apply the Section 49.3 two-step positive response (off exposure + recheck next month)—move them off the job first, recheck after.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: people withdrawn 10 min; gather 10 min after the sulfur goes down; one week of boosted ventilation for the area; two spills at one post within a year triggers the process review; mercury work is run by two people in rotation, never one person alone month after month. Calibration: the sulfur dose is judged by "no silver-white glint from any bead or seam" (not by weight); conversion in the jar is judged by "no silver-white bead visible" (Section 49.4.3, sulfur until it turns black).
  5. Observations to record: location and extent of the spill, estimated amount, number of sulfur passes, whether any silver-white bead remained in the jar, the second sprinkling, start and end of ventilation and rotation, the double entry in ledger and exposure file, and the symptom inquiry for the cleaner.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = visible beads at zero + jar sealed and red-marked + double entry in ledger and exposure file + rotation executed; rework = a seam still glints silver-white → sprinkle sulfur again and re-gather; scrap (management failure) = sweeping with a broom, flushing with water, or dumping into ordinary slag—registered as a red-line event, that batch of slag quarantined and re-sorted, the event taken into review.
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order (most frequent first): ① reaching for the broom (commonest and worst) → stop at once, switch to the stiff card, increase the sulfur dose and the ventilation time; ② seams missed → sprinkle sulfur again and re-inspect along the seams in raking light; ③ cannot find every landing spot of scattered mercury → compensate with full-coverage sulfur sprinkling (a UV lamp is a far-term means, not part of this procedure now); ④ work carried on after a spill with no registration and no rotation → check the spill ledger and retrain on this card; ⑤ gathered material mixed into ordinary slag → trace and re-sort per the Section 49.4.3 heavy-metal red line, and quarantine the whole batch of building material.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one drill: 10 min withdrawal + sulfur + gathering into the jar + one ledger page; L2 = one real spill handled to standard, double entry in ledger and exposure file, rotation at that area executed; L3 = a year with no "broom / water flush / ordinary slag" violations + the process review closed after two spills at one post + one person brought up to handle a spill independently.

Acid spill: small areas—cover with dry sand to absorb, shovel into the waste-acid vat, neutralize by slow addition of ash lye (stirring, indicator to near neutral); large areas—first build a sand berm to keep it out of the ditches, then as above; never flush directly with water into the drain (berm first, then flush).

Chlorine / acid-mist leak: all personnel evacuate upwind; close the clamps, stop the reaction; spray an ash-lye mist over the leak area to settle it; those with coughing or stinging go to Chapter 44 observation.

docs.title: 49.6.3 Drill System
docs.text: One comprehensive drill each year (one specialized plan drawn at random + the universal sequence): time it (leaving the exposure ≤1 min is the pass line, an empirical value), record it, debrief into the file. A plan never drilled equals no plan.

docs.title: Master Parameter Table
docs.text: Parameter Value Class Wet work Breaking / dry grinding always sprayed with water Hard rule Lead post discipline No eating or smoking in the work area; wash hands and face after operations Red line Mercury work Shallow tray + sulfur for spills + lidded jar + job rotation Chapter 33 linkage Arsenic site ≥100 paces downwind of the residential area Section 17.8 linkage Acid-mist off-gas All through lye absorption bottles Chapters 23/26 linkage Noise posts Per person ≤2 h cumulative daily at forging positions (empirical) Empirical CO posts Single person ≤30 min continuous per shift Section 6.8 linkage Examination frequency Six-source posts, observation items table once a year Institution Slag-yard distance to water ≥30 paces + salt-tracer verification Criterion Heavy-metal slag Dedicated bucket, dedicated burial + lime + location registration Red line Waste acid disposal Neutralize with ash lye to near neutral Procedure Drills Once a year; leaving the exposure ≤1 min Criterion

docs.title: Failure Modes and Diagnosis
docs.text: Symptom Candidate causes (by probability) Verification Response Multiple people, same symptoms, same period A common exposure source surfacing Split lines by post / address (49.5) Immediate removal from exposure + environmental source hunt Child anemia and abdominal pain clustering Environmental pollution (water / food chain) Child-sentinel rule Seal the slag yard + change the water source Protection exists only on paper Gear out of repair / no one checking Workstation spot checks Gear acceptance system (15.6) + roll call Slag yard "feels fine" Never tracer-verified Repeat the salt tracer Verify retroactively; if connected, seal Examinations "all normal" year after year Observation items skipped, box-ticking Check each item against the table Examiners tested; records filed Waste slag dumped secretly into ditches Disposal too cumbersome, no convenient alternative Patrol along the ditches Place official slag buckets nearby (convenience is the compliance rate) Work continues as usual after a mercury spill No registration, no rotation Check the mercury-spill ledger Retrain on Card 49-03

docs.title: Process Card Index
docs.text: Card Name Section Purpose Posted at 49-01 Occupational Exposure Registration Card end of 49.3.5 Four-field post file, eleven annual-examination items, two-step response to positives Foreman's station; medical station 49-02 Waste Slag Classification and Disposal Card end of 49.4.5 Three-way slag sorting, mutual neutralization, three-bucket deep burial, ledger reconciliation Slag yard; workshops 49-03 Mercury Spill Emergency Card end of 49.6.2 Clear the people first, no sweeping or flushing, sulfur and gathering, withdrawal and review lines Mercury work area; medical station

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• L1: six-source post files created; each of the four waste categories through one compliant disposal with a paper trail; one mercury spill or acid spill handled successfully per card.
  • L2: the four disposal chains running one season (ledger continuous); the post rotation table in force; the annual examination covering all six-source posts; one comprehensive drill passing (leaving the exposure ≤1 min).
  • L3: examination data as curves for two consecutive years (able to answer "which post is getting worse"); slag-yard–case association monitoring running (child-sentinel line + annual salt-tracer verification); disposal cost and epidemic cost as parallel columns in the Chapter 38 ledger. Evidence: exposure files, examination curves, the slag-yard registry, drill records.

docs.title: Work Hours, Manpower, and Consumption
docs.text: Item Manpower Hours (empirical) Six-source post files 1 person 2–3 days One examination round (30–50 people) Medic + assistant 3–5 days Slag-yard construction and salt tracer 2 people 3 days + 7 days observation One mercury-spill response 2 people Half a day Comprehensive drill All hands Half a day/year Consumption Sulfur, lime, dry sand, neutralizing lye Into the Chapter 38 ledger

docs.title: Safety Boundary
docs.text:
Hard gate restated (implementing the part-level declaration): where any medical card in this chapter writes a criterion that falls "beyond the boundary," stop at once; the only remaining responses are warming / rehydration / pain relief / attendance / recording (see Chapter 44's part declaration).

  • Those handling mercury- and arsenic-bearing waste are trained before posted; after work, follow that poison's washing procedure;
  • Guard against inhaling sulfur powder; guard against splashes during neutralization (acid into lye, add slowly, stir gently);
  • Waste-slag deep-burial pits ≥2 cubits + a lime layer + marker posts—the location registry is for those who come after;
  • Every measure in this chapter is engineering and institutions, not medicine: suspected occupational disease symptoms are managed under Chapter 47's case system with removal from exposure; [Background/Outlook] specialized occupational medicine awaits a mature medical system.

docs.title: A. Existing Tools List
docs.text: Chapter 45 sanitation and isolation systems; Chapter 47 case registry and death account; Chapter 38 ledger; Chapter 44 first-aid procedures; Chapters 23/26 chemical management and off-gas absorption; Chapter 33 mercury discipline; Section 17.8 arsenic-site procedures.

docs.title: B. New Tools in This Chapter
docs.text: The six-source analysis and the twenty-year list; post exposure files + annual observation items table + post rotation system; occupational disease registration (Chapter 47 plus an exposure column); the four waste disposal chains (classification–siting–interception–tracing–registration); the salt-tracer connectivity verification method; the child-sentinel rule; the backfire simulation and remediation cost account; the three emergency plans (mercury spill / acid spill / gas leak) and the annual drill system.

docs.title: C. Unsolved Dependencies
docs.text: Specialized occupational medicine ([Background/Outlook]); quantitative exposure testing (no instruments; indirect monitoring via the observation items table + registry, declared honestly); large-scale tailings revegetation (a Chapter 10 long-term topic); remediation technology for already-contaminated sites (sealing + changing the water source stops the loss, it does not cure).

docs.title: Next Dependencies
docs.text: Chapters 41/42: disposal costs and sick-leave labor conversion into the ledger's twin columns. Chapter 40: the waste lines listed in disaster redundancy and degraded-operation plans. Chapters 50–53: environmental variants—salt-fog corrosion (islands), frozen-season slag yards (permafrost), desert dust. Chapters 44–47: poisoning first aid, case registration, exposure epidemiology. Loop back to the master outline: Iron Law Seven's "labor is the first asset" lands in this chapter as three institutions—registry, examination, disposal—twenty years of rebuilding first requires people who can work all twenty years.

docs.title: Chapter Objectives
docs.text:
After reading this chapter, the settlement should produce five documents and run them on the wall:

Deliverable Acceptance criterion Rainforest environment assessment conclusion Card 50-01 with measured values for all ten dimensions (water / fuel / clay / metal / silicon / wood / power / transport / maintenance / labor), linked to the master outline's Assessment Form G04 Fails-first order table (local version) Local ordering of the seven failure lines of Section 50.3, each line's "precursors" written onto the duty board Annual rhythm table Dry season (build, burn, store) and rainy season (make, repair, heal) scheduled month by month (Section 50.7) Rainforest maintenance cycle table Every item of the Section 50.4 comparison table implemented, with ten-day inspection signatures as proof Rainforest substitution matrix ≥5 entries registered in the Chapter 40 four-column format, each trial-produced

Acceptance for this chapter is not "what has been built" but whether the rainy-season assessment has been passed: only when the four ledgers — mold, fever, leakage, corrosion — all reach target at the end of the rainy season has this chapter been executed.

docs.title: Capability Boundaries
docs.text:
Can do:

  • Give the sequencing differences, the consolidated failure table, and the frequency-multiplied maintenance cycles for the Part 1–6 technology library under rainforest conditions (Sections 50.2–50.4).
  • Build four-column substitution matrices for the scarce resources, with boundaries stated honestly (Section 50.5, Chapter 40 format).
  • Place the engineering defense lines against malaria and waterborne disease ahead of all industry, and give the trigger thresholds of the default fever protocol (Section 50.6).

Cannot do:

  • Cannot change the climate. Dry-season window length is a hard constraint; in a rainy year the window shortens or even vanishes, so the rhythm table must carry a "rainy-year contingency column."
  • Cannot conjure resources from nothing. With no salt springs and no refractory clay outcrops inside the territory, the corresponding matrix cells can only say "no route"; padding them with "theoretically obtainable through distant trade" is not allowed (Iron Law 5 of Chapter 40).
  • Cannot eradicate mold, malaria, or corrosion; can only stretch failure cycles beyond the maintenance cycle — the definition of every institution in this chapter is one sentence: make "decays slowly" outrun "repairs diligently."
  • Does not re-teach processes. Each technology point cites only a chapter number plus one sentence of rainforest difference; building while skipping that chapter's process card counts as an incomplete work step.

External dependencies (counted into List C): the master outline's Assessment Form G04 and Ledger Regulation No. 02; the Chapter 40 register, contingency box, and post-flood drying procedure; the medical line's fever handling and mosquito-control rules (interface in Section 50.6).

docs.title: Pre-Construction Verification
docs.text:
Checkbox style. Any dimension not measured (copying "typical rainforest values" does not count) means the corresponding later subsections may only be marked as drafts.

# Dimension Typical rainforest rating Check criteria (confirm you hold ××, by the standard ××) 1 Water Quantity A · Quality D ≥1 year of rain-gauge records (calibrated per Chapter 3); dry-season lowest-month flow measured (Chapter 29 method); ten-year highest flood level staked 2 Fuel Biomass A · Dry firewood C Firewood-sample moisture content measured (stir-dry weighing method, Section 50.4); count of consecutive dry-season ten-day periods fixed 3 Clay Refractory D Local clays tested by the side-by-side test-bar bend-down method (Section 40.2.4); refractoriness numbers on the register 4 Metal Open-pit D · Alluvial tin B Riverbed heavy-mineral concentrate survey at ≥3 points (Chapter 16 panning-pan method); cassiterite present/absent conclusion on the register 5 Silicon River sand B–C River sand test-fired through a small glass item (Chapter 14 procedure); without a test firing, treat as no silicon source 6 Wood A+ Rotation-harvest zoning map on the register: annual allowable cut = annual growing-stock increment × 0.8; "cut one, replant three" register in operation; mother-tree and watershed-bank no-cut zones demarcated 7 Power Water A Head × dry-season flow annual ledger (Chapter 29); a diagram of flood level vs. weir sites in hand 8 Transport Land C · River B Measured months of dry-season road passability; one loaded trial voyage of a river raft completed 9 Maintenance D (heaviest in the whole book) Corrosion coupons hung the full 90 days (Section 50.3 ③ method); mold observation samples (3 each of leather, rope, paper) placed in the observation shed 10 Labor C Weekly fever-register baseline established (Section 50.6); shift-covering roster for a 30% staffing loss trial-drafted

Two overall checks. First, dry-season length is set by measurement — the dry season begins after 3 consecutive ten-day periods with rainfall <30 mm per period; settlements with a dry season <60 days run under the "no-dry-season regime" (all sun-drying switches to the drying room, fuel ledger doubled, Section 50.2). Second, every workstation sits above the ten-year highest flood level +500 mm (siting criterion, Chapter 37), with evacuation lines staked and gong signals publicly posted.

docs.title: 50.1 Resources: Rainforest Resource Quick Reference
docs.text:
The rainforest's abundance and scarcity are two sides of the same coin: abundant rainfall means scarcity of dryness; abundant biomass means abundance of mold sources. So this section's quick reference is organized not by products, but by "which raw-material line each abundant item feeds, and which failure and substitution line each scarce item enters."

Item Rating Destination Water Abundant Power and drinking water assured (Chapter 29 waterwheel line); the cost enters failure ④ (waterborne disease) and ⑤ (flood) Wood and bamboo Very abundant Construction, fuel, and vessels all run on bamboo and wood (Chapter 13); the cost enters failure ① (mold and borers) Plant fibers (rattan, palm, bast) Abundant Rope and textile feedstock uninterrupted (Chapters 7 and 15); the cost enters failure ① Ash potash (wood ash) Abundant Industrial alkali assured: soapmaking, glass fluxing (Chapter 14), pickling aid — a chemical resource unique to the rainforest Drying Scarce All "sun-drying" operations downgraded, drying rooms moved forward; enters failure ⑥ Refractory clay Scarce High-temperature interfaces lack material; go with substitute furnace linings + frequent patching (Section 50.5) Open-pit mines Scarce The metal line falls back on the heavy-mineral concentrate survey (Chapter 16) and the recycling loop (Chapter 17) Salt Scarce Table salt is the rainforest's number-one trade item and number-one substitution problem (Section 50.5) Stone Scarce No outcrops except dry-season riverbeds; go with bamboo-reinforced rammed earth substitution + dry-season window quarrying

Core judgment: the rainforest's scarcity is not "absence" but "cannot be stored." Water, firewood, grain, leather, paper, iron — all present, and all molding, rusting, rotting. This chapter therefore manages "dryness" as the first resource: every sunny day of the dry season is rationed, allocated centrally by the rhythm table of Section 50.7.

Four rainforest-specific resource items:

  1. Bamboo — the capital for fast housebuilding. It matures in 3–5 years (trees take 20–60), the rainforest's "steel stand-in": tubes (scaffolding, water pipes, air ducts), split strips (woven walls, mats), vessels (bamboo-tube cookware). One-sentence difference from Chapter 13: in the rainforest the construction line is led by elevated bamboo-timber framing. Boundary: bamboo is not durable; the two borer-proofing methods (soaking 30–60 days, or charring the surface over fire to a light scorch) are empirical practices whose effect is verified by registered borer-hole counts; expected life after treatment is 8–15 years indoors and 3–6 years outdoors (empirical values), written into the ledger with mandatory due-date inspection.
  2. Alluvial tin — the rainforest's only welcome gift to metallurgy. Alluvial cassiterite is surveyed by the panning heavy-mineral-concentrate method (Chapter 16): with tin, the copper–tin alloy line opens early; without tin, the metal line falls back to "recycling loop + small-scale bloomery smelting" (Chapters 17 and 18), without forcing capacity. Boundary: alluvial deposits pan out — a ≥30% decline in panned output over 3 consecutive months triggers a standing alert, with an early pivot to prospecting primary ore or to trade.
  3. Rattan — king of rope sources. The backbone material for suspension bridges, lashing, and weaving (the rainforest enhancement of the Chapter 7 fiber library); freshly cut rattan enters the anti-mold process (Card 50-02) within 10 days of cutting, otherwise the strength ledger starts leaking from day one.
  4. Ash alkali — potash is not sodium salt. Leaching and evaporating slash-burn ash and charcoal-kiln ash yields potassium carbonate: soapmaking and glass fluxing (Chapter 14) can be fully self-sufficient — this is the rainforest's chemical advantage. But it must not be eaten as salt — it is bitter and purgative; the food-use boundary is in Section 50.5, written honestly.

[Card 50-01 Rainforest Site Assessment] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: the land under assessment and its surroundings; existing population and tool inventory. Do this before breaking ground — the rainforest error is "we built it and then found it will not keep," and rework costs far more than one more survey.
  2. Tools required: record board, staff gauge or flood-mark reference (mud lines on trunks, color bands on banks), rainfall proxies (moss and lichen belts, elders' accounts). Calibration source: the dry season and the flood line are measured or read from physical marks, never estimated by feel.
  3. Sequence and control points: (1) grade all nine resources in 50.1 (water; wood and bamboo; plant fiber; ash potassium; dryness; refractory clay; open-pit ore; salt; stone) → (2) walk all seven failure lines in 50.3 looking for precursors (mold and fungus; damp insulation; metal corrosion; waterborne disease; flood and landslide; drying failure; borers) → (3) map each "abundant" and each "scarce" rating onto the failure line it feeds → (4) set countermeasures and pre-emptive works for the weak items. Control points: both halves are mandatory — resources alone miss the failures, failures alone miss the usable wealth.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: dry season = three consecutive ten-day periods with under 30 mm of rain (the construction window is defined this way, not by month); flood safety line = highest flood in ten years +500 mm (hard rule — workshop and granary floor levels must sit above it). The core judgment in one sentence: what the rainforest lacks is not "things" but "keeping" — water, fuel, grain, hides, paper, iron are all present, and all of them are molding, rusting or rotting.
  5. Observations to record: all nine ratings / precursor sightings along the seven failure lines / measured flood-mark elevation / measured start and end of the dry season / weak-item list with countermeasures.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = all nine and all seven concluded, weak items have countermeasures, floor level above the flood line; rework = any item left blank (go back and measure); scrap = the site sits below the flood line and cannot be raised (move).
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) no drying capacity discovered in the rainy season → dryness was graded as abundant during assessment; it is scarce, and drying houses must move to the first construction batch (50.2); (2) the first flood fills the workshop → the flood line was never measured, replaced by a few years' memory; (3) dry-season window opened too early → judged by month instead of three consecutive ten-days under 30 mm; (4) bamboo structures collapse in two years → the borer line was not assessed and no treatment was applied (Card 50-02).
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = a complete assessment sheet (nine plus seven); L2 = the assessment's conclusions match the actual failure record of the following year; L3 = a second person assesses the same site from this card alone, flood-line readings within 300 mm.

docs.title: 50.2 Sequence: The Rainforest Technology Route
docs.text:
List of differences from the master outline's order (each with a reason; re-sequence the chapter start-ups accordingly):

Technology item Master-outline position Rainforest adjustment Reason Drying and storage facilities (drying rooms, elevated storehouses, smoke houses) With Chapters 6/10 Moved forward to the first batch The rainforest's "cannot store" precedes "cannot make" — without drying rooms, firewood, grain, green ware, and paper are all constrained Anti-malaria engineering (drainage, gauze, mosquito nets) Chapter 45 Moved forward to the settlement-siting stage Fever-driven attrition is the rainforest's number-one capacity killer, ahead of every workshop Waterwheels and bamboo-timber construction Chapters 21/13 Moved earlier, before the mining-metallurgy line Use the water-A, wood-A abundant items to the full first Salt making — Promoted early as a special project Without salt, both the food-preservation line (Chapter 10) and physiological needs are constrained; ash potash cannot substitute Pottery and glass Chapters 11/14 Glass postponed Silicon source B–C and drying scarce — the fuel/drying cost of crucibles and annealing is highest in the rainforest; pottery proceeds as usual Metal line Chapters 16–19 Start with heavy-mineral tin + the recycling loop; bloomery smelting at small scale Open-pit mines scarce; capacity waits on the alluvial-tin survey conclusion Electrical line Chapters 30–32 Postponed until the insulation system passes rainforest-adapted acceptance High-humidity insulation is the electrical line's rainforest gate (Section 50.3 ②) Paper and archives Chapter 41 Moisture-proofing add-ons moved earlier (smoke house + oil sealing) One molded batch of archives collapses a corner of the whole record-keeping system

Dry-season window discipline: all operations needing "sun" (grain, green ware, paper, firewood, leather) are completed within the dry season and sealed into storage; the rainy season does only indoor work (making, repair, medicine, teaching). Settlements with a dry season <60 days: all sun-drying switches to oven-drying (the drying-room fuel ledger goes into Chapter 42's doubled column).

docs.title: 50.3 Failure: Which Line Fails First in the Rainforest (Core of This Chapter)
docs.text:
Ordered by "fails first." Each line gives precursors (observable signals for the duty board) and the consequence chain.

No. Failure line Precursors (observable before failure) Consequence chain ① Mold and fungi (leather, rope, grain, paper — products of Chapters 15/10/45) White frost spots on leather; green patches on rope with falling tensile strength; damp caking on grain-bag inner walls; curled paper edges with mold specks Gear lost → archives destroyed → grain stores damaged — all three main lines collapse simultaneously ② High-humidity insulation failure (electrical line, Chapters 30–32) Coarse leakage test (Section 31.4.3 method) readings pronounced after rain; water beads chaining on insulators; "tingling" switch handles Shock accident → grid shutdown → whole-plant blackout ③ Metal corrosion (hot-humid year-round) Accelerated coupon weight loss (see Section 50.4); rust spots merging across tool faces Cutting-tool life halved → tool-ledger consumption doubled → capacity down ④ Waterborne disease (Chapter 45: cholera/dysentery class) Weekly fever and diarrhea counts above baseline (Section 50.6) Attrition → roster collapse (Chapter 37) → epidemic quarantine (Chapter 45) ⑤ Flood and landslide Sudden rise in river turbidity; the sound of rain upstream (water sounds at midnight) Workshops flooded → furnaces and kilns destroyed → ledgers and archives soaked ⑥ Drying failure Firewood burns sluggish when lit; grain bags warming (Chapter 10 pre-mold sign) Fuel heating value drops → furnace temperature collapses (Chapter 12 ①: check fuel) → grain stores mold ⑦ Borer insects (bamboo-timber structures) Frass powder piling at member bases; hollow knocking sound Load-bearing members of elevated structures fail → house collapse

docs.title: 50.4 Maintenance: The Rainforest Maintenance Cycle Table (All Cycles Shortened Against Earlier Chapters)
docs.text:
