docs.title: 51.10 Process Card Index
docs.text: [51-01] Ice-thickness measurement and clearance card (abstract: bore at three points, take the minimum; tiered clearance table; re-measure every ten days, plus extra measurements on any sudden temperature rise; red line = early-spring and late-winter prohibition is non-negotiable) [51-02] Pre-winter maintenance card (abstract: replace grease with thin-oil graphite grease / full re-greasing of leather / clearance recheck / belt tensioning / drain or insulate the water system — tick off item by item, complete before first frost; missed items get a hang-tag and operations are forbidden) [51-03] Three seasonal-storage ledgers card (fuel / food / spare parts: autumn storage = winter consumption × ice-season days × 1.3 redundancy; ten-day stocktakes; red line = use restricted once stock is down to half)

docs.title: 51.11 Kang Heat-Storage Stove Construction Card (Card 51-04)
docs.text:
The heat-storage stove is frozen ground's "heat battery" — the principle of one burn warming the whole night is stone-bed heat storage + a long flue:

  • Construction: firebox (stone-built, interior clear size about 2 chi square) → stone-slab kang surface (3–5 courses of large flat slabs stacked, each bedded on refractory mortar — a gap leaking smoke = CO red line) → the flue snakes through the kang interior for 2–3 bends (total flue length ≥4 m, empirical — too short and the heat runs off with the smoke; too long and draft is insufficient and smoke reverses) → smoke outlet higher than the eaves (12.3: low in, high out);
  • Firing regime: one hard burn of 1–2 h before sleep (three stages: kindling — full fire — banked fire); once the fire bed is sealed under ash, the stone bed releases heat slowly all night; in the morning the kang surface "tolerates a long touch of the back of the hand" (40–50 ℃ band) = pass;
  • Acceptance: a new kang's first firing must be a "curing burn" — three days of empty small fire to drive out moisture (a wet stone bed will condense water and steam the first night); every flue joint leak-checked with a smoke thread (burn damp grass in the firebox; wherever a seam smokes, patch it with clay);
  • CO red line restated: smoke leaking through kang seams is an odorless night killer — one smoke-thread leak check per month + watching the flame of an indoor torch (a weakening flame triggers a ventilation check).

[Card 51-04 Kang Heat-Storage Stove: Construction and Firing Regime] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: stone for the firebox (internal clear about 2 chi square), large flat stone slabs (3–5 layers for the kang surface), refractory clay mortar, ash (for banking), fuel.
  2. Tools required: masonry tools, damp straw for the smoke-line leak test, a torch for flame watching indoors. Calibration source: CO leakage is found by smoke-line testing and torch flame observation, never by smell — CO has none.
  3. Sequence and control points: stone firebox → long flue (the heat-storage body) → 3–5 layers of slab for the kang surface with refractory clay mortar bedded between slabs (a leaking joint is a CO red line) → three days of gentle test firing on a new stove (dry-out: a damp stone bed condenses water and steams the first night) → normal firing regime. Control points: bedding the slab joints and the three-day dry firing — economizing on either costs lives.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: firebox clear about 2 chi square; 3–5 slab layers; firing regime: one hard burn of 1–2 h before sleep (kindle — full fire — bank), the banked ember bed releasing heat through the stone all night; a morning kang surface you can hold the back of your hand against (40–50 °C) is the normal band; smoke-line leak test monthly plus torch flame check indoors (a weakening flame means ventilate and investigate).
  5. Observations to record: per firing — start and end times / the three phases' durations / banking time / morning hand test / flue cleaning date / leak test result.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = morning surface holds the hand, leak test shows no seep, indoor flame normal; rework = surface stays cold (too few slab layers or flue too short), or a leak (lift slabs and re-bed); scrap = firebox cracked through (rebuild; do not patch).
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) waking cold at night → the three firing phases were not completed (especially banking), or too few stone layers; (2) headache and nausea indoors → open windows, evacuate, check the flue for leakage — this is CO poisoning; (3) chimney fire → flue not cleaned monthly, tar accumulation; (4) part of the surface stays cold → flue routing short-circuits the gas path.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one stove built with dry-firing and first-month firing records; L2 = a full winter fired to the regime, no CO incident, monthly leak tests unbroken; L3 = a second person builds one from this card alone and passes both the leak test and the dry-firing acceptance.

docs.title: 51.12 Winter Bog-Iron Harvesting and Roasting (Card 51-05)
docs.text:
• Winter harvesting: select iron-rich stretches of lakes and marshes (marked in summer: oily-film water color / rusty springs on the bank); after ice clearance per Card 51-01, chop ice holes (1 chi square, spaced 3 paces apart in a line); a long-pole scoop (hemp net bag + hardwood pole) dragged along the bottom — the nodules (limonite spheres, 1–5 cm in diameter) have a distinct feel on the bottom (◎ drag feel: sand is soft, spheres are hard; half a day of practice makes it recognizable); scoop each hole 20–30 min; daily output 30–80 kg of raw ore (empirical, must be field-calibrated);
  • Sorting: drop nodules into water — sinking = real (iron nodule density 3–4); floating = mud egg, discard;
  • Roasting (critical — removes water and organic matter): spread on a stone-slab bed 3 fingers thick; gentle fire → strong fire for 2–4 h, turned twice — criteria: color turns dark red, rings clean when struck, no black core in the fracture (black core = organic matter not burned out; in the furnace it absorbs heat and makes slag); record roasting weight loss (weight loss around 30% is the normal band, empirical);
  • Into the furnace: roasted nodules are the Chapter 18 bloomery furnace's "selected ore" (grade about 40–55%; bog iron's advantage is almost no gangue — less slag, less charcoal);
  • Reserve ledger: two winters of harvesting data + a swamp-area estimate → "annual iron output" enters the Chapter 38 ledger — bog iron is sustainable, but the annual output ceiling is governed by the swamp's regeneration rate (iron-bacteria deposition adds millimeters per year; overdraft means exhaustion).

[Card 51-05 Winter Bog-Iron Harvesting and Roasting] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: bog-iron concretions (marked in summer — iridescent films on water, rusty springs at the shore; find the rich beds before winter); fuel for roasting. Ice must first be cleared per Card 51-01.
  2. Tools required: ice chisel (cutting 1 chi square holes), long-handled rake or basket, stone slab bed for roasting, mallet for the ring test. Calibration source: grade and roast completion read from the fracture and the ring, not from instruments.
  3. Sequence and control points: ice cleared → chisel holes (1 chi square, one every 3 paces) → haul concretions → sort by dropping in water (sinks = true ore, floats = mud balls, discard) → roast (spread 3 fingers thick on the slab bed, gentle fire then strong for 2–4 h, turned twice) → charge the furnace. Control points: the water-drop sort and the turning count.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: holes 1 chi square, one per 3 paces; roast criterion — color turns dull red, rings clear, no black core on the break (a black core means organics not burned out, which eats charcoal in the furnace); grade about 40–55%; bog iron's advantage is almost no gangue, so little slag and less charcoal; smelting season concentrated in summer, winter forging only (production red line).
  5. Observations to record: per winter — bed locations / hole count / total concretions / discard ratio from sorting / roast batches and turning counts / fracture readings / iron yield.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = dull red, clear ring, no black core, normal slag in the furnace; rework = black cores, spread out and roast again; scrap = heavy mud-ball contamination (the water-drop sort was skipped).
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) excessive slag in the furnace → under-roasted or poorly sorted; (2) furnace will not hold heat and charcoal burn soars → roasting incomplete, organics competing for oxygen inside; (3) mostly mud balls hauled → the summer marking was wrong, re-mark the beds; (4) holes caving in → went out on ice below clearance, back to Card 51-01.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one winter's harvest and roasting records plus one acceptable furnace charge; L2 = two consecutive winters of data, with annual iron output and bog-area estimate entered in the Chapter 38 ledger; L3 = a second person runs a winter's work from this card alone and produces acceptable ore.

[Card 51-01 Ice Thickness Measurement and Clearance] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: the ice surface to be measured (river or lake reach); a pole or rope as a safety line, one measuring and one watching. This card governs lives; the clearance criteria are not negotiable.
  2. Tools required: ice drill or chisel (to cut through), a graduated sounding rod (Chapter 3), colored marker flags. Calibration source: thickness measured with the graduated rod — never "it looks thick enough".
  3. Sequence and control points: three-point sampling (near shore, center, and any doubtful spot, one hole each) → measure thickness → take the minimum as the criterion for that reach → set the clearance class from the table → plant flags → re-survey every ten days. Control points: minimum of three points (ice varies; an average will lie) and re-measure at once when temperatures rise sharply, do not wait for the next ten-day round.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: person on foot ≥2 fists of ice, sledge load ≥3 fists (empirical, calibrate to local ice quality); red line: late winter and early spring are closed regardless — no argument — that ice is "white ice," structurally unsound however thick; re-survey every ten days.
  5. Observations to record: per survey — date and temperature / three thickness readings / the minimum used / clearance class / flag positions / interval to next survey.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = minimum meets the class and it is not a closed period; rework = short of class, narrow the clearance (foot traffic to closed) or detour; scrap = gray-blue ice or water seeping through (structure gone) — close that reach entirely.
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) a vehicle goes through → an average or single reading was used; (2) the same reach held yesterday and collapsed today → spring or thermal influence under the ice, not avoided at route selection; (3) late-spring ice thick enough yet failing → the closed-period red line was ignored; (4) readings vary widely → flowing water or air pockets beneath, take the minimum and add measurement points.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one complete three-point survey with a clearance decision; L2 = a full ice season with no gap in the ten-day surveys, and at least one active downgrade or closure in response to falling readings; L3 = a second person judges the same reach from this card alone, reaching the same clearance class.

docs.title: 51.13 Ice-Road and Sledge Transport Regulations
docs.text:
• Ice-road route selection: straight river reaches, slow current (freezes solid in winter), avoiding spring eyes and warm-spring influence stretches (locally thin ice) — route survey identical to Card 51-01's ten-day re-measurement;
  • Sledge specifications: hardwood bottom board (oak/birch) + bottom surface poured with water to freeze an ice shell (the ice shell's friction coefficient is far below a wood surface — on freezing nights pour water three times to form the shell; re-pour before each trip); load ≤1.5 times the dry-season cart load (ice-bearing redundancy);
  • Convoy discipline: spacing between sledges ≥10 paces (one ice crack does not claim the whole convoy); heavy sledges take the old ruts (compacted old ruts are safer); during spring thaw the ice road closes along its whole length regardless of load (structural degradation);
  • Efficiency ledger: ice-road freight efficiency is 1.5–2 times that of dry-season dirt roads (empirical) — winter is the frozen ground's bulk transport season, the ledger expression of the 51.4 conclusion: seasonal redistribution of transport labor hours.

docs.title: 51.14 Dugout Workshop Construction Specifications
docs.text:
• Excavation depth: half into the frozen-ground active layer (about 1–1.2 m, fixed after measured frost depth) — digging into the permafrost layer means the summer-thaw/winter-freeze cycle destroys the walls; dig only into the active layer;
  • Structure: round-log cribbed walls (each course interlocked, seams chinked with moss) + round-log floor grillage + double floor (ventilation channel underneath guards against thaw subsidence — the 51.6 gate) + sod pitched roof (soil cover ≥1 chi);
  • Zoning: furnace end (kilns, forging — flue straight through the roof) and precision end (measurement, assembly — the constant-temperature end) separated by one insulating wall; the temperature difference between the two ends can reach the 20 ℃ scale (empirical);
  • Vestibule mandatory: double-door buffer (prevents heat loss on door opening + keeps frost from striking straight into the precision end);
  • Acceptance: on an outdoor −30 ℃ class night (the team's historical extreme band), the precision end holds ≥5 ℃ and the furnace end remains workable, with the fuel ledger within Chapter 37 quotas.

docs.title: 51.15 Using the Constant-Temperature Resource (Free Precision Room)
docs.text: The cold of the frozen ground is an enemy and also a resource: the underground constant-temperature layer's temperature barely changes all year (below the active layer it stays near the annual mean year-round; 0–4 ℃ level in cold regions) — - The dugout precision end's temperature drift is far smaller than a surface building's (surface: 50 ℃ annual drift; dugout: within 10 ℃, empirical) — the "constant-temperature discipline" of Chapter 22 micrometer verification and Chapter 35 photolithography alignment is naturally half met in frozen ground; - Winter precision scheduling: the processes most afraid of temperature drift (gauge calibration, wafer measurement, instrument assembly) are fixedly scheduled at the dugout end, and kept clear of the furnace end's firing periods (firing raises the whole dugout by 2–3 ℃; calibration pieces must be offset in time from the furnace); - The food ice cellar (51.1) and the constant-temperature precision room share the same ground-temperature principle — the one-pit-two-use design is entered as a Chapter 13 building variant.

docs.title: 51.16 Frozen-Ground Farming and Fisheries: Fish-Run Calendar, Dried-Fish Line, and Cellared Vegetables
docs.text:
The frozen-ground growing season cannot feed the whole team; fishing and storage are the backbone of the winter protein ledger — this section rearranges Chapter 10's farm-storage processes for the cold region, introducing no new equipment.

Fish-run calendar (a forecasting system for the spring shore-landing window): - Principle: fish wintering under the ice come shoreward to feed during the melt period; the window is short (about 10–20 days start to finish, floating with ice conditions — empirical, needs local calibration); missing the window = losing a whole winter's protein ledger; - The three-piece calendar kit, recorded for two consecutive years: ① ice-crack day (the day structural water-permeable cracks appear in the ice) ② first-catch day (shore catch first reaches ≥10 kg of fish in a single day) ③ water-temperature signal (≥4 ℃ for 3 consecutive days at 10 cm water depth near shore); the three are cross-compared year by year into a calendar; from the third year the window can be forecast (calibration method: back-substitution testing year by year; forecast error ≤3 days = usable; if out of tolerance, add an air-temperature item the next year); - Under-ice winter fishing kit: chop ice holes and set nets (hole-chopping process same as Card 51-05; hole diameter matched to net width); net-hauling discipline — shake the net the instant it leaves the water, strip the fish the instant they leave the net (a wet net freezes hard within 10 min in low temperature; a hard net's strands snap at a single fold); - Scheduling linkage: the fish-run window = the raw-material flood peak of Card 51-07's dried-fish line; processing manpower rostered half a month ahead (the food version of the Chapter 29 redundancy law: losing people during the run = a ledger shortfall).

Dried-fish line (cold-region edition of Chapter 10 drying and Chapter 53 fish salt-drying; full operating text in Card 51-07): - Cold-region advantage: cool shade drying naturally suppresses bacteria and fly maggots; salt can be cut to under half the temperate formula (with daytime temperature in the <10 ℃ band, salt-free shade drying is possible); - A cold-region-specific reverse risk: the repeated freeze–thaw of day-sunning and night-freezing cracks the flesh tissue and squeezes out water — dehydration is fast but the tissue turns mushy, storage life shortens, and pests are attracted; rule: out by day, in by night, or favor shade drying in a ventilated shed (no direct sun, through-draft) — shade drying is the proper cold-region road; sun drying is the backup; - Dryness criterion: single-fish dry weight = 30–35% of fresh weight (empirical range, calibrated on the first run); ◎ hand-feel band: fold the fish double — the backbone snaps while the flesh face shows no water = pass; practice method: on the first run take 10 fish, weigh them through the whole process, and build an archive (archive kept in the ledger); thereafter practice 2 runs comparing the fold-snap feel against the archive; misjudgment compensation: any hand-feel doubt goes back on the scale for re-weighing.

Cellared vegetables (freeze-proof retrofit of the Chapter 10 cellar): - The only hard retrofit: burial depth below the frozen-ground line — the cellar floor must lie below the local maximum frost depth (measured frost depth entered in the Chapter 3 overwinter archive; with no data, dig test pits and measure first; copying the convenient southern depth is forbidden); - The frozen-ground cellar's risk is "too cold and freeze–thaw," not "not cold enough" (51.8 already lists thawed-then-refrozen = discard): target cellar temperature 0–4 ℃; ◎ temperature-control criterion (bowl-ice method): hang a bowl of water at the cellar mouth — a full bowl of ice by morning = too cold (add a straw seal layer), no ice = too warm (enlarge the vent), a one-finger ice shell not filling the bowl = pass; practice method: calibrate by comparing two consecutive ten-day periods of bowl appearance against actual vegetable condition at cellar opening; misjudgment compensation: one max-min thermometer (Chapter 3 temperature-measurement item) kept in the cellar; - Stacking and cellar-entry safety: frost-hardy vegetables (Chinese cabbage, turnip) by the door side; frost-tender vegetables (potato, radish) in the middle and upper layers; potatoes turn green and poisonous in light — use a shaded lamp with weak light inside the cellar; lamp test before entering (Chapter 6 oxygen-deficiency red line: carry a lantern in; if the flame weakens or goes out, the person withdraws and the cellar is ventilated); cellar work in two-person teams.

Short-season crop seed selection (cold-region reweighting of Chapter 10's three criteria): - Weights become: earliness > cold hardiness > yield — without enough growing days, the yield criterion is meaningless; - Hard criterion: keep only varieties with "growing period ≤ local frost-free period × 0.8" as seed stock (20% redundancy against early frost); fields still green on first-frost day are registered as "late-ripening abandoned fields" and excluded from seed stock the following year; - Directed domestication: each year, separately harvest and store the earliest-ripening 10% of plants as seed — after 5–8 consecutive generations clear earliness is visible (empirical; register ripening date and grain weight yearly in the ledger; a break in the generations undoes all prior work).

docs.title: 51.17 Fur and Leather Processing (Cold-Region Edition of Chapter 15)
docs.text:
In frozen ground, pelts are both clothing raw material and hard currency of trade. Chapter 15's tanning mostly takes dehaired leather as its main line; the cold-region specialization is hair-on tanning — hair that does not mat, underfur that does not shed, a pelt that does not rot.

Two routes of hair-on pelt tanning: - Brain tanning (first choice for next-to-skin clothing): brush an emulsion of animal brains on the flesh side — 1–2 brains per pelt (the starting ratio to pelt area is empirical; in the first season build an archive of brain amounts matched to pelt sizes); mash the brain with warm water into an emulsion (enough that rubbing between fingers yields no grittiness), coat the flesh side fully, roll up and leave half a day, scrape off the excess and spread out; half of success lies in stretching: repeatedly pull and knead throughout, from half-dry to fully dry; a skin that hardens after drying = insufficient stretching; rework method: let the pelt re-dampen overnight wrapped in a wet cloth, then re-coat and re-stretch; pass criteria: rustles softly and feels supple when kneaded, no dead crease when folded, hair stands when shaken with the fur side out; - Smoke tanning (first choice for tent curtains and boot uppers): hang the pelt above a smoke pit to smoke; aldehydes in the smoke fix the skin while repelling insects and moisture; start with the pelt 30 cm from the smoke source (empirical; calibration: hold the back of your hand between pelt and smoke source — a long touch without scalding means the distance is right; if it scalds, raise it); smoke material: decayed wood and birch-bark shavings (resin-rich open-flame smoke turns sticky and deposits black — reject); turn the pelt every 2 h; 4–8 h in total; - Combined route: brain tanning followed by smoke tanning is the most durable but doubles labor hours — choose by use and enter it in the ledger; the whole team's pelts may not all be double-processed (labor-hour discipline).

Pelt grading (three tests, one unified trade standard): - First test, underfur depth: part the guard hairs and look at the underfur layer — skin not visible = top-grade winter pelt; needle substitute: a fine needle inserted into the underfur disappears with no tip showing = top grade (this is the compensation for tactile misjudgment of the second test); - Second test, skin softness: fold, squeeze, release — the crease smooths out at once = soft skin (usable for next-to-skin clothing); the crease stays = stiff skin (downgraded to straps and gear wraps); - Third test, hair shedding: push the palm against the grain three times — no hair falls = sound; up to 3–5 hairs fall = downgraded to lining; hair falls in clumps = hair roots damaged (acid rot or decay already deep); shave the hair, keep the skin, handle as a separate case; - ◎ grade-banding practice: blind-sort 20 pelts into three grades and compare against a skilled hand's results; ≤4 errors to graduate; misjudgment compensation is the needle test / fold test / stroke count from the three tests above — any doubt in hand feel defers to the physical-evidence tests; grading by eye alone is not permitted.

Moth-proof winter storage: - The insect-damage window is the warming-back period and summer cellar storage, not deep winter: smoke once before storage (same pit as smoke tanning; doubles as insect proofing); hang mugwort or camphor bundles in the store (use if available locally); shake out and air once per ten days on a clear day (in ventilated shade; direct sunlight forbidden — sunning fades the underfur color and embrittles the skin); - Bookkeeping: grading results enter the team ledger as "grade × count"; in trade, keep the standard unified — top-grade winter pelts and off-grade pelts differ severalfold in price; selling mixed grades = a loss on the books.

docs.title: 51.18 Hypothermia and Frostbite Protection (Chapter 44 Interface)
docs.text:
In frozen ground the bulk of casualties is cold injury, not industrial injury. This section is the cold-region specialization of the Chapter 44 medical general principles; the handling discipline is trained to the whole team — cold-injury first aid cannot wait for medics to arrive; the first handler is the workmate at your side.

Hypothermia grading and rewarming procedure: - Grade by behavior, not by self-report (a hypothermia victim's self-assessment cannot be trusted): stage one, shivering phase — unceasing shivering, clumsy movements, normal answers; stage two, dullness phase — shivering weakens, speech slows, "paradoxical undressing" appears (feels hot and wants to remove clothing; an extremely dangerous sign); stage three, rigid phase — shivering stops, cannot walk unaided. Shivering stopping is not improvement but worsening — the frozen ground's most lethal misjudgment (posted verbatim on the duty board); - Rewarming procedure (field handling for stages one and two): move into a warm room → strip wet clothes and change into dry → warm sugar water for anyone who can swallow → warm-water bags placed over clothing against the torso (bag temperature not above 45 ℃, the "long touch of the back of the hand without scalding" band); rapid heating is forbidden (fire-roasting, pouring hot water directly, rubbing the limbs) — principle: in severe hypothermia, the limbs' cold blood surging back to the core makes core temperature first fall and then destabilize (rewarming shock); and frost-numbed skin has lost sensation, so fire-roasting inevitably burns without the victim knowing; - For stage three the field does one thing only: stop further heat loss — wrap in dry clothes and dry blankets, carry flat with no jolting (rough handling can trigger arrhythmia); rewarming is handed to medical care (Chapter 44 interface; transport observation records in Chapter 44 format); - Observation record: consciousness, shivering, and breathing recorded every 10 min (a dedicated recorder for the whole rescue; reconstructing from memory afterward is not allowed).

Four-degree frostbite interpretation and handling boundaries: - First degree, frost-reddened: pale turns red and swollen, tingling and itching — after rewarming and warming, apply grease; may remain on a light-duty post; - Second degree, blisters: clear blisters appear after rewarming — do not pierce them (an intact blister is a sterile natural dressing); for blisters too large for bandaging, puncture-drain at the blister edge and keep the blister skin as a cover; - Third degree (purplish-black necrosis through the full skin layer) and fourth degree (deep into muscle and bone): on site, only keep warm and send for care; all debridement, piercing-scraping, and ointment attempts are forbidden (Chapter 44 handling boundary; any field "treatment" manufactures infection); - Rewarming operation: immerse the frozen limb in 38–42 ℃ water for 20–30 min — water temperature must never be set by the casualty (a frozen limb has no sensation and will certainly be scalded); the standard is a healthy person's elbow finding it acceptable; effective-rewarming criteria = skin reddens and sensation returns in the "numbness → pain → itch" sequence (pain is good news); - Red lines: an un-rewarmed frozen limb must not be rubbed (ice crystals are cutting tissue; rubbing = doubled mechanical damage), must not be fire-roasted, must not be walked on (walking on frostbitten feet = crushing tissue with every step).

Snow-blindness prevention (smoke-darkened slit goggles): - Mechanism: strong light reflected off snow burns the cornea; symptoms appear only that evening (eye pain, tearing, photophobia) — same-day snowfield exposure is easily missed as the cause and mistaken for "caught a chill getting up at night"; - Making them: birch bark or thin wood slats with horizontal slits (slit length about 30 mm, slit width about 5 mm, empirical; calibration: being able to clearly make out the ground within three steps of your feet = slit width acceptable), inner face smoke-darkened to cut glare, cords on both sides, worn goggle-style; - Handling: rest shielded from light 1–3 days, cold compress for pain; self-healing is possible; repeated snow blindness = cumulative corneal damage — goggles on snowfield work are discipline, not an option (add one line to the morning checklist: "goggles carried").

Winter clothing layering system: - Three-layer system: inner layer wicks sweat (fine soft fabric next to the skin, changed as soon as it is sweat-soaked — wet underwear is hypothermia's first accomplice); middle layer stores heat (many thin fluffy layers beat one thick wrap; layer counts set for the three bands −10/−20/−30 ℃); outer layer blocks wind (fur or dense weave; the point is wind blocking); - Work discipline: at the first light sweat from work, open the outer layer to shed heat; for static posts (night watch, ice fishing, sentry duty), changing into a dry inner layer before going on duty is mandatory; personnel with a frostbite history are registered by post (the risk of refreezing the same site is doubled); - Morning mutual check: before setting out, two people face each other — white cheeks or fingertips (first-degree frostbite omens) are rubbed warm on the spot before work resumes; white patches that do not recede mean stopping work for treatment.

docs.title: 51.19 Frostbite Treatment Card (Card 51-06, eight-field abstract)
docs.text:
• ① Input materials: warm water 38–42 ℃ (≥10 L per session, must submerge the injured limb), dry clothes and dry blankets, warm-water bags placed over clothing, warm sugar water, clean dressings; substitute: mild stage one/two cases may use mutual body-heat warming (armpit, abdomen); alcohol rubbing forbidden; snow rubbing forbidden.
  • ② Required tools: water thermometer (Chapter 3 temperature-measurement item, ice-point calibrated); emergency compensation: crushed-ice chips floating up in the water mean temperature out of tolerance — discard and do not use.
  • ③ Operation sequence and control points: remove frozen shoes and gloves (pour warm water where stuck to skin to separate; hard tearing forbidden) → immerse in 38–42 ℃ water 20–30 min → remove, wrap in dry dressings, elevate the injured limb → blisters not pierced → keep warm under observation or send for care. Control point: water temperature maintained throughout; when changing or heating water, lift the injured limb out first, then add hot water.
  • ④ Empirical parameters and calibration: water temperature 38–42 ℃ — calibration: a healthy person's elbow immersed 5 s finding it "warm but not hot" = the acceptable band; the rewarming-duration criterion takes precedence over the clock (stop when skin reddens and sensation gradually returns).
  • ⑤ Process record items: body part / color at first sight / blisters present or not / water temperature and rewarming time / consciousness and shivering state — recorded item by item in the Chapter 44 medical-record format.
  • ⑥ Pass / rework / handover: pass = reddening, sensation returning; rework = still pale (recheck water temperature and re-immerse, at most two rounds); handover = purplish-black, cloudy blister fluid, severe pain after rewarming that will not stop (third degree or above; keep warm and send for care).
  • ⑦ Failure troubleshooting (verify in order for the same symptom): no reddening after 30 min of rewarming — ① water temperature insufficient (re-measure by thermometer or elbow test) → ② incomplete immersion (shoes, socks, gloves not fully removed) → ③ third-degree or worse frostbite (send for care immediately).
  • ⑧ L1/L2/L3 evidence: L1 one treatment record; L2 whole-team training assessment (simulated treatment, everyone passes; roster archived); L3 archive of actual winter cases and review records.

[Card 51-06 Frostbite Treatment] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: water at 38–42 °C (at least 10 L per immersion, enough to submerge the limb); dry clothing and blankets; warm water bottles wrapped in cloth; warm sugar water; clean dressings. First- and second-degree cases may use body-warmth rewarming; third degree and above require water.
  2. Tools required: water thermometer (Chapter 3 instrument, ice-point calibrated); fallback — if ice crystals float in the water it is over temperature, discard it. No thermometer is not a reason to skip treatment.
  3. Sequence and control points: remove frozen boots and gloves (separate stuck skin with warm water pouring, never tear) → immerse in 38–42 °C water for 20–30 min → wrap in dry dressings and elevate → give warm sugar water → record → decide on referral. Control points: no rubbing, no fire, no snow (these three cause most frostbite disability); err on the cool side of the temperature range.
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: water 38–42 °C (calibrated by a healthy elbow: 5 s feels "warm, not hot"); rewarming time is judged by tissue, not by clock — skin turning pink and sensation returning means done; the clock does not.
  5. Observations to record: site / initial color / blisters present / water temperature and rewarming time / consciousness and shivering state — recorded item by item in the Chapter 44 case format.
  6. Pass / rework / referral criteria: pass = pink and sensation returned; rework = still pale (recheck water temperature and immerse again, at most twice); referral = purple-black, cloudy blister fluid, no sensation after rewarming (to surgery — Chapter 44 debridement, Chapter 49 amputation red lines).
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) still pale after 30 min → (a) water too cool (measure or elbow-check) → (b) immersion incomplete (boots, socks, gloves not fully off) → (c) water too shallow to submerge; (2) large blisters turning black after rewarming → third degree reached, stop rewarming and refer; (3) patient shivering uncontrollably → whole-body hypothermia; rewarm the trunk before the extremities (Chapter 44 hypothermia-first rule).
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one treatment record; L2 = whole-team training with every member passing a simulated case, names on file; L3 = actual winter case files with review records.

docs.title: 51.20 Dried-Fish Line Card (Card 51-07, eight-field abstract)
docs.text:
• ① Input materials: fresh run fish (into the line within ≤2 h of leaving the water; if over time, salt first, then dry), salt (if available: 5–10% of fish weight; salt-free if daytime temperature is in the <10 ℃ band), drying-rack poles and rope netting; hang 30–50 fish per rack, one fist apart, not touching back-to-back.
  • ② Required tools: fish-splitting knife (Chapter 7 blade, sharpened its full length), scale (Chapter 3; rechecked against standard stones on the first day of the run), drying shed (ventilated, no direct sun).
  • ③ Operation sequence and control points: gut (a broken gall = the whole fish downgraded; excise the bile-contaminated section of the cavity) → split along the back and spread flat, backbone unbroken → salt-cure 0.5–1 day (salt-using band) → hang on racks to shade-dry → turn every 2 days → take down when the dryness standard is met. Control point: out by day and in by night, or shade-dry inside the shed the whole time, to prevent freeze–thaw cycles.
  • ④ Empirical parameters and calibration: dryness = 30–35% of fresh weight (calibration: on the first run take 10 fish, weigh through the whole process, build the archive into the ledger); drying period 5–10 days (governed by the dryness criterion, not the calendar).
  • ⑤ Process record items: fresh weight / salt amount / dry weight at take-down / drying days / weather — entered in the ledger rack by rack; compute the shrink ratio (dry weight ÷ fresh weight).
  • ⑥ Pass / rework / scrap: pass = backbone snaps on fold, no wet fingerprints on the flesh face, no mold, no maggots; rework = wet-soft fingerprints (re-hang 2–3 days); scrap = mold patches joining up, maggot burrows, gray foul rot after freeze–thaw (discard or into field fertilizer; eating forbidden).
  • ⑦ Failure troubleshooting (verify in order for the same symptom): fish racks going slimy in batches — ① hang spacing too dense, no ventilation → ② left out in the rain and re-dampened → ③ raw material out of water too long (salt the next batch earlier).
  • ⑧ L1/L2/L3 evidence: L1 one sample fish kept from the first qualified rack; L2 three consecutive racks with pass rate ≥8/10; L3 full-run shrink-ratio table and winter consumption review.

[Card 51-07 Dried-Fish Line] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: fish from the run (into the line within 2 h of leaving water; beyond that, salt first then dry); salt if available (5–10% of fish weight; may be omitted when daytime temperature is below 10 °C). Time out of water is this line's first criterion, not its last.
  2. Tools required: filleting knife (Chapter 7 edge, fully sharpened), balance (Chapter 3, rechecked against the standard stone on the first day of the run), drying rack (ventilated, not in direct sun).
  3. Sequence and control points: gut (a cut gallbladder downgrades the whole fish; the bile-contaminated section must be removed) → split along the back and flatten, backbone intact → salt 0.5–1 day (if using salt) → rack and dry → weigh down. Control points: gallbladder removal and backbone left intact (a broken backbone will not flatten, and an unflattened fish will not dry through).
  4. Empirical parameters and calibration: dryness = 30–35% of fresh weight (calibrate by weighing 10 fish through the full process on the first run and filing the record); drying period 5–10 days (governed by the dryness criterion, not the calendar); salt 5–10%; salt-free band when daytime is below 10 °C.
  5. Observations to record: per rack — fresh weight / salt used / dried weight off the rack / drying days / weather — every rack into the ledger, with the yield ratio (dry ÷ fresh) computed.
  6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = backbone snaps when folded, no damp fingerprint on the flesh, no mold, no maggots; rework = damp and soft (rehang 2–3 days); scrap = continuous mold or maggots (discard the rack, never mix it in).
  7. Common failures and diagnosis order: (1) racks go tacky in bulk → (a) hanging too close for air movement → (b) rain-damp and not taken in → (c) fish held beyond 2 h out of water (salt the next batch); (2) dries hard outside, wet inside → rack in direct sun, move to ventilated shade; (3) mold → humidity high or drying period short; check whether the yield ratio was met; (4) abnormally low yield ratio → fish not fresh and already dehydrated (held too long).
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one acceptable dried fish kept as a sample from the first rack; L2 = three consecutive racks at ≥8/10 pass rate; L3 = a full-run yield-ratio table plus a winter consumption review.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• L1: insulated house + heat-storage stove pass a real winter test (fuel ledger meets target); the three seasonal-storage ledgers established; first bog iron into the furnace; the ice-thickness tiered table field-measured and archived.
  • L2: one full season of continuous winter production in the dugout workshop; dual-power switchover running; pre-winter maintenance card two years with no missed items; thaw-subsidence observation system running.
  • L3: ice-road freight in routine operation; battery room at full capacity in winter; "winter does not reduce output" — proven by the output ledgers of two full winters.

docs.title: Safety Boundaries
docs.text:
• CO discipline doubled (sealed-space heating = the most dangerous combination under the Chapter 6 red line; vents-stay-open rule); solo outdoor travel forbidden (hypothermia rescue windows are counted in minutes);
  • On ice, trust only measurement, never appearance; cast iron forbidden for impact in winter; monthly chimney cleaning for fire prevention.

docs.title: Chapter Objectives
docs.text: Gives the complete reconstruction execution plan for desert conditions: water resource survey → five-stage route → special-risk sections. This chapter introduces no new technology; it does only reordering and desert adaptation; the core proposition is "process basket selection" under the doubly tight constraint of the water ledger and the fuel ledger.

docs.title: Capability Boundaries
docs.text: Can do: the four water-source steps (survey–store–convey–conserve) and the qanat; low-water-use buildings and wind towers; solar-heat-assisted kilns and the salt–nitrate chemistry line; the anti-sand machinery system; adjudicating the industrial basket with the water unit-consumption table. Explicitly cannot: large-scale supply of non-mineralized fresh water (distillation covers drinking only); high-water-use industries (papermaking / wet chemistry at restricted output); photovoltaics (a far-generation item); changing sandstorms and drought (only contingency plans possible). External dependencies: fuel (the vegetation regrowth rate is the production ceiling — trading for fuel is the norm, not a failure); the annual groundwater ledger.

docs.title: Environmental Assumptions (Assessment Table Conclusions)
docs.text: Item Typical Desert Answer Consequence for the Route Water Scarce / point-sourced (oases, groundwater) Water is the first line of every ledger Sunshine Extremely abundant Solar heat and the photovoltaic horizon (Section 52.5) Biomass Sparse (shrubs, date palms) An extremely tight fuel budget Minerals Salts / gypsum / (possibly metals) A distinctive salt chemistry line Temperature swing Large between day and night Thermal fatigue in buildings and materials

docs.title: Minimum Preconditions
docs.text: The Parts One-through-Six technology library + water resource reconnaissance (oasis yield, groundwater depth, rainy-season patterns — the desert version of the Chapter 2 survey; settlement is forbidden until this step is complete).

docs.title: 52.1 Stage One: The Water Resource Survey
docs.text:
• Three water-source surveys: ① oasis yield (measured by day-and-night pumping + dry-season recheck); ② groundwater (digging under dry riverbeds, seepage at the mountain-front gobi — plant indicators: shallow water beneath reed/tamarisk clusters); ③ rainy-season flash floods and lowland ponding (collection windows);
  • Water storage: underground cisterns (Chapter 13 mortar + bitumen/clay sealing) — cover slab + soil cover against evaporation (an open pool in the desert is a sieve);
  • The qanat (underground-channel conveyance): mountain-foot groundwater is led by gravity through a gently descending underground channel to the oasis — evaporation loss far below that of an open channel; excavation in segments via vertical shafts (Chapter 16 surveying + Chapter 13 masonry); yield registered by the Chapter 25 volumetric method;
  • Water-saving discipline: every process registers its unit water consumption (first place in the desert version of the Chapter 23 ledger); washing water reused in grades (clean–grey–foul, three grades);
  • Solar distillation (a starter device for brackish-water desalination): Chapter 24 glass/transparent sheet + a black-bottomed shallow pool; seawater/brackish water evaporated and the condensate collected — low yield but zero fuel; serves as the drinking-water bottom line (enough to sustain life, not enough to support industry — an honest positioning).

[Card 52-01 Three Water-Source Checks and Qanat Yield] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: three candidate water-source points (① oasis ② dry riverbed / mountain-front gobi seepage ③ rainy-season flash-flood and lowland ponding windows); the qanat outlet (completed test section); a water-point ledger. No large group moves in before the annual water survey is done — this card is the gate on settlement.
  2. Tools required: a measuring vessel (Chapter 25 volumetric method), pacing bow and rope-and-line (Chapter 3), test-digging tools (for probing shafts), a dedicated tasting spoon (salinity, one person's own). Calibration source: yield is accepted only from consecutive volumetric measurements, never from "it looks enough".
  3. Operation sequence and control points: ① oasis yield — day-and-night pumping measured + dry-season recheck; ② groundwater — dig under dry riverbeds and at mountain-front gobi seepage, reading the plant indicators (shallow water beneath reed/tamarisk clusters); ③ rainy-season flash floods and lowland ponding — register the collection windows; ④ the qanat outlet measured by the volumetric method three consecutive days; ⑤ ten-day tasting of salinity / turbidity / flavor into the ledger. Control points: both the day and the night readings are required (daylight-only measurement overstates the yield); the dry-season recheck is the one that decides "can we settle"; missing one of the three days means measuring again.
  4. Experiential parameters and calibration method: warning line = down twenty percent for two consecutive ten-day periods → investigate silting/collapse; inspection shafts one per 60 paces, ten-day siltation checks in the sandstorm season, one major cleanout a year; water quality tasted every ten days (salinity / turbidity / flavor, dedicated spoon and taster); the qanat is depreciated over fifty years. These are the chapter's master-table and Section 52.11 values; local yield is re-calibrated yearly by the volumetric method.
  5. In-process observation items: per point record date / day-and-night pumped volume / dry-season recheck value / water-struck depth in the test shafts (the basis for the water-table trend) / salinity, turbidity, flavor / the ten-day value and the two-period decline.
  6. Accept / rework / scrap criteria: accept = all three surveys complete, three-day flow stable, no consecutive rise in salinity; rework = down twenty percent over two ten-day periods (investigate silting: ten-day checks locate the shaft section for desilting); scrap = the well site is irreversibly salinized or a collapsed channel section cannot be repaired (that well or section is retired and the backup source opened).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: ① ten-day yield decline → check silting first → then collapsed sections → finally the water table (the annual water-level ledger assigns responsibility); ② water turning salty period by period → check for over-abstraction → cut withdrawal and open the backup; ③ test digging strikes no water → plant indicators misread or the water-table trend mis-set (back to 52.11 route selection); ④ water in the rainy season, dry in the dry season → only one survey was done, the dry-season recheck was skipped.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one complete triple survey plus the qanat outlet's three-day measurement; L2 = a full year's ledger including the dry season, with the warning line triggered at least once and a disposition recorded; L3 = a second person independently re-measuring the same source per this card, the two volumetric readings agreeing.

docs.title: 52.2 Stage Two: Low-Water Materials and Building
docs.text:
• Building: thick adobe walls (thermal inertia — absorbs heat by day, releases it at night, a time-lag regulator) + high small windows + inner courtyard; wind tower (wind catching + evaporative cooling: air crosses a wet curtain carrying moisture into the rooms — desert air conditioning); arches and domes (large spans in unreinforced adobe — the desert specialization of Chapter 13 masonry);
  • Stone and gypsum: sandstone cuts easily (extractable with Chapter 5 stone tools alone); gypsum calcination (Chapter 23) for plastering and molds;
  • Wind and sand control: lattice sand fences (fences of upright shrub branches that pile drifting sand into ridges); double-layer doorway porches (entering the house first passes through a dust-settling vestibule — the same principle as the permafrost cold-porch, intercepting a different intruder).

[Card 52-02 Anti-Sand Day Procedure] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: the day's sandstorm warning (yellow dust / black wind, two levels); machinery (bearings / guideways / gearboxes), optical surfaces, electrical insulators, water pools; grease (dust sealing), rags, boxes and covers.
  2. Tools required: blow-off device (air blower / bellows), soft cloth, grease gun, box-type storage containers, pool covers. Calibration source: whether the blow-out is done shows in the oil colour and the running noise, not in "I swept it once".
  3. Operation sequence and control points: grade the day in the morning (yellow dust = stop outdoor machinery + cover optical surfaces; black wind = everyone indoors, doors and windows sealed) → daily blow-out of machinery on dust days (machine by machine) → optical surfaces by the three steps "blow – wipe – cover" (wiped and boxed immediately after use + blow-off with the air blower) → clear dust off insulators at once, special patrol immediately after rain → remove dust from pools and cover them. Control points: blow before wiping (wiping straight away = grinding the mirror with sand grains; a scratch is irreversible); graded actions follow the warning level — no improvising up, no discounting down.
  4. Experiential parameters and calibration method: daily blow-out (dust days) + weekly oil change; optical surfaces wiped and boxed immediately after use; insulators patrolled immediately after rain (dust meeting water = a leakage eruption point); routine blow-out is 0.5 man-hour per day on the duty post; sandstorms run the two-level yellow-dust / black-wind plan, and once warned, high-place and outdoor machinery work stops.
  5. In-process observation items: daily record wind force and warning level / number of machines blown out / oil colour / optical-surface disposition / insulator patrol result / pool dust removal.
  6. Accept / rework / scrap criteria: accept = every machine blown out and signed for that day, no scratched optical surface, no leakage on the post-rain patrol; rework = grey oil or raspy running noise (precursor of dust ingress) → change the oil and check the dust seal; scrap = a seized bearing, or a scratched optical surface (irreversible).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: ① raspy running noise, temperature rise early → dust ingress (seal failed; check the dust seal and the grease); ② scratched optical surface → the "blow – wipe – cover" steps were not all done; ③ leakage after rain → insulator dust not cleared, patrol not done; ④ pool water green and salty → not covered, dust not removed.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one sandstorm season of daily blow-out records; L2 = a whole season with zero seized shafts, zero scratched optics, and no gap in the post-rain patrols; L3 = a second person independently running one day's procedure per this card with every item signed.

docs.title: 52.3 Stage Three: Heat Energy and Basic Chemistry
docs.text:
• Kiln strategy under the tight fuel constraint: ① solar preheating (materials sun-dried through the day before charging, saving over one tenth of fuel; experiential value, must be field-calibrated); ② doubled kiln-body insulation (Chapter 12 thermal insulation) + miniaturization (match daily output, not scale vanity); ③ a shrub-firewood quota system (annual regrowth = the cutting cap; the same discipline as Chapter 50);
  • The salt chemistry line (desert specialty): salt pans and salt lakes → table salt + Glauber's salt + (where present) nitrate-bearing soil layers (identification per Chapter 23); nitrates (Chile-saltpeter-type deposits) are a natural treasury of gunpowder and nitrogen feedstock — the desert may leap at a bound into a "chemistry-rich zone" (coexisting with fuel poverty; record this contradiction truthfully);
  • Direct-sun processes: evaporative crystallization (the zero-fuel version of Chapter 26 crystallization), sun-curing of salt, partial pre-calcination of gypsum;
  • Glass: good quartz sand is often at hand (the desert = a glass raw-material bank) — but melting consumes fuel, clashing with the tight fuel constraint: glass in the desert is a candidate for "export in exchange for fuel," not a local consumer good (route economics, adjudicated by Chapter 29 accounting).

[Card 52-03 Fuel Quota] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: measured shrub regrowth (quadrats), the cutting ledger, quota tags (to household and to kiln), measured cutting-radius records.
  2. Tools required: quadrat rope and pacing bow (Chapter 3), scales, the reconciliation ledger (Chapter 38). Calibration source: regrowth is accepted only from quadrat measurement, never from last year's consumption.
  3. Operation sequence and control points: measure regrowth by quadrat → set the annual cutting cap = regrowth × 0.8 → issue quotas to households and kilns (tagged) → monthly reconciliation → measure the cutting radius → a 10 percent expansion = yellow warning → cut quotas or trade for fuel. Control points: the cap is computed from measured regrowth, not from last year's usage; the cutting radius is the most sensitive gauge (expansion = the vegetation is being eaten through).
  4. Experiential parameters and calibration method: cutting cap = regrowth × 0.8; quotas to households and kilns; radius expanding 10 percent = yellow warning (Chapter 42 linkage); monthly reconciliation + radius measurement; the vegetation regrowth rate is the production ceiling — trading for fuel is the norm, not a failure.
  5. In-process observation items: per season record quadrat regrowth / the annual cap / each household's and kiln's quota and actual use / cutting radius / warning dates and dispositions.
  6. Accept / rework / scrap criteria: accept = annual use within the cap and the radius not expanded; rework = radius expanded 10 percent (cut quotas + trade for fuel, and re-measure regrowth); scrap = quota breach stopping the kiln line (review and reset the cap — eating the vegetation bare in three years is the desert version of a historical failure).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: ① kiln fuel exhausted → quota breach (activate the red line, trade for fuel); ② cutting radius expanding year by year → the cap was set too high (regrowth mismeasured, or the cap set from usage); ③ damp wood, weak fire → a dry-storage problem, not a quota problem; ④ quota disputes → quotas never reached household and kiln (no tags, no ledger).
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one year of quota and reconciliation ledgers; L2 = two consecutive years with no radius expansion and no fuel-driven stoppage; L3 = a second person re-measuring the same quadrats and independently computing the cap, with consistent results.

docs.title: 52.4 Stage Four: Metals and Machinery
docs.text:
• Ore-source determinism (Chapter 16 general survey first): desert-type deposits (residual/slope-wash, placer, open oxidized zones) are easy to mine, hard to smelt (fuel and water lacking) — smelting schedules are capped by the "fuel transport radius";
  • A closed water loop for metallurgy: reuse pools for quench and ore-wash water (brine concentrated by evaporation handled separately — every liter of water must have its destination registered);
  • Machinery: dust is the killer of bearings and guideways (the desert version of the Chapter 33 three protections) — sealed bearings + grease dust seals + daily blow-out; fully enclosed gearbox design takes priority over open belts (better low efficiency than ingress of sand).

docs.title: 52.5 Stage Five: Power Generation and Electronics
docs.text:
• The early phase unchanged: waterwheels (qanat flow is small, often enough only for small machines) or animal power / a little steam (constrained by the fuel ledger);
  • Wind as the mainstay: the desert's day–night thermal convection winds plus perennial wind belts — windmill + elevated reservoir (the Chapter 29 wind–pool pairing) is the desert's standard powerplant;
  • Solar power generation (registered as a long-range item): the heat-engine route (concentrator-made steam driving a Chapter 28 engine type — the concentrator mirror = the Chapter 24 mirror process scaled up, registered as a key-attack item); photovoltaics belong to the far generation of the Chapter 34 purity ladder and are not promised;
  • Electronics: sand-proof sealed packaging (the Chapter 36 harsh-environment grade) + thermal-cycling qualification (large day–night temperature swings = heat-fatigue accelerated aging; add this page to the failure atlas).

docs.title: 52.6 Special Sections of the Desert Version
docs.text:
1. How water limits industrial scale: the "water unit-consumption table" for every class of process decides the industrial basket — high water use (papermaking, wet chemistry, steam) is restricted; low water use (dry chemistry, machinery, optics) has priority;
  2. The applicable boundary of solar heat: preheating and sun-drying processes are zero-risk; concentrated high temperature demands tracking and safety (the Chapter 24 focused-ignition risk); "solar abundance" does not equal "high-temperature processes for free" — collection, storage, and temperature control are independent engineering problems (the executed version of the Chapter 29 warning);
  3. The effects of dust on machinery / optics / electrics: optical surfaces (lenses and mirrors) are never stored exposed (box storage + unboxed only for use); dust on electrical porcelain skirts turns conductive (special patrol after rain — in the desert "after rain" is the high season for leakage);
  4. Water storage and chemical operations under high evaporation: open chemical pools are forbidden (concentration runs away); reagents are made up "at the moment of use";
  5. A system minimizing dependence on external transport: a spares localization-rate metric (the desert weighting of the Chapter 36 inventory) — long supply lines themselves consume water and fuel; "make it rather than buy it" is, in the desert, a survival algorithm and not merely an economic one.

docs.title: 52.7 Failure: Which Line Breaks First in the Desert (Second of the Five Review Angles)
docs.text: No. Failure Line Precursor Consequence Chain ① Dust ingress into machinery (bearings / guideways / gears) Running noise turning raspy, oil turning grey, temperature rise arriving early Seized shaft → shutdown; scratched optical surfaces (irreversible) ② Water-line supply cut (qanat silting/collapse, wells turning saline) Ten-day yield decline, changing taste and salinity (under registration) Whole-plant water outage — the king of desert failures ③ Day–night thermal fatigue (glass / metal / seals) Morning-and-evening "clicks" from glass, hairline cracks in welds, seeping seals Vessels shatter, lines leak, electronic packages die young ④ Fuel quota breach (shrub regrowth outpaced by cutting) Cutting radius expanding year by year (checked against the Chapter 38 ledger) Kiln lines stop — eating the vegetation bare in three years is the desert version of a historical failure ⑤ Evaporation miscalculation (open pools / reagents / stored water) Pool liquor concentrating daily, reagents crystallizing Runaway concentration = a wellspring of chemical accidents (the desert version of the Chapter 26 red line) ⑥ Stored-water contamination (dust into pools / algae) A floating dust film on the pool, water taste changing Waterborne disease (Chapter 45) — the desert's "wet" diseases kill just the same

docs.title: 52.8 Maintenance: The Desert Periodic Table
docs.text: Item Conventional Cycle Desert Cycle Machinery blow-out / oil change Weekly check Daily blow-out (on dust days) + weekly oil change Qanat shafts and underground channel Quarterly check Ten-day siltation checks (in the sandstorm season) + annual major cleanout Optical surfaces Boxed after use Wiped and boxed immediately after use + blow-off with the air blower Insulators / electrics Special patrol after rain Immediate post-rain special patrol (dust meeting water = a leakage eruption point) Water quality Monthly check Ten-day taste registration (salinity / turbidity / flavor — a dedicated spoon and a dedicated taster) Fuel quota reconciliation Monthly Monthly + measured cutting radius (checked against the Chapter 38 red line)
