docs.title: 52.10 Process Card Index
docs.text: [52-01] Water-Source Triple Survey and Qanat Yield Card (summary: measured day-and-night pumping × dry-season recheck; daily yield registered by the volumetric method (Chapter 25); ten-day salinity tastings entered in the ledger; warning line = yield down twenty percent for two consecutive ten-day periods → check for silting/collapse) [52-02] Anti-Sand Day Procedure Card (summary: graded sandstorm warnings — yellow dust = stop outdoor machinery and cover optical surfaces; black wind = everyone indoors, doors and windows sealed; after sand = daily machinery blow-out + special insulator patrol + dust removal from water pools; optical surfaces follow the three steps "blow – wipe – cover") [52-03] Fuel Quota Card (summary: annual cut = measured shrub regrowth × 0.8; quotas issued to households and kilns; radius expanding 10% = yellow warning — Chapter 42 linkage) [52-04] Qanat Construction Card (summary: probe shafts at 50-pace intervals fix the route and record the water-struck depth; floor drops 1–2 finger-widths per 10 paces; shafts every 20–30 paces during excavation, half sealed on completion with inspection shafts every 60 paces; cross-section 2.5–3 chi; three-lamp alignment; acceptance by volumetric measurement over three consecutive days) [52-05] Solar Distillation Card (summary: shallow pool with black bottom + 25–30° transparent pitched cover + collection trough; pool depth 2–3 finger-widths; 1.5–3 L per square meter per day (experiential, field calibration required); charge in the morning, collect in the afternoon, clear the salt crust before charging; water streaming in strings on the cover at noon is normal; the drinking-water bottom line — not enough to support industry)

docs.title: 52.11 The Qanat Process Card (Card 52-04)
docs.text:
The qanat is the desert's lifeline works — an underground channel carries mountain-foot groundwater by gravity, with evaporation loss a small fraction of an open channel's:

  • Route selection: where the mountain-foot water table sits high (probe for water with shafts: test-dig at 50-pace intervals until water is struck, recording the water-struck depth — joining the points traces the water table's trend; lay the conveyance channel along the water-table contour with a gentle descent);
  • Longitudinal gradient: the channel floor drops 1–2 finger-widths per 10 paces (same method as the Chapter 13 open channel — too steep scours the floor and caves it in; too shallow silts up and cuts the flow); each shaft serves both as an excavation opening and later as an inspection and ventilation opening;
  • Shaft spacing: one shaft every 20–30 paces during excavation (ease of spoil removal); after completion half the shafts are sealed (inspection shafts kept at one per 60 paces + an outlet shaft at the end — sealed-shaft covers guard against sand and against people falling in);
  • Cross-section: channel height and width each 2.5–3 chi (the minimum section in which one person stooping can desilt); lining supports only in loose sections (dry-laid cobble or adobe arch, Chapter 13);
  • Excavation organization: driving from both ends + segmented multi-face excavation via shafts (Chapter 37 shift scheduling: 2 persons per shaft face × rotating shifts); direction control — straightness inside the channel is held by the three-lamp alignment method (a lamp at each end + a lamp in the middle; three lamps in one line = straight);
  • Yield acceptance: outlet daily flow measured by the volumetric method for three consecutive days (Chapter 25 baseline); warning line = down twenty percent for two consecutive ten-day periods → check for silting/collapse (Card 52-01);
  • Maintenance ledger: one major cleanout per year (silt removal + repair of collapsed sections), monthly inspection of shaft-head covers — the qanat is an "ancestral-estate project"; the books depreciate it over fifty years.

[Card 52-04 Qanat Construction] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: the mountain-foot water-table section (route fixed by probe shafts), masonry materials (cobble / adobe / mortar, Chapter 13), shaft-head covers, three lamps (three-lamp alignment).
  2. Tools required: test-digging tools, a water meter (Chapter 25 volumetric method), pacing bow and rope-and-line (Chapter 3), masonry tools. Calibration source: gradient and cross-section are measured with rules, not estimated by eye.
  3. Operation sequence and control points: probe shafts fix the route (test-dig at 50-pace intervals until water is struck, record the water-struck depth; joining the points gives the water-table trend; lay the line along the contour with a gentle descent) → excavate in segments via shafts (one shaft every 20–30 paces) → channel cross-section 2.5–3 chi in both height and width → line loose sections with dry-laid cobble or an adobe arch → hold straightness with the three-lamp method (a lamp at each end + one in the middle, three in one line) → acceptance by volumetric measurement over three consecutive days at the outlet → on completion seal half the shafts (inspection shafts one per 60 paces + the end outlet shaft; covers against sand and against people falling in). Control point: the floor drops 1–2 finger-widths per 10 paces (too steep scours and caves in, too shallow silts up and cuts the flow).
  4. Experiential parameters and calibration method: gradient 1–2 finger-widths per 10 paces; shafts every 20–30 paces (excavation) / 60 paces (inspection); cross-section 2.5–3 chi; probe interval 50 paces; acceptance over three consecutive days; warning line = down twenty percent for two consecutive ten-day periods; one major cleanout a year + monthly shaft-cover inspection; depreciated over fifty years; one segment (10 shafts) takes 4–6 persons 30–60 days (experiential).
  5. In-process observation items: per shaft record water-struck depth / shaft spacing / cross-section dimensions / lined sections / three-lamp alignment result / three-day outlet flow / ten-day siltation check.
  6. Accept / rework / scrap criteria: accept = outlet flow stable for three consecutive days, gradient and cross-section on spec, three-lamp alignment with no deviation; rework = insufficient flow or fast silting (re-measure the gradient, desilt and re-align); scrap = a collapsed section beyond repair or a salinized well site (seal that section, open the backup well).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: ① ten-day yield decline → silting → collapsed section → falling water table; ② the two headings fail to meet → the three-lamp check was skipped or the gradient ran away; ③ floor scoured and caved in → gradient too steep; ④ channel silted and flow cut → gradient too shallow; ⑤ someone fell down a shaft → the shaft cover was missing.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one 10-shaft segment completed + the three-day acceptance record; L2 = the whole line supplying water stably for a year with no gap in ten-day checks; L3 = a second person independently driving one segment per this card and meeting the heading by three-lamp alignment.

docs.title: 52.12 The Solar Still Device Card (Card 52-05)
docs.text:
Positioning: the drinking-water bottom line — enough to sustain life, not enough to support industry (daily yield 1.5–3 L per square meter, experiential value, must be field-calibrated):

  • Construction: shallow pool (stone-built + black bottom — pot-bottom soot mixed into a paste and painted on; the key to heat absorption) + transparent cover (glass plate / mica sheet, built as a 25–30° pitched roof) + collection trough (along the lower edge of the slope); pool water depth 2–3 finger-widths (too shallow and it dries out fast; too deep and it warms slowly — 2 fingers is the compromise);
  • Operation: charge water in the morning (brackish or turbid water both fine — what distills out is clean water), collect water in the afternoon; before charging, clear the salt crust off the pool bottom (a crust insulating the black = efficiency drops sharply);
  • Efficiency self-check: at noon, beads of water streaming down the cover's inner wall in strings = normal; condensing but not streaming = the cover is too hot (shade and ventilate one corner with a straw mat to cool it, or switch to a double cover);
  • Winter / sandstorms: cover the pool for heat retention (at night, prevent condensate dripping back and contaminating); after a sandstorm, clear the sand before running again;
  • Upgrade path: multiple pools in series (stage one's waste heat feeds stage two) — yield can rise fifty percent (experiential value); scheduled as a second-batch project.

[Card 52-05 Solar Distillation] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: brackish or turbid water (what distills out is clean water), a stone-built shallow pool with a black bottom (pot-bottom soot mixed into a paste and painted on), a transparent cover (glass plate / mica sheet, 25–30° pitched roof), a collection trough.
  2. Tools required: collection vessels, a measuring vessel (Chapter 25), a straw mat (shade cooling), a pool cover (for night). Calibration source: yield is calibrated by on-site measurement; the experiential value in this chapter is only a starting point.
  3. Operation sequence and control points: charge water in the morning (pool depth 2–3 finger-widths, 2 fingers the compromise) → collect in the afternoon → clear the salt crust off the pool bottom before charging (a crust insulating the black = efficiency drops sharply) → noon efficiency self-check → after a sandstorm clear the sand before running. Control points: beads of water streaming down the cover's inner wall in strings = normal; condensing but not streaming = the cover is too hot (shade and ventilate a corner, or switch to a double cover); never leave the still unattended (dry-boil bursting).
  4. Experiential parameters and calibration method: daily yield 1.5–3 L per square meter (experiential value, must be field-calibrated); pool depth 2–3 finger-widths; cover pitched 25–30°; multiple pools in series can raise yield by fifty percent (experiential value, a second-batch project). Positioning stated honestly: enough to sustain life, not enough to support industry.
  5. In-process observation items: daily record water charged / water collected (converted to yield per square meter) / salt crust cleared / noon cover behaviour (strings or mere condensation) / pool-water salinity.
  6. Accept / rework / scrap criteria: accept = water streaming in strings at noon and daily drinking output meeting the ledger; rework = condensing but not streaming (check cover temperature and shading, clear the salt crust); scrap = the black layer has come off or the cover is broken (recoat / replace the cover).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: ① yield collapsing → check the salt crust first → then the black bottom → then sand on the cover and its sealing; ② condensing but not streaming → cover too hot (shade it, double cover); ③ water at night but none by day → night condensate dripping back, the pool was not covered; ④ cracked pool → unattended dry boiling (the safety-boundary red line).
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = daily yield records for one bank of pools; L2 = a full season of yield accounting that covers the daily drinking bottom line; L3 = a second person independently building one bank of pools per this card and reproducing the same yield.

docs.title: 52.13 Salt-Evaporation Ponds and Glauber's Salt Separation (the Civil-Works Face of the Salt Chemistry Line)
docs.text:
• Evaporation ponds: level gentle-slope ground into cascading pond groups (3–4 stages, a one-finger-width drop per stage) — brine moves stage by stage, thickening stage by stage: stage one clarification pond (sand settling), stage two evaporation pond (main sunning), stage three crystallization pond (salt precipitates out). Pond bottoms compacted + mortar render (Chapter 13 hydraulic formulation) against seepage;
  • Harvest rhythm: harvest only when the crystallization pond's salt layer is 2–3 finger-widths thick (early harvests carry mud); harvest by "scrape first, then wash" — the surface salt is scraped off and rinsed once with concentrated brine (removes mud and bitterness);
  • Glauber's salt separation (the winter nitrate harvest): brine cold-precipitates in winter — Glauber's salt (sodium sulfate) solubility falls steeply with temperature; in winter it grows out of the brine by itself, while table salt stays in solution (the reverse side of the same coin as the hot-filtration principle of Section 23.9.2: hot filtration strips salt from saltpeter; winter cold precipitates Glauber's salt by itself); haul Glauber's salt in winter, sun table salt in spring and summer — one pond, two seasons, two products;
  • Product destinations: table salt enters the food and chemical ledgers (Chapter 38); Glauber's salt for papermaking / glass flux / soda feedstock (the local feedstock for the Section 23.9.5 Leblanc line).

docs.title: 52.14 Wind Tower Construction Parameters
docs.text:
• Tower body: a square vertical shaft (3×3 chi clear inside), standing 2–3 zhang above the ground — the higher, the steadier the wind (no vortex at the top);
  • Orientation: the shaft mouth opens toward the prevailing wind (or four-way openings + movable guide panels adjusted with the wind direction);
  • Cooling fittings: water pan at the tower base + wet curtain (layers of hemp cloth hanging into the pan, kept moist by capillary uptake — incoming air crossing the wet curtain cools by evaporation); the wind, cooled in passing down the tower, enters the corridor outside the living quarters;
  • Criterion: at noon the tower-base outlet air is 5–8 ℃ below ambient (hand-feel grade comparison; experiential value, must be field-calibrated); a dry, white wet curtain = the pan has lost its water (daily refill is a duty item);
  • Limits, stated honestly: on windless days the wind tower is out of action — thick-wall thermal inertia (52.2) is the desert's first line of cooling; the wind tower is the second.

docs.title: 52.15 The Process Water Unit-Consumption Table (the Adjudication Table for the Industrial Basket)
docs.text:
For every candidate process, fill this table before starting work — the desert's industrial basket is ranked by "water consumed per kg of product":

Process Unit Consumption (experiential; must be measured) Adjudication Machining / dry grinding ≈0 (cooling can be air cooling) Priority Optical cold working Low (abrasive-slurry water can settle and be reused) Priority Forging Low (closed quench-water loop) Priority Kilns Low (no water) Priority Glass melting Medium (wet feedstock / cooling) Conditional Papermaking / wet chemistry High (tens of liters per kg) Restricted — output capped or purchased externally Steam power High (boiler + condensation) Restricted — shut down only in the low-water season Ore washing / beneficiation High Adjudicated by ore price; reuse pools mandatory

How to use the table: deduct the water red line first (the Chapter 45 drinking bottom line); with the remaining water, "buy" industries top-down per the table above — the ranked table is the desert version of the priority formula (the single-variable extreme form of the master-outline formula).

docs.title: 52.16 Drought-Resistant Agronomy: Date Palm as the Frame, Water Runs in Pipes
docs.text:
• Seed selection: the Chapter 10 three standards with desert weighting — the general three standards (drought tolerance / storability / yield) are re-ranked in the desert as drought tolerance > storability > yield: the yield champion dies first in drought years (count its loss at one hundred percent); the storability champion is famine-year reserve grain; only the drought-tolerance champion is year-in year-out rations. Execution: candidate crops (barley, millet, sorghum, forage — three lines each) split across two comparison plots — Plot A under conventional irrigation, Plot B on a sixty-percent water ration; for two consecutive seasons register the five columns "emergence date — maturity date — yield per mu — thousand-grain weight — water actually applied"; selection criterion = Plot B's per-mu yield down no more than thirty percent, and thousand-grain weight down no more than ten percent (two indicators guard against "yield puffery" — a line propped through one season by one-time deep roots will surely be exposed in the second). Selected lines are harvested and stored separately, with duplicate seed samples kept (one in use, one in reserve; wax-sealed in pottery jars).
  • Date palm as the skeleton: alkali-tolerant, heat-tolerant, fruit high in sugar and storable, trunk usable, fronds and palm fiber weavable — five uses from one tree, the load-bearing wall of desert agriculture. Planting row spacing is set by the shadow: the noon shade radius of an adult crown is experientially 1.5–2 zhang. Calibration method: pick three local adult trees, measure the noon shadow length three days running around the summer solstice, and average (values differ with latitude; copying from books is forbidden).
  • Shade intercropping: tree rows run east–west — inside the shade band plant forage (the alfalfa family) and shallow-rooted vegetables; in the full-sun band outside, plant millet and sorghum. The evaporation advantage under shade must be measured and registered: two identical shallow basins each charged with equal water, one set in shade and one in full sun for half a day; the water difference is the half-day evaporation difference (experiential value: shade loss is roughly thirty to fifty percent of full-sun loss; local calibration required); if measured shade loss still exceeds sixty percent, the row orientation or spacing is wrong — adjust by transplanting next year.
  • Clay-pipe seepage irrigation (a native method of drip/seepage irrigation): unglazed clay pipes (the Chapter 13 pottery line; inner diameter 2–3 finger-widths, segment length 1.5–2 chi) are buried beside the root zone; the pipe head connects to the field ditch, the pipe tail is plugged, and water seeps through wall pores into the root zone — no wet surface above ground, and evaporation is only a small fraction of basin irrigation (comparison method: one basin-irrigated bed and one seepage-irrigated bed given the same measured quantity of water; on the third day dig a profile and compare wetting-front depth; enter it in the ledger);
  • Burial depth: cereals 0.5–1 chi (the upper edge of the main root layer); young date palms 1–1.5 chi (experiential; recheck against local soil with a test-seepage profile — if the wetting front has not reached the root layer, deepen by half a chi and retry);
  • Seepage-radius calibration: bury a single pipe section as a test, pour in one measured bucket of water, and after 24 hours dig a profile perpendicular to the pipe; the farthest horizontal reach of the wetting front is the radius r — wet sand is dark, dry sand light, and the boundary is discernible; ◎ practice method: before going to the field, train the eye ten times on paired trays of dry and wet sand; compensation for misjudgment is probing with bamboo skewers (a skewer pulled out carrying damp sand = past the wetting front); pipe spacing = 2r−1 finger-widths (leaving a one-finger dry-soil band, preventing cross-seepage between lines and keeping one cracked pipe from waterlogging the whole band);
  • Head–seepage table: for each one-finger-width raise of the pipe-head water head, record one hour's seepage output by the volumetric method (Chapter 25); post the small table in the well house — irrigation is timed by the table, never by feel.
  • Salt-alkali pioneer-crop observation registration: newly cleared salt-patch land is forbidden to go straight into food crops — drill three observation strips in salt-tolerance order: saltbush/salt-sage strip → barley strip → (once seedlings take) date-palm strip; every ten days register "emergence rate — seedling death rate — plant height," for three consecutive periods. Promotion criterion: barley-strip emergence above fifty percent and plant height above one chi; failing that, the plot is kept salt-suppressing for another year, and leaching water may only be return water (the 52.17 account), never fresh water. Observation strips are "using crops as the geological survey party" — cheaper than digging soil for assay and more honest than guessing. [Card 52-06 ] (eight fields)
  • Input materials: unglazed clay pipes (inner diameter 2–3 finger-widths, wall 3–4 fen; a light two-finger tap rings clear; a dull sound means a longitudinal crack — scrap; substitute — bamboo with the nodes bored through, a drilled bamboo pipe, service life roughly halved); hemp oakum + clay slip to seal the joints; tail caps of pottery sheet of the same material.
  • Tools required: calibrated water bucket (graduations checked by the water-weighing method), pacing bow / rope-and-line (Chapter 3), profile spade, a bundle of bamboo skewers.
  • Operation sequence and control points: ① pipe-trench excavation (depth = burial depth + pipe diameter) → ② joints wrapped with two turns of hemp oakum and sealed with slip → ③ a small sand-settling well at the pipe head + an overflow port holding the head constant → ④ single-pipe test seepage to fix r → ⑤ lay pipes at 2r−1 finger-widths → ⑥ backfill and tamp; no cart traffic over the pipe lines.
  • Experiential parameters and calibration method: two burial-depth settings (see main text); the test-seepage method for r; the head–seepage table — once the three items are finalized, transcribe them into the ledger; thereafter consult the book only, never memory.
  • In-process observation items: the opening head at irrigation (bamboo-scale reading), monthly profile dig at one point for wetting-front depth, whether the pipe tail seeps (water at the tail = head too high or a cracked pipe — investigate at once).
  • Accept / rework / scrap criteria: accept = the wetting front forms a continuous band and the surface soil stays dry (no wet patches); rework = dry spots inside the strip — first raise the head half a finger-width for a ten-day trial; if that fails, dig up and inspect the joints and reseal; scrap = a longitudinal crack producing visible flow — replace the pipe and relay that section.
  • Common failures and troubleshooting order: dry spots — check the head first → then dig open the joints → then remove the tail cap and back-flush the sand with water → finally check for root intrusion; wet patches — check for a cracked pipe first, then for an excessive head.
  • L1/L2/L3 evidence: L1 = traced test-seepage profiles + the r table and the head–seepage table; L2 = a one-mu, one-season "seepage vs basin irrigation" comparison ledger (water quantity and harvest, two columns); L3 = the ledger + a second person independently laying one mu per the tables with consistent results.

docs.title: 52.17 The Irrigation Network: A Three-Tier Ledger from Well Head to Root Zone
docs.text:
• The main distribution pool and proportional weirs: qanat output first enters the main distribution pool (doubling as a sand settler — two compartments rotated for desilting), then water is distributed in two tiers: the main pool's weir boards carry large apertures cut per plot, the field-ditch heads small apertures per work team. Principle of the proportional weir: at equal head, discharge is approximately proportional to weir-mouth width (the thin-plate weir empirical formula), so the "division ratio" is realized as a "weir-width ratio" — but for it to hold, every weir must be calibrated once by the volumetric method, recording a "weir width — head — output per shichen" table; an uncalibrated weir is mere decoration. Disciplinary red line: privately altering a weir mouth = stealing water — a ten-day water fine plus registration; any weir change must pass the three steps "report — recalibrate — replace board."
  • The rotation irrigation timetable: open irrigation in the desert happens only in low-evaporation windows — open at sunset, close at sunrise; the timetable is arranged by night: at each ten-day period's start, deduct from the total water in the order "human and livestock drinking → salt-alkali observation strips → food-grain fields → forage fields"; the remainder is converted, by "area × crop grade," into time slots filling all seven nights. The execution trio: the duty officer calling the change (open/close irrigation times reported into the book), the bamboo-scale head reading before each weir, and estimating return water at the drain. Linked with the Chapter 37 shift system: irrigation-night duty and workshop night shifts hang on the same scheduling wall — one person, one post, one signature — preventing "two night shifts each assuming the other is watching the water."
  • Field anti-evaporation: mulch as soon as irrigation closes. Stone mulch — gravel spread between plants and along both sides of the field ditches, 1–2 finger-widths thick (dew condenses among the stones at night, vapor is blocked by day, and day–night soil temperature swings under stone are smaller too); straw mulch — date-palm fiber or dry grass spread around the tree disks, 2–3 finger-widths thick (grass sources are tight; young trees get priority). Acceptance criterion: the morning of the second day after irrigation the surface soil is still damp; daytime drying with cracking = mulch insufficient — thicken by one finger-width and retry (local values are found by gradient trials; do not copy books).
  • Collection and reuse of irrigation return water: the drain ditches at each plot's lowest point feed a return-water pool (lidded against evaporation — the same discipline as the 52.1 water storage); return water is booked in three grades: ① residue not over 2 g/L (evaporate one liter of return water to dryness and weigh; an experiential line; recheck: scorched leaf edges three days after irrigation = drop a grade) → re-irrigate the salt-alkali observation strips; second-pass water is just right for the salt-tolerant crops; ② over the line but still usable → into the dedicated salt-leaching account; ③ ◎ salinity judged by taste: a dedicated spoon and a dedicated taster practice taste judgment ten times each ten-day period against reference samples weighed after evaporation to dryness; compensation for misjudgment = the weighing always prevails — the over-concentrated goes into the salt-evaporation ponds as brine (linking to 52.13). Every drop of water passing two pairs of hands is the baseline courtesy of the desert water ledger. [Card 52-07 ] (eight fields)
  • Input materials: the well head's ten-day average flow (Chapter 25 volumetric method), each plot's area and crop water-demand grade, wooden tags or ceramic tallies for per-household identification.
  • Tools required: weir boards with a rectangular notch cut in, bamboo scale, sundial + water clock for timing (the water clock calibrated against the sundial's noon).
  • Operation sequence and control points: ① settle the ten-day total at period start → ② deduct in the order human and livestock drinking → salt-alkali observation strips → food-grain fields → forage fields → ③ convert the remainder into time slots across seven nights → ④ divide water with proportional weirs; once weir-mouth widths are calibrated, no one may alter them privately.
  • Experiential parameters and calibration method: discharge ∝ weir-mouth width (the thin-plate weir empirical formula at equal head) — calibrate each weir once by the volumetric method into a table; repair the water clock if its daily error exceeds a quarter hour (checked against the sundial).
  • In-process observation items: each plot's irrigation open/close times (the duty officer's called registration), the head before each weir, return-water volume at the drain.
  • Accept / rework / reschedule criteria: accept = each plot's actual water within ten percent of plan; rework = the next ten-day period compensates by adjusting time slots per the deviation; full re-schedule = well flow down twenty percent in a ten-day period (triggering the 39-01 warning line), the whole table re-arranged and posted publicly.
  • Common failures and troubleshooting order: downstream short of water — first re-measure all weir-mouth widths with the bamboo scale (checking for private alteration) → check field-ditch silting → check the total well-head flow account.
  • L1/L2/L3 evidence: L1 = the call-roll book from three trial nights; L2 = a full season executed with every ten-day account balanced and no adjudication records; L3 = the timetable carved on a ceramic tablet standing in the well house + the successor re-arranging one ten-day period from the tablet with consistent results.

docs.title: 52.18 Trade Routes and Camel Caravans: Walking the Desert into a Road Network
docs.text:
• The camel load standard: a single-camel load is experientially 120–150 kg (±10 kg). Calibration method: a new camel starts its first season at 100 kg and adds 10 kg per ten-day period, watching two signs — unable to rise after lying down, and footpads worn through — if either appears, drop back one grade (individual variation exceeds breed variation, so files are kept per camel and grades are not set per breed). Three loading principles: heavy low, light high; water forward, cargo aft (water skins go ahead of the hump so they do not chafe against the cargo); every load carries a quick-release tie (in danger, one knife cut drops the load and saves the life). ◎ load-balancing practice method: time three rounds of loading and stripping an empty pack, and check saddle skew with a plumb line; compensation for misjudgment = weigh the two sides of the pack separately on a steelyard; a difference over 5 kg means reload. Schedule: the pack pace covers 4–5 shichen (two-hour periods) of travel per day, about 25–35 li (registered and revised line by line according to terrain).
  • The water-and-feed carrying ledger: humans drink 4–6 L per day (experiential; carry 8 L per person in the hot season); camels drink 20–30 L per day and eat 3–5 kg of feed per day (dry grass / date residue); carrying quantity = schedule × daily consumption × safety factor 1.5. The factor is not a fixed number: on each return leg settle "actual water remaining ÷ planned water carried"; if the five-trip average runs above 1.3 over the long term, lower the factor back to 1.3 — spare water becomes dead weight that breaks camels down, and a padded ledger is more dangerous than no ledger. On segments with mowable pasture along the way, feed counts at half quantity (pasture grade registered into the water register).
  • Watering-point spacing and the "water register": before opening a new route, dispatch a pathfinding party and register all watering points along the line into an inter-point schedule (trade jargon calls it the "water register"): for each pair of points, five lines — mileage, days of travel, whether shade exists en route, pasture grade, spare-water factor. New-route rule: no more than two days between waters (a green route with two-day water gaps may not carry loaded camels). The water register is revised once at each season's end — in the dry season sources shrink, in the rainy season flash floods move them; a past-its-season register harms more than no register at all.
  • Caravan signals and the night-camp system: by day, smoke talk (three short rising puffs = halt; one long straight column = move; twin columns = water found); by night, lamp talk (a lantern swung left and right = danger; held high and circled = assemble); the horn's three calls (rising call = load up; level call = move slow; falling call = strike camp). All three signal sets are rehearsed by the whole party before departure; those who have not mastered the signals may only follow the local camel drivers and may not lead off alone with the whistle. Night camp: camels formed in a ring (cargo stacks centered, camels' heads facing outward); paired sentries posted at diagonal corners (with a single sentry, one man's sleep stakes every life in the party on his eyelids); camp on the waist of a dune's lee slope (wind is savage at the crest; sand piles at the foot and buries cargo); the campfire sits downwind and no nearer than three paces to the cargo stacks.
  • Value-density ranking of trade goods (the desert borrowing of Chapter 53 trade thought): the desert caravan's transport account = fuel/grain equivalent recovered per kg of load. Ranked by it: saltpeter, glassware, refined salt (low weight, high value) list as prime cargo; coarse salt and gypsum (high weight, low value) only ride along in passing; ironware and grain are return-leg priority cargo. Red line: an empty-camel return leg = a double loss — before every caravan departs, recompute the ranking table against the prices at both ends, enter it in the trade ledger, and re-audit once per quarter.

docs.title: Master Parameter Table

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
• L1: The four water-source steps complete; the solar still meeting its daily drinking-water output; one anti-sand building through a summer; the six failure lines posted on the wall.
  • L2: The qanat supplying water stably (agriculture included); wind–pool power continuous; the water unit-consumption table having adjudicated one round of industrial-basket trade-offs; the fuel quota executed for one year.
  • L3: The concentrator key attack producing its first prototype; the salt–nitrate chemistry line exporting outward; the concentrator prototype produced; the localization rate on target; two full sandstorm seasons with zero major sand losses.

docs.text: All of Parts One through Six; this chapter is reordering + desert clauses.

docs.text: The triple water-source survey method and the qanat; soil-covered anti-evaporation cisterns; the solar-distillation bottom-line device; the process water unit-consumption table and three-tier reuse; thick-adobe building + wind tower + sand fences; solar-preheat kilns and miniaturized scheduling; the salt–nitrate chemistry line; the fuel quota system; the concentrator-mirror key-attack registration; sealed machinery and daily blow-out; wind–pool power as standard; sand-proof packaging and thermal-fatigue qualification; the localization-rate metric; the drought-resistant seed-selection comparison method and pioneer observation strips; the clay-pipe seepage irrigation system and test-seepage calibration method; proportional weirs and the rotation irrigation timetable; stone and straw mulch against evaporation; three-tier return-water accounting; the inter-point schedule (water register) and caravan loading standards; the trade-goods value-density ranking table.

docs.title: C. Unresolved Dependencies
docs.text: The annual groundwater ledger; nitrate deposit reserves; concentrator-mirror technology (the Chapter 24 mirror process, scaled up) awaiting the key attack.

docs.title: Safety Boundaries
docs.text:
• Large groups may not settle before the annual water survey is complete; the brackish-water still may never be left unattended (dry-boil bursting);
  • Fire prevention in the concentrator zone (Chapter 24 focused ignition of objects); sandstorm warnings halt high-place and outdoor machinery work;
  • Solo departure from the party is forbidden (the windows for water loss and disorientation are extremely short) — caravan rules follow the century-old custom of the trade routes.

docs.title: Next-Step Dependencies
docs.text: • Trade complementarity with Chapters 37, 38, and 53: the desert's salt, nitrate, and glass vs the outside world's fuel, fiber, and iron.

docs.title: Chapter Objectives
docs.text: Presents the complete restart execution plan for island conditions: island-type determination → five-stage roadmap → special-risk sections. This chapter introduces no new technologies; it only performs reordering and island adaptation; its core thesis is to recognize "limited local industry + external exchange" as a legitimate finished state.

docs.title: Capability Boundaries
docs.text: What can be done: three freshwater sources with lens-water abstraction-limit management; the fish-salt drying-and-storage system; catamarans and star navigation for inter-island voyaging; the shell-lime–seaweed-ash–volcanic-ash chemical line; salt-spray-resistant electrics and the island-group communication network; "limited local industry + external exchange" as an official route (each of the three island types sets its metallurgical depth by its resources). Explicitly cannot be done: local metallurgy on coral islands (strategic non-metallurgy); wave/tidal power (registered as a research target, no promises); eliminating typhoons (only early warning and contingency plans). External dependencies: stability of trading partners (chain-break contingency plans kept ready at all times); boat-timber plantations (a century-scale project — today's boat timber is a tree planted by our forebears).

docs.text: Item Typical island answer Route consequence Fresh water rainwater / lens water / streams, variable in quantity the water ledger sets the population ceiling Food abundant marine protein the fish-and-salt system carries high weight Minerals volcanic islands (obsidian / sulfur / iron); coral islands (almost none) three types, three routes Alkali shell lime + seaweed ash (twin specialties) a unique chemical line Power wind, small temperature-difference flows, waves (long-term prospect) wind is primary Corrosion salt spray — the most severe corrosion environment in this book electrical anticorrosion tightened

docs.title: Minimum Prerequisites
docs.text: The Parts 1–6 technology library + island-type determination (volcanic / coral / continental island — the island version of the Chapter 2 geological survey).

docs.title: 53.1 Stage One: Water, Food, and Transport
docs.text:
• Three freshwater sources: rainwater harvesting (the roof-to-urn system, Chapter 11 large urns); the island freshwater lens (the fresh water floating atop seawater on coral islands — only small, slow withdrawals, over-abstraction causes salinization; dispersed well siting + registered daily withdrawal quotas); streams (volcanic islands often hold bulk fresh water — this directly unlocks the population ceiling);
  • Food: fish (fish spears / nets / traps) + shellfish (filter-feeding shellfish are forbidden during red tides — toxin accumulation; register sea-state precursors) + coconut starch; salted-dried fish (salt = sun-dried seawater; the Chapter 52 salt-drying method costs nothing on an island) — a protein storage system = lean-season insurance;
  • Transport is the lifeline: dugout canoe → outrigger canoe → catamaran (stability leaps upward, cargo becomes possible). Navigation: star navigation (Chapter 3 time + Chapter 25 angles — self-made rising/setting azimuth tables for stars; a preserved-knowledge version of the Austronesian millennium system) + coastal landmarks + monsoon windows (the sailing window = the monsoon calendar; register the no-sail periods);
  • Coastal work zone: slipway (launch–recovery ramp) + net-drying ground + salt pans — laid out along the tide lines (a combination of Chapter 2 hydrology + Chapter 13 building).

[Card 53-01 Lens-Water Abstraction Limit] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: the lens-water wells (well sites spread apart), each well's daily-withdrawal register and ten-day salinity records, colour-coded tags (marked in different colours from the rainwater jars).
  2. Tools required: a measuring vessel (Chapter 25 volumetric / water-weighing method), a dedicated tasting spoon (salinity, one person's own). Calibration source: withdrawal is registered by the volumetric method, not estimated in bucket counts.
  3. Operation sequence and control points: register each well's first-month daily withdrawal to fix its baseline → draw water within the ceiling (sites spread apart, small amounts drawn slowly) → taste salinity every ten days into the ledger → two consecutive salty ten-day periods close the well and the backup well opens → colour-code against the rainwater jars and keep a separate account for each source. Control points: the ceiling is per well, not per island (concentrating on one well = local over-abstraction); two consecutive salty periods means stop at once, do not wait for a third (salinization is irreversible).
  4. Experiential parameters and calibration method: per-well daily ceiling = the registered baseline; water quality tasted every ten days, every lens well on the books; two consecutive salty periods close the well (master-table red line); lens water may only be drawn in small amounts and slowly — over-abstraction means salinization, and a salinized freshwater lens is a death sentence for the island.
  5. In-process observation items: per well record daily withdrawal / ten-day salinity (taste judgment) / dates of closure and reopening / the well's converted days of supply.
  6. Accept / rework / scrap criteria: accept = no well exceeding its baseline all year and a steady salinity curve; rework = a single salty ten-day period (cut withdrawal at once, tighten tasting, see whether it freshens); scrap = salinity in two consecutive periods (that well is closed, irreversibly; open the backup and re-set the baseline).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: ① well water turning salty period by period → over-abstraction (withdrawal above baseline, or sites too close together); ② the whole island salty at once → several wells over-drawn together (re-arrange sites and the water ledger); ③ withdrawal pushed up in the dry season → the rationing regime was not accounted per well; ④ disagreement over taste judgment → dedicated spoon and taster, compared every ten days; when in doubt treat it as salty.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one year of per-well registers; L2 = a steady salinity curve plus at least one voluntary closure and reopening; L3 = a second person independently making one closure / reopening decision per this card with the same conclusion.

docs.title: 53.2 Stage Two: Woodwork, Fiber, and Marine Materials
docs.text:
• Hull timber (straight-grained lightweight wood, selectively bred — Chapter 7 material selection + the long horizon of Chapter 10 plantations: today's boat timber is a tree planted by our forebears; boat-timber plantations are listed as a century-scale project). Canvas and rope (coconut fiber / sisal — the marine-fiber version of Chapter 15, salt-resistant and rot-resistant);
  • Obsidian (a volcanic-island birthright): natural glass-grade stone-tool material (Chapter 5 — its sharpness crowns all stone tools); edge tools and scrapers go straight to top grade. But it is brittle (forbidden for impact tools) and non-renewable (registered sites, quota-limited extraction);
  • Anticorrosion treatment: anti-fouling for hull bottoms (burned dried-oyster ash mixed into paint / multiple coats of tung oil); monthly inspection of ironware for salt-spray corrosion (a strengthened version of the Chapter 50 system — island ironware rusts at a "respiration rate"; wherever wood / stone / ceramics can substitute, iron is not used).

[Card 53-02 Salt-Spray Anticorrosion Inspection] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: the three-tier exposure-surface checklist (tier one = hull hardware; tier two = outdoor structures; tier three = indoors), fresh water (to wash salt frost), anticorrosion grease and tung oil, corrosion coupons (test pieces).
  2. Tools required: brushes, grease gun, soft cloth, coupons and a monthly scale (Chapter 3). Calibration source: corrosion rate is logged by monthly coupon weighing, not judged by eye.
  3. Operation sequence and control points: weekly rounds over the three-tier checklist (tier-one parts inspected after every use) → on white frost: fresh water wash → dry → oil → contacts grease-sealed (monthly + after rain) → coupons weighed monthly to log the rate → review the graded material choice (where wood / stone / ceramic can replace iron, use them; hull bottoms get dried-oyster lime paint or multiple coats of tung oil). Control points: patrol immediately after rain; wash before oiling (oiling without washing seals the salt under the paint).
  4. Experiential parameters and calibration method: weekly rounds + rounds immediately after rain; tier-one parts inspected after each use; electrical contacts monthly + after rain; coupons weighed monthly; island iron rusts at a "respiration rate"; insulators get extra skirts + silicone sealing coat + sealed distribution boards.
  5. In-process observation items: per round record date / tier patrolled / location of white frost / treatment (wash–dry–oil) / contact condition / monthly coupon weight / parts replaced.
  6. Accept / rework / scrap criteria: accept = weekly and post-rain rounds with no gaps, no green contacts, steady coupon weight loss; rework = white frost recurring (tighten to a round after every voyage and recoat); scrap = green, powdery contacts or corroded terminals (replace, switching to non-iron parts or sealing).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: ① contacts failing in batches → no post-rain round (make it up + grease-seal + seal the board); ② iron life halved → the three-tier material choice was not followed (switch to substitutes, re-baseline the coupons); ③ blistering under the paint → oil applied before washing (salt sealed under the paint); ④ pitting on hull hardware → tier-one parts not inspected after use.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one season of weekly-round records + monthly coupon weights; L2 = a full year with no batch contact failures and a coupon-rate curve; L3 = a second person independently running one round per this card with the same white-frost judgment.

docs.title: 53.3 Stage Three: Pottery, Lime, and Glass
docs.text:
• Pottery: clay or none (coral islands usually lack soil — sea-shipped clay is listed as a regular trade item, or transition with lime-mortar wooden vessels); on volcanic islands, volcanic ash + lime give a natural cement formula (pozzolanic cement, Chapter 13) — the mainstay material for island construction and slipways;
  • Shell lime (the mother of island chemistry): kiln-burning of shells (the Chapter 13 lime process) — one kiln, two products: lime (construction / mortar) and lye (after causticizing: soap, glass, and the whole Chapter 23 line);
  • Seaweed ash: burn seaweed to get ash — rich in iodine and alkali (iodine is a strategic material for wound disinfection and thyroid health; registered extraction: ash-water leaching with graded crystallization). Soda supplies the glass line;
  • Glass: the coral island's white sand + seaweed soda = a complete glass batch — glassware and lenses (Chapters 14 and 24) actually proceed smoothly on islands (coral islands are an "optically rich zone" — a registered paradox).

docs.title: 53.4 Stage Four: Metallurgy and Machinery
docs.text:
• Three routes by island type:
  • Volcanic island: basalt (building material / millstones) + magnetite sand (black sand = an iron source; the island form of the Chapter 16 heavy-mineral-concentrate method — smelting sand-iron has heavy fuel costs, so scale is decided by the fuel ledger) + sulfur (crater vents, Chapter 23);
  • Continental island: conventional ore deposits (follow the main route of Parts 1–6);
  • Coral island: essentially no minerals — local metal = the recycling loop (Chapter 17) + driftwood iron fittings + trading for metal (strategic non-metallurgy);
  • Guano (where rookeries exist): phosphorus-nitrogen fertilizer (the Chapter 10 agriculture leap) and raw material for phosphate dopants (Chapter 35) — a remote island may in fact be one of the environments closest to semiconductors in this whole book (the odd combination of guano + shell-lime alkali + seaweed iodine + white-sand glass + wind-generated electricity); registered as a "long-line opportunity";
  • Machinery: ship-repair capability outranks machine building — the woodworking and rigging system for masts / rudders / pumps is the body of the seafaring industry.

docs.title: 53.5 Stage Five: Electricity and Electronics
docs.text:
• Power: wind as the mainstay (sea winds are steady) + small hydropower (volcanic-island streams); waves and tides (registered as a research target, no promises);
  • Salt-spray-resistant electrics: skirting added to porcelain insulators + silicone-oil sealing coats + sealed distribution boards (the island version of the Chapter 32 three-piece set). The grounding-electrode trap on islands: coral sand conducts poorly — backfill a saltwater pit + multiple electrodes in parallel (measure the grounding resistance; do not close the switch until it meets spec);
  • Electronics and communication (the greatest value of the island edition): telegraph / radio stations (Chapters 32–33) link the island group — fishery warnings, rescue calls, trade inquiries. Navigation lights (harbor wind lamps + focused beams) — a public good of a seafaring society;
  • Packaging: the Chapter 36 harsh-environment grade + salt-spray accelerated-aging qualification (the first island entry in the failure atlas = electrochemical migration).

docs.title: 53.6 Special Sections of the Island Edition
docs.text:
1. Seawater cannot directly replace fresh water (all process ledgers are still kept in fresh water); a seawater-use register (cooling / salt drying / rinsing — wherever seawater is used, anticorrosion design is mandatory);
  2. The general corrosion strategy: grade the metal exposure surfaces (Tier-1 exposure = hull hardware, use copper / tin fittings; Tier-2 = outdoor construction; Tier-3 = indoors) — graded material selection replaces "iron everywhere";
  3. The economic trade-off between sea freight and local manufacture: goods whose value per unit weight is below the freight cost (stone, wood, coarse ceramics) are made locally; high-value low-weight goods (salt, iodine, glassware, dried fish, guano fertilizer) are exchanged for metal, fuel, and seed — the trade list is the technology roadmap (the nautical version of Chapter 29 full-cost accounting);
  4. The ship–harbor–rope-and-net system is the island's "first industry": repairing one ship is as comprehensive as a joint examination in metallurgy + woodworking + textiles + chemistry — ship-repair capability is the acceptance touchstone of island industry;
  5. The typhoon/storm protocol: warning (register cloud forms and swell precursors) → boats hauled onto the slipway → supplies stored → personnel sheltered (in bone-built structures); after a disaster, the "communication network + repair fleet" is the first recovery sequence.

[Card 53-03 Storm Contingency] (eight fields)

  1. Input materials: the sky-watch post's daily register (swell / cloud forms / hand-feel barometric grade), boats awaiting haul-out, supplies awaiting storage (including the three-tier water storage), the storm-shelter bone-frame building, the radio set.
  2. Tools required: the register, the slipway and keel blocks (Card 53-08), mooring lines, the storage checklist, a hot-standby radio set. Calibration source: precursors are read against the daily register, not by last-minute feel.
  3. Operation sequence and control points: register the precursors daily (swell direction shift / cloud forms / sudden sky-glow) → grade and issue the warning → boats hauled out and secured → supplies stored (three-tier water storage full, sail-and-rigging spares doubled) → personnel sheltered (bone-frame building) → post-disaster recovery order: communications → ship repair → power → production. Control points: the recovery order must never be inverted (without communications first, the repair crews cannot be dispatched); once warned, boats come ashore regardless of how the sky looks.
  4. Experiential parameters and calibration method: three tiers of precursors; the sky-watch post registers 15 min daily; recovery order communications → ship repair → power → production (master-table iron rule); before the typhoon season rigging spares doubled and three-tier water storage full; slipway gradient re-measured once before and after each typhoon.
  5. In-process observation items: daily three precursors / warning level and issue time / number of boats hauled out and how secured / items stored / number of people sheltered / damage and the time of each recovery step.
  6. Accept / rework / scrap criteria: accept = warning issued on time, all boats ashore and secured, recovery run in order; rework = a late warning or a missed boat (sky-watch post held to account + whole-crew drill); scrap = an inverted recovery order causing second-round losses (register and review, retrain).
  7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: ① typhoon losses concentrated → late warning or boats not hauled out; ② slow recovery → communications not restored first (repair crews cannot be dispatched); ③ boats damaged on the slipway → hauled out but not blocked up and secured; ④ water run out during the storm → three-tier storage not full before the season.
  8. L1 / L2 / L3 evidence: L1 = one typhoon season of daily registers + one drill record; L2 = an actual storm run through in order with losses contained; L3 = a second person independently running one drill with the same sequence and checklist.

docs.title: 53.7 Failure: Which Line Breaks First on an Island (Second of the Five Review Angles)
docs.text: No. Failure line Precursor Consequence chain ① Salt-spray corrosion (the strongest in this book) white salt frost creeping onto hardware, contacts turning green, wire terminals powdering ship lost → communications cut → electrical accidents — every island failure is layered on top of this one ② Lens-water over-abstraction salinization well water tasting saltier with each ten-day period (registration system) irreversible salinization of the freshwater lens = a death sentence for the island ③ Storm damage (typhoon / cyclone) swell direction shifts, cloud forms, the barometric hand-feel notch (bird-behavior and swell-precursor registration) fleet wiped out, houses destroyed, sailing halted for several ten-day periods ④ Boat-timber generational gap (the shipbuilding forest not renewed) harvestable boat-timber diameters shrinking year by year no boats = trade and fishing both severed — boat timber is a century-scale project; its failure arrives a generation later ⑤ Red tide and fish poisoning sea-surface discoloration, noctiluca glow, dead fish drifting ashore mass poisoning (the Section 10.1 red line) ⑥ External-dependency chain break (trading partner defaults / route severed) anomalies in the quarterly trade-list carryover metal / seed supply cut — the unique weak point of a trade-based economy
