docs.title: 56.1 The Geometric Construction-Methods Set
docs.text: Three general rules: ①every method has four complete columns — given conditions, construction steps, verification method, error registration; ②the accuracy ceiling of construction is set by line width: scriber + line reading is 0.5–1 mm, which on a 1 m format is the ±0.1% order — all construction methods share this ceiling, and no promised precision may cross it; ③the error-registration system: for each method's first execution and for quarterly spot checks, register the verification readings in the Section 3.4 error-record format; out of tolerance, that board and that tool are immediately decommissioned.

docs.title: 56.1.1 Perpendiculars (three methods)
docs.text:
Method 1 (the 3-4-5 rope method, for outdoor layout): already in Chapter 3; one added registration item — flipping it back against its original position with an even gap counts as pass; the crossing-angle verification reading goes into the error table.

Method 2 (the perpendicular-bisector method, for the board): given segment AB — ①with center A and radius R (0.7–1.2×AB, empirical window) draw two arcs above and below; ②with center B and the same R draw arcs meeting the first pair at C and D; ③join CD, crossing AB at M — then CD⊥AB and M is the midpoint. Verification: measure the four distances AC, BC, AD, BD — all must equal R; and MC=MD. Error point: when the two arcs are nearly tangent, the intersections smear — redraw outside the R window; fudging an intersection reading is not allowed.

Method 3 (the tangent method, for long perpendiculars): given line L and an external point P — ①with center P draw an arc cutting L at E and F; ②with centers E and F and equal radius (>EF/2) draw arcs meeting at Q; ③PQ⊥L. Verification: the midpoint of EF must fall on PQ (Method 2 cross-check; the two methods verify each other — double insurance).

docs.title: 56.1.2 Parallels (two methods)
docs.text:
Method 1 (the equidistant double-perpendicular method): pick any two points on the known line L, erect a perpendicular at each (Method 3), measure distance d along both perpendiculars to get two points; the line joining them is the parallel. Verification: pick another point on the new line and measure its perpendicular distance to L — it must =d; the three points' mutual difference ≤1 line-width passes.

Method 2 (the double-perpendicular method, a parallel through a point): through external point P erect the perpendicular to L, with foot H (Method 3); then through P erect the perpendicular to PH (Method 2 reduced to the "pick two points on a line" case) — the result is the parallel through P. Verification as in Method 1. The meaning of the double perpendicular: it reduces "parallel" to two applications of "perpendicular", and perpendicularity is a primitive already verified in this chapter.

docs.title: 56.1.3 Angle Bisection
docs.text: Steps: given ∠BAC — ①with center A and radius R draw an arc cutting both sides at D and E; ②with centers D and E and equal radius r (0.5–1.0×R, empirical window) draw arcs meeting at F; ③AF is the bisector. Control point: AD=AE must be laid out in one and the same compass opening for the two leg positions (two separate openings = systematic error). Verification: AF crosses DE at G; then GD=GE and DG⊥AF (perpendicular-bisector mutual check). Error registration: the bisector deviates from the midpoint of the line joining the two equidistant points by ≤1 line-width.

docs.title: 56.1.4 Regular Polygons (3/4/5/6/8 sides)
docs.text:
General method: first construct the circumscribed circle, then step around it with fixed chord lengths — the same idea as the Chapter 22 angle blocks: closure error distributed evenly over the full circle.

Sides Construction Verification 3 Step around the circle with the compass opened to the radius, connecting alternate points (chord=√3×R, taking two radii with 120° between them) Mutual difference of the three sides ≤1 line-width 4 Construct a diameter; construct its perpendicular bisector (56.1.1 Method 2) to get the other diameter; connect the four points The two diagonals are equal and bisect each other at right angles 6 Step the radius opening around the circle six times Six chords walked around return to the start; closure gap ≤2 line-widths 8 On the 4-side basis, bisect each 90° central angle (56.1.3) to get four points in the 45° directions Mutual difference of the eight sides ≤1 line-width; closure gap ≤2 line-widths 5 Method A (approximate construction): draw the circle and two perpendicular diameters; take K as the midpoint of radius OM; with center K and radius KN (N the endpoint of the other diameter) draw an arc cutting the adjacent diameter at P; NP is the side length — a classical approximation, side-length deviation about 0.5% (empirical value). Method B (computed chord): sin18°=0.309 (56.5 table) → side=0.618R, set the compass directly Mutual difference of the five sides ≤1 line-width; closure gap distributed back over the five sides per the Chapter 22 closure rule

The 3-, 4-, 6-, and 8-side cases are exact constructions; the 5-side case is approximate + closure correction — the registration sheet must state which side count used the approximate method (an honest precision account).

docs.title: 56.1.5 Scaling Up and Down (the similar-triangle grid method)
docs.text:
Use: enlarging a 1:1 drawing to the layout yard, or shrinking a large yard layout onto a clay tablet.

Steps: ①grid the original drawing with squares whose side = 2–4 times the smallest feature size of the original (empirical window: each cell contains at least one feature point; too fine doubles the work, too coarse distorts); ②grid the target surface at magnification k, cell sides scaled by k in step — k may only take integer ratios and simple fractions such as 2, 3, 1/2, 1/3 (Section 3.6 discipline: use only re-checkable ratios); ③transcribe cell by cell: feature points are recorded as "which row, which column + position within the cell", the in-cell position transcribed as readings like "so many finger-widths from the left edge, so many from the bottom edge"; ④verification: pick any 3 feature lines spanning multiple cells and measure their lengths — the ratio must =k (±2 line-widths); for circular features re-verify that the radius ratio =k. Error registration: grid lines are stepped off at equal spacing with dividers + cell-by-cell checking; mutual difference of cell spacings ≤1 line-width.

docs.title: 56.1.6 Dividing a Circle (construction methods + error registration)
docs.text:
A graded route; each level uses only already-verified operations:

  • 2/4/8/16 divisions: diameters + successive perpendicular bisection (56.1.1 Method 2 applied to radius segments); a closure check at every level.
  • 3/6/12 divisions: chord stepping with the radius opening (chord = radius).
  • 5/10 divisions: the 56.1.4 pentagon Methods A/B.
  • 24 divisions (15° per division): make 12 and 8 divisions independently, by two routes; check coincidence at the common-multiple points — intersections of two independent routes coinciding to ≤1 line-width is the hard test of division quality.
  • 90 divisions (4° per division): serves 56.5 and the angle gauge; using the chord table (fed back after 56.5 builds it), re-verify one point every 6 divisions.
  • Error registration: after any division is completed, walk the whole circle and register the "start-to-finish closure error", distributing it evenly back over the segments by division count (the Chapter 22 system) — this compass thereby gains its own "division-correction account", filed.
  • Boundary: prime-number divisions like 7/9/11 have no construction method — once the sine table exists, route around by computing the chord as "chord=2R·sin(θ/2)"; until then, 7 divisions may only use the approximate chord 0.868R + even closure distribution, registered as a downgraded accuracy class.

docs.title: 56.2 Building the Logarithm Table
docs.text:
What a logarithm is (one-sentence engineering statement): the logarithm demotes multiplication and division to addition and subtraction — log(ab)=log a+log b, log(a/b)=log a−log b. Two lookups, one addition or subtraction, one reverse lookup: three table operations replace one long multiplication. Engineering payoff: multiplication and division of two-digit numbers (two reliable digits (±1%), third digit for interpolation reference only) goes from "half an incense stick of longhand work + error-prone" to "ten breaths + cross-checkable"; and the log table is also the key to roots — divide by two and reverse-lookup: that is a square root.

Precision budget first (silent failure first): errors are computed before building — square-root anchor ±0.3% (empirical), cumulative-multiplication drift ±0.5% (empirical), table-lookup interpolation ±0.3%; the relative errors of multiplication/division add (Section 25.11 Rule 2), combining to ≤±1.5%. Commitment: the first two digits of a result are reliable, the third digit is suspect (interpolation reference only). That is nothing to be ashamed of — spurious precision is.

docs.title: 56.2.1 Four Steps to Build the Table
docs.text:
Step 1: square root by construction (the geometric-mean method) — the whole table's only external input is the single geometric fact that "the square root can be constructed":

  1. On a line take O and B with OB=a+1; on OB take A so that OA=1, AB=a;
  2. Draw a semicircle on OB as diameter (find the center by 56.1.1 Method 2; peg it in place and draw the circle);
  3. Erect the perpendicular to OB through A (Method 2), meeting the semicircle at C — AC=√a;
  4. Principle: the right-triangle altitude theorem, AC²=OA×AB=1×a. Verification: build a square on side AC and compare areas with an a×1 rectangle by cutting and rearranging; take the median of three independent constructions (the 3.4 procedure). Self-check anchor: a=4 must give exactly 2; a=9 gives 3 — a technique that fails this gate may not go further. Precision: ±0.3% (empirical, must be field-calibrated: the self-check anchor deviation is the demonstrated precision of the technique, entered in the ledger).

Step 2: the anchor chain: starting from √10=3.162, construct square roots six times in succession: 10^(1/2)=3.162 → 10^(1/4)=1.778 → 10^(1/8)=1.3335 → 10^(1/16)=1.1548 → 10^(1/32)=1.0746 → 10^(1/64)=1.0366 → common ratio c=10^(1/128)=1.0182 (the fourth digit is untrustworthy; write only four digits). At each level take the median of three constructions. Closure check: the theoretical value of c is 10^(1/128)=1.0182; the constructed value must differ from the table by ≤0.5%; the whole-chain gate is c multiplied back out to 10, with stepwise verification against the master table substituted for physical repeated multiplication (c multiplied by itself 7 times ≈1.13, not a return to 10).

Step 3: the master table by cumulative multiplication: a 128-row geometric sequence; row 0=1.000; each row multiplied by c gives the next; row 128 must=10.000; the logarithm of row number m is m/128.

  • Drift control (critical): set check anchors every 16 rows — row 16=1.3335, row 32=1.778, row 48=2.371 (=1.3335×1.778), row 64=3.162, row 80=4.217, row 96=5.623, row 112=7.499 (=10÷1.3335), row 128=10.000. The anchor values follow from multiplying one another; the anchor system is self-consistent and needs no new measurements. When a row value differs from its anchor by more than 0.005, the deviation is distributed proportionally back over that 16-row run (corrected directly when the table is transcribed).
  • Cross-check system: two people each build the master table once; per-row mutual difference ≤0.005; out-of-tolerance rows are adjudicated by a third builder (transplanted 3.4 procedure).

Step 4: transcribing the main table (90×10 cells): rows = true values 1.0–9.9 (step 0.1); columns = second decimal digit (0–9); each cell holds the logarithm to two decimal places (two reliable digits (±1%), third digit for interpolation reference only), the value read from the master table + linear interpolation:

  • Interpolation procedure: if x falls between master-table rows m and m+1, then log x≈m/128+(x−row value)÷(next row−row value)×(1/128);
  • Densification points: the master-table row spacing is 0.018 at 1.0 and 0.18 at 10 — in segments where the row spacing exceeds 0.1 (roughly x>6), insert midpoint rows first: midpoint value=√(upper row×lower row); each inserted point is cross-checked by two methods, "square root via the log table" and the arithmetic midpoint; identical values pass;
  • The main table's 900 cells take about 2 person-days; spot-check 10 cells by hand computation (multiply 10^log back to the true value, ±0.5%).

docs.title: 56.2.2 Usage Procedures and Three Worked Examples
docs.text:
Five rules: ①table readings give two reliable digits (±1%), third digit for interpolation reference only; mental arithmetic never enters the table; ②magnitude self-check (the Section 25.8 four-piece set) — fix the power of 10 first, then compute the mantissa; ③spot-check one in ten of the critical numbers entering the archive with manual multiplication; ④error annotation per 25.11; ⑤"the slide rule estimates the scheme, the tables fix the numbers" (56.3).

Example 1 (multiplication): 472×36.5. log 472=2.674, log 36.5=1.562; sum=4.236; reverse lookup 0.236→1.72; result=1.72×10⁴=17200. Magnitude check: 500×37≈18500, same order ✓. Error: about ±1.5%; report 1.72×10⁴.

Example 2 (division): 850÷46. log 850=2.929, log 46=1.663; difference=1.266; reverse lookup 0.266→1.845; result≈18.5. Magnitude check: 850÷50=17 ✓. Report 18.5 (±2%).

Example 3 (square root): √200. log 200=2.301; ÷2=1.1505; reverse lookup 0.1505→1.414; result≈14.1. Magnitude check: 14²=196 ✓. Report 14.1 (±2%).

(Square = the special case of multiplication, log×2; reciprocal = 0−log — one table covers five operations: multiplication, division, squaring, square root, reciprocal.) [Card 56-01 Logarithm table compilation ] (eight fields) 1. Input materials: 1 construction board (passing the two-position fit check), standard rods, two carriers for the master table; one 128-row pass takes about 2 tablets. Substitute: all-clay-tablet in the paperless period (raises transcription frequency). 2. Required tools: compass and dividers (repeatable opening), right-angle square and scriber (Chapter 19), certified straightedge, magnifier; calibration: the compass's two trial circles coincide; the straightedge passes the two-position check against the light. 3. Operation sequence and control points: square-root self-check (a=4→2, a=9→3) → six anchor-chain levels in succession (median of three at each level) → c checked against the table value 1.0182 (difference ≤0.5%) — failing this, going further is forbidden → master table by cumulative multiplication → anchor verification every 16 rows, deviation distributed back proportionally → two independent builders, mutual difference ≤0.005 → main table transcribed with interpolation (densify the x>6 segment first) → spot-check 10 cells by back-multiplication (±0.5%). 4. Empirical parameters and calibration: c=1.0182 (±0.3%; calibration: median of three constructions + the self-multiply-7-times closure check); anchor-deviation red line 0.005 (calibration: from the first table, tally whole-table anchor deviations and take the measured P95; transcribe into the ledger, Chapter 43). 5. In-process observation records: three readings per square-root level; anchor deviations entered in an "anchor-deviation column" every 16 rows; both builders and the date in the table header; any change of compass opening noted by row number. 6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = all anchor deviations pass, mutual differences on target, all spot checks pass; rework = individual rows out of tolerance (re-multiply and re-distribute that 16-row segment); scrap = c^7 closure failure (>0.5%) — return to the self-check anchors, retrain the construction technique, then rebuild. 7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: the master table drifting ever further off → first check for a miscopied fourth digit of c, then skipped rows, finally miscopied anchor values; isolated wrong cells in the main table → first check whether they lie in the un-densified x>6 region, then transcription line-skips, finally identical errors by both builders (identical errors mean a bad master-table row — return to the master table). 8. L1/L2/L3 evidence: L1 = master table + the three worked examples on paper; L2 = main table + spot-check records + a third person's blind check passed; L3 = dual backup at separate sites, the c value and anchor table entered in the ledger, the next generation reproducing it independently from the card.

docs.title: 56.3 Slide-Rule Manufacture
docs.text: Why it is worth making: the log table is "compute by lookup" — three lookups per problem; the slide rule is the logarithm table engraved on a stick — push the slide and read directly — ten breaths per problem. Input versus output: the master rule costs 3–5 person-days; thereafter each working rule takes 1–2 days to copy; consumption is near zero; the whole settlement uses it for ten years — the same investment class as machine-tool metrology.

docs.title: 56.3.1 Scale Principle and the Three-Scale System
docs.text:
• Principle: on the rule, the mark for x sits at distance L·log(x) from the left end — "multiplication of numbers" becomes "addition of lengths". Push the slide so that C's 1 aligns with D's a; then the D reading under C's b = ab (two lengths added).
  • Rule length L=250 mm class (empirical, must be field-calibrated: the longer L, the finer the reading; a short 150 mm-class rule degrades to ±4% error — carry-along quick-calculation only, no ±2% promise).
  • The C/D/A three-scale system: the D scale (lower fixed stock) runs 1–10; main line positions = L×log value, each computed from the 56.2 master table and registered into a "scale-line position table" — this is the construction drawing for engraving the rule; estimating lines by eye in the field is forbidden. The C scale (the slide) is graduated exactly like D. The A scale (second row of the lower fixed stock) runs 1–100, line positions = L×log(x)/2 — when the cursor line reads a on D, the same line on A reads a²; conversely, read N on A and look at D to get √N.
  • The line-density trade-off (honest): graduating all of 1–10 to two reliable digits (±1%), third digit for interpolation reference only, would take about 500 lines on 250 mm — beyond hand methods. The trade-off: the 1.0–2.0 segment at 0.02 per division, 2.0–5.0 at 0.05 per division, 5.0–10 at 0.1 per division — a log scale is naturally dense on the left, sparse on the right; this segmentation follows the density, about 120 secondary lines in all, within scriber reach.
  • The master-rule system: build one master rule first; after it passes inspection it serves as the template from which working rules are copied (the Chapter 22 first-article-inspection concept); the master rule is sealed away, and working rules are checked against it monthly (the Chapter 3 monthly-check system transplanted).

docs.title: 56.3.2 Engraving and Cursor Workmanship
docs.text:
• Rule blanks: bamboo/linden, shade-dried one season (dryness test: weighed across two weeks with no weight change — Chapter 3 standard transplanted), wax-soaked against moisture; the working face mated to the surface plate shows no gap against the light (Chapter 20 concept).
  • Engraving: scribe along a certified straightedge, depth judged by "a fingernail stroke can feel it, yet it does not prick the hand"; after engraving, rub soot ink in to raise contrast.
  • Slide groove: the slide sits between the upper and lower stocks, running freely over the whole travel with no lateral play — lateral play = systematically wrong readings. Criterion: push to mid-travel and lift the slide lightly; verify 0.3 mm with the paper-gauge method (two 0.3 mm sheets together will not enter; a single sheet will — empirical value).
  • Cursor: a wooden frame clamping a glass window (Chapter 24), a fine copper wire waxed at the window's center as the hairline; line-straightness criterion: rotate the window 45° and the line shows no kink.
  • Reading technique ◎: the line of sight must be perpendicular to the rule face — parallax is the slide rule's number-one error. Practice: stand a small mirror of polished copper sheet beside the rule; when the hairline and its mirror reflection join into one line, the sight line is perpendicular. With no mirror, two people cross-check (one reads, one watches the sight angle from the side). Misjudgment compensation: for critical readings, nudge the cursor half a division left and right and take the midpoint of the two readings.

docs.title: 56.3.3 Graduation Criterion and Typical Usage
docs.text:
Graduation (the 10-problem method): the quiz-setter works out 10 problems by hand (4 multiplications, 3 divisions, 2 proportions, 1 square — all two-digit numbers, two reliable digits (±1%), third digit for interpolation reference only); the trainee completes them on the slide rule within half an incense stick. All errors <2% and not a single magnitude error passes; three groups, all passed, on 3 consecutive days, graduates. A magnitude error (a 10× error) is an automatic veto — the slide rule reads only significant figures; the power of ten must be held by your own mental arithmetic: this is the procedure's second maxim.

Table of typical uses:

Task Operation sequence Worked example Multiplication Set C's 1 against D's a; read the D line under C's b 4.72×3.65→read 17.2 (actually 17.23); magnitude check 4.7×3.7≈17 Division Set C's b against D's a; read under C's 1 850÷46: set 4.6 against 8.5, read 1.85 under the 1→18.5 Proportion chain Set C's a against D's b; thereafter read below any number on C for the answer Saltpeter boiling 5:1 (Chapter 23): after 60 is set against 12, any nitre-earth quantity on C reads its required ash quantity directly below Square Set the cursor line to a on D; read A on the same line D 2.41→A 5.81 Square root Set the cursor line to N on A (N<10 use the left half, 10–100 the right half — the place-determination mnemonic), read D A 2.00→D 1.41

Accuracy division-of-labor statement: the slide rule is ±2% (the first two digits reliable); numbers entering the archive are re-verified with the log table or by hand — "the slide rule fixes the scheme, the tables fix the numbers" is written into the system. [Card 56-02 Slide-rule engraving ] (eight fields) 1. Input materials: shade-dried bamboo/wood blanks (2 fixed stocks + 1 slide, straight grain, knot-free), 1 thin-glass window, 1 length of fine copper wire, 20–30 g beeswax, soot ink. Substitute: with no glass, read the rule face directly (parallax risk rises — switch to a two-person mutual-reading system). 2. Required tools: scriber (Chapter 19, trial-scribes 10 lines without a break), certified straightedge, surface plates for mutual fitting, magnifier, an accepted logarithm table (56.2, the data source for the scale lines); calibration: the blank faces mutually fitted show no gap against the light. 3. Operation sequence and control points: compute the scale-line position table (register L×log values line by line) → engrave the master rule D/C → inspect (field 6) → engrave working rules by copying the master → cut the groove and fit the slide (play ≤0.3 mm) → fit the cursor hairline → wax-soak and ink-fill → engrave the serial number and the L value on the rule's underside. Control points: the position table must come from an accepted logarithm table; a master rule that has not passed inspection may not be copied into working rules. 4. Empirical parameters and calibration: L=250 mm (calibration: actually measured with a standard rod, engraved into the rule's underside); line segmentation 0.02/0.05/0.1 (calibration: trial-engrave a 50 mm stretch and set the class by whether the second digit is readable); play 0.3 mm (the two-sheet paper gauge). 5. In-process observation records: a "computed/actually engraved" comparison column for every main scale line; slide paper-gauge records; hairline rotated-window checks; an error list from 5 trial calculations. 6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = all main-line position errors ≤0.3 mm, all 5 multiplication trials <2%, the slide running freely over the whole travel; rework = individual lines out of tolerance (scrape the wax and re-engrave that line); scrap = warped blank (gaps show in mutual fitting) or groove play beyond repair — new blank, remake. 7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: trials biased in the same direction → first check whether the measured L and the position table carry the same value, then whether the slide is mounted reversed, finally whether the hairline is not perpendicular to the rule's long axis; the second digit unreadable in the 1.0–2.0 segment → wrong segmentation boundaries (return to field 4 and re-set); the slide sticky → wax lumps or uneven groove width (scrape the groove and refit). 8. L1/L2/L3 evidence: L1 = one master rule + the 5-problem trial sheet; L2 = monthly-check records for 2 working rules + the graduation records of 3 groups of 10 problems; L3 = the position table archived, the master-rule seal system, a second person building a rule independently from the card.

docs.title: 56.4 Calendar and Farming-Season Calculation
docs.text: The engineering essence of a calendar: turning "when to sow, when to open the stores and check the grain" from memory into tables that can be registered, re-checked, and handed over. The error red line: a farming-season drift of ±5 days ruins a season — the Chapter 10 reserve system presumes that farming seasons are predictable; this chapter's solstice determination is ±2 days, leaving double the margin against the red line.

docs.title: 56.4.1 The Shadow Solar-Term Table
docs.text:
• Site: the 3.2.1 true-north-line site (scribed lines and set pegs in place) and the same gnomon pole (about 1.5 m tall, plumbed straight in two directions).
  • Daily registration: every day at noon, measure the "pole base to shadow tip" length and enter it on the calendar board (one board per season; two columns, date + shadow length). Noon-fixing method: mark the shadow tip twice before and twice after noon and take the shortest position — watch the shadow, never the sun (a Chapter 3 red line).
  • Solstice determination (the ±2-day method): near the solstice, the change in shadow length approaches zero — criterion: for 3 consecutive days, mutual differences in shadow length ≤1/5 of the average daily change over the previous 10 days (empirical value, must be field-calibrated: after the first full-year table is complete, look back at the solstice window, re-verify this threshold, and transcribe it into the ledger); take the median day of the 3 as the solstice. Winter solstice = the longest-shadow window; summer solstice = the shortest-shadow window.
  • Why only ±2 days (honest): near the solstice the shadow curve is "flat-topped", its day-to-day differences flattened to the same order as measurement error — ±2 days is the single-year limit of hand methods; ±1 day would need multi-year averaging, listed as a multi-year system and kept out of the first-round commitment.
  • Measuring the year's length: register the number of days between consecutive years' solstices (median days) on counting tallies (one notch per day, five dots to a bar, 3.6) — a single year must yield 365 or 366; deciding the leap on 1 year alone is forbidden; average 4 consecutive years and it converges to near 365¼.

docs.title: 56.4.2 Leap-Year Correction (hand-method re-synchronization)
docs.text:
• The regular system: the calendar face runs 365 days/year; the measured mean is about 365¼ → insert 1 leap day after the winter solstice every 4 years;
  • The re-synchronization red line (harder than the leap-year rule): the measured winter solstice must be taken every year; when the calendar-face solstice and the measured solstice differ by ≥3 days, insert a leap day to re-synchronize immediately — waiting for the next scheduled leap year is forbidden — the farming-season red line is ±5 days; re-synchronization triggers at ±3 days, leaving a buffer;
  • The precision correction "subtract 1 day every 128 years" is declared as it stands: that is a millennial system — not promised in the first rebuild, only written into the ledger notes, so later generations do not mistake it for a first-round task.

docs.title: 56.4.3 Fixing the Season by Star Risings and Settings (cross-validation)
docs.text: The shadow table fears long overcast spells — in the cloudy season, stars stand in. Choose 3–5 bright stars in the local eastern sky and register their "morning first-appearance" dates (first seen above the eastern horizon before dawn). Three institutional rules: ①the same site (the true-north-line site), the same observing position; ②the "first-appearance" criterion = visible on two consecutive days (a single day may be a misidentification); ③the same observer throughout — changing observers requires a two-season handover star-check (Chapter 43). Source of the star table: the Chapter 53 island edition already has the "self-made star rising/setting azimuth table" system — this chapter converts it from a navigation tool into cross-validation for the solar-term calendar: each star's morning first-appearance recurs on the same date every year; cross-check it against the shadow table's solstice; a disagreement between the two routes of more than ±3 days sends you back to the observation records (the astronomical version of the Chapter 23 dual-route mutual check).

docs.title: 56.4.4 The Farming-Season/Grain-Storage Cycle Alignment Table
docs.text:
Three-column comparison (calendar-face skeleton × farm work × grain storage; action items reference Chapter 10):

Solar-term anchor (calendar face) Farm action (Chapter 10) Storage/ledger action Winter solstice (year-start anchor) Annual seed-selection plan; cold-moist stratification started Whole-store inventory; accounting-year settlement (Chapter 38) Sowing window (local shadow-length value + phenological anchors) Field sowing Verify the reserve seed quantity (next season's sowing quantity ×2) Summer solstice Intertillage; mid-season irrigation inspection Semiannual spot check: open and inspect one batch each of the dried/smoked/fermented/pit stores Autumn-equinox slot (the shadow length falls back through its registered value) Harvest begins; ear-selection seed-saving in parallel Into the store, onto the books 30 days after the solstice (locally fixed slot) Late-autumn field-care wrap-up Stored-grain seasonal pest-and-damp inspection (Chapter 10 cycle)
  • The system: the sowing window and the harvest window are locally measured phenological values — the first year relies entirely on registered shadow-length values + 3 local phenological anchors (apricot blossom opening, first frog calls, and the like — chosen locally and registered year by year); from the second year on, alignment corrections apply; the "phenological-anchor-to-shadow-length correspondence book" is this chapter's most important agricultural asset, transcribed into the ledger (Chapter 43) with an off-site copy (3.6). [Card 56-04 Solar-term calendar table ] (eight fields)
  • Input materials: 1 true-north-line site (scribed lines and pegs intact), 1 gnomon pole (1.5 m class), calendar boards (one per season), counting tallies. Substitute: in the no-clay-tablet period, notched wooden strips + a knotted-cord index (3.6, as index only).
  • Required tools: standard rod (measuring shadow lengths), A-frame level (annual site check), plumb line; calibration: the pole plumbed in two directions against the line; the true-north line's annual check — the intersection angle re-measured on two days differs ≤half a finger-width (3.2.1).
  • Operation sequence and control points: register noon shadow lengths day by day (missed days are back-filled the next day, marked "back-filled") → identify the solstice window → fix the solstice anchor → count the year's length → star first-appearance cross-validation → at year's end transcribe the next year's calendar face and the alignment table. Control point: the solstice may never be judged by "feeling that the shadow has stopped shortening" — you must back-calculate the average daily change over the previous 10 days against the threshold.
  • Empirical parameters and calibration: solstice threshold = 1/5 of the average daily change over the previous 10 days (re-calibrated with the first year's data); re-synchronization trigger ±3 days (basis: the ±5-day red line minus the shadow table's own ±2 days, then halved); 3 phenological anchors (their class set by two years of alignment correction).
  • In-process observation records: daily shadow length, weather (overcast days entered as "no shadow", not counted), observer; star first-appearance dates and the consecutive-visibility judgment; leap-day insertion dates and reasons.
  • Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = the solstice has 3-day window evidence + star-table mutual difference ≤±3 days; rework = insufficient window evidence (carry on with the interval median and mark the class downgraded); scrap = the site was disturbed (true-north annual check out of tolerance) — that season's data voided and re-measured.
  • Common failures and troubleshooting order: solstices misaligned between two years → first check for a change of observer and of stance, then pole-base settlement (if the pole's height changes, every shadow changes), finally the density of missed records (a season with >10 missed days is downgraded); a large star-table/shadow-table disagreement → first check the star criteria (single-day misrecords), then the true-north site, finally a missed leap-day insertion.
  • L1/L2/L3 evidence: L1 = one season's shadow-length board + solstice determination records; L2 = two consecutive years' solstices + year-length counting + leap-day system operation records; L3 = the alignment table and phenological-anchor book entered in the ledger with dual backup, handover star-check records, the next incumbent continuing the tables from the card.

docs.title: 56.5 Practical Trigonometric Tables
docs.text: Why needed: ramp layout (Chapter 13), the ice road's descending gradient (Chapter 51 Section 51.13), measuring tower and tree heights, judging the sun's angle — every case of "know the angle, find the side; know the side, find the angle". This chapter builds only a sin/tan table over 0–90° in 7.5° steps: 13 rows suffice, interpolation covers the gaps between rows.

docs.title: 56.5.1 Building the Sine Table by Dual Routes
docs.text:
Route A (geometric square-root chain, paper computation):

  1. Three base angles constructed exactly: sin30°=0.5 (opposite side over side in an equilateral triangle), sin45°=0.707 (diagonal over side in a square, √2 by constructed square root), sin60°=0.866;
  2. The half-angle chain downward: sin²(θ/2)=(1−cosθ)/2 — apply square roots repeatedly (the log-table method: log÷2 then reverse lookup, 56.2 Example 3) to get 15°, 7.5°, 3.75°;
  3. Angle-sum accumulation: sin(α+β)=sinα·cosβ+cosα·sinβ — generate the whole table cell by cell in 7.5° steps (multiplications via the log table);
  4. Precision: the whole table at the ±0.01 absolute-error class (empirical); small-angle rows have large relative error but small absolute values — the 3.75° row is ±2% relative, registered as it is.

Route B (large-circle chord measurement, physical measurement, cross-checked against A):

  1. On level ground draw a large circle of R=1 m (radius measured independently twice with a standard rod, difference ≤2 mm);
  2. Lay out central angle 2θ (24 circle divisions give 15° central angles — verified in 56.1.6; angle blocks from Chapter 22 can reinforce it) and measure the subtended chord s;
  3. sinθ=s/2R (inscribed-angle theorem: the chord subtending central angle 2θ = 2R·sinθ) — chord readings ±2 mm → sin to the ±0.001 class (when R=1 m);
  4. Mutual check: the two tables compared row by row; mutual difference ≤0.005 passes; out-of-tolerance rows are adjudicated by a third method — re-measure the construction or re-do the arithmetic — and the agreeing value taken.

tan column: tanθ=sinθ/cosθ (log-table division); guaranteed only over 0–45° — tan diverges at large angles; above 45° use the cot reverse lookup (written into the system; forcing a direct lookup is not allowed).

Table sample (first 5 rows illustrative; the full 13-row table enters the archive):

θ sinθ (value taken after A/B mutual check) tanθ 7.5° 0.131 0.132 15° 0.259 0.268 22.5° 0.383 0.414 30° 0.500 0.577 45° 0.707 1.000

docs.title: 56.5.2 Three Application Procedures
docs.text:
Procedure 1 (slope-to-rise conversion, serving Chapter 13 layout and the Chapter 51 ice road): slope is uniformly expressed as "a rise of n finger-widths per rod" (avoiding percentage mental arithmetic). Worked example: a slope run 20 rods long, rising 6 finger-widths per rod → total rise 120 finger-widths (about the 2.2 m class, per the local finger-to-rod conversion); reverse the table for the angle: 6 finger-widths per rod is roughly a 5–6° slope angle (interpolated in the tan table). Ice-road routes should be gentle — the ≤3 finger-widths per rod class (within 3°): Chapter 51 only gives route selection and haulage-formation discipline; the slope class is set by reverse lookup in this table, entered in the ledger.

Procedure 2 (measuring heights, tower/tree/cliff): stand d rods from the target, measure the elevation angle θ with the chord angle-gauge; height=d×tanθ+eye height. Worked example: 15 rods from a tower, elevation 10° (±1°) → height=15×0.176=2.64 rods; error: at ±1°, tan10° changes by about ±10% relative (25.11: the angle error dominates) → report 2.6 rods (±10%). Error-reduction method: switch to the two-station method — measure the angle at two stations and take the difference; the gauge's systematic bias cancels in the difference (the dividend of comparative measurement).

Procedure 3 (the chord angle-gauge, an extension of the Chapter 22 angle blocks): a semicircular plate with main graduations at 24 divisions (the 15° class, 56.1.6), chord interpolation down to the 5° class; two pins as the sighting device. Accuracy commitment: the ±5° class — criterion: reading back a known 90°/45° angle on the true-north site differs by ≤1 class; falsely labeling it ±1° is forbidden (spurious-precision discipline). [Card 56-03 Sine table by measurement ] (eight fields) 1. Input materials: level ground ≥2.5×2.5 m (stone slab/tamped earth), thin wooden strips as chord rules, several pegs. Substitute: with no large ground available, draw an R=0.5 m circle (sin precision degrades twofold to the ±0.002 class — registered as an honest downgrade). 2. Required tools: standard rod (R=1 m measured twice), long-arm compass (pole + rope substitute), scriber, right-angle square, angle block set (Chapter 22); calibration: the long-arm compass draws a full circle whose 8-direction radii differ by ≤2 mm. 3. Operation sequence and control points: draw the large circle → 24 divisions (closure check passed) → connect chords angle by angle → measure each chord three times and take the median (one pass by a different person) → divide by 2R to get sin → compare row by row with the Route A table, mutual difference ≤0.005 → transcribe the passing rows into the main table. Control points: both chord ends must be read at scribed-line centers; the pegs are checked once on the day. 4. Empirical parameters and calibration: R=1.000 m (calibration: two independent radius measurements differing ≤2 mm; re-measured across seasons); chord readings ±2 mm (calibration: demonstrated by the range of three passes by two people on the same chord); mutual-difference red line 0.005 (after the first table, the class is re-set from the measured distribution and entered in the ledger). 5. In-process observation records: three chord readings per angle and the observer; temperature anchor (cool/warm class — the ground expands and contracts); the source of each central angle (division number or angle block number). 6. Pass / rework / scrap criteria: pass = all 13 rows meet the mutual-difference target; rework = individual rows out of tolerance (re-draw the chord at that angle and re-measure; if 3 passes still fail, adopt the Route A value and annotate "measured check failed, computed value used"); scrap = the circle center has shifted or the re-measured radius differs >2 mm — the whole table voided and re-measured. 7. Common failures and troubleshooting order: the whole table biased high → first check whether the measured R came out small, then whether chords were read on the outer arc line (line-width reading bias), finally whether central angles ran large (closure error not distributed); individual rows off → first check peg looseness at that angle, then bowing of the chord rule (two-position straightness check). 8. L1/L2/L3 evidence: L1 = one 13-row table + A/B mutual-difference records; L2 = a second person's independent re-measurement on target + the angle gauge's readback records on known angles; L3 = the main table archived with dual backup, red-line values entered in the ledger, the slope-conversion worked example entered into the teaching materials (Chapter 43).

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria L1/L2/L3
docs.text:
• L1: every method of the construction set executed once with verification and registered; one master table + three worked examples; one master rule + a 5-problem trial sheet; one season's shadow-length board + solstice determination records; one 13-row sine table + A/B mutual-difference records.
  • L2: the main table's 900 cells transcribed, the 10-cell spot check fully passed; 2 working rules under monthly check against the master rule, on record; the two-person master-table cross-build within mutual-difference target; two consecutive years' solstices + star-table corroboration; the sine table independently re-measured by a second person, on target; the angle gauge reads back known angles to ≤1 class.
  • L3: the slide-rule graduation system running (graduation records for ≥3 people); the alignment table and phenological-anchor book entered in the ledger with dual backup; any damaged master item (master table / master rule / calendar site) rebuilt within 7 days per the card and meeting the mutual-difference target; a second settlement independently reproducing one table and one rule from the card (blind-build verification, 3.7).

docs.title: Safety Boundaries
docs.text:
• The long-arm compass and scriber are passed point-down, gripped by the handle, never carried in the mouth; while scribing, the other hand stays out of the line's extension direction (extension of the Chapter 3 red line);
  • Looking directly at the sun is forbidden during shadow observation — fix noon by watching the shadow, not the sun; avoid bright light for the 10 min before star observation to preserve dark adaptation, and clear the site of obstacles;
  • Keep wax-soaking work away from fire (wax is flammable); mix soot ink at a ventilated spot (echoing 25.8);
  • Night visits to the calendar site go in pairs; lamps stay clear of the peg zone.

docs.title: A. Existing Tool Inventory
docs.text: Standard rods and bisection-scribed lines, the true-north line and shadow yard (Chapter 3); three-rod mutual check and surface plates (Chapter 20); hardened scribers (Chapter 19); angle blocks and even closure-error distribution (Chapter 22); magnifiers and thin glass (Chapter 24); rough error-propagation calculation, the five recording elements, and the engineering-estimation four-piece set (Chapter 25); the star rising/setting azimuth table system (Chapter 53); the ledger and blind-build verification (Chapter 43, 3.7); paper-and-ink carriers (Chapter 41); ice-road route-selection standards (Chapter 51 Section 51.13).

docs.title: B. New Tools Added in This Chapter
docs.text: The geometric construction-methods set (three perpendicular methods / two parallel methods / angle bisection / regular polygons 3-4-5-6-8 / grid scaling / circle division with closure-error registration); the square-root construction (geometric mean + self-check anchors); the local logarithm table (master table 128 rows + main table 90×10, ±1% class) with the three worked-example procedures for multiply, divide, and square root; the slide rule (C/D/A three scales, cursor hairline, mirror parallax check, 10-problem graduation system, master-rule seal system); the shadow solar-term table and ±2-day solstice determination; year-length counting and the leap-day re-synchronization system (±3-day trigger); the star first-appearance cross-validation table; the farming-season/grain-storage alignment table and the phenological-anchor book; the dual-route sine table and tan column; the slope-to-rise conversion procedure (n finger-widths per rod); the chord angle-gauge (±5° class, two-station method).

docs.title: C. Unresolved Dependencies
docs.text:
• Four-digit precision for the log table (needs more anchors; an open problem, not scheduled); chord-table methods for prime-number divisions like 7/9 (unlocked once the sine table feeds back);
  • Precision angle measurement at the ±1° class (graduated-dial turning, an extension of Chapter 22); densifying the sine table to 1° (ten times the work; a project on demand);
  • A precision astronomical calendar (lunar phases, eclipses) — explicitly not done; old-world-class calculators — permanently "not done";
  • 500-line-class dense engraving and replication processes for slide rules (the Chapter 27 instrument line).

docs.title: Next-Step Dependencies
docs.text:
• All parts of the book: the log table and the slide rule directly serve every multiplication and division in Section 25.8 estimation, the Chapter 38 ledger, and Chapter 37 population balancing — "estimate first, then fix the scheme" now has tools underneath it;
  • Chapters 10/13: the farming-season alignment table back-fills the sowing window; slope conversion back-fills building and canal layout;
  • Chapter 51: ice-road slope classes are set using 56.5.2 Procedure 1;
  • Chapters 22/27: angle blocks and the angle gauge cross-calibrate each other; the graduated-dial upgrade line;
  • Chapter 43: the phenological-anchor book, the sealed master table and master rule, and the graduation records enter the inheritance chain — losing the ledger is treated as this chapter's processes being demoted back to Tier 1 (the G02 inheritance rule).

docs.title: Appendix C · Safety Red Lines and Fatal Errors Master Table
docs.text: A compilation of the red lines of the whole book. If any single one is violated, the rest of the chapters, however well written, may all come to nothing. The "Safety Boundaries" section of each chapter's main text gives the context and handling details; this table is for posting at workstations and for patrol checks. Rounds two and three add red lines for Chapters 28–56 (including the renumbered 44–49 medical line) (marked with ◆).

docs.title: I. Life Red Lines (a violation may kill someone)
docs.text: # Red line Source chapter 1 Carbon monoxide: enclosed heating/furnace areas must have vents; withdraw at the first dizziness 6 2 All raw water is forbidden to drink; "clear does not mean safe" (doubly so in rainforest/on islands) 10/50/53 3 Mandatory registration and mosquito protection for fever patients in the rainforest 46 4 After a boiler has boiled dry, never add water immediately (remove the fire first and let it cool through) 28 5 Vessels that have not passed a 2× hydrostatic test are barred from steam service; cast iron is barred as a pressure-bearing shell 28 6 Molten metal/glass must never touch water (explosion); no wet charge into the furnace 17/18/14 7 High-pressure tests (electrical/steam) require two people present; rewire only with power off 28/32 8 Electric-shock first aid: cut the power first, never grab the person with bare hands; sustained artificial respiration 32 9 Test hydrogen for purity before every ignition; flammable gas mixed with air explodes 26 10 Chlorine/HF handled at a ventilated position; acid into water, never water into acid 26 11 No loose clothing or long hair at rotating machinery; never step over a running belt 20/21 12 No solo entry: outdoors on permafrost, leaving the group in the desert, furnace areas, work over water 37–40 13 Ice crossing permitted only by thickness grade; barred in early spring and late winter 47 14 The established evacuation order under typhoon/sandstorm/flood warning must not be inverted 50/52/53 15 No shellfish during red tide; never eat unknown mushrooms (no exceptions) 40/prior volume 16 Lead never enters food or vessels; lead-bearing glazes barred on tableware 8/13 17 A charged Leyden jar must always be discharged with a discharger; electric-shock games strictly forbidden 30/33 18 High-voltage capacitors hold charge after power-off — discharge before touching 33 ◆19 Adits: torch in front, people behind; where the sound is dull, pry first; withdraw at the first headache; no ore is worth a life 16 ◆20 Never load weights onto a safety valve (lead-sealed, one designated keeper); after dry-boiling, never add water immediately 28 ◆21 Never force out a broken tap; no added force beyond the set-torque line 22 ◆22 Nitric acid only in glass bottles; the delivery tube must never dip under the liquid; acid into water, never water into acid 23/26 ◆23 Never keep nitric acid in ceramic vessels; keep Leblanc residue away from water sources; mercury work uses shallow trays + sulfur to gather spills 23/53 ◆24 Generator "spinning but no power": follow the seven-step troubleshooting table; no skipped steps, no blind disassembly 31 ◆25 Never substitute copper wire for a fuse; never thicken and force supply through repeated blowing; if full load burns the hand, switch to thicker wire at once 32 ◆26 The human-body unit must not be handed across persons; change the clepsydra vessel and the table changes with it 3 ◆27 Mercury displacement pump and McLeod gauge work: shallow tray + sulfur + ventilation + handwashing; spilled mercury handled per Card 49-03 33/53 ◆28 Cellars/old workings: ventilate first + verify oxygen with a torch before entry; descend roped with a person left topside 10/16 ◆29 First law of first aid: the rescuer protects self first; every tourniquet must carry a written time mark 44 ◆30 The three cleans of delivery are all indispensable; postpartum hemorrhage: massage first, then refer at the capability boundary 48 ◆31 Medicine-trial subject system: healthy consenting adults, one person one drug, first aid standing by; no induced vomiting for coma/convulsions/strong acid or alkali 46 ◆32 The authority to start epidemic quarantine rests with the sanitation officer; each day of delay roughly doubles the cost; austere mourning is a system, not heartlessness 49/51 ◆33 Arsenic-roasting grounds at least 100 paces downwind of dwellings; anyone showing Mees' lines is permanently reassigned immediately 17/53 ◆34 Heavy-metal slag: dedicated barrels, dedicated burial + location registered; waste slag must never enter ditches (secret dumping = the 49.5 blowback projection) 49 ◆35 Stop lens-water extraction once it has been salty for two ten-day periods running (salinization is irreversible); no shellfish during red tide 40/10 ◆36 Confined-space entry: ventilate first, rope up, two people; a flame turning weak and blue is an auxiliary warning (flames extinguish around 16–19% oxygen, before a person becomes severely hypoxic), but an open flame must never be the sole criterion, and open flames are barred from spaces that may hold flammable gas; withdraw at the first headache 16/49

docs.title: II. Capability Red Lines (a violation means heavy loss but no immediate injury)
docs.text: # Red line Source chapter 1 No tool traversal: only the results of chapters with smaller numbers may be used General Outline 2 No seed-saving from hybrid varieties; register seed batches 10 3 Good fuel (charcoal/coke) goes first to high-temperature processes 23 4 Measuring tools must never serve as working tools; measure hot parts only after cooling 22 5 A higher reference may only calibrate a lower one; calibrating upward is strictly forbidden 22/27 6 Never substitute copper wire for a fuse; never thicken and force supply through repeated blowing 32 7 The temperature-rise red line (about 60 °C hand-touch limit) is the load-reduction line 21/31 8 No single power source may carry >50% of base load 29 9 Chemical scale-up proceeds one order of magnitude at a time, with calibration at each step 26 10 A reagent without a label is discarded; store niter–sulfur–charcoal separately 26 11 No iron implements may touch the semiconductor line (ceramic/quartz ware discipline) 34 12 Process-card freeze rule: changing a parameter = opening a new version; verbal changes forbidden 4/35 13 Never overload the balance; weights handled only with tweezers 25 14 Rainforest no-cut line / desert fuel quota / permafrost seasonal-store ledger — overdrawing the ecosystem = overdrawing the future 50/52/51

docs.title: III. Edition-Specific Quick Reference for Each Environment
docs.text:
• Rainforest (50): clean water and the four defenses against malaria; no wet charcoal into the furnace; pre-flood checklist; the rotational-felling line.
  • Permafrost (51): doubled CO discipline; no impact loads on cast iron in winter; thaw-subsidence observation; the three seasonal-store ledgers.
  • Desert (52): no settling until the water-source survey is complete; fire prevention in solar-concentration zones; open chemical ponds forbidden.
  • Island (53): capped lens-water extraction; go to sea by the monsoon calendar; grounding electrodes field-measured; post-disaster recovery order (communications → power → production).

docs.title: IV. The Post-Accident Learning System
docs.text: Every accident (near-misses included) is recorded under the Chapter 4 failure classification: course of events – direct cause – root cause – system correction. Accident records are the highest-density knowledge asset in the whole book — when revising any edition of this manual, the accident library takes precedence over theory.

docs.title: Appendix D · Master Table of Terminology and Units
docs.text: Unified conventions for the whole book (an expansion of the G02 terminology section). Wherever the body text conflicts with this table, the body text is to be revised to match this table.

docs.title: 1. Core Terms
docs.text: Term Definition First appears 工艺卡／工位卡 (process card / workstation card) Same object, two names: an eight-field worksheet numbered "chapter-sequence" (e.g., 20-01) G02 八字段 (eight fields) Input materials / required tools / operation sequence and control points / empirical parameters and field-calibration method / in-process observation record items / pass, rework, or scrap criteria / common failures and troubleshooting / L1–L3 evidence G02 九块骨架 (nine-block framework) Capability boundary / pre-start verification / materials / tools / steps / parameters / failure diagnosis / acceptance / work-hours and staffing G02 固定块 (fixed blocks) End of every chapter: failure modes and diagnostics / process card index / acceptance criteria / safety boundaries / next dependencies G02 三档标准 (three-tier standard) Tier 1: know of it / Tier 2: manage to make it once by trial / Tier 3: repeatable manufacture, diagnosable G02 L1/L2/L3 Proof of principle / repeatable manufacture / sustainable production G02 铁律 (Iron Law) The seven constitutional rules of the whole book (no anachronism / precision must have a source / material chain / verifiability / line of retreat / evidence / labor) G01 预告 (preview) A forward declaration of the form "will be established in Chapter N"; preview items may NOT be counted as already existing Chapter 4 沉默失败 (silent failure) A failure that is not immediately visible when done wrong (annealing / vacuum / winding / cement-curing class) G01 Iron Law 6 经验值，需现场标定 (empirical value, must be field-calibrated) Default numbers: a value plus a field calibration method must both be given before they may be used for acceptance G02 降档声明 (tier-down declaration) An explicit statement at the start of a subsection when the process has not reached Tier 3 G02 ◎标记 (◎ marker) Hand-feel (tacit-judgment) steps: must be accompanied by a practice method plus a measurable compensating criterion G02 【背景/展望】 ([Background/Outlook]) Marker for long-range passages kept separate from executable content G02 三实检 (three live tests) Scratch + bend + in-use test (steel/iron acceptance) Chapter 19 整流比 (rectification ratio) Ratio of forward to reverse current at the same voltage (selecting detector points) Chapter 33 双液淬火 (interrupted quenching, water-then-oil) Two-bath relay: water (rapid cooling through the mid-temperature range) → oil (slow cooling through the low-temperature range) Chapter 19 渣棒法 (slag-rod method) Judge furnace temperature by the length of wire drawn from a slag-coated iron rod Chapter 18 四栏替代 (four-column alternatives) Performance loss / resource cost / applicable boundaries / final bottleneck Chapter 40
